docs.title: Apogee Engine
docs.text:
A free, open-source C# 3D engine made for crunching numbers: big worlds in double precision, a data-oriented ECS, SIMD, and the best libraries that exist for everything else.

Apogee is a set of small Apogee.* libraries, each with its own interop, on top of SDL3, Vulkan, Flecs, Luau, Jolt, OpenAL Soft, GameNetworkingSockets, Steamworks, Dear ImGui and RmlUi. The editor and dev builds run on CoreCLR; shipped games are NativeAOT, so engine code never uses runtime reflection. The engine is C#; games and mods are written in Luau and data. It is licensed under the Apache License 2.0.

Pre-alpha

APIs change without notice. The engine is developed on Linux with Vulkan; Windows is built and tested by CI, and the Metal backend for macOS has never run on a GPU. See Help wanted.

The editor is very bare-bones for now: it cannot import 3D models or other assets (it only places and re-imports files already in the game folder), and it has no materials, no animations and no Export dialog (a game is exported from the command line).

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text:
Is Apogee ready to make a game with? Not yet in the sense of a stable engine: it is pre-alpha and APIs change. It is complete enough to build on if you read the code, and every library has tests and a Manual page.

Why not Unity, Unreal or Godot? Use them if they fit: for many games they are the right choice. Apogee is for games where the engine's assumptions get in the way of numbers: very large worlds, heavy simulation, custom data layouts. There you want to own the stack and have a foundation instead of a framework.

Why C#? Modern C# (unsafe code, spans, function pointers, SIMD, NativeAOT) is fast enough for the hot paths and much faster to work in than C++. Shipped games are NativeAOT, so there is no JIT and no runtime reflection.

Why Luau and not C# for games and mods? Scripts must be sandboxed, limited in time and memory, and reloadable while the game runs, and a mod must not be able to run native code. Luau was built for that. The engine is C#; the games made with it and their mods are Luau and data.

Which platforms? Windows, Linux and macOS, on x64 and Arm64 where the libraries allow. Vulkan 1.3 is the graphics API on Windows and Linux; macOS uses Metal 3, which is written but untested (help wanted). There is no console, mobile or web target.

Is there a Direct3D 12 backend? No, and it is not planned: Vulkan covers Windows. The graphics page says what it would take.

Do I have to use Steam? No. Apogee.Steam is a separate library, and a game that does not start it never touches Steam.

Can I use FMOD or Wwise? Not out of the box: the repository only ships libraries it may redistribute, so audio is OpenAL Soft. If your game needs one of them, replace Apogee.Audio in your project.

Do I have to credit Apogee in my game? The Apache License asks you to keep the license and NOTICE with copies of the engine you redistribute. The third-party libraries ask for their notices in your credits or documentation: Third-party notices lists what each one needs. We do not ask for royalties or a logo.

Is the engine written with AI? Parts of it are written with an AI assistant, under the maintainer's review and with tests. CONTRIBUTING.md says what we expect when you do the same.

docs.title: What Apogee is
docs.text:
Apogee is an engine for games that crunch numbers: simulations with big worlds, many entities and a lot of arithmetic per frame. Its choices follow from that.

  • Numbers first. Positions are double so a world can be thousands of kilometers wide without jitter; everything the GPU sees is float. The ECS is Flecs. Hot paths use unmanaged memory, unsafe code and SIMD, and do not allocate.
  • The best library for each job. SDL3 for windows and input, Vulkan 1.3 with VMA and the Slang shader compiler for graphics, Jolt for physics, Luau for scripting, OpenAL Soft for audio, GameNetworkingSockets for networking, Dear ImGui for tools, RmlUi for game UI. Our work is the thin, fast layer between them and the game.
  • Small libraries. One Apogee.* project per concern, each with its own interop. Take what you need; nothing forces the rest on you.
  • Our own bindings. The raw bindings (Apogee.Native.*) come from our own generator, checked by tests that every entry point resolves and every struct has clang's size. They are committed; nothing is hand-edited.
  • AOT by default. Shipped games are NativeAOT. No runtime reflection, no Reflection.Emit, no loading managed code: a source generator writes the registry that gives scripts, serialization and the editor's inspectors their view of the engine's classes.
  • Luau for games and mods. The engine core is C#. Game developers and modders both write Luau and data, so scripts can be sandboxed, limited per owner and hot-reloaded.
  • Everything redistributable. The repository ships only libraries whose headers and binaries we may redistribute, so a clone builds and runs with nothing to download.
  • You own your stack. Apache-2.0, no royalties, no logo screen. If the project goes somewhere you do not want to follow, fork it.

docs.title: What Apogee is not
docs.text:
• It is not a general-purpose engine for every kind of game, and it is not a drop-in replacement for Unity, Unreal or Godot. Pull requests that drift from the purpose above are declined, because adding everything is how engines end up doing nothing well.
  • It targets desktop platforms: Windows, Linux and macOS. No consoles, no mobile, no web.
  • Games and mods are written in Luau, not C#. There is no visual scripting.
  • It has no feature toggles: everything is always compiled. Options are build modes and dev tools only.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Pre-alpha. The libraries below are all there and tested, but APIs will change and some corners are thin. The maintainers develop on Linux with Vulkan. Windows is built and tested by CI; Metal (macOS) is written, its shaders pass Apple's compiler, but it has never run on a GPU. Direct3D 12 is not planned. The editor is very bare-bones for now: it cannot import 3D models or other assets (it only places and re-imports files already in the game folder), and it has no materials, no animations and no game export. Help wanted lists what we need.

docs.title: License
docs.text: Apogee's own code, tools and documentation are under the Apache License, Version 2.0: you may use, modify and distribute them, in open or closed source, for free games and commercial ones, with no royalties. The license text is LICENSE in the repository, and NOTICE is the notice to keep with it when you redistribute the engine. Contributions are accepted under the same license (see Contributing).

docs.title: Third-party libraries
docs.text:
The engine links, loads or vendors third-party libraries, each under its own license (MIT, BSD, Zlib, Apache-2.0, the FreeType License, LGPL for OpenAL Soft). ThirdParty/README.md says where each came from, at what version and how its binaries were built. Legal/THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md lists what a game that ships a library has to include with it (most ask for their copyright notice in the credits or documentation).

Two things worth knowing:

  • OpenAL Soft is LGPL, so it is its own shared library beside the program, loaded at run time and replaceable, never linked statically.
  • Steamworks is Valve's. Only its redistributable_bin libraries are in the repository, as the SDK Access Agreement allows. The C# bindings generated from its headers carry Valve's terms, not the Apache License, and using Steamworks needs a partner account and an agreement with Valve.

docs.title: API reference

Two references, both generated from the code so they cannot drift from it:

The raw native bindings (Apogee.Native.*) are not listed: they mirror the C headers of their libraries, which document them.

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text: Call once a frame, after the world has progressed (it reads the entities' world transforms). Files are read through , so sounds live in res://, mods and packs. One audio system per process: OpenAL's current context is process-wide. The OpenAL listener stays at the origin; every voice is placed relative to the nearest , in double precision, so sound stays exact far from the world's origin. To use another audio middleware, replace this library (the engine has no backend layer).

docs.title: Class AssetDatabase
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Content.Assets Assembly: Apogee.Content.dll

Which file an asset's UID names, and which UID a file has. The UID of an imported file is in its .import.xml, the UID of an authored one (a scene) is in its root element (); the database reads them from the files, so it is always about what is on disk. To find a UID it first asks the project's list, imported/assets.xml (written by : one read per root), and when that has nothing (or is out of date: the file moved after the import) it scans the files of its once. It never writes: giving files UIDs is the importer's job, so a read-only root (a pack, a mod, a shipped game) is fine, and its assets with no UID just have none.

Results are remembered until (call it after an import, or when files change on disk). Safe to use from several threads.

docs.title: Move(string, string, IReadOnlyList<string>?, bool, bool)
docs.text:
Moves or renames the asset at from to to (both in the game folder, res://) and keeps everything that names it working:

  • the file, its .import.xml (so the UID goes with it) and its imported artifact move together;
  • the references in documents are rewritten (: scenes and the definition folders in defFolders), keeping their UIDs;
  • imported/index.xml and imported/assets.xml say the new path. The artifact is still good (the import key does not depend on the path), so nothing imports again; an editor that wants to be sure can call .

All or nothing for what matters: the documents are checked and prepared before anything is touched, the files are then moved, and if that fails the documents and the files are put back. The import data is a cache; if it cannot be updated that is a warning and the next import repairs it. .luau scripts are never rewritten: the ones that mention the old path are listed in . Only a file can be moved here (a folder is moved by moving what is in it, one call each).

public MoveReport Move(string from, string to, IReadOnlyList<string>? defFolders = null, bool dryRun = false, bool allowSkipped = false)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
from string

The asset's path. It must be a file, and not an .import.xml (that follows its asset) or something in imported/.

to string

The new path. Nothing may be there, neither a file nor a folder, and no .import.xml.

defFolders IReadOnlyList<string>?

Virtual folders whose .xml files are searched for references as well as the authored files.

dryRun bool

Report what would happen and change nothing.

Namespace: Apogee.Content.Assets Assembly: Apogee.Content.dll

Finds the documents that refer to an asset and rewrites them when the asset is renamed or moved: what the editor's rename calls. A document is an authored file (: scenes now) or an .xml file in one of the definition folders the caller names, in any root of the . A reference is an attribute whose whole text is an (Model="res://models/car.glb|uid://4k2m9x7q1w3ze"); text inside elements is not looked at.

What counts as a reference to the asset: an attribute whose path is the asset's path (as the engine writes it: the two addresses of a package file, res://packages/id/x and mod://id/x, are the same), or whose UID is the asset's UID and whose path does not lead to some other file. That last condition is the engine's own rule, the path wins while its file exists (): a reference that carries the UID of a copied file and the path of the copy means the copy.

Rewriting changes the characters of the path part of each reference and nothing else (); a UID is never touched, so a reference keeps resolving through it even if a document is missed. It is all or nothing: every new text is made and checked before the first file is written, a file that changed in between stops the whole thing, and if a write fails the files already written are put back. Nothing here deletes or half-writes a file.

docs.title: Class DirectorySource
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Content.FileSystem Assembly: Apogee.Content.dll

A folder of the real file system. Paths are joined to the folder after they were checked to hold only plain names, and the result is checked to be inside it. A link inside the folder that points out of it is followed, as the operating system does: do not mount a folder whose contents you do not trust to be links-free.

A write is durable and whole: the bytes go to a hidden file of a unique name beside the target, are flushed to the disk, and the file is then renamed over the target, so a crash or a full disk leaves the old file, and not an empty one. A file that is a symbolic link is written through: the new bytes go to the file the link leads to, and the link stays a link. A file that has several hard links is replaced by a new file: the other names keep the old bytes (the operating system does not say which names a file has, so this cannot be seen from here).

Namespace: Apogee.Content.FileSystem Assembly: Apogee.Content.dll

Notices when files of a change, for hot reload. It watches every folder that backs a mount (zips and packs do not change under a running game) and gives the changes as virtual paths: the one the file has through the mount it was found in, and every other path that is a view of it (a package at res://packages/core is also mod://core). A link inside the folder that points out of it is followed, as the operating system does: do not mount a folder whose contents you do not trust to be links-free.

docs.title: Class AssetImporter
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Content.Import Assembly: Apogee.Content.dll

Turns the assets of a game into the engine's own formats. It is a small registry: each takes some extensions (models, images, shaders…) and writes an artifact for each asset, in res://imported/ beside an index.xml that says which source each came from ( reads it). Artifacts are kept: an asset is imported again only when its key changes, the SHA-256 of the importer's name and fingerprint, the asset's .import.xml settings, the asset, and every file the import read for it (a model's buffers and textures, the modules a shader imports). Artifacts whose source is gone are deleted. Importers run in the order of the list, and a file that an earlier import read (a model's image) is not imported on its own. res:// has to be writable.

Importing also gives assets their UID (): an imported file gets one in its .import.xml (made if there is none), an authored one () in its root, and imported/assets.xml lists them all for . The UID is not part of the key (), so minting one never imports anything again. A UID that is already there is never changed, except to tell a copy from its original.

docs.title: Class BasisEncoder
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Content.Import Assembly: Apogee.Content.dll

Encodes an RGBA8 texture and its mip chain as UASTC in a KTX 2 file, with libktx's Basis Universal encoder: the blocks go through RDO (rate-distortion optimization, which makes them compress better) and the levels are supercompressed with zstd. A color or data texture and a normal map get different settings: normal maps skip RDO and take a slower, more accurate encoder level, because errors in a normal are visible as lighting noise. Normal maps stay RGB (libktx's own "normal map" mode would keep two channels as RRRG, which the shaders do not read). The encoder is slow, which is what the import cache is for; it is deterministic.

docs.title: KeyText(string)
docs.text:
The text of a sidecar as the import key sees it: the same text without the root's uid attribute, so that minting a UID into a sidecar (or into a new one) does not change the key and make the asset import again, and every key made before UIDs existed is still the one a sidecar without a UID makes.

  1. The empty text stays empty.
  2. A sidecar that says nothing but a UID (<Import uid="…"/>, which is what minting makes when there was no sidecar) is the same as no sidecar: empty. (A sidecar that already existed with no settings at all, <Import/>, keeps its own key, so adding a UID to it imports the asset once more: it says nothing, and nobody writes it.)
  3. Otherwise the uid attribute and the white space before it are taken out textually (only that attribute changes), and everything else is returned byte for byte: it is the text people wrote, and it was part of the key before UIDs existed.

Text that is not valid XML is returned as it is (reading it as settings fails on its own).

docs.title: Classes
docs.text:
AssetImporter

Turns the assets of a game into the engine's own formats. It is a small registry: each takes some extensions (models, images, shaders…) and writes an artifact for each asset, in res://imported/ beside an index.xml that says which source each came from ( reads it). Artifacts are kept: an asset is imported again only when its key changes, the SHA-256 of the importer's name and fingerprint, the asset's .import.xml settings, the asset, and every file the import read for it (a model's buffers and textures, the modules a shader imports). Artifacts whose source is gone are deleted. Importers run in the order of the list, and a file that an earlier import read (a model's image) is not imported on its own. res:// has to be writable.

Importing also gives assets their UID (): an imported file gets one in its .import.xml (made if there is none), an authored one () in its root, and imported/assets.xml lists them all for . The UID is not part of the key (), so minting one never imports anything again. A UID that is already there is never changed, except to tell a copy from its original.

BasisEncoder

Encodes an RGBA8 texture and its mip chain as UASTC in a KTX 2 file, with libktx's Basis Universal encoder: the blocks go through RDO (rate-distortion optimization, which makes them compress better) and the levels are supercompressed with zstd. A color or data texture and a normal map get different settings: normal maps skip RDO and take a slower, more accurate encoder level, because errors in a normal are visible as lighting noise. Normal maps stay RGB (libktx's own "normal map" mode would keep two channels as RRRG, which the shaders do not read). The encoder is slow, which is what the import cache is for; it is deterministic.

ContentLoader

A game that was never imported loads from its sources, so the same call works everywhere. A package's files have artifacts when the package shipped them (it was imported as a folder of its own, its imported/ is at mod://id/imported). It does not check that the artifact is current: importing is the step that does.

docs.title: Class PackageSolver
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Content.Packages Assembly: Apogee.Content.dll

Decides which packages load and in what order. There is one version of each id: the first candidate with an id wins and later ones are ignored with a problem. A package is disabled, with a reason, when it needs a newer API or another game version, the player switched it off, a dependency is missing, disabled, or out of its version range, it is in a dependency cycle, or it is a base package that needs a mod; disabling cascades to what depends on it. What loads is ordered so that dependencies come first, base packages before mods and otherwise by id, so that the order is the same on every machine.

public static class PackageSolver

docs.title: Class SchemaSet
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Content.Xml Assembly: Apogee.Content.dll

XSD, the parts content definitions need: checking XML against a schema and turning it into data (). A set is every .xsd file loaded into it (and the ones they include), so that a package can bring the schema of the definitions it adds, and the children it adds to an open element of another's.

Supported: element and attribute declarations (type, ref for elements, default, fixed, use, minOccurs, maxOccurs), complexType with sequence, choice and all (the order of children is not checked; a choice's members each repeat as they say, so a choice repeated stands for any order), group and attributeGroup, complexContent and simpleContent extensions, any and anyAttribute, simpleType restrictions (enumeration, minInclusive, maxInclusive, minExclusive, maxExclusive, pattern, minLength, maxLength, length) and lists, the built-in types, annotation, and include/import of a file by its location (no namespaces: names are plain). Anything else is a that names it, so a schema never means less than it says.

docs.title: Decode(XmlNode, string?, string?)
docs.text:
Checks node against the schemas and turns it into data. An element with a complex type is a record: its attributes (numbers, booleans and text by their types, a list type as a list), the defaults of the attributes it leaves out, and its child elements by name; a child that may repeat is a list; an element that holds nothing but one repeatable element (<units><unit/><unit/></units>) is that list; an element with a simple type is its value. Two conventions are read from an element's xs:appinfo: map (a container of <entry key="…"> items is a record by the keys; an item that has nothing but a key and a value gives the value) and defaults (the element left out is decoded as an empty one, so that the defaults of its attributes apply; a list left out is empty). An open element (xs:any) gives each child the global element <its name>.<child name> when the schemas have one, and keeps the others as they are.

public DecodeResult Decode(XmlNode node, string? origin = null, string? asElement = null)

A binary encoding of an XML document, for cooked packs (APXB): the tree holds, with every name and value in one string table and the nodes in document order. It is smaller than the text and read without parsing it, and it gives back exactly the tree that was written: names, attributes in their order, text, lines and children. Read a file that may be either form through .

public static class XmlBinary

docs.title: Inherited Members
docs.text: object.Equals(object?), object.Equals(object?, object?), object.GetHashCode(), object.GetType(), object.MemberwiseClone(), object.ReferenceEquals(object?, object?), object.ToString()

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text:
Little-endian; a varint is an unsigned LEB128 of at most 32 bits.

header   u32 magic "APXB" (0x42585041) · u16 version · u16 flags (0) · u32 string count · u32 node count
strings  count x { varint byte length, UTF-8 bytes }    first-appearance order, string 0 is ""
nodes    pre-order, root first: varint name, varint line, varint attribute count,
         attributes x { varint name, varint value }, varint text, varint child count

The reader checks every count against the bytes that are left before it allocates for it, so a damaged or hostile file can only make it throw a , or allocate in proportion to the file's own size. is not stored; the reader sets it to the path it was given.

GltfLoader

Reads glTF 2.0 (.gltf with its files, or .glb) into a : the default scene's meshes placed in the world, metallic-roughness materials with their textures decoded, and punctual lights. Supported extensions: KHR_texture_transform, KHR_texture_basisu, KHR_materials_emissive_strength, KHR_materials_unlit, KHR_lights_punctual. Draco and meshopt compression are refused with a clear error.

ImageDecoder

Decodes PNG, JPEG, BMP, TGA and the other formats stb_image reads into RGBA8 textures with a full mip chain.

Ktx2Loader

Loads KTX 2 files. Basis Universal data (ETC1S and UASTC) is transcoded to the best format the GPU samples: BC7, ASTC 4x4, or RGBA8.

LightData

A KHR_lights_punctual light in world space. Intensity is in lux (directional) or candela (point and spot), as glTF defines it.

MaterialData

glTF's metallic-roughness material.

MeshData

One glTF primitive: triangles with one material.

MeshProcessing

Mesh clean-up and the vertex attributes glTF lets a file leave out.

ModelData

A glTF file, flattened: the meshes the default scene uses, where they are, their materials and textures, and its lights.

ModelMerge

Combines models into one scene: the way a sample or a level puts several glTF files and generated shapes together.

Png

A minimal PNG writer for 8-bit RGBA images: screenshots and test files. Reading goes through stb_image.

ProceduralMeshes

Simple shapes built in code: for sample scenes, tools and tests. Every mesh has normals, UVs and tangents, and counter-clockwise front faces.

TextureData

A decoded texture ready to upload: the GPU format, the size, and the bytes of every mip level (largest first, each tightly packed).

AssetRef

A reference to an asset by its path and its . The path is what people read and is tried first; when the file is no longer there, the UID finds it where it was moved. Either part may be missing. The path is kept exactly as given: this type does not normalise it (the asset database does).

The text form is res://models/car.glb|uid://4k2m9x7q1w3ze; a path alone and a UID alone (uid://4k2m9x7q1w3ze) are also valid, and the empty text is the empty reference. | cannot be part of a path.

docs.title: Class DebugDraw
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Core.Graphics Assembly: Apogee.Core.dll

Immediate-mode debug drawing: lines and triangles in world positions that live for one frame. Anything may add to it (gameplay, physics, tools) with no knowledge of rendering; the renderer draws what is in it when a frame is rendered and the owner then s it for the next. Positions are double precision, like the world's, and are turned into offsets from the camera only when drawn. The number of lines and triangles is capped (); what does not fit is counted in and left out, so a loop that draws too much costs a frame's detail and not the program's memory.

docs.title: Class FileLogSink
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Core.Logging Assembly: Apogee.Core.dll

Writes each entry as a line of a file that is this run's own: <yyyyMMdd-HHmmss>-<pid>.log (UTC) in a folder that keeps the newest few. The file is flushed after every line, so that a crash keeps the last ones. Next to it, a .running marker (the process id, when it started and the log's name) lives until : a marker whose process is gone is a run that did not end cleanly (). The sink never throws: a file that cannot be written disables it, with one line on stderr.

public sealed class FileLogSink : ILogSink, IDisposable

docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Core.Numerics Assembly: Apogee.Core.dll

A position in the double-precision world: three doubles (24 bytes). Float has 24 bits of precision, so at 5 km from the origin a float position moves in 0.5 mm steps; a double keeps sub-micrometre steps for thousands of kilometres. Only positions are double. Directions, rotations, scales and everything the GPU sees stay float: positions are turned into float offsets from a nearby origin (the camera) with before they are used. Plain scalar code on purpose: positions are added and subtracted, not crunched in bulk.

docs.title: Struct Frustum
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Core.Numerics Assembly: Apogee.Core.dll

The view volume of a perspective camera with an infinite far plane, as five planes (left, right, bottom, top, near) in the camera-relative space the renderer works in. A plane is (nx, ny, nz, d) and a point is inside when n·p + d >= 0 for all five. The four side planes pass through the camera, which is the origin, so their d is zero; moves the origin for a scene whose coordinates are relative to something else. The normals are not unit length (the side ones are forward * tan + right); the culling kernel takes that into account.

public readonly struct Frustum

docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Core.Numerics Assembly: Apogee.Core.dll

A placement in the double-precision world: a position, a rotation and a scale (not a matrix, so a position far from the origin keeps its precision). A point is scaled, then rotated, then moved. Non-uniform scale is allowed, but there is no shear: the scale of a child under a rotated, non-uniformly scaled parent is the product of the two scales, which is exact only when the parent's scale is uniform or its rotation lines up with the child's axes (the usual rule of game engines).

docs.title: Classes
docs.text:
DevOverlay

The engine's debug window: frame time graph, GPU pass timings, the render graph, and lighting statistics and controls. Call every frame between and .

DevOverlayData

What the overlay shows. Fill it each frame from whatever the game has; leave out what it does not have.

DevToolsLibrary

The devtools table of scripts: when to draw, and what to show in the debug window.

ImGuiHost

A Dear ImGui context wired to the engine: SDL input, display size and the dark style. Draw widgets between and ; then puts the result on the screen.

ImGuiLibrary

Dear ImGui for Luau scripts, as the global table imgui: snake_case functions over the same calls the dev tools use. A widget returns changed, value; a window or tree that can be open returns whether it is; every begin has its end (ImGui recovers from a script that forgets, at the end of the frame). With no frame open every call does nothing and returns what it was given, so tool code can stay in a shipped game. Ids are the labels, with ImGui's ## and ### conventions.

ImGuiRenderer

Draws Dear ImGui's draw data onto the frame's output as a render-graph pass: its textures (the font atlas) become images in the bindless heap as ImGui asks for them, and its vertices and indices go through per-frame buffers that the shader pulls from. Use it as the of , or call on your own graph.

OverlayToggle

A checkbox the host adds to the overlay's Debug section: it reads and writes a switch of the host's (physics debug drawing, say).

Plots

Plots with ImPlot, for the overlay's graphs and the editor's profiler: a small surface over the binding that takes strings and spans. Use it between and : if (Plots.Begin("id", size)) { Plots.Axes(...); Plots.Line(...); Plots.End(); }.

docs.title: Class PrefabLibrary
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Ecs Assembly: Apogee.Ecs.dll

The prefab files a session knows, as numbers: one handle per file (the same file asked for by its path, its uid:// or both is the same handle), and each file's document, read once. A handle is what and hold; it only means something in the run that made it, which is why snapshots and scenes name the file instead (). A reference that names no file still gets a handle that keeps its text, so an instance of a prefab that is missing keeps what it was made from. Safe to use from several threads.

docs.title: SavePrefabFile(string, Entity)
docs.text:
Writes root and everything below it as the prefab file at path. The ids in the file stay the same from one save to the next: an entity that came from this file ( of it) keeps its id, and a new one takes the file's nextId and raises it, so an id that was deleted is never used again. The file keeps its UID (a new one gets a new UID). Every entity written is marked as a member of the file, with its id there, so that saving again keeps it. Entity fields that point outside what is saved are left out. An instance of another prefab inside the tree is written as it is in a scene: one element with only what differs from its prefab, numbered in this file. The root itself is written as a plain entity even when it is an instance (a prefab saved from an instance of itself, or of another prefab, holds its entities).

public void SavePrefabFile(string path, Entity root)

root Entity

The prefab files a session knows, as numbers: one handle per file (the same file asked for by its path, its uid:// or both is the same handle), and each file's document, read once. A handle is what and hold; it only means something in the run that made it, which is why snapshots and scenes name the file instead (). A reference that names no file still gets a handle that keeps its text, so an instance of a prefab that is missing keeps what it was made from. Safe to use from several threads.

A Flecs world: entities, components, queries and systems. Components are the unmanaged structs marked [Component] (reflected, so Flecs knows their fields too) or ones a script defined at run time. Not thread safe: use it from one thread.

PrefabInstance

Marks the root of a prefab instance: the entity returned. is a handle of the world's ; a snapshot holds the it names instead (the prefab asset type), so it means the same prefab in another run. It is never written as a component: a scene writes the instance as one <Entity prefab="…"> element with only what differs from its prefab.

PrefabMember

Marks an entity that came from a prefab file (or was saved into one): is its number in that file, the number that stays the same each time the file is saved, and is the file the number belongs to. It is never written to a scene file.

QueryTerm

One term of a query: a component (or a pair), how it must match, and where it is read from.

TableView

The entities of one table and their components, valid only inside the call that got it. A field is the component of the term with that index; components are arrays, one element per entity (a field a term gets from elsewhere, such as a singleton, is a single element).

Transform

Where an entity is, relative to its parent (the ChildOf relationship); for an entity with no parent, in the world. The position is a : the world is double precision, so a position stays exact for thousands of kilometres. Set the to one: a zeroed transform (from Add) has no size. the world's transform system keeps up to date from it.

docs.title: Class PackKeySlot
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Export Assembly: Apogee.Export.dll

A reserved place in the engine's executable for the key of the game's packs, so that an exported game opens its packs without the environment variable. The executable holds (68 bytes in its read-only data: a 16 byte magic, a format byte, a "used" byte, 2 reserved bytes, a 16 byte salt, and 32 bytes for the key); an export finds every copy of the template in the copy of the executable it makes, and writes the key into each, masked: key XOR SHA-256(salt + magic) (the same salt and bytes in all). The running game reads it back with .

There is normally one copy, but a compiler may emit the data twice (the NativeAOT compiler does in the arm64 macOS executable), and the game reads whichever copy its code refers to: so every copy is patched.

This is obfuscation, not protection. The key is in the file, one XOR from anyone who reads this code or finds the magic; and a running game has the key in memory. It keeps the key out of strings, out of a quick look in a hex editor, and out of the packs' reach, nothing more. It stops nobody who wants the game's files. 

public static class PackKeySlot

docs.title: Class MetalBindlessHeap
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Graphics.Metal Assembly: Apogee.Graphics.dll

The bindless textures, samplers and storage images as one Metal argument buffer, buffer 1 of every shader that reads them (see ParameterBlock<BindlessResources> in common.slang). In an argument buffer of tier 2 each resource of an array takes one 8-byte slot and a struct's members follow one another, so the buffer is the runs of in the order the shader block declares them: the 16 384 2D textures, the 256 samplers, then the cube, 2D-array, 3D and unsigned-integer texture arrays (16 384 each) and the 256 storage images. A slot holds the resource's GPU resource id. Metal has no aliasing: on Vulkan all the sampled arrays are one descriptor binding, here each is a run of its own, so a sampled texture's id is written into the same index of every sampled run and the shader reads it through the array of its type. The textures and samplers are made resident through the device's residency set.

docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Graphics.Metal Assembly: Apogee.Graphics.dll

A Metal command buffer being recorded. Metal has encoders where Vulkan has one command buffer: this opens the one the next command needs (render, compute or blit) and ends the one that is open. Metal does not order what a shader reaches through an address or an argument buffer, so the encoders form a chain, each waiting for a fence that the one before it updates: that is what the barriers of the render graph mean here (there are no image layouts to change, so does nothing by itself).

docs.title: Classes
docs.text:
MetalBindlessHeap

The bindless textures, samplers and storage images as one Metal argument buffer, buffer 1 of every shader that reads them (see ParameterBlock<BindlessResources> in common.slang). In an argument buffer of tier 2 each resource of an array takes one 8-byte slot and a struct's members follow one another, so the buffer is the runs of in the order the shader block declares them: the 16 384 2D textures, the 256 samplers, then the cube, 2D-array, 3D and unsigned-integer texture arrays (16 384 each) and the 256 storage images. A slot holds the resource's GPU resource id. Metal has no aliasing: on Vulkan all the sampled arrays are one descriptor binding, here each is a run of its own, so a sampled texture's id is written into the same index of every sampled run and the shader reads it through the array of its type. The textures and samplers are made resident through the device's residency set.

MetalBuffer

A Metal buffer. Device-local buffers are private (the GPU's), upload and readback buffers are shared and mapped for their whole life.

MetalCommandRecorder

A Metal command buffer being recorded. Metal has encoders where Vulkan has one command buffer: this opens the one the next command needs (render, compute or blit) and ends the one that is open. Metal does not order what a shader reaches through an address or an argument buffer, so the encoders form a chain, each waiting for a fence that the one before it updates: that is what the barriers of the render graph mean here (there are no image layouts to change, so does nothing by itself).

MetalDevice

The Metal implementation of (macOS 15 and later, on a GPU with Metal 3 and tier 2 argument buffers: Apple silicon and the Intel Macs of 2017 and later). It owns one command queue and a residency set: everything the GPU reaches through an address or an argument buffer must be resident, so every buffer and texture is added to the set when it is made.

MetalException

A Metal call failed or the machine cannot do what the engine needs; the message says which.

MetalFrameLoop

The Metal frame loop: a few frames in flight, each with its own upload arena and command buffer, and one shared event as the timeline (its value is the number of frames the GPU has finished). With a swapchain it takes the next drawable and presents it; without one it renders headless. GPU timings are not measured yet, so stays empty.

MetalImage

A Metal texture, or a window's drawable texture that is borrowed for a frame ().

MetalImageView

A view of a Metal texture. The image's own view borrows the texture; views made with own theirs.

MetalImmediateContext

Records a command buffer, commits it and waits for it: for loading and tools. The calls are serialized.

MetalPipeline

A Metal compute pipeline, or a render pipeline with the fixed-function state Metal sets on the encoder (depth test, culling, winding).

MetalSampler

MetalSwapchain

The images of a window: a CAMetalLayer that SDL made for it (the window needs ). The format is BGRA8 UNORM, like the Vulkan swapchain's: shaders write sRGB-encoded values themselves. A frame takes the layer's next drawable (Acquire) and presents it with its command buffer.

docs.title: Classes
docs.text:
BindlessHeap

The one set of resources every pipeline sees: arrays of sampled images, samplers and storage images that shaders index with integers, plus the push constants. Slot 0 of the images and samplers is a white texel and a linear repeat sampler, so an unset index still reads something sane; slot 0 of the storage images is never handed out (0 means "none").

CommandRecorder

A command buffer being recorded, with the operations the engine needs on it. Everything here is on the one queue family the device uses.

Frame

One frame in flight: its command buffer, the window's image, per-frame upload memory, and deferred destruction.

FrameLoop

Keeps frames in flight (two by default): each has its own command buffer, upload arena and timer queries, and waits only for the frame that used its slot two frames ago. Without a swapchain it runs headless: the same frames with no window image, for screenshots, tests and servers. Made by .

GpuBuffer

A buffer in GPU memory. Every buffer has a device address, so shaders reach it through a pointer in push constants.

GpuImage

An image with a view of the whole of it (the aspect a shader samples).

GpuInfo

A GPU a backend found, and whether the engine can use it.

GpuSampler

GraphicsDevice

The logical device of one graphics API and everything created with it. The renderer talks to this class and the abstract classes it hands out (buffers, images, pipelines, a command recorder, a swapchain and frame loop); Apogee.Graphics.Vulkan has the Vulkan implementation, and a Metal one follows. The engine's baseline is the same on every API: dynamic rendering, explicit barriers, buffer device addresses and bindless textures; a GPU without them is rejected with the reason.

GraphicsDeviceOptions

GraphicsException

A graphics call failed or the machine cannot do what the engine needs (no usable GPU, a missing feature); the message says which. Each backend has its own subclass.

GraphicsPipelineDescription

Everything that makes a graphics pipeline (front faces are counter-clockwise by default, as in glTF). Geometry is pulled from buffers by the vertex shader (no vertex input state), depth is reverse-Z (the near plane is 1, so is greater-or-equal), and the pipelines render with dynamic rendering into attachments of these formats.

ImageView

A view of (part of) an image, as the API of a backend sees it. Opaque: the backend that made it knows what is in it.

ImmediateContext

Records a command buffer, submits it and waits for it: for loading and tools, where stalling is fine. A frame never uses this. Safe to call from several threads (the calls are serialized).

Pipeline

A compiled pipeline; bind it with .

ResourceStates

Which states write a resource.

Swapchain

The images of a window, which the frame loop acquires, renders to and presents. Made by .

docs.text:
Backbuffer

The image of the window the frame renders to. It starts in and must end in .

BufferBarrier

ColorTarget

A color attachment to render into: its view (the image is in ), cleared or loaded, and kept or discarded.

DebugLabelScope

Closes a debug label group when disposed.

DepthTarget

The depth attachment. The engine uses reverse-Z, so the usual clear value is 0 (the far plane).

DispatchIndirectCommand

The arguments of one indirect dispatch, as reads them from a buffer (a compute shader can write them). Twelve bytes.

DrawIndexedIndirectCommand

The arguments of one indexed indirect draw, as reads them from a buffer (a compute shader can write them). Twenty bytes, the same layout in Vulkan and Metal.

FrameAllocation

Space in a frame's upload arena: an address for shaders and memory for the CPU to fill.

FrameScope

A debug label with a GPU timer; dispose it to end the section.

GpuTiming

How long a named part of a frame took on the GPU.

ImageBarrier

One image transition: from the state it was last used in to the state the next use needs.

ImageDescription

What an image is: format, size, mip chain, layers and what it will be used for.

ImageRegion

Where in a staging buffer the bytes of one image subresource are.

SamplerDescription

What a sampler does. other than the average needs and is not combined with .

ShaderCode

One shader stage: the compiled code for the device's (SPIR-V for Vulkan, Metal shading language source for Metal) and the entry point in it to run. A compute shader also says its size.

ThreadGroupSize

The size of a compute shader's thread group, [numthreads(x, y, z)]. Vulkan pipelines have it inside; a Metal dispatch has to be told.

docs.text:
AssetLibrary

Asset identity for scripts, as the global assets: an asset is named by its path (res://models/car.glb), which people read, and has a UID (uid://4k2m9x7q1w3ze), which stays the same when the file is renamed or moved. A reference is the text path|uid://…; a path alone and a uid://… alone are also references. models.load and the other loaders take a path or a uid:// directly.

EngineSettingDefaults

What a game's game.xml says about its window, as the defaults of the engine's window settings.

EngineSettings

The engine's own settings (window., graphics., audio.*) and what makes them do something.

FrameOverlay

What goes over the finished picture: the game's UI, then the dev tools on top of it. The UI renderer is made the first frame after a document was loaded, so a script that only has ImGui panels never compiles the UI shader.

GameLibrary

What a game asks of the program that runs it, as the script table game: ending the run (a menu's Quit), and whether the Escape key still ends it. A shipped game's menu does the first; one with a pause menu of its own does the second, since Escape is its key.

GameStart

What starts: a game folder and how to run it.

RunDiagnostics

The log file and the crash reports of a run, in the player's folder (user://logs and user://crashes).

ScriptSession

A script running in a world: the entry script has been executed and its callbacks are registered; the loops step it frame by frame.

SettingDef

The schema of one setting: its key (dotted lower-case words, such as audio.volume or mod.coolmod.show_hints), its type, its default, and for a number its range or for a choice its choices. The values themselves live in a .

SettingsStore

The player's settings, as the settings global: typed values under dotted keys (audio.volume, mod.coolmod.show_hints) that the engine and the game define (), kept in user://settings.xml as the ones that differ from their defaults. Keys the game does not define (a mod that is switched off) are kept as they are. The store belongs to the main thread.

WindowSettings

Keeps a window and the window.* settings together: fullscreen follows the setting, and the size the player gives the window while it is not fullscreen is stored.

WorldView

The session's world drawn through its main camera (the entity with ), with the ImGui frame over it. Nothing is made until a world has such a camera: a script that only has panels never compiles the scene shaders, and keeps drawing its panels over the plain background.

docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Input Assembly: Apogee.Input.dll

Turns the player's input into the actions of an that fire in the active contexts, and says how far analog actions are pushed. Of the bindings on an input whose modifiers are all held, the one with the most modifiers wins, so Shift+Tab isn't also Tab, and a key still fires while running with Shift. A key with a hold binding fires its press on a quick release instead; a key with a double tap waits a moment for the second tap before firing its press. feeds it from SDL; , , and feed it by hand, with explicit times (seconds, any origin), for tests and replays. Call once a frame to raise , and after the frame's logic ran.

docs.title: Class FileDialog
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Platform Assembly: Apogee.Platform.dll

SDL's native file dialogs (open file, save file, open folder), asynchronous. SDL shows the dialog and later reports the result on a callback that it may run on another thread (Windows, the Linux portal and zenity backends) or before the call returns, so the result is never handed to the caller there: the callback only copies it into a queue, and (called by , on the main thread) runs each request's continuation.

What is shared between threads: only s_completed, a that the callback enqueues into (any thread) and drains (main thread). Everything else (s_pending, s_nextId, the request memory) is touched by the main thread alone. The callback receives a request id as its userdata (never a pointer or a GCHandle), so it cannot reach managed objects of the requests, and a result whose id is unknown (the platform was shut down meanwhile) is dropped.

Memory: SDL keeps the filters table, the filter strings and the default location, and requires them to stay valid until it has called back. Each request therefore gets one unmanaged block () that is freed only when its result is dispatched (a dialog still open at keeps its block: see Reset). The list of paths in the callback belongs to SDL and is freed when the callback returns, so the callback copies every string into managed memory before it returns.

docs.title: Classes
docs.text:
FileDialog

SDL's native file dialogs (open file, save file, open folder), asynchronous. SDL shows the dialog and later reports the result on a callback that it may run on another thread (Windows, the Linux portal and zenity backends) or before the call returns, so the result is never handed to the caller there: the callback only copies it into a queue, and (called by , on the main thread) runs each request's continuation.

What is shared between threads: only s_completed, a that the callback enqueues into (any thread) and drains (main thread). Everything else (s_pending, s_nextId, the request memory) is touched by the main thread alone. The callback receives a request id as its userdata (never a pointer or a GCHandle), so it cannot reach managed objects of the requests, and a result whose id is unknown (the platform was shut down meanwhile) is dropped.

Memory: SDL keeps the filters table, the filter strings and the default location, and requires them to stay valid until it has called back. Each request therefore gets one unmanaged block () that is freed only when its result is dispatched (a dialog still open at keeps its block: see Reset). The list of paths in the callback belongs to SDL and is freed when the callback returns, so the callback copies every string into managed memory before it returns.

FileDialogResult

What a native file dialog ended with. A chosen file or folder is in (operating system paths, one or several); a dialog that was closed without a choice is ; a dialog that could not be shown (no dialog backend on this machine, a failure) has an with SDL's reason.

A component field as text and back: what a scene file holds in an attribute, and what prefab overrides and the clipboard will hold. The text is the same in every culture (): booleans are true and false, integers decimal, floats the shortest text that reads back as the same number (with NaN, Infinity and -Infinity), and a , or is its numbers separated by single spaces (1 2 3, 0 0 0 1).

and are not here: what they hold only means something in a world (an entity's id, an asset handle), so whoever has that context writes and reads them.

A component field as text and back: what a scene file holds in an attribute, and what prefab overrides and the clipboard will hold. The text is the same in every culture (): booleans are true and false, integers decimal, floats the shortest text that reads back as the same number (with NaN, Infinity and -Infinity), and a , or is its numbers separated by single spaces (1 2 3, 0 0 0 1).

What a module registered while it loaded, so that loading it again can take it back: a function that draws, a signal connection, a system. A reload makes a new scope, runs the new module in it, and then either runs the old scope's cleanups (the new code worked) or this one's (it did not, and the old registrations stay).

ScriptCaller

Which script is calling the engine right now, on this thread: the scripting layer sets it around every method a script calls, so that an engine class that does work for the script (the UI loading a document that has scripts of its own) can run that work as the same owner, under the same limits. Null outside a call from a script.

ScriptEnvironment

A place for the scripts of one thing to run in, such as one UI document: a table of globals of its own that falls back to the caller's, so the functions a <script> defines are visible to the document's onclick="..." attributes and to nothing else. ScriptTable

A table a script handed to the engine, kept by reference and read when needed: what UI data models are made of. A place in it is a path of fields and list elements; reading the same path later gives what the script has put there since.

docs.title: Class Camera
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Rendering Assembly: Apogee.Rendering.dll

A perspective camera in a right-handed world (+Y up, looking down -Z at yaw 0). The projection is reverse-Z with an infinite far plane: the near plane maps to depth 1 and infinity to 0, which spreads float precision evenly over the whole depth range. Normalized device y points down, as in Vulkan, so no viewport flip is needed; the image, and so the winding of triangles (counter-clockwise for front faces, as in glTF), is unchanged. The position is a (the world is double precision) and the renderer works relative to it: has the camera at the origin, and everything else is turned into an offset from the camera before it reaches the GPU.

docs.title: Class ExposureMath
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Rendering Assembly: Apogee.Rendering.dll

The photographic exposure maths of the renderer, on the CPU: the twin of exposure.slang and of the exposure functions in common.slang, which the tests compare it with.

Scene light is photometric: the forward pass writes luminance in cd/m2 (a sun of E lux on a white diffuse surface gives E / pi cd/m2). The camera's exposure is an EV100, the exposure value at ISO 100: EV100 = log2(N^2 / t) - log2(S / 100) for an aperture f/N, a shutter time t in seconds and a sensitivity S. The forward pass multiplies its result by , the saturation-based exposure of a camera at that EV100, so the HDR image holds exposed values: 1.0 is the luminance that just saturates the sensor, 1.2 * 2^EV100 cd/m2, and a fp16 image cannot overflow with a bright sun.

docs.title: Struct Gt7ToneMapping
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Rendering Assembly: Apogee.Rendering.dll

The Gran Turismo 7 tone mapping operator, on the CPU: the twin of the one in tonemap.slang, which the tests compare it with. It is a port of Polyphony Digital's sample implementation gt7_tone_mapping.cpp (version 1.0, MIT licence, Copyright (c) 2025 Polyphony Digital Inc.; the notice is in Legal/THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md).

The operator works on linear Rec.2020 colors in "frame-buffer" units, where 1.0 is (100) cd/m2. It tone-maps each channel with a curve (a toe, a linear section and an exponential shoulder that converges on the display's peak), then blends that with a version whose lightness comes from the curved color but whose chroma (in ICtCp) is kept and faded out near the peak, so bright colors desaturate towards white instead of changing hue. In SDR mode the peak is (250 cd/m2) and the result is scaled so that 1.0 is the display's white, ready for the sRGB transfer function.

docs.title: Class ReloadablePipelines<T>
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Rendering.Shaders Assembly: Apogee.Rendering.dll

The pipelines a renderer builds from some shader modules, rebuilt when one of them changes (or a module it imports) without stalling the frame. A change starts a build on another thread: the shaders are compiled through the and the pipelines made, while the renderer carries on with . The renderer calls at the start of a frame; if a build has finished, the new pipelines become current there, and the old ones are destroyed through once the GPU is done with the frames that used them. A build that fails (a shader that does not compile) leaves as it was, is logged, and shows in until a later build works. Changes that arrive during a build start another one right after it.

docs.title: Class ShaderLibrary
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Rendering.Shaders Assembly: Apogee.Rendering.dll

Where renderers get their shaders. takes the compiled artifact of a shader module when its project was imported (), which is how a shipped game and a mod that ships its shaders work: the Slang compiler is never loaded. A module without an artifact is compiled, as in development, if the compiler is there, and the error says what to do when it is not. The engine's own shaders are mounted as shaders:// (); a mod's are at mod://id/…, with their artifacts in mod://id/imported. The library remembers which files each module it loaded was made from, so that when files change (, from HotReloader.ShadersChanged or a ) it can say which modules are out of date (): rebuilds on that. It is thread safe.

docs.text:
PipelineScope

The pipelines one build made. Disposing destroys them all; they go through when a rebuild replaces them.

ReloadablePipelines<T>

The pipelines a renderer builds from some shader modules, rebuilt when one of them changes (or a module it imports) without stalling the frame. A change starts a build on another thread: the shaders are compiled through the and the pipelines made, while the renderer carries on with . The renderer calls at the start of a frame; if a build has finished, the new pipelines become current there, and the old ones are destroyed through once the GPU is done with the frames that used them. A build that fails (a shader that does not compile) leaves as it was, is logged, and shows in until a later build works. Changes that arrive during a build start another one right after it.

ShaderImporter

Slang modules into s (.ashader): each module with entry points is compiled to SPIR-V (Vulkan) and to Metal shading language (Metal), with its reflection, once without defines and once for each <Variant> its .import.xml lists. The files the compiler read (import, #include) are the artifact's dependencies, so editing a library re-imports every shader that uses it, and the library is not imported on its own. A module with no [shader(…)] entry point is not an asset: it only serves the others.

ShaderLibrary

Where renderers get their shaders. takes the compiled artifact of a shader module when its project was imported (), which is how a shipped game and a mod that ships its shaders work: the Slang compiler is never loaded. A module without an artifact is compiled, as in development, if the compiler is there, and the error says what to do when it is not. The engine's own shaders are mounted as shaders:// (); a mod's are at mod://id/…, with their artifacts in mod://id/imported. The library remembers which files each module it loaded was made from, so that when files change (, from HotReloader.ShadersChanged or a ) it can say which modules are out of date (): rebuilds on that. It is thread safe.

docs.title: Classes
docs.text:
Camera

A perspective camera in a right-handed world (+Y up, looking down -Z at yaw 0). The projection is reverse-Z with an infinite far plane: the near plane maps to depth 1 and infinity to 0, which spreads float precision evenly over the whole depth range. Normalized device y points down, as in Vulkan, so no viewport flip is needed; the image, and so the winding of triangles (counter-clockwise for front faces, as in glTF), is unchanged. The position is a (the world is double precision) and the renderer works relative to it: has the camera at the origin, and everything else is turned into an offset from the camera before it reaches the GPU.

ClusterGrid

The grid lights are culled against: 16 x 9 cells over the screen and 24 slices in depth, spaced exponentially from the camera's near plane to so that near slices are thin. This is the CPU twin of the shaders (cluster_build and common.slang), for tests and tools.

DebugDrawLibrary

Debug drawing for Luau scripts, as the global table debug_draw: lines and shapes that last one frame, drawn over the world. Call them every frame (from a system, or from the devtools.on_gui function) for as long as they should show. Colors are vectors of red, green and blue from 0 to 1; without one a line is white. Positions are the world's. With nowhere to draw (no renderer) the calls do nothing.

ExposureMath

The photographic exposure maths of the renderer, on the CPU: the twin of exposure.slang and of the exposure functions in common.slang, which the tests compare it with.

Scene light is photometric: the forward pass writes luminance in cd/m2 (a sun of E lux on a white diffuse surface gives E / pi cd/m2). The camera's exposure is an EV100, the exposure value at ISO 100: EV100 = log2(N^2 / t) - log2(S / 100) for an aperture f/N, a shutter time t in seconds and a sensitivity S. The forward pass multiplies its result by , the saturation-based exposure of a camera at that EV100, so the HDR image holds exposed values: 1.0 is the luminance that just saturates the sensor, 1.2 * 2^EV100 cd/m2, and a fp16 image cannot overflow with a bright sun.

GpuModel

A on the GPU: its vertices, indices, materials and textures in buffers and in the bindless heap. It is placed in the world any number of times (by a , or by entities with a ); each placement costs one instance record per mesh instance, never another copy of the data.

ModelLibrary

The models that entities draw ( is an id from here; scripts see this as models). A model is loaded once per path whatever the number of entities that show it, and reloaded in place when its file changes, so entities keep their id. Ids are never reused.

OverlayChain

Several overlays as one, drawn in order over the finished image: the game's UI first, the dev tools on top of it.

RenderScene

One placed in the world, with the lights and sky it is lit with. The lights can be changed every frame. The model's own coordinates (instance transforms, light positions, bounds) are relative to the scene's , a position in the double-precision world; every frame the renderer turns them into offsets from the camera, so a scene can be anywhere in the world. For many models, or for models placed by entities, see .

RenderSettings

RenderStats

RenderWorld

An ECS as something to draw: every entity with a and a shows its model there, every lights it, and the entity with is the eye (). Nothing is copied: the world is read when a frame is rendered, so what the systems moved this frame is what is drawn.

SceneRenderer

The Forward+ renderer. Every frame it builds a render graph: a depth prepass, a light-culling compute pass over the 16 x 9 x 24 cluster grid, the PBR forward pass (opaque and alpha-masked, then blended draws far to near), and a tone-mapping pass into the target.

docs.text:
CameraComponent

A perspective camera at the entity's , looking along its -Z. The entity that also has is the one the world is drawn through. Roll is ignored: the camera turns about +Y (yaw) and then up or down (pitch).

GpuDebugPush

GpuFramePush

GpuInstance

GpuTonemapPush

Gt7ToneMapping

The Gran Turismo 7 tone mapping operator, on the CPU: the twin of the one in tonemap.slang, which the tests compare it with. It is a port of Polyphony Digital's sample implementation gt7_tone_mapping.cpp (version 1.0, MIT licence, Copyright (c) 2025 Polyphony Digital Inc.; the notice is in Legal/THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md).

The operator works on linear Rec.2020 colors in "frame-buffer" units, where 1.0 is (100) cd/m2. It tone-maps each channel with a curve (a toe, a linear section and an exponential shoulder that converges on the display's peak), then blends that with a version whose lightness comes from the curved color but whose chroma (in ICtCp) is kept and faded out near the peak, so bright colors desaturate towards white instead of changing hue. In SDR mode the peak is (250 cd/m2) and the result is scaled so that 1.0 is the display's white, ready for the sRGB transfer function.

Light

A light at the entity's , shining along its -Z (as glTF lights do). A directional light is the world's sun: its color and direction set the sun (the first one wins), and its position does not matter.

MainCamera

Marks the the world is drawn through (the first one found, when several have it).

ModelRenderer

Draws a model at the entity's : its position, rotation and scale place every mesh of the model. is an id from the (models.load in scripts); 0, or an id the library no longer knows, draws nothing. Many entities may share a model.

RenderTarget

Where the final image goes: the window's image, an offscreen one that is read back, or one that is drawn as a texture afterwards (an editor's viewport).

docs.title: Class PackageLoader
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Scripting Assembly: Apogee.Scripting.dll

Runs the packages of a in a VM. Each package's scripts run in the order its manifest lists them, packages in load order; a package's base-game scripts run as the VM's base owner, a mod's as an owner of its own (its own memory category and limits), with:

  • @<id>/… as a require alias for each package, so that a mod can use a dependency's modules;
  • confinement: a mod may require files of its own package and of the packages it depends on (and res://), nothing else;

  • modules that run as the owner of the package they are in, whoever required them.

A script that fails stops its package (the error is logged and in the result), and what depends on it is not run; it never stops the game. Content the package brought stays loaded.

docs.title: Class ScriptScheduler
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Scripting Assembly: Apogee.Scripting.dll

The tasks of one VM (and its tweens, which it steps and cancels along with them): what task.spawn, task.defer, task.delay and task.every start, and what task.wait puts to sleep. A task is a Luau thread the scheduler resumes: at once (spawn), at the next drain (defer), when its time comes (delay, wait, every). There is no clock in here: says how much game time and real time passed, so a test drives it with a fake clock and the engine drives it with the frame. Every resume is a protected resume under the time budget of the task's owner, and the thread keeps the memory category of the script that started it. Not thread safe: use it from the thread that made the VM.

docs.title: Class SteamSystem
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.Steam Assembly: Apogee.Steam.dll

The game's connection to Steam: the user, the overlay, achievements, stats and leaderboards, rich presence, cloud files and Workshop items. Steam's library is Valve's redistributable and is in the repository; the client is the player's. When Steam is not running, or the game was not started with an app id, is false and every call does nothing and returns something inert, so a game works the same without it.

public sealed class SteamSystem : EngineObject, IDisposable

docs.title: Remarks
docs.text: Call once a frame: it pumps Steam's callbacks (manual dispatch, all on the calling thread) and turns them into signals. Steam's ids (users, Workshop items) are 64-bit and cross into scripts as decimal strings, because a script number cannot hold them. Mods cannot use this object: it is the game's.

docs.title: Class UiElement
docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.UI Assembly: Apogee.UI.dll

An element of a document (a div, a text node, a whole document) as scripts hold it. The object is a handle: it names the element without keeping it alive, so one whose element has been destroyed (its document was closed, an ancestor was destroyed) is false and every call on it does nothing or answers "none". An element made with or belongs to the object that holds it until it is put in a tree with or ; an element nobody ever put in a tree is destroyed when the script lets go of it, and one in a tree lives as long as the tree does. Elements are made, moved and changed here.

docs.text:
Namespace: Apogee.UI Assembly: Apogee.UI.dll

Draws what RmlUi hands the host onto the frame's output, as a pass of the render graph: use it as (part of) the of SceneRenderer.Render. RmlUi compiles geometry once and renders it many times; the renderer keeps the compiled vertices and indices in memory and, when a frame is built, packs the geometry that frame draws into per-frame upload buffers (as the ImGui backend does), so nothing on the GPU depends on when RmlUi releases or re-renders a piece of geometry. Textures are images in the bindless heap, and the handle RmlUi holds for one is its bindless index (0 is the white texel that untextured geometry samples).

docs.text: Call when the window changes size, once a frame (it lays out and runs animations and delivers nothing by itself: events are delivered when input is given), and let the draw (it is the render overlay: it asks for the picture when the frame's graph is built). UiDataModel

A data model: a script's table tied to documents. <p data-model="stats">{{score}}</p> shows score of the table; data-if, data-for, data-class-, data-style- and data-value (which writes back what the player types) use it too, and data-event-click="buy(1)" calls the table's function buy. The table is read when RmlUi needs a value: change it and say so with (or change a top-level field with ), and the elements that show it are updated at the next frame.

UiElement

An element of a document (a div, a text node, a whole document) as scripts hold it. The object is a handle: it names the element without keeping it alive, so one whose element has been destroyed (its document was closed, an ancestor was destroyed) is false and every call on it does nothing or answers "none". An element made with or belongs to the object that holds it until it is put in a tree with or ; an element nobody ever put in a tree is destroyed when the script lets go of it, and one in a tree lives as long as the tree does. Elements are made, moved and changed here.

docs.title: Globals
docs.text:
What the host sets in the VMs it runs scripts in.

  • world: World. The world the script runs in (--run sets it).
  • physics: PhysicsWorld. The physics of the world: give entities bodies with physics:add_body, ask what is where with physics:raycast. It is stepped before the world each frame.
  • audio: AudioSystem. The game's sound: audio:load_sound and the sounds it plays need OpenAL Soft installed (audio.is_active says); an entity with the AudioListener component is the ear.
  • steam: SteamSystem. The game's connection to Steam (the base game only; mods cannot use it): achievements, stats, leaderboards, rich presence, the overlay, cloud saves and Workshop mods. steam.is_active says whether Steam is running; when it is not every call does nothing.
  • net: NetSystem. The game's network (the base game only; mods cannot use it): net:listen(port) and net:connect(address) make NetConnections, connection:send(text) sends, and the signals connection_requested, connected, message and disconnected say what happened. net.is_active says whether the network library is installed; when it is not every call does nothing.
  • models: ModelLibrary. The models entities draw: models:load(path) returns the id to put in a ModelRenderer component (the same id for the same path, 0 means none). A game with an entity that has the MainCamera component is drawn through it; Light entities light it.
  • ui: UiSystem. The game's user interface: ui:load_document(path) loads RML from a file, ui:create_document() makes an empty one; documents can carry <script>s, on* attributes and data models (ui:open_data_model); elements are UiElements you make, move and listen to. It is sized to the screen, fed the player's input, and drawn over the picture.
  • input: InputActionRouter. The player's input as actions: define them on input.map, set input.contexts each frame, read input:get_strength(action) and connect input.action_fired.
  • settings: Settings. The player's settings, kept in user://settings.xml: settings:define(key, spec) the ones your game or mod needs, settings:get and settings:set them, and connect settings.changed. The engine's own (window.*, graphics.vsync, audio.volume) are defined; a mod can change only mod.<its id>.*.

docs.title: Classes
docs.text:
• AssetLibrary: Asset identity for scripts, as the global assets: an asset is named by its path (res://models/car.glb), which people read, and has a UID (uid://4k2m9x7q1w3ze), which stays the same when the file is renamed or moved.
  • AudioBus: A bus of the mix: a group of sounds with a volume, a mute and a pause of its own (Music, Vehicles, Environment, UI).
  • AudioSound: A sound file loaded by AudioSystem.LoadSound: play it any number of times, on any bus.
  • AudioSystem: The game's audio, on OpenAL Soft: sounds (WAV, FLAC, MP3, Ogg Vorbis) played in 3D around the entity that has an AudioListener, on buses, with reverb zones and occlusion.
  • AudioVoice: Something that is playing, or about to: a sound on a source (AudioSound.Play).
  • BodyDesc: What a body is made of and how it behaves: the shape, how it moves, its mass, surface and layers.
  • CharacterController: A walking character: a capsule that slides along walls, climbs stairs and slopes, sticks to the ground going down and stands on moving platforms, without being a rigid body (Jolt's CharacterVirtual).
  • Hitch: A hitch on a vehicle: a point on its body where an attachment or a trailer is attached.
  • InputActionMap: Every action the player can bind, where each works (its contexts) and what it is bound to.
  • InputActionRouter: Turns the player's input into the actions of an InputActionMap that fire in the active contexts, and says how far analog actions are pushed.
  • ModelLibrary: The models that entities draw (ModelRenderer.Model is an id from here; scripts see this as models).
  • NetConnection: One connection to another program, made by NetSystem.Connect or accepted by a NetSystem.Listen.
  • NetSystem: The game's network: connections to other programs over UDP, with encryption, in order and reliably or not as each message asks (GameNetworkingSockets, Valve's open-source transport).
  • PhysicsShape: A collision shape: an immutable thing a body (or another shape) is made of, in the body's local space.
  • PhysicsWorld: The physics simulation of one ECS World: Jolt Physics with double-precision positions, stepped at a fixed rate.
  • Settings: The player's settings, as the settings global: typed values under dotted keys (audio.volume, mod.coolmod.show_hints) that the engine and the game define (SettingDef), kept in user://settings.xml as the ones that differ from their defaults.
  • SteamSystem
  • Tween: An animation that tween.value, tween.property and tween.field start: a number, a vector, a colour (a linear-RGB vector) or a rotation (slerped) moving from one value to another over some seconds, with an easing curve.
  • UiDataModel: A data model: a script's table tied to documents.
  • UiElement: An element of a document (a div, a text node, a whole document) as scripts hold it.
  • UiEvent: An event that reached a listener (UiElement.Listen).
  • UiSystem
  • Vehicle: A vehicle on a dynamic body: wheels with suspension and tires, or tracks, an engine and a clutch (Jolt's VehicleConstraint).
  • VehicleDesc: A vehicle: its engine, drivetrain and wheels.
  • WheelDesc: One wheel of a vehicle.
  • World
