Source/Apogee.Rendering/Shaders/exposure.slang, tonemap.slang, Tests/Apogee.Rendering.Tests/MetalShaderTests.cs MetalShaderTests passes with exposure.slang in it, and ExposureTests passes on Metal GPU timings. FrameLoop.Timings is empty on Metal. Counter sample buffers (MTLCounterSampleBuffer) sample at encoder boundaries, and not on every GPU. MetalFrameLoop, MetalDevice.SupportsTimestamps, apogee_metal.h GpuScopesAreTimedAndLabelled runs (is not skipped) and passes on Metal Shader library cache. Metal shading language is compiled with newLibraryWithSource every start; an MTLBinaryArchive would keep the result. MetalDevice.CreateComputePipeline and CreateGraphicsPipeline the second start does not compile A CI runner with a real Metal GPU. A self-hosted Mac makes APOGEE_REQUIRE_METAL=1 possible: point macos_builds.yml at it (the probe step already turns the requirement on when a GPU qualifies). .github/workflows/macos_builds.yml, "GPUs (Metal probe)" the Metal tests are required in CI Check the Intel (osx-x64) NativeAOT build. CI publishes it as an artifact, but it has only been built. the apogee-osx-x64 artifact the fixture game, a sample and the Luau tests run from it

docs.title: Windows testing
docs.text:
What exists. CI builds and tests Release on windows-latest (a software GPU at best), and the NativeAOT runtime runs the fixture game headless. Nobody has run the editor, the samples or the GPU tests on real Windows hardware.

Needs: a Windows 10 or 11 machine with a Vulkan 1.3 GPU (AMD, NVIDIA or Intel; Windows on Arm too).

Task Done when Run it. ./build.sh test, then the viewer sample and the editor (dotnet run --project Source/Apogee.Editor -- Samples/Mods/game). Report what fails, with --gpu-info's output. an issue per problem, or a "works" note in the Windows discussion with your GPU and driver Controllers, high-DPI, multi-monitor, fullscreen. The input and window code is checked on Linux only. what breaks is reported or fixed NativeAOT on Windows. ./build.sh aot and the games' commands in Building. the fixture game and the Luau tests run from the published binary

docs.title: Game export on real hardware
docs.text:
What exists. Apogee.Runtime --export <game folder> <out dir> --target <linux-x64|win-x64|osx-arm64|osx-x64> (wrapper: ./build.sh export) copies the platform's runtime, native libraries and cooked packs into a folder that runs on its own. The exporter writes Windows icon/version resources into the .exe, switches it to the windowed subsystem, builds a macOS .app bundle with an ad-hoc code signature repair, and for Linux sets the executable bit and writes an icon and a .desktop file. Everything is tested from Linux with synthesized and vendored binaries; nothing has been run on Windows or macOS.

Needs: a Windows 10/11 machine, a Mac with Apple silicon, and a Linux distribution older than the one the runtime was built on.

Task Where to look Done when Windows: export Tests/Fixtures/ShippedGame for win-x64 from a published NativeAOT runtime and double-click the .exe. Docs/manual/tools/export.md, Source/Apogee.Export/Windows/ it starts with no console window, Explorer shows the icon, the Details tab shows the version, and the loader accepts the rewritten image (or the problem is reported). macOS: export for osx-arm64, copy the executable out of the bundle and run codesign --verify --strict --verbose=4 on the copy, run plutil -lint on Contents/Info.plist, then launch the .app on Apple silicon. Source/Apogee.Export/Mac/, the macOS section of Docs/manual/tools/export.md the signature verifies and the game starts, or the failure is reported. Linux: run an exported folder on the oldest distribution you can (the runtime needs the glibc of the machine that built it). the Linux section of Docs/manual/tools/export.md it starts without LD_LIBRARY_PATH, or the missing library or glibc version is reported.

Building the release runtimes in CI on the oldest supported distribution is part of this work.

docs.title: Reviewing
docs.text: The maintainer works alone, so every kind of review helps: the unsafe and interop code (Apogee.Interop, the generated bindings' layout checks, the native shims in Native/), the public APIs (naming, ownership, what throws), the shaders, and the Manual (a page that does not match the code is a bug). Open an issue with what you found, or a pull request.

docs.title: Expanding the engine
docs.text: Features that fit the scope in CONTRIBUTING.md are welcome: rendering features (shadows, post-processing, terrain), editor panels, tools, samples, the editor (importing models and assets, materials, animations, exporting a game: it is very bare-bones), more Luau API, performance work with a benchmark in Samples/Benchmarks. Every feature comes with tests and a Manual page. Ask first if it is big.

docs.title: Tell us if you hit this
docs.text: The Apogee.Ecs.Tests test program crashed twice on the Intel macOS CI runner (that job is experimental, so a failure does not fail the run) with a floating-point exception (SIGFPE) in a non-main thread, and passed on other runs. It has not been explained. The CI prints the crash report's faulting thread when it happens again.

docs.title: Writing docs
docs.text:
The documentation is Markdown in Docs/, built with MkDocs and the Material theme, and published at apogeeengine.github.io/docs. It lives next to the code so that a pull request changes both.

Docs/
  about/            introduction, FAQ, license
  getting-started/  building, samples
  manual/           one folder per area: core, native, platform, graphics, physics, audio, network, scripting, content, ui, tools
  api/              the generated reference (not committed, see below), with a committed index page each
  contributing/     for people who work on the engine

docs.title: Building the site
docs.text:
pip install mkdocs-material
./build.sh docs          # the API reference, then the site into Bin/site (mkdocs --strict: a broken link fails the build)
./build.sh docs serve    # the same, then a local server that reloads when a page changes

./build.sh docs first writes the API reference, which is why you do not run mkdocs directly:

  • C#: DocFX (a pinned local dotnet tool, .config/dotnet-tools.json) reads the XML documentation comments of the libraries listed in Tools/docfx/docfx.json and writes one page per type into Docs/api/csharp. The raw bindings (Apogee.Native.*) are left out. Document public members with /// comments: that is the C# reference.
  • Luau: Apogee.Runtime --luau-docs Docs/api/luau writes one page per class and library from the registry. The text comes from the same /// comments of [ApogeeClass], [Property], [Method] and [Signal] members, so documenting them documents the script API too.

Both folders are git-ignored apart from their index.md.

docs.title: Style
docs.text:
• A page explains how a feature fits together and why; the API reference lists the members. Show the smallest example that runs.
  • Say what is missing and what is untested. A page that does not match the code is a bug.
  • Relative links between pages (../core/ecs.md), so the strict build checks them.
  • No screenshots of samples as references: samples are run by hand.

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
Requires the .NET 10 SDK, CMake and Ninja (native libraries), Git LFS (prebuilt binaries are LFS objects: run git lfs install once before cloning) and clang (only to regenerate bindings).

./build.sh                       # dotnet build Apogee.slnx
./build.sh test                  # dotnet test
./build.sh native                # the shared libraries in Native/ (Flecs, Luau, cimgui) into Bin/native/<rid>
./build.sh aot                   # NativeAOT publish of Apogee.Runtime and Samples/Viewer into Bin/publish, then their shaders compiled ahead of time
./build.sh docs                  # this Manual and the API reference, built with mkdocs --strict into Bin/site (see Writing docs)
./build.sh bindings [lib…]       # regenerate Source/Apogee.Native.*/Generated

build.ps1 is the same on Windows. A .env file (gitignored) is loaded by both wrappers.

docs.title: Native libraries
docs.text:
Libraries that are vendored as binaries live in ThirdParty/<lib>/lib/<rid>; libraries built from source are built by ./build.sh native into Bin/native/<rid>. Either way ThirdParty/NativeLibraries.props copies the ones for the current platform next to a project's output, where NativeLibraries finds them (see Interop). ThirdParty/README.md says where each library comes from and how it was built.

Steamworks is proprietary. Valve lets us publish the SDK's redistributable_bin libraries, which are in the repository; ./build.sh sdk steam <zip> refreshes them from a newer SDK and unpacks the headers (git-ignored) that regenerating the bindings needs. Which files are unpacked, and why, is in ThirdParty/README.md.

Shared libraries on Linux are linked with --no-undefined: a missing source file fails the build instead of the first call.

docs.title: Warnings
docs.text: Warnings are errors, including the trimming and NativeAOT analyzers, for everything under Source/.

docs.title: Continuous integration
docs.text: Every push to main and every pull request builds, tests and publishes on Linux, Windows and macOS: see Continuous integration.

docs.title: Mods sample
docs.text:
Samples/Mods is a small game made only of packages, with mods that change its data and run scripts, shown by two panels. It is also what CI runs end to end: the package loader, definitions with schemas and patches, the sandbox, packs, and a rendered image.

Apogee.Runtime --game Samples/Mods/game --user /tmp/mods-user              # a window with the panels
Apogee.Runtime --game Samples/Mods/game --user /tmp/mods-user --watch      # and edit while it runs (see Hot reload)

game/ is the game's folder (res://): packages/base_game is its one base package, and dev_mods/ holds the mods of a development build (a player's mods go in user://mods, the same layout). --user is where user:// is; mods may write only user://moddata/<their id>/.

Package Shows base_game a schema for Crate (an enumeration, a default, a repeated Tag, a map of prices), two crates, a module (lib/util.luau) and a script with the two panels bigger_crates a dependency on base_game (^1.0) and gameVersion; a patch of the wooden crate (weight, size, and <Tag append="true">) and a new crate (gold); require("@base_game/lib/util"); writing its own data folder broken_mod a script with a bug: the error is logged with its file and line, the package is marked failed, and the game goes on needs_ghost a dependency on a mod that is not there: it does not load, and packages.list() says why

The Packages panel is packages.list(): which packages loaded, in load order, and for those that did not, why. The Crates panel is defs.all("Crate") after every package's content was merged: the wooden crate is 20 kg and large with three tags (the base game's two and the mod's), and the gold crate is the mod's. Delete bigger_crates and run again, and the panel shows the base game's numbers: nothing else changes.

docs.title: Things to try
docs.text:
• --watch, then change weight in dev_mods/bigger_crates/data/crates.xml, or a line in lib/util.luau: the panel changes without a restart.
  • Misspell an attribute in crates.xml: the schema reports it (defs.problems(), and the log) with the file and line, and the crate is still there.
  • Make needs_ghost load by adding a ghost_mod package next to it; make bigger_crates stop loading with <Dependency id="base_game" version=">=2.0"/>.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
• Samples/Mods/tests/util.test.luau: the module's functions, with --luau-test (run by hand).
  • Nothing in CI runs this sample. What it shows is tested on a fixture game of its own: Tests/Fixtures/ShippedGame (a package, a mod, a UI document with a script and a data model, and an ImGui panel) runs headless, from a pack and rendered on lavapipe in CI, and Tests/Apogee.Runtime.Tests and Tests/Apogee.Mods.Tests cover the loading, patching, dependency and failure rules.

docs.title: Scripting sample
docs.text:
Samples/Scripting is a program in Luau only: boxes that move and bounce in a cube, a panel with their count and a speed slider, and tests. It uses the scripting layer, and shows how a game's scripts are laid out.

  • sim.luau is a module. sim.install(world, settings) defines the components (Position, Velocity, the Box tag) and two systems: Move carries every box by its velocity times settings.speed and the frame's time step, and Bounce runs after it ("post_update") and puts a box that left the cube back on the wall, turned around. sim.spawn makes boxes from a small deterministic generator, so a run is the same every time. The settings table is read by the systems each frame: the panel's slider changes it.
  • main.luau is the program. The host gives it world; it installs the simulation, spawns 50 boxes, and registers a gui function with devtools.on_gui that draws the panel (imgui.begin_window, imgui.slider_float, imgui.button) and devtools.watches the speed and the frame in the debug window.
  • tests/sim.test.luau runs sim in a world of its own for as many frames as each case needs: spawning, the same places every run, motion by velocity, the speed setting, a bounce at the wall, and sixty boxes staying inside the cube for ten seconds.
Apogee.Runtime --luau-test Samples/Scripting
Apogee.Runtime --run Samples/Scripting/main.luau                    # in a window, with the panel and the dev overlay
Apogee.Runtime --run Samples/Scripting/main.luau --frames 120 --headless

This is a sample: you run it by hand, and nothing in CI runs it (the Luau library it uses is tested by Tests/Luau and the engine's own test projects). For luau-lsp, Apogee.Runtime --luau-defs Bin/defs writes the definitions and the sample's .luaurc points the engine alias at them. See Scripting, Runtime and Luau tests and Dev tools.

docs.title: UI sample
docs.text:
Samples/UI is a small game whose UI is plain RmlUi: a main menu, an options screen, a pause menu, and a HUD over a physics scene, written as RML and RCSS documents with Luau scripts and data models, plus a mod that adds a panel to the HUD. It is the model for how a game and its mods build UI with the ui surface: documents that carry their own scripts and data models.

Apogee.Runtime --game Samples/UI/game --user /tmp/ui-user          # Start, play; Esc pauses and resumes
echo playing > /tmp/ui-user/autostart.txt                          # menu, options, playing or paused: where the game starts
Apogee.Runtime --luau-test Samples/UI                              # the sample's own tests

A window, a keyboard and a mouse are all it needs. Like the other samples it is run by hand (and with --watch to edit while it runs), and nothing in CI runs it: the engine's behavior it relies on is tested in the engine's own tests.

docs.title: The game
docs.text:
game/packages/base_ui is the base package. Its files are small, and each has one job:

File What it holds main.luau Ties the scene to the screen (the world is paused except while playing; Start builds the scene and launches the ball), and starts the screens. lib/state.luau The game's state as plain values (screen, volume, theme, the speeds), the flow between screens (start, open_options, close_options, to_menu, escape) and the formatting helpers. It tells whoever registered (on_screen, on_theme) when something changed. Nothing else knows what a screen is called, and nothing here knows what a document is. lib/screens.luau Loads the four documents once, shows and hides them as the screen changes (the pause menu is shown after the HUD, so it is drawn over it), puts the theme class on their bodies, and sends Escape to state.escape. lib/hud.luau The hud data model ({{speed}}, {{top_speed}}, {{fps}}, the minimap dot) and the slots: hud.add_panel("hud_right", rml, rcss) puts a panel in a place the HUD document reserves. lib/options.luau The options data model (the theme's name, the volume as text and as a bar width) and what the buttons do to it. lib/scene.luau The scene behind the UI: a ground, a pyramid of crates and a ball (physics bodies, drawn as debug wireframes: the sample ships no models), a camera entity, and a system that reads the ball into the HUD's model every frame. ui/theme.rcss The look: colors are custom properties on body (--surface, --fg, --primary...), and body.light redefines them, so putting the class light on a document's body switches the theme. Cards, buttons, rows and the volume bar are rules here. ui/*.rml, ui/*.luau A document and its script for the menu, the options, the pause menu; the HUD has no script, only its data model. A script is a <script src> of the document, and its functions are what the onclick="on_start()" attributes call.

Things the sample shows on purpose: the state is separate from the documents (the scripts of a document only call into state, and the tests exercise state without any UI); a theme is a set of custom properties and the Options button restyles every document by changing a class; values that change continuously are a data model (data-style-left on the minimap dot, {{speed}}), updated once a frame with model:dirty(); and the data models are opened before the documents that use them load.

The game says game.set_escape_quits(false): in a window the runtime ends a run on Escape, which a game with a pause menu cannot have. game.quit() is what its Quit button calls. physics.paused is what the pause menu sets: no time is added to the simulation while it is true, so the world stays where it was and resumes from there.

docs.title: The mod
docs.text:
game/dev_mods/crate_panel is a mod: a mod.xml that depends on base_ui, a script, an RML fragment and its RCSS.

local hud = require("@base_ui/lib/hud")
local scene = require("@base_ui/lib/scene")

local panel = hud.add_panel("hud_right", fs.read_text("mod://crate_panel/panel.rml"), fs.read_text("mod://crate_panel/panel.rcss"))
panel:by_id("crate_boost"):listen("click", function() scene.boost() end)

It uses the game's modules (@base_ui/..., a dependency's, which a mod may require) and nothing in the base game mentions it: delete the folder and the panel is gone. It is Luau, RML and RCSS only, as every mod is. The mod listens on its own elements instead of writing onclick attributes in its fragment: an attribute a script writes runs as that script (as the mod, with the mod's limits, and without the base document's functions), so it could not call the game's functions anyway. What is not confined yet is what the UI may load: ui:load_document and ui:load_font read any mounted path, like the audio and models libraries, because the engine's classes do not know which mod called them; a document's <script src> is confined to what the document's owner may read.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Samples/UI/tests holds Luau tests of the pieces that need no UI (the formatting, the volume and the minimap arithmetic, the screen flow); run them by hand with Apogee.Runtime --luau-test Samples/UI. The things the sample uses are tested where they live: scripts and data models in documents (Tests/Apogee.UI.Tests, Tests/Apogee.Runtime.Tests), physics.paused (physics), game.quit (runtime).

docs.title: Viewer sample
docs.text:
Samples/Viewer (Apogee.Samples.Viewer) is the engine's first program that shows something: a procedural colonnade, six small glTF models on pedestals and 256 animated colored lights, drawn by the Forward+ renderer. It opens a window with the dev overlay, or renders offscreen (--headless) for screenshots. Everything scene-specific lives in the sample, next to its assets; the libraries it uses are Apogee.Platform, Content, Graphics, Rendering and DevTools.

dotnet run --project Samples/Viewer                 # the window
./build.sh aot && Bin/publish/viewer/Apogee.Samples.Viewer --help

docs.title: Controls
docs.text: WASD move, Q/E down and up, Shift is faster, hold the right mouse button to look, the wheel changes the speed, F1 shows or hides the dev overlay, Esc quits.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option --scene <courtyard\|file.gltf> what to show; a .gltf or .glb is lit with the light show --assets <dir> where the sample models are (default: Samples/Viewer/Assets, found by walking up from the program) --no-models leave the sample models out of the courtyard --lights <n> animated point lights, 256 by default --camera x,y,z,yaw,pitch start position in meters, angles in degrees --headless no window: render offscreen --frames <n> stop after n frames (headless default: 1) --size <w>x<h> window or image size (default 1280x720) --overlay draw the dev overlay in headless images --screenshot <file.png> headless: write the last frame --gpu <name> prefer the GPU whose name contains this (sets APOGEE_GPU) --no-vsync do not wait for vertical blank --watch window: use the shaders' source files (found in the repository above the program) and rebuild the pipelines that use a shader when you save it, with no hitch; an edit that does not compile keeps the old image and shows the error in red in the overlay

Exit codes: 0 fine, 1 bad arguments, 2 failure (no GPU, a file that does not load, a shader that does not compile), 3 the validation layer reported errors.

docs.title: Headless runs
docs.text:
Headless frames advance by a fixed 1/60 s, and the light show is a function of time only, so a given --frames always renders the same image on the same GPU:

Apogee.Samples.Viewer --gpu llvmpipe --headless --size 640x360 --frames 4 --screenshot viewer.png

The Viewer is a sample: people run it by hand, and neither CI nor any test runs it (there is no reference image to compare with). What the renderer must get right is tested, with its own fixtures, in Tests/Apogee.Rendering.Tests. ./build.sh aot-viewer publishes it with NativeAOT.

docs.title: Models
docs.text: The six models in Samples/Viewer/Assets are CC0 glTF-Sample-Assets files kept as Git LFS objects (see their README.md); where LFS was not pulled the courtyard still builds, without them. Larger scenes are not in the repository: Amazon's Lumberyard Bistro is CC BY 4.0 and a conversion to glTF is a local step, and Sponza and DamagedHelmet were left out because their licenses do not fit a repository that is freely redistributable.

docs.title: Audio
docs.text:
Apogee.Audio is the game's sound: OpenAL Soft behind one AudioSystem, playing WAV, FLAC, MP3 and Ogg Vorbis files in 3D around the entity that has an AudioListener, on buses, with reverb zones and occlusion. In a game, scripts see it as the global audio.

OpenAL Soft is LGPL, so it is its own shared library beside the program (libopenal.so.1, OpenAL32.dll, libopenal.1.dylib in ThirdParty/openal-soft/lib), loaded at run time and replaceable: see Legal/THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md for what a game that ships it does. Without the library audio.is_active is false: every call does nothing and returns an inert object, and the game runs in silence (the log says so once). The files are decoded by dr_wav, dr_flac, dr_mp3 and stb_vorbis in our audio_decode library (Native libraries).

local horn = audio:load_sound("res://sounds/horn.ogg")   -- a file from the game or a mod
local voice = horn:play("vehicles", 0.8, 1.0, false, truckEntity)   -- bus, volume, pitch, loop, entity
audio:get_bus("music").volume = 0.5

local music = audio:load_sound("res://music/field.ogg", true, false, true)   -- stream, is_3d, loop
music:play("music")

Another audio engine. There is no backend layer: the engine has one audio library. Middleware such as FMOD or Wwise is built around authored events, which a "play a file" API does not cover, so a shared seam would only get in the way; a game that needs one replaces Apogee.Audio.

docs.title: The system
docs.text:
new AudioSystem(world, options, files) (a session makes it for you): the device and context start with it; audio.is_active says whether they did (no library, a library that cannot start: both give an inactive system and a line in the log). Update(dt) is called once a frame after the world has progressed (ScriptSession.Progress does), because it reads world transforms.

AudioOptions: the output, the sample rate (48 kHz), and the Doppler and rolloff scales and the distance factor. - AudioOutput.Default is the platform's device, in real time. With no device at all the system mixes into nowhere and says so. - AudioOutput.None is OpenAL Soft's loopback device: nothing is played, but Update(dt) mixes the dt seconds it is given and drops the samples, so sounds start, loop and end exactly as they would be heard. Headless runs, script tests and the editor (when not playing) use it, and it needs no sound card. - AudioOutput.WavFile is the same, written to WavPath as a 32-bit float WAV when the system is disposed: what the tests record and measure.

audio.volume is the master volume (the listener's gain, which is also the volume of the master bus).

The player's volumes are settings: the setting audio.volume sets the master volume at the start and whenever it changes, and a game that defines a number setting audio.bus.music (settings:define("audio.bus.music", { type = "number", default = 1, min = 0, max = 1 })) gets the volume of the bus music kept in the player's file and applied from the start.

Files. Sounds are read through the game's virtual file system: res://, mod://<id>/, packs and zips, so a mod brings its sounds and a pack can hold them. Only virtual paths are read: a path with no scheme:// is an error, so a script cannot ask for a file by its place on the disk. (A mod can still read any res://, mod:// or user:// file: the audio classes do not know which mod called them, like the UI and model classes.) The format is told from the file's first bytes, not its name. A file that is missing or is not audio we read is an error with the reason. OpenAL's current context is process-wide: one audio system per process.

Loading. load_sound(path, stream, is_3d, loop) decodes the whole file into one OpenAL buffer, unless stream is true: then the file stays in memory and each voice decodes it as it plays, into four buffers of a quarter of a second (music, long ambience). Files with more than two channels are folded down to stereo.

docs.title: 3D, the listener and far from the origin
docs.text:
An entity with the AudioListener component (Index, 0 by default) is the ear: it looks along its local -Z with +Y up, as a camera does. Up to eight listeners (split screen). OpenAL's own listener stays at the origin. Each voice is placed relative to the nearest AudioListener, in that listener's frame, taken in double precision and then narrowed, so a source 10 000 km from the origin is as exact as one near it. The voice's velocity relative to that listener drives the Doppler effect (clamped to 300 m/s: a teleport must not shift the pitch to nonsense).

A voice is positional when its sound is 3D and it has an entity (the last argument of play): each frame it is placed at that entity's world transform. A sound loaded with is_3d = false is not. Sound fades with distance by OpenAL's inverse-distance rolloff, clamped: no quieter-than-full inside min_distance (1 m), no quieter than it is at max_distance (10 000 m). Set them on a sound (sound.min_distance, sound.max_distance: every voice it makes starts with them) or on one voice.

docs.title: Voices
docs.text: AudioVoice is what is playing: sound:play(bus, volume, pitch, loop, entity). volume, pitch, paused, is_playing, position (seconds), min_distance, max_distance, occlusion, muffling, stop(). Letting go: a sound that does not loop plays to its end whether you keep the voice or not; a looping sound is stopped when the voice is destroyed, which is when a script drops it, so keep the voice of whatever loops. Destroying a sound cuts every voice that is playing it.

docs.title: Buses
docs.text: audio:get_bus(name) returns the bus of that name (the same object each time): master or an empty name is the whole mix, and any other name is a bus of our own, made on first use, that sounds are played on (sound:play("vehicles")). volume, muted, set_paused(bool) and stop_all(). A voice's gain is its volume times its bus's times the master's. The old project's four buses (Music, Vehicles, Environment, UI) are the game's to make; the engine defines none.

docs.title: Reverb zones
docs.text: The ReverbZone component is a box centered on its entity (HalfExtents, scaled by the entity's scale) with a Preset, a Priority and a Level (dB added to the wet level). Where the first listener is in several, the highest priority wins, then the smallest. Only that zone applies; there is no crossfade (one EFX reverb effect carries it, and the change is heard at once). audio.current_reverb is the preset the listener hears now. The presets (generic, room, hallway, garage, barn, hangar, cave, forest, plain; off outside every zone) are our own approximations of those spaces, in ReverbPresets as OpenAL Soft's EAX reverb parameters, to be tuned by ear. Every voice sends to the one effect slot. Without the EFX extension (OpenAL Soft has it) there is no reverb and no occlusion filter.

docs.title: Occlusion
docs.text: A voice with occlusion = true and an entity, in an audio system with its physics set (audio.physics = physics; a session does), casts a ray from the nearest listener to the voice each frame and, when something blocks the way, puts a low-pass and an attenuation on its direct sound and its reverb send (OpenAL's filters), moving smoothly toward the target (8 · dt a frame). voice.muffling is how much (0 to 1). The ray ignores sensors and passes the voice's own body; it is one ray, so a source behind a thin pole is not muffled and behind a thick wall is.

docs.title: Not done
docs.text: HRTF settings (OpenAL Soft's own defaults apply), the other effects (echo, chorus…) from scripts (the C bindings have all of EFX), geometry-based occlusion, crossfading between zones, more than one reverb at a time, recording, .pck-style sound banks, and audio in the editor's own viewport (the editor plays sound in play mode only).

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Tests/Apogee.Audio.Tests mixes into a WAV file (AudioOutput.WavFile) and measures it, with no sound card, so they run in CI: a sound from the virtual file system is heard and ends, every format plays, only virtual paths are read, a stream plays to its end and a streamed loop goes on, a source on the left is louder in the left speaker and the sound follows when it moves, a far source is quieter and the distances of a voice change that, a bus scales what plays on it by exactly its gain (4:1 for 0.25), the master bus mutes the mix, mute and pause silence a bus, pitch and stop, destroying a sound cuts its voices, a reverb zone leaves a tail that no zone does not, zones are picked by priority then size, and a wall between the listener and the source muffles it (with the physics world's rays). Tests/Apogee.Native.Tests renders a source on the loopback device and tests the decoders. Tests/Luau/audio.test.luau runs the script surface, passing with or without the library, in the NativeAOT binary too.

docs.title: Asset identity: paths and UIDs
docs.text:
An asset is named by its path (res://models/car.glb), which people can read, and has a UID (uid://4k2m9x7q1w3ze), which stays the same when the file is renamed or moved. A reference holds both, so that a path which no longer leads to a file can be followed by its UID to where the file went.

res://models/car.glb|uid://4k2m9x7q1w3ze

The path is tried first and wins while its file exists. When it does not, the UID finds the file (and the engine logs that the reference is out of date, so that whoever saves the document that holds it writes the new path).

docs.title: The values
docs.text:
AssetUid and AssetRef are in Apogee.Core.Assets.

  • AssetUid is 64 random bits, never zero (zero is AssetUid.None, "no UID"). Its text is uid:// and 13 characters of lower-case Crockford base32 (0-9 a-h j k m n p-t v-z, no i l o u): uid://[0-9a-hjkmnp-tv-z]{13}. Parsing ignores case and refuses anything else, including all zeros.
  • AssetRef is a path and a UID. Its text is path|uid://…; a path alone and uid://… alone are valid too. A | cannot be part of a path, so the text splits without doubt, and a reference moves through an XML attribute or a Luau string as one value: a patch that replaces the path replaces the UID with it.

docs.title: Where a UID lives
docs.text:
Asset UID in Example An imported file (.glb, .png, .slang…) the uid attribute of its <asset>.import.xml <Import uid="uid://4k2m9x7q1w3ze" srgb="false"/> An authored file (.ascene, .aprefab) the uid attribute of the document's root <Scene version="1" uid="uid://…">, <Prefab version="1" uid="uid://…" nextId="4"> The whole project imported/assets.xml, a list written by the import <Asset uid="uid://…" path="res://models/car.glb"/>

AuthoredAssets.Extensions lists the authored kinds: scenes and prefabs. The sidecar and the document are the truth; assets.xml is a copy that makes lookups fast. It is rewritten by every import (only when its text changes), sorted by path, and a pack carries it, so a shipped game finds a UID without scanning. The paths in it are written as the folder looked when it was imported (res://…); a package that was imported on its own and is mounted at mod://id/ is read with its paths under mod://id/. In a --pack --cooked pack the list is cooked XML and is the only record of the imported assets' UIDs (their sidecars and sources are left out), so AssetDatabase believes a cooked list without looking for the files.

docs.title: When a UID is made
docs.text:
• Apogee.Runtime --import (AssetImporter.Run) gives a UID to every imported file that has none, by creating or editing its .import.xml, and to every authored file that has none, by adding the attribute to its root. Only those two attributes are written: comments, indentation, quote style, line endings and a byte order mark in the file stay as they were, and an attribute that is already there is never changed. The editor's single-asset Reimport does the same for its asset.
  • Never at run time, except when a scene is saved. A game, a mod, a pack or a read-only folder is never written to by the engine. Their assets without a UID simply have none, and a reference to them is by path.
  • A file that is not XML (a damaged document) has nowhere to hold a UID and is left alone.

Something that rewrites a .import.xml (a settings panel) must keep the UID: ImportSidecar.SetUid(newText, ImportSidecar.ReadUid(oldText)). Likewise AuthoredAssets.SetUid for a document that is saved over an existing one. World.SaveSceneFile does this for scenes: it mints a UID for a new file and keeps the one an existing file has (see scene files), and a scene that is saved from the editor is therefore an authored asset with a UID from its first save, without waiting for an import.

docs.title: The UID does not change the import key
docs.text: An artifact is imported again when its key changes, and the key hashes the text of the .import.xml. A UID is written into that text after the first import, so the key is made from ImportSettings.KeyText(text): the same text without the root's uid attribute (and a sidecar that holds only a UID counts as no sidecar). Minting or changing a UID therefore imports nothing again, and the keys made before UIDs existed are still valid. Changing a real setting still imports the asset again.

docs.title: Moves, deleted sidecars and copies
docs.text:
• Rename or move an asset together with its .import.xml: the UID goes with it, and every reference that has it still finds the file (AssetDatabase.Resolve).
  • Move without the sidecar: the file is a new asset with a new UID, and references to the old UID cannot follow. The import says so in the log when UIDs disappeared in a run that made new ones.
  • Delete the sidecar (and leave the file): the next import makes it again with the same UID, from assets.xml.
  • Copy an asset with its sidecar: two files now have one UID. The import keeps the UID on the original (the path assets.xml recorded for it, or the first path in order when there is no record) and gives the others a new one, and lists them in ImportReport.Reassigned. A copy made on a root that cannot be written to keeps the shared UID with a warning; the UID then names the original.

docs.title: From C
docs.text:
var assets = new AssetDatabase(files);        // or new ContentLoader(files).Assets
assets.Roots.Add("mod://cool/");               // res:// is the default; add each mounted package, in load order

AssetRef car = assets.RefOf("res://models/car.glb");          // path and UID
string? where = assets.Resolve(car);                           // the path if the file is there, else wherever the UID's file is, else null
string path = assets.ResolvePath("uid://4k2m9x7q1w3ze");      // a uid:// becomes a path; a path is returned as it is; an unknown uid is a ContentException
AssetUid uid = assets.UidOf("res://textures/ground.png");
  • The database reads the files and never writes. To find a UID it reads each root's imported/assets.xml, checks that the file it names is still there and still has that UID, and otherwise scans the files of its roots once. It remembers what it read until Refresh() (ContentLoader.Refresh() calls it, after an import).
  • When two files have the same UID, the one assets.xml names wins, or else the first root in the list (load order, for mods), and Duplicates lists the group.
  • Package paths: a package under res://packages/<id>/ (or res://dev_mods/<id>/) is also mod://<id>/. If mod://<id>/ is one of the roots, PathOf answers with the mod:// address, the one the rest of the engine uses, and the scan does not count the files twice.
  • ContentLoader.ResolveAssetPath(text) is what a loader that takes "a path or a uid://" calls first.

docs.title: Renaming and moving assets (for tools)
docs.text:
An editor that renames or moves an asset has two jobs: move the file with its identity, and make the documents that name it say the new path. A reference that carries a UID keeps working without the second job (the UID finds the file, and the engine logs that the path is out of date), but a path-only reference does not, and out-of-date paths are noise. AssetDatabase.Move does both; AssetReferences has the pieces.

MoveReport preview = assets.Move("res://models/car.glb", "res://vehicles/truck.glb", defFolders: ["res://data"], dryRun: true);
MoveReport done    = assets.Move("res://models/car.glb", "res://vehicles/truck.glb", defFolders: ["res://data"]);

IReadOnlyList<AssetReferenceSite> uses = AssetReferences.Find(assets, assets.RefOf("res://models/car.glb"), ["res://data"], includeScripts: true);
RewriteReport report = AssetReferences.Rewrite(assets, "res://models/car.glb", "res://vehicles/truck.glb", ["res://data"], dryRun: true);

docs.title: What is searched
docs.text:
• Documents: every authored file (AuthoredAssets.Extensions: scenes and prefabs) in the roots of the database, and every .xml file under the defFolders you name (definitions). Sidecars (.import.xml) hold settings, not references, and are not searched; they move with their asset.
  • References: an attribute whose whole text is an AssetRef. Text inside elements is not rewritten (it is reported, see below).
  • What counts as the asset: an attribute whose path is the asset's path, or whose UID is the asset's UID and whose path does not lead to some other existing file. The second condition is the rule of Resolve (the path wins while its file is there): a reference that carries the UID of a file and the path of its copy means the copy, and renaming the original must not touch it. When a UID is on two files (a copy that was not imported yet), the engine resolves it to the one PathOf names; renaming the other file does not take a stale-path reference with that UID, only the references that spell its own path.
  • Package files: the two addresses of a package file, res://packages/id/x and mod://id/x, are the same path, and a rewritten reference keeps the form it was written in. A mod://id/x is searched and rewritten as both res://packages/id/x and res://dev_mods/id/x (the mount does not say which folder backs it): if the same id exists in both folders, their references are treated alike.
  • Scripts: with includeScripts (always, in Rewrite and Move) the .luau files that spell the old path (or, in Find, the UID) are listed with an empty Attribute. They are reported and never rewritten: a string in code may be built, compared or logged. A uid:// in a script follows the file and is not reported by Rewrite. The search is linear in the size of the script, and at most 10,000 mentions are listed per script.
  • Paths that are not attribute references: RewriteReport.Unrewritable lists, and Move adds a warning for each, the places that name the old path and are not rewritten: <EntryScene path> and <Icon path> in game.xml, <Script path> in a package's mod.xml (relative paths there; the site's value is the full path), and the text inside an element of a document (<Model>res://models/car.glb</Model>; Attribute is empty). Edit them by hand; they break if the file moves. A path in a .rml or .rcss file is not looked at.

docs.title: What is written
docs.text:
Rewrite changes the path part of each matching reference and nothing else. It edits the text of the file, so comments, indentation, quote style, line endings, a byte order mark and the order of every other attribute stay exactly as they were (a scene is under version control, and a diff of a rename should show the renamed paths). Everything from the | on stays character for character: a UID written in capitals is still in capitals. The UID is never changed; a UID alone has nothing to rewrite and is listed in Unchanged, as is a reference that already says the new path. It may be called before the file moves or after (the UID is read from whichever path has the file). A scene that is a symbolic link is written through: the file it leads to is rewritten and the link stays. A file with several hard links is replaced by a new file, and the other names keep the old text.

Each edit is checked twice: before it, the attributes found in the text must be the attributes of the parsed document, in the same order with the same names, and a value to change must decode to what the parse says; after it, the new text is parsed again and must be the old document with only the chosen values changed (same elements, text and attributes). A file that fails a check is skipped.

Every file is written the same way (DirectorySource): the new bytes go to a hidden file beside it with a unique name, are flushed to the disk, and are then renamed over the file, so a crash or a full disk leaves the old file whole and never an empty one. The file keeps its permissions.

docs.title: All or nothing
docs.text:
1. Every new text is made and checked in memory first. Nothing is written if the request is wrong: the same path, a missing file, both paths existing, a folder as either path, and for Move a target inside the source or inside a file, game.xml and mod.xml, and a package's own imported/. A rename that only changes the case of a name on a file system that ignores case is refused with that explanation (paths are compared with their case: do it in two steps).
  2. Files that cannot be used are skipped with a reason in RewriteReport.Skipped, never half-written: unreadable, larger than AssetReferences.MaxDocumentBytes (64 MB), naming the asset more than AssetReferences.MaxReferencesPerDocument (100,000) times, over the memory a rewrite may take (MaxPlannedBytes, 256 MB for the old and the new text of all the documents), not valid UTF-8 (the text is written back, so a replaced byte would be damage; a file that cannot be read as UTF-8 and does not name the asset is no concern), not well-formed XML or with a document type, a cooked document (rewritten from its edited source instead), and anything in a read-only root such as a pack or a mod (its references are found, and not rewritten; their UIDs still find the asset).
  3. A skipped document that could have been written refuses the rename. Its references to the asset would break silently, so Rewrite and Move throw a ContentException before any write or move (a dryRun does not throw: its Skipped list is what to show the user, with SkippedDocument.Blocking true for these). Pass allowSkipped: true to go on after the user agreed. Documents in read-only roots never block: nothing could have rewritten them.
  4. Before the first write every file is read again and must be what the plan was made from: a scene the editor saved in between stops the rename, with nothing written. Then the files are written one by one, each checked again just before its own write (the editor can save while the earlier ones are being written). If a check fails or a write fails, whatever the exception, the ones already written get their old bytes back, but only a file that still holds what was written: one saved since is left as the person saved it and named in the error (saved since, left as it is), never overwritten with older text. A file that cannot be put back is named in the error.
  5. dryRun: true runs all of it except the writes and returns the same report with Applied false: use it for a confirmation dialog.
  6. Everything that can go wrong before the first write (a folder that cannot be listed or that is deleted during the scan, a file that cannot be opened, a source of your own that throws) comes out of Find, Rewrite and Move as a ContentException that says nothing was changed; only a null argument is an ArgumentNullException. Listing the project is bounded (24 folders deep, 100,000 folders), so a link that leads back to a folder above it ends in an error, not in a tree without end.

docs.title: Move
docs.text:
AssetDatabase.Move(from, to) is for a file in the game folder (res://; a pack or a mod is read-only). It refuses a folder (move the files in it, one call each), an .import.xml (it follows its asset), the imported/ cache (also a package's own) and hidden folders, game.xml and mod.xml, and a target that exists. Then, in this order: the references are rewritten, the file and its .import.xml move (so the UID goes with it), the imported artifact moves to the name the importer would give it, and imported/index.xml and imported/assets.xml say the new path. If a file cannot move, the files already moved (the last first) and then the documents are put back. If a moved file cannot be put back, the undoing stops there with the asset at its new path, where the documents (left as they are) name it: a document never names a file that did not move. The import data is a cache: if it cannot be updated that is a warning, and the next import repairs it. The artifact stays valid, because the import key does not depend on the path: nothing imports again (call AssetImporter.Reimport if you want to be sure). MoveReport.Warnings also says when another asset reads the moved one by path (a glTF's image), or the moved asset reads others by relative path and changed folder: those imports can fail until their files are updated; and one line for each place in RewriteReport.Unrewritable.

Running the same Move again finishes an interrupted one. If the process died, or an error left things half done, after the documents were rewritten (the references then already say the new path and are listed as Unchanged) or after the asset moved but before its .import.xml and import data did, call Move(from, to) with the same arguments: it moves what is left and brings the import data up to date.

docs.title: From Luau
docs.text:
Everything that loads an asset by path takes a uid:// as well: models:load("uid://4k2m9x7q1w3ze") gives the same id as models:load("res://models/car.glb") when that UID names that file, and it follows the file if it was moved. A uid:// that no file has is an error. The global assets (AssetLibrary) is for asking about identity:

assets:uid_of("res://models/car.glb")            -- "uid://4k2m9x7q1w3ze", or nil when the file does not exist or has none
assets:ref_of("res://models/car.glb")            -- "res://models/car.glb|uid://4k2m9x7q1w3ze": what to store to find it again
assets:resolve("uid://4k2m9x7q1w3ze")            -- "res://models/car.glb"
assets:resolve("res://old/car.glb|uid://4k2m9x7q1w3ze")  -- the path if its file is there, otherwise where the UID's file is; nil if neither

resolve takes a path, a uid:// or a path|uid://… reference and returns a path or nil; text that is none of these is an error. The UIDs are looked for under res:// and in each package that loads, in load order. ModelRenderer.Model is a number in scripts (models:load's id) and is saved in scenes as such a reference: see asset fields.

A game cooked with --pack --cooked has the artifacts of its imported assets and not their sources. A path that names an imported source still resolves (the pack's index says it was imported), and models:load accepts it, so scenes and scripts written with source paths run the same shipped.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
Tests/Apogee.Core.Tests/AssetRefTests.cs covers the text forms. Tests/Apogee.Content.Tests/AssetUidTests.cs covers the UID in sidecars (made, kept, edited in place with comments, quotes, CRLF and a byte order mark), the key that ignores it (nothing is imported again; a real setting still does), a deleted sidecar, copies and the file that moved with its UID, authored files, assets.xml, read-only roots, packages, and an asset that is renamed and still resolves.

Tests/Apogee.Content.Tests/AssetReferencesTests.cs covers finding and rewriting references (by path and by a stale path's UID, comments, quotes, CRLF and a byte order mark kept, similar paths left alone, packages, read-only roots, hostile and cooked files, a writable document that was skipped, a failed write put back for any exception, a file saved since or in between, a file that cannot be put back, symbolic links, reading that goes wrong, a script with 500,000 mentions, a UID on two files, a UID in capitals, game.xml, mod.xml and element text, previews) and Move (sidecar, artifact and lists, a model used by two scenes that still resolves through its UID, refusals, a failed move put back, a move that cannot be undone and the same call finishing it, an interrupted one finished). Tests/Apogee.Content.Tests/FileSystemTests.cs covers the durable write and the limits of a listing.

Tests/Apogee.Ecs.Tests/SceneAssetTests.cs covers asset fields in scenes (saved as path and UID, loaded from either, a moved asset found through its UID, an unregistered type), GamePackerTests the path-only reference in a cooked pack, Tests/Apogee.Rendering.Tests/ModelLibraryPathTests.cs uid:// in ModelLibrary.Load, and RuntimeTests.AModelLoadsByUidAndASavedSceneFindsAModelThatWasMoved the assets global and a scene saved by a script that loads after the model moved.

docs.title: Content loading
docs.text: Apogee.Content is how the engine gets its files: the virtual file system (below), and the readers that turn model and texture files into plain CPU data that the renderer uploads (no GPU types except the PixelFormat enum). XML definitions, packs and mods build on the file system and come next.

docs.title: File system
docs.text:
A VirtualFileSystem gives the engine, and the scripts of mods, one view of where files are. Paths are scheme://a/b/c.txt:

Prefix Holds Writable res:// the game's content: its folders, and its packs and patch packs over them no user:// what the player's machine keeps for the game: saves, settings, downloaded mods yes mod://<id>/ one mod's own files no

The program decides what is mounted where, with Mount(prefix, source); a source is an IFileSource: a DirectorySource (a folder, read-only unless asked to be writable), a ZipSource (a zipped mod), and later a pack. A path is looked up in every source mounted at a prefix of it, the one mounted last first, so a mod's folder or a patch pack overrides what is under it. A source can also remove a file (a patch pack does): it is gone for everything mounted before that source. Prefixes nest (res://mods/cool over res://), and a folder that only exists because something is mounted below it (mod://) is listed.

var vfs = new VirtualFileSystem();
vfs.Mount("res://", new DirectorySource("Content"));
vfs.Mount("user://", new DirectorySource(VirtualFileSystem.DefaultUserDirectory("Acme", "Truck"), writable: true));
vfs.Mount("mod://cool", new ZipSource("mods/cool.zip"));

byte[] bytes = vfs.ReadAllBytes("res://textures/ground.png");
string text = vfs.ReadAllText("mod://cool/mod.xml");                 // UTF-8, without a byte order mark
foreach (string file in vfs.EnumerateFiles("res://defs", "*.xml", recursive: true)) { ... }   // sorted by ordinal order
vfs.WriteAllText("user://saves/slot1.xml", xml);                     // user:// only; res:// is read-only

Rules that keep a path meaning the same everywhere (and a script inside its mounts): a path has a lowercase scheme, / separators, and segments that are plain names: no . or .., no empty segment, no \ : * ? " < > | or control characters, nothing that ends in a dot or a space, and no Windows device name (nul, con.txt). A path that breaks a rule is a VfsException (an IOException) when it is read or written, and simply not there for Exists and its kin. Paths are case-sensitive, even on a file system that is not (a texture asked for as Ground.PNG would load on Windows and fail on Linux): write them as they are on disk, in lowercase by convention. Only a writable source takes a write, a missing file is a FileNotFoundException, and a write goes to a hidden temporary file of a unique name, is flushed to the disk and is renamed over the target, so that a crash or a full disk leaves the old file whole (a symbolic link is written through and stays a link; a file with several hard links is replaced by a new file). EnumerateFiles takes maxDepth and maxDirectories for a folder that may hold links leading back to a folder above them. Zip entries whose names break the rules are skipped (with a warning), so no entry can name a place outside the zip. A DirectorySource follows links inside its folder as the OS does: do not mount a folder that you do not trust to be free of links.

CanWrite(path) says whether a write would be accepted, and Move(from, to) moves a file to a path that has nothing yet (inside one folder source it is a single rename that refuses to replace anything; between two sources it is a copy and a delete). Tools use them to rename an asset (see renaming and moving assets).

VfsPath has the helpers: Parse (strict), and lenient Normalize, Combine, DirectoryOf for resolving what a file refers to, where .. climbs but stops at the root of the scheme. TryGetPhysicalPath gives the real path of a file that a folder holds (to watch it, or for a library that only takes paths).

docs.title: What reads through it
docs.text:
• Scripts: new LuauVm(new LuauVmOptions { Files = new VfsScriptFiles(vfs) }) and vm.AddRoot("res://") (or "mod://cool"): require("./x"), .luaurc aliases and init.luau work on virtual paths, and chunk names, errors and OwnerOfModule see them (res://main.luau:12).
  • Models: ContentOptions.ReadFile = vfs.ReadAllBytes and GltfLoader.Load("res://models/car.gltf", options). The textures and the external .bin buffers a model refers to are read through it too (cgltf is given our allocator and file reader), relative to the model, so a model in a pack or a zip loads like one on disk.
  • Textures: ImageDecoder and Ktx2Loader take bytes: pass them vfs.ReadAllBytes(path).
  • Not yet: shaders. Slang compiles from real files and finds its imports itself, so the engine's shaders stay next to the program.

docs.title: glTF models
docs.text:
ModelData model = GltfLoader.Load("Models/Sponza/Sponza.gltf", new ContentOptions
{
    TextureCaps = new TextureCaps(Bc: device.SupportsBc, Astc: device.SupportsAstc),
});

GltfLoader reads .gltf (with its .bin and images) and .glb, and turns the default scene into a ModelData:

  • Meshes — one MeshData per glTF primitive that the scene uses: Vertex[] (48 bytes: position, normal, tangent+handedness, UV0 — the struct the vertex shader pulls from a buffer), uint[] indices, a material index and bounds. A mesh used by several nodes is loaded once.
  • Instances — each mesh placed in the world with its node hierarchy's world matrix (System.Numerics row-vector convention).
  • Materials — glTF's metallic-roughness model: factors and TextureRefs (texture index, UV set, KHR_texture_transform), emissive already multiplied by KHR_materials_emissive_strength, alpha mode and cutoff, double-sided, KHR_materials_unlit.
  • Textures — decoded and ready to upload (below). The same image used as a base color (sRGB) and as a normal map (linear) is two entries.
  • Lights — KHR_lights_punctual lights in world space (position, direction, color, intensity in lux or candela, range, cone angles).

What the file leaves out is filled in as glTF specifies: no normals gives flat normals; a normal-mapped material without tangents gets them computed from the UVs. By default (OptimizeMeshes) meshoptimizer merges duplicate vertices and reorders both buffers for the vertex cache and memory fetch, keeping exactly the same triangles. Triangle strips and fans become lists; points and lines are skipped with a warning. Only TEXCOORD_0 is read. Draco and EXT_meshopt_compression models are refused with an error that says so; any problem with a file is a ContentException naming the file.

docs.title: Textures
docs.text:
PNG, JPEG, BMP and TGA go through stb_image to RGBA8 with a full mip chain, built with a box filter; sRGB images are averaged in linear light, as the GPU's filtering does, and alpha never is. KTX 2 files (the glTF KHR_texture_basisu extension, or any .ktx2) are read by libktx, and Basis Universal data is transcoded at load to what the GPU has: BC7 (TextureCaps.Bc), else ASTC 4x4 (TextureCaps.Astc), else RGBA8. The file's own mip levels are kept. A TextureData carries the PixelFormat (the sRGB variant for base color and emissive, linear for the rest — decided by how the material uses it, not by the file), the size, the bytes of every mip, and the sampler state (filter, mipmaps, wrap).

Png.Encode(width, height, rgba) writes a PNG, for screenshots and test files.

docs.title: Definitions and schemas
docs.text: A game's data is XML: definitions (a crate, a machine, a crop) that mods can add to, change and remove, checked against schemas (XSD) that say what a valid one looks like. Apogee.Content reads both (Apogee.Content.Xml) and gives code and scripts typed data, with the line of every mistake.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text:
A definition is an element with an id. Its name is its type; type and id together identify it.

<!-- res://data/crates.xml: one definition, or a list of them under any root -->
<Crates>
  <Crate id="wooden" weight="12.5">
    <Tag>fragile</Tag>
    <Tag>stackable</Tag>
  </Crate>
  <Crate id="steel" weight="80"/>
</Crates>

A file holds one definition (its root has an id) or a list (the root's children are the definitions). DefDatabase.Load(files, folders, schemas) reads the .xml files of the folders you give it, in load order: the folders in order, in each folder its files sorted by name and then its subfolders the same way. In a game the folders come from the packages (base game first, then mods in dependency order).

What a later file may do with a definition:

Written Effect <Crate id="x" …/> again replaces it (it keeps its place in the list), with a warning that names both files <Crate id="x" patch="true" …/> patches it: see below <Crate id="x" remove="true"/> removes it

A patch or a removal of a definition that is not there is a warning, and does nothing. A patch merges into the definition (DefDatabase.Merge): its attributes replace the definition's (and add new ones), its text replaces the text, and its children are matched with the definition's children by name and id, or, with no id, by name and place (the second <Tag/> of a patch is the second <Tag> of the definition, even when the patch removed the first). A matched child is merged the same way; a child with remove="true" takes its match away; a child that matches nothing is added at the end. The patch and remove attributes are not kept.

<Crate id="wooden" patch="true" weight="14"><Tag remove="true"/><Tag append="true">reinforced</Tag></Crate>

Every Def knows Type, Id, its merged Node, its decoded Value, and Sources: the file that defined it and each file that patched it (with package, path, line), so a mod that patches a definition can find the files beside the original. Comments are not read.

docs.title: Problems
docs.text:
Everything wrong goes in database.Problems, each with a severity, the file and line, a path inside the definition, and a message:

mod://base/data/crates.xml:2: Crate.weight (wooden): 'heavy' is not a number
mod://base/data/crates.xml:4: Crate (steel): 'colour' is not an attribute of <Crate> (it has: id, weight).
mod://mod/data/crates.xml:1: warning: Crate: replaces Crate 'wooden' defined in mod://base/data/crates.xml (package 'base').

Errors are content that does not match its schema, a file that is not well-formed XML, a definition without an id. Warnings are things that load but are odd: a replacement, a patch of nothing, a type with no schema. A definition with errors is still in the database, with what could be made of it (a value that does not convert stays as text), so one mistake does not take a whole game down; the caller decides what to do with HasErrors. A problem in a patched definition names the file of the line it is on.

docs.title: Schemas
docs.text:
SchemaSet loads .xsd files (LoadFile, LoadFolder, LoadText), with the files they xs:include (found beside them, read once). A package brings the schema of the kinds of definitions it adds. The engine reads the part of XSD that content needs, and says so when a schema asks for more (<xs:key> is not supported, with the file and line), so a schema never means less than it says:

  • element, attribute (type, default, fixed, use; minOccurs, maxOccurs; elements may use ref), complexType with sequence, choice, all, group, attributeGroup, complexContent and simpleContent extensions, any, anyAttribute;
  • simpleType restrictions with enumeration, minInclusive, maxInclusive, minExclusive, maxExclusive, pattern (a regular expression that must match all of the text, with a time limit), minLength, maxLength, length, and list;
  • the built-in types: strings (string, token, ID, date…), boolean, decimal, float, double, and the integers with their ranges (int, long, byte, unsignedByte, positiveInteger…), and the engine's own vector3 (three numbers, "1 2.5 -3" or "1, 2.5, -3", decoded as a DefVector and a vector in Luau);
  • annotation with documentation (kept, for tools) and appinfo (the two conventions below). There are no namespaces: names are plain.

Order is not checked. Children may come in any order; each element is checked for how often it appears. The members of a choice have no minimum (any one may be the one chosen), and a repeated choice stands for "any order".

docs.title: What a definition decodes to (SchemaSet.Decode)
docs.text:
An element with a complex type is a record: its attributes, typed (numbers, booleans, text; a list type is a list), with the defaults of the attributes it leaves out, and its child elements by name. A child that may appear more than once is a list. An element that holds only one repeatable element (<Units><Unit/><Unit/></Units>) is that list. An element with a simple type is its value. simpleContent (text with attributes) is a record with the attributes and value, or just the value if it has no attributes. The example above decodes to:

{id: "wooden", weight: 12.5, Tag: ["fragile", "stackable"]}

Numbers are doubles, so whole numbers beyond 2^53 lose precision. Two conventions, written in the declaration's xs:annotation/xs:appinfo:

  • map: a container of <entry key="…"> items is a record by the keys (<Prices><entry key="wheat" value="2.5"/></Prices> is {wheat: 2.5}); an entry with nothing but key and value gives the value, any other entry is its record without the key. A key used twice is a problem.
  • defaults: an element that is left out is decoded as an empty one, so the defaults of its attributes apply, and a list that is left out is empty (without it a missing element or list is simply not there).

An open element (one with xs:any) is how a package adds a kind of child to another package's definition. Each child is checked against the global element named <open element>.<child> when the schemas have one (<components><motor power="90"/></components> is described by an element named components.motor), and kept as it is otherwise: attributes as text, children by name (a repeated name is a list), text as value. xs:anyAttribute keeps unknown attributes as text.

patch, remove, append, xmlns and xsi:… attributes are accepted on any element. An element the schemas have no declaration for decodes the same generic way, with no problems (DecodeResult.Declared is false), which is how a database without schemas reads everything.

docs.title: From Luau
docs.text:
Two global libraries (hand-written natives, declared in apogee.d.luau):

-- defs: the game's definitions, set with LuauVm.Defs (a game sets it when it has loaded its content)
local crate = defs.get("Crate", "wooden")          -- a table, or nil: crate.weight, crate.Tag[1]
for _, c in defs.all("Crate") do print(c.id) end   -- in load order
defs.types()                                       -- {"Barrel", "Crate"}
for _, s in defs.sources("Crate", "wooden") do print(s.package, s.path, s.line, s.role) end   -- "definition", "replacement", "patch"
for _, p in defs.problems() do print(p.severity, p.file, p.line, p.message) end

-- xml: XML text or files to and from tables
local node = xml.decode('<Crate id="a"><Tag>x</Tag></Crate>')   -- { name, attrs, order, children, text, line }
local text = xml.encode(node)
local file, err = xml.load("mod://core/data/crates.xml")         -- the same table from a file, or nil and a message

xml.load(path) reads a file as xml.decode reads text, with the same table and the same lines, and the path rules of fs (a mod sees what fs.read_text lets it see). It takes a text file and a cooked one alike, which fs.read_text and xml.decode do not: a shipped pack holds its definitions as binary, at the same paths (below), and reading one as text gives bytes. A file that is missing, not allowed, not well-formed or a damaged cooked file gives nil and a message that names the path (and the line); xml.decode raises an error instead, since it has no file to name. Use defs for definitions, and xml.load for XML you read yourself.

docs.title: Cooked definitions
docs.text:
./build.sh pack … --cooked (Packs) writes the definition files of the base packages (the .xml files in the Content folders of each packages/<id>/mod.xml) in the binary form of cooked XML, at the paths they have in the folder, so a shipped game parses no text for them. DefDatabase reads every file with XmlFile.Read, so cooked and text definitions load, merge, patch and report problems alike (a cooked file keeps the lines of its source, so a problem still points at the line you wrote). The folder in development is unchanged and a mod's files are never cooked, so a mod can patch a cooked definition of the base game as it patches a text one. The manifests mod.xml and schemas .xsd stay text.

A definition's table is made the first time it is asked for and is read-only all the way down (assigning to it is an error), and it is the same table for every script, so scripts cannot change each other's view of the game; copy what you need to change. Setting LuauVm.Defs again (a reload) makes later calls see the new definitions, and tables that scripts already hold stay as they were. Without a database the library is there and finds nothing. xml.encode writes attributes in the order of order and then the rest sorted by name, so the text is the same every time; elements nest at most 128 deep, both ways.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Tests/Apogee.Content.Tests: the XML reader and writer (lines, entities, a DTD refused), each schema feature with the exact problem messages, the merge rules including place counting and removal, and the database (load order, replace, patch, remove, sources, problems with file and line, kinds without a schema). Tests/Apogee.Scripting.Tests runs xml and defs from scripts (read-only tables, identity, sources and problems, reloads, xml.load of a text and a cooked file), and Tests/Luau/xml.test.luau runs them in the NativeAOT binary. Cooked definitions load and merge like text ones (CookedDefsLoadAndMergeLikeText), GamePackerTests checks which files a cooked pack cooks, and Tests/Apogee.Runtime.Tests packs the shipped-game fixture --cooked and encrypted and runs it from the pack.

docs.title: The game manifest (game.xml)
docs.text:
A game folder describes itself in a game.xml at its root, next to packages/ and data/. It says what the game is called, who made it, which version it is, where the player's files go, its Steam app id, and what its window looks like. The runtime reads it when it starts a game (Apogee.Runtime --game <folder>, the editor's Play), and a game that is exported needs it.

A folder without a game.xml still runs, as it always did: it has no version (so the gameVersion of its mods is not checked), its player's files go in a folder named after the game folder, and its Steam app id is the one in a steam_appid.txt, if there is one. Add a game.xml to give it all of that.

<Game name="Fixture Game" organization="Apogee" version="1.0.0" executable="FixtureGame" identifier="org.apogee.fixturegame"
      description="The shipped-game fixture of the CI." copyright="Copyright 2026 The Apogee Engine Authors">
  <EntryScene path="scenes/main.ascene"/>
  <Icon path="icon.png"/>
  <Window width="1280" height="720" fullscreen="false" resizable="true"/>
</Game>

docs.title: What it holds
docs.text:
Attributes of <Game>:

Default name the game's name, required: the window title, the bundle name, the product name of an executable none organization who made it, required: the folder that holds the player's files of all your games, the company of an executable none version major.minor.patch, required (all three parts): the version of the game that mods are checked against, the file and bundle version none executable the name of the executable of an export, without extension: letters, digits, _, ., -, up to 64, starting with a letter or digit the letters and digits of name (Game if there are none) identifier the reverse-DNS name of the game, lowercase letters, digits and dashes in at least two parts (org.apogee.fixturegame): the macOS bundle identifier, the Linux application id com.<organization>.<executable>, lowercase, letters, digits and dashes only userFolder the name of the folder of the player's files, under the organization's name steamAppId the game's Steam app id (a number) 0, none description, copyright text for the executable's properties and for installers empty

Children, each at most once:

<EntryScene path="…"/> a scene that is loaded before the packages' scripts run, as a path inside the game folder (scenes/main.ascene). The scripts then find its entities. A file that is not there is an error of the game. <Icon path="…"/> a square PNG inside the game folder, 256 pixels or more (1024 for macOS). An export makes the icons of each platform from it. <Window width height fullscreen resizable/> the window the game opens with: 16 to 16384 pixels wide and high, defaults 1280 x 720, windowed, resizable.

Paths are plain relative paths inside the game folder: no .., no drive or scheme, and the icon is a .png. The file is checked against the engine's schema (game.xsd, embedded in the Apogee.Content library) and then for what a schema cannot say; every problem comes with the file and line, and a game.xml with problems is an error of the game: it does not start (exit code 2).

docs.title: What it drives
docs.text:
• The player's folder (user://). --user <dir> wins; otherwise it is <local application data>/<organization>/<userFolder> with <>:"/\|?*, control characters and trailing dots and spaces left out of both names (~/.local/share on Linux, AppData/Local on Windows, ~/Library/Application Support on macOS). Without a game.xml it is <local application data>/Apogee/<game folder name>.
  • The game version. version is what each package's gameVersion range is checked against (Packages and mods): a mod that needs ^2.0 does not load in game 1.4.0, with a reason the game can show the player.
  • The Steam app id. steamAppId is the app id that StartGame hands to Steam (see Steam). A game that has none in its game.xml but a steam_appid.txt in its folder still works, with a warning in the log that the file is deprecated.
  • The entry scene, when the game starts without a scene of its own (the editor's Play starts from the scene being edited).

docs.title: How the runtime finds it
docs.text:
A runtime started with no command looks for game.xml in the folder of its executable, then in ../Resources (the Contents/Resources of a macOS app whose executable is in Contents/MacOS), and the folder it finds is the game's root: data/*.pack is there too. That game is run with its packs only (nothing else in the folder is res://), with the window of <Window> and the name of name as its title (--size <w>x<h> overrides the size). Both places are tried on every system. Arguments the runtime does not know are logged and ignored when a game is found that way, because Steam adds +connect_lobby <id> to the command line when a player accepts an invitation, and an older macOS adds -psn_…; after any command (--game, --pack, …) they are still mistakes. A development run (--game <folder>) takes the title and the window from game.xml too, but the whole folder stays res://. With no game.xml anywhere the runtime exits with code 1 (use --game <folder>, --smoke or --help).

The window gets the application's name, version and identifier from the manifest before it is created (SDL's application metadata: the macOS menu, Wayland's application id, the audio stream's name). On Linux the icon of the window is <Icon>'s file, read from the game's root when it is there; on Windows and macOS it is the executable's icon and the bundle's.

docs.title: From code
docs.text:
GameManifest? game = GameManifest.Load(folder, out IReadOnlyList<string> problems);   // null and no problems when there is no file
GameManifest.TryParse(text, "game.xml", out GameManifest? parsed, out problems);       // problems are "file:line: ..." and the manifest is null when there are any
string folder = game!.UserDirectory();                                                  // the player's folder
string xml = game.ToXml();                                                              // every value written out, so that reading it again gives the same manifest
ScriptSession.StartGame(new GameStart { Folder = folder, RealAudio = true });           // reads game.xml itself

GameManifest.SanitizeFileName is the rule that makes a name a folder name on every platform.

docs.title: Hot reload
docs.text:
While a game runs in development (and in the editor, which uses the same pieces), changing a file takes effect without a restart: a script you saved, a definition, an image.

Apogee.Runtime --game Samples/Mods --watch

--watch goes with --game. It makes res:// writable (so that a changed asset can be imported again into res://imported) and reloads, every frame it has something to do:

What changed What happens a .luau file that a script has required the module is run again and updated in place (below) a definition or a schema in a package's Content or Schema folder the definitions are read again, LuauVm.Defs is replaced, the defs.on_change listeners are called a .glb, .gltf, .bin, image or .import.xml imported again when the project has been imported (imported/index.xml), then HotReloader.AssetsChanged says which, for the host to load them again a .slang file imported again when the project has been imported (so its .ashader stays current), then HotReloader.ShadersChanged says which. The runtime hands them to its ShaderLibrary, and the renderers rebuild the pipelines that use them, off the render thread and swapped in at a frame boundary (Rendering); a shader that does not compile keeps the old pipelines and shows its error in the dev overlay a package's mod.xml, or an entry script (a package's <Script>, which runs once) listed as needs a restart, with a warning in the log

Files and folders that start with a dot, editors' temporary files (~, .tmp, .swp), and imported/ itself are ignored. Zips and packs are not watched (they do not change under a running game).

docs.title: Modules are updated where they are
docs.text:
LuauVm.ReloadModule runs the changed file again and then makes the table that every script got from require be the new module: it gets the new fields and loses the ones the new code does not have (and the new metatable). So every script that required the module sees the new functions, without being reloaded itself.

  • If the new code fails (syntax error, runtime error, timeout) nothing changes: the old module stays, and so does everything it registered. Fixing the file reloads it. The error and its line are in the log and in ReloadReport.Failures.
  • What a module registers while it loads is taken back and registered again by the new run: functions given to devtools.on_gui, signal connections, world:systems, defs.on_change listeners. (What a script registers later, from an event handler, is the script's to manage.) If the new run fails halfway, what it had registered is removed again and the old registrations stay.
  • Tasks are taken back too: what the module started with task.spawn, task.delay or task.every while it loaded (and what those tasks started) is cancelled, and the new run starts its own (Tasks). The same goes for the tweens it started with tween.value, tween.property and tween.field (Tweens).
  • A function copied into a local stays the old one: local f = module.f keeps the old function after a reload. Read module.f when you call it (or call module.f() directly).
  • State: the functions of the new module work on the new module table, while holders keep the old one, so a counter kept as a plain field (M.count) would split in two. Keep state in a table of its own and hand it over in on_reload(new, old), which the module may define and which is called before the update:
local M = { state = { count = 0 } }
function M.on_reload(new, old) new.state = old.state end   -- the new code carries on with the old state
function M.inc() M.state.count += 1 end
return M
  • A module that returns a frozen table (table.freeze) or something that is not a table is replaced in the cache only: scripts that already hold the old one keep it, new requires get the new one.
  • A module that nothing has required yet is not loaded by a change (it would run code nobody asked for).

docs.title: From code
docs.text:
using var reloader = new HotReloader(files, vm, packages);        // watches every folder behind the mounts
reloader.AssetsChanged += paths => { /* load the assets again */ };

// each frame, on the thread that owns the VM:
ReloadReport report = reloader.Poll();        // modules, DefsReloaded, assets, shaders, NeedsRestart, Failures
