VfsWatcher is the part that notices changes: it reports virtual paths (a file in res://packages/core is also mod://core/…, and both are reported), waits until a path has been quiet for 150 ms (saving a file is usually several events) and gives each path once. A new folder is scanned, because the operating system starts watching it a moment after it exists.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Only what require loaded is reloaded; an entry script needs a restart. Entities and components a script created stay as they are.
  • Pipelines are rebuilt from shaders, not state: a pipeline that a shader edit made differently (a different push constant layout, say) still has to agree with the code that draws with it. Texture and model reloading is the host's, from AssetsChanged.
  • While watching, base-game scripts can write res:// (mods still cannot: their fs rules do not change).

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Tests/Apogee.Scripting.Tests: module updates (identity, removed fields, the old module kept when the new one fails to compile or run, on_reload, a failing on_reload, frozen and non-table modules, listeners and signal connections moved to the new code, a module that failed its first load leaving nothing registered) and HotReloader over real files (a module edit, a broken edit then a fix, definitions and schemas, changes that need a restart, modules nothing required, an image imported again, sources and shaders without an import). Tests/Apogee.Content.Tests: the watcher (debounce, once, new and deleted files, ignored names, package views, zips). Tests/Apogee.Runtime.Tests: --watch, and a game's shader edits reaching its ShaderLibrary. Tests/Apogee.Rendering.Tests: a shader edit changing the rendered image (with its before and after), only the pipelines that use the file rebuilt, a broken edit then a fix, rebuilds while frames are in flight, changes during a build. Tests/Apogee.DevTools.Tests: the same for the overlay's shader, and the error section.

docs.title: Asset import
docs.text:
Source assets (glTF models, PNG and JPEG images, Slang shaders) are made for artists; a game wants its own formats, ready to load. Importing turns one into the other and keeps the result, so that it is done once, not at every start.

Apogee.Runtime --import Samples/Mods/res            # import what changed (in the folder's imported/)
Apogee.Runtime --import Samples/Mods/res --force    # import everything again
./build.sh pack Samples/Mods/res Bin/data/game.pack --cooked   # pack the artifacts instead of the sources they replace

docs.title: What it makes
GPU texture compression
docs.text:
Textures are cooked to Basis Universal UASTC inside KTX 2: one file for every platform, which Ktx2Loader transcodes when it loads to what the GPU samples (BC7 on desktop, ASTC 4x4 on mobile and Apple, RGBA8 where neither exists; TextureCaps says which). The encoder is the one in libktx (KTX-Software 4.4.2, Native libraries); BasisEncoder drives it:

  • Colour and data maps: UASTC level 2 (the default speed/quality trade-off) with RDO at quality 1.0, which shapes the blocks so that zstd squeezes them further, then zstd level 18 over the levels.
  • Normal maps (a material's normal texture inside a model, or an image whose settings say normalMap="true"): UASTC level 3, no RDO, and linear whatever srgb says: errors in a normal show as lighting noise, so these take the slower and more accurate settings. They stay RGB, so shaders read them as they always did. (libktx has a "normal map" mode that keeps two channels as RRRG, which would need the shaders and a BC5 target to go with it; it is not used.)
  • sRGB or linear is written in the file (the data format descriptor's transfer function); ContentLoader reads it from there, so a caller cannot get it wrong. The mip chain is the one the importer built (sRGB averaged in linear light).
  • A texture with a side under 4 pixels stays RGBA8 (a block would be bigger than the texture). compression="none" in the settings keeps RGBA8 for anything, such as a UI image that must not show block artifacts.
  • The encoder is deterministic (the same bytes on any number of cores) and slow, which is what the import cache is for: nothing is encoded again until the image, its settings or the encoder settings (part of the importer's fingerprint) change.

Measured on the 11 MB BoomBox.glb sample (four 2048 x 2048 PNGs; Linux, 28 threads, Release):

RGBA8 + zstd (compression="none") UASTC (the default) .amodel artifact 11.7 MB 5.5 MB (5.2 MiB) in a --cooked pack 11.7 MB 5.5 MB textures on the GPU (all levels) 85.3 MiB 21.3 MiB (BC7: 4x less) first import 1.0 s 18.7 s (139 s of CPU) import with nothing changed 0.07 s 0.07 s

The artifact used to be about the size of its source; now it is half, and a GPU holds a quarter of the memory.

docs.title: When something is imported again
docs.text: Each artifact has a key: the SHA-256 of the importer's version, the asset's .import.xml settings, the asset itself, and every file the import read for it. --import makes an artifact again only when its key is different, so changing a texture of a model, or a model's buffer, re-imports the model, and touching nothing re-imports nothing. An artifact whose source is gone is deleted. A failed import (a file that is not a PNG, a settings file that is wrong) is reported with its file, does not stop the others, exits with code 2, and leaves the artifact the game had (and its index entry) until the source is fixed.

docs.title: UIDs and the key
docs.text: Importing also gives each asset a UID in its .import.xml (<Import uid="uid://…"/>, made if there is no sidecar) and lists them in imported/assets.xml. The uid attribute is not part of the key (ImportSettings.KeyText leaves it out), so a UID that is added, or that changes, imports nothing again.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
An <asset>.import.xml next to an asset (checked against the engine's schema) changes how it is imported; every attribute is optional:

<Import srgb="false" mips="false" optimize="false"/>

srgb (default true) is for images: colour maps are sRGB, normal maps, roughness and masks are linear. mips (default true) builds the mip chain. compression is uastc (the default) or none, for images and for the textures of a model; normalMap (default false) says that an image is a normal map (linear, encoded for accuracy). optimize (default true) is for models: merge duplicate vertices and reorder for the GPU's vertex cache. A model's textures take their sRGB or linear setting, and whether they are normal maps, from how its materials use them.

For a shader, <Variant> children each list the preprocessor defines of one more version to compile (the version with no defines is always compiled); the shader is loaded in a variant by passing the same defines to ShaderLibrary.Load:

<Import>
  <Variant><Define name="SHADOWS"/><Define name="QUALITY" value="3"/></Variant>
</Import>

docs.title: Loading
docs.text:
ContentLoader is what a game calls: it takes the artifact when there is one and the source otherwise, so the same call works in the editor (sources), in a development run that has imported (artifacts) and in a shipped game (artifacts in a pack). A mod's files are not imported by the game, but a mod may be imported as a folder of its own and ship its imported/ (a mod that brings compiled shaders does); the loader finds it at mod://id/imported:

var content = new ContentLoader(files);
ModelData car = content.LoadModel("res://models/car.gltf");
TextureData ground = content.LoadTexture("res://textures/ground.png", srgb: true, caps);

It does not check that an artifact is current: importing is the step that does (and hot reload, in the editor, runs it when a file changes). The textures of an imported model or image are transcoded for the GPU in ContentOptions.TextureCaps / the caps argument, as those of a source model are.

docs.title: Packing
docs.text:
--pack … --cooked leaves out every source that has an artifact, the files it was made from and its .import.xml, and packs the rest with imported/. It needs an import first. A shipped game therefore holds models/car.gltf.amodel and textures/ground.png.ktx2, not the glTF, the .bin and the PNGs, and ContentLoader.LoadModel("res://models/car.gltf") finds the artifact by the path of the source it replaced.

A cooked pack also holds the authored documents (.ascene, see AuthoredAssets.Extensions) and the UID list imported/assets.xml as cooked XML, each at the path of its source, so a shipped game parses no text for them and a UID still names its asset after the sidecar has been left out. So are the definitions of the base packages: the .xml files in the content folders (<Content path="data"/>) of each packages/<id>/mod.xml that reads. Everything else stays as it is: other .xml files, the manifests mod.xml, schemas (.xsd), RmlUi documents, the scripts, and everything under dev_mods/. The packing is GamePacker (Packs); --pack is a thin command on top of it. A scene or a definition file that is not well-formed XML stops the pack, with its path and line.

docs.title: Shaders
docs.text: Shipped games never load the Slang compiler. ./build.sh aot publishes the runtime and then runs Apogee.Runtime --import on its Shaders folder, which writes Shaders/imported/*.ashader; the renderers load those (ShaderLibrary, Rendering). In development nothing needs importing: a shader without an artifact is compiled and cached, as before. The bundle records the engine's shader ABI, so a mod's old compiled shader is refused with "import it again" rather than crashing the driver; to make a mod's shaders, import the mod's folder with the engine's dev runtime. CI runs the published runtime with the compiler libraries and every .slang source deleted, running the fixture game, to prove it.

docs.title: Cooked XML
docs.text:
Authored XML (scenes, and later prefabs and materials) and definitions are small, but a shipped game still gains from not parsing text: a cooked file is the same document in a binary encoding, APXB, in Apogee.Content.Xml.XmlBinary. It is not typed by the reflection registry: it holds the XmlNode tree (names, attributes in their order, text, the line each element started on, children) with every distinct name and value stored once, so it works for any XML file, does not depend on which components the engine had when the file was cooked, and gives back exactly the tree that was written. A scene with a thousand entities is less than half the size of its text.

Part What it is Header, 16 bytes the magic APXB, a format version (1), flags (none are defined), the number of strings and the number of elements; little-endian Strings each one a length and its UTF-8 bytes, in the order the writer first used them, so the same tree always gives the same file Elements in document order, root first: name, line, attributes (name and value), text, number of children; every number is a varint (7 bits per byte) 
byte[] cooked = XmlBinary.Write(XmlNode.Parse(text));
XmlNode again = XmlBinary.Read(cooked, "res://scenes/start.ascene");   // a ContentException if it is damaged
XmlNode either = XmlFile.Read(files, "res://scenes/start.ascene");     // text or cooked, whichever the file is

XmlFile.Read(files, path) is the one way to read an authored or definition file: it takes a file that starts with the magic as cooked (no text XML file can: those begin with <, a byte order mark or white space) and anything else as UTF-8 text, so the same code runs on the sources in development and on the cooked files of a shipped pack. A cooked file keeps the path of its source, which is why a script that reads it as text (fs.read_text) gets bytes, and reading it with XmlFile is the way that works for both. --pack --cooked writes it for authored documents, the definitions of the base packages and the UID list (see Packing).

Everything in the engine that reads such a file goes through XmlFile.Read: DefDatabase (the definitions, so defs in scripts), World.LoadSceneFile (and world:load_scene_file), the asset database's UID list, and the Luau xml.load(path), which gives scripts the table xml.decode gives for a text or a cooked file (Definitions). What is not read that way is never cooked: the package manifests mod.xml, schemas (.xsd), .rml documents, the import index and the sidecars, game.xml, and the files of mods, which stay text because players and tools open them.

The origin of an element is not stored: the reader gives every element the path it was asked to read, so an error in a cooked file still names the file and the source line. The reader accepts the versions up to the one it knows; a file from a newer engine, or with a flag it does not know, is refused with "cook again". A file cut short or damaged is a ContentException, never anything else, and a count in it (strings, elements, attributes, children) is checked against the bytes that are left before the reader makes room for it, so a hostile file cannot make it allocate more than a small multiple of its own size. Nesting is limited as in the text parser (XmlNode.MaxDepth).

AuthoredAssets.ReadUid also reads the uid of a cooked document, from its root only.

docs.title: What gets cooked, and what does not (the plan)
docs.text:
A rule first: source formats always load. Mods are Luau and data, are never imported, and ship as folders or zips; the editor works on sources. So every loader keeps a source path (as ContentLoader does), and cooking is only an optimization for the base game: a faster, sometimes smaller artifact that is a cache of the source. No format exists only cooked.

Use a standard container where there is one, and an engine format only where there is none. So no .atex: textures stay KTX 2, which the engine already reads (including GPU-compressed data that is transcoded at load). That leaves .amodel as the one engine-specific binary so far, because glTF is an interchange format and there is no standard runtime one.

Kind Authored as Cooked? Artifact Models glTF yes, done .amodel (meshoptimizer) Textures PNG, JPEG yes, done: Basis UASTC in KTX 2, transcoded to BC7/ASTC/RGBA8 at load .ktx2 Shaders Slang yes, done: SPIR-V and Metal shading language and reflection ahead of time, in one bundle (DXIL has a slot), so a shipped game does not carry the compiler .ashader Materials XML definition (a Material type with a schema: textures by path, factors, alpha mode) not for now. They are small data, which mods must be able to author and patch like any definition; a model's built-in materials are already in .amodel none (an .amat only if profiling asks) Scenes, prefabs XML: entities and their components, written and read through the reflection registry yes, done: APXB in place (Cooked XML): --pack --cooked writes the tree of the document as a binary file in place of the source, under the same path, so that scenes, prefabs and definitions share one format and one reader; the definitions of the base packages are cooked the same way (a mod's are not: mods are never cooked) binary XML (APXB), same path Audio WAV, FLAC, MP3 and Ogg Vorbis, decoded when loaded (streamed if asked) already compressed by the formats; a cook would only trade load time for size none Scripts Luau no (a bytecode cache could come later; it is not needed to ship) none

How it grows. AssetImporter is a small registry. An importer (IAssetImporter) is a name, the extensions it takes, a fingerprint (part of the key: its version, and the versions and options of the tools it calls, such as Slang's, so changing what it writes imports again), and a function from the source and its settings to an artifact, or to nothing for a file that is not an asset on its own. It reads files through the ImportContext, which records them as the artifact's dependencies. new AssetImporter(files, importers) runs them in the order of the list (a file an earlier importer read is not imported by a later one); AssetImporter.Defaults is models and images and the runtime adds ShaderImporter, which lives in Apogee.Rendering because Content does not reference Graphics. A new kind of asset is a new importer and a Load… that takes its artifact; the index, the keys, the sidecar settings, --import and --pack --cooked stay as they are.

What is open for you to decide: whether a .amat is ever worth having. It blocks nothing.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Tests/Apogee.Content.Tests: GPU compression (transcoding to BC7, ASTC and RGBA8 and how close it stays, the colour space read from the file, normal maps, determinism, the sidecar, a model's textures and the caps of the loader), the registry (order, an asset that is not one, what an earlier importer read, the fingerprint, a package's own artifacts, shader variants in the settings), the KTX 2 writer read back by libktx's reader (sRGB and linear, odd sizes, one level or a chain, the data format descriptor), the model file (every field bit for bit, deterministic, a mesh that is not a triangle list, damaged and foreign files), and the importer (artifacts and the index, nothing imported twice, a change to the source, a dependency or the settings, deleted sources, failures that keep the old artifact, hidden folders, a damaged index, settings checked against their schema) and ContentLoader (the artifact is the one used, a source otherwise, a mod's files). cooked XML (XmlBinaryTests: every field of a tree back, escapes and non-ASCII text, the same bytes every time, size against the text, text and cooked read alike, a newer version or a flag refused, every truncation and a thousand flipped bytes, counts that do not fit the file, nesting). Tests/Apogee.Graphics.Tests: the shader bundle (variants, damaged files, another ABI, backends that are not written yet). Tests/Apogee.Rendering.Tests: the shader importer and ShaderLibrary (dependencies, variants, the compiler never started when an artifact exists, no compiler no artifact, a mod's artifacts). Tests/Apogee.Runtime.Tests runs --import and --pack --cooked end to end, for shaders too.

docs.title: Status and re-importing one asset
docs.text: AssetImporter.StatusOf("models/car.glb") says where one asset stands (AssetStatus: NotImportable, NotImported, UpToDate, or Stale when the file, its .import.xml or what the import read changed) and Reimport(source) imports just that asset again, leaving the rest of the index as it is. The editor's asset browser uses them, and so does the editor when files are dropped on it from the system: it copies them into the game and calls Reimport for each, on a worker thread, with the import gate held so that nothing else imports at the same time.

docs.title: Packages and mods
docs.text:
The game's content and the mods that change it are all packages: a folder (or a .zip) with a mod.xml at its root. The game's own packages are base packages; mods are packages too, with the same layout and the same tools, so the base game is just the first thing that loads. Mods are Luau and data, never native code.

my_mod/
  mod.xml          what it is, what it needs, what it brings
  main.luau        scripts listed in mod.xml
  data/*.xml       definitions (see Definitions and schemas)
  schemas/*.xsd    schemas for the definitions it adds

docs.title: mod.xml
docs.text:
<Mod id="bigger_crates" name="Bigger Crates" version="1.2.0" author="Ada" description="Crates, but bigger."
     apiVersion="1" gameVersion=">=1.0 <3">
  <Dependency id="base_game" version="^1.0"/>
  <Script path="main.luau"/>
  <Content path="data"/>
  <Schema path="schemas"/>
</Mod>
id lowercase letters, digits and underscores, up to 64; the name of the package's folder (or of its .zip without the extension). Not engine, self, res, user or mod. version major.minor.patch; missing parts are 0, a leading v and a -suffix are ignored apiVersion the package API it was written for (default 1); a package that needs a newer one than the engine has does not load gameVersion which versions of the game it works with (a version range, default any), checked against the version of the game's game.xml; a game without one has no version and the range is not checked Dependency a package that must be there, and which versions of it (a range, default any) Script a .luau file inside the package, run when it loads, in the order written Content, Schema folders of definitions and of schemas inside the package

Paths are plain relative paths inside the package: no .., no drive or scheme. The manifest is checked against the engine's schema (mod.xsd), then for what a schema cannot say; every problem comes with the file and line.

Version ranges are comparators separated by spaces or commas, all of which must hold: >=1.2, <=, >, <, =1.2 (or 1.2), ^1.2.3 (at least that, below the next version of its first non-zero part: <2.0.0; ^0.2.3 is <0.3.0), ~1.2.3 (below the next minor: <1.3.0), * (any).

docs.title: Finding, solving and mounting
docs.text:
PackageSet.Load(files) looks in:

Where Kind Can the player switch it off? res://packages/<id>/ base no res://dev_mods/<id>/ dev (a development build's mods) yes user://mods/<id>/ and user://mods/<id>.zip the player's mods yes workshop://<id>/ the player's Steam Workshop mods (when Steam runs; see Steam) yes

The player's switched-off mods are in user://mods.xml (<Mods><Disabled id="cool"/></Mods>), which only the game writes (UserModSettings), never a mod. There is one package per id: the first one found wins, and a later one with the same id is ignored with a problem.

A package does not load, with a reason you can show the player, when: it needs a newer package API or another game version, the player switched it off, a dependency is missing, does not load, or is out of its version range (this cascades through whatever depends on it), it is part of a dependency cycle, or it is a base package that needs a mod. What loads is ordered dependencies first, base packages before mods, and otherwise by id, so the order is the same on every machine. Everything that loads is mounted at mod://<id>/ in the file system, whatever it is made of, so a package's files have one address everywhere (mod://bigger_crates/data/x.xml).

using PackageSet packages = PackageSet.Load(files, new PackageOptions { GameVersion = new PackageVersion(1, 4, 0) });

foreach (SolvedPackage p in packages.Packages)
    Console.WriteLine($"{p.Id} {p.Manifest.Version}: {(p.Enabled ? "loads" : p.Reason)}");   // "needs 'base_game', which is not installed"

DefDatabase defs = packages.LoadDefs();    // the packages' schemas and content folders, in load order
foreach (var (package, path) in packages.Scripts) { /* run the scripts */ }

Trouble with the search itself (a mod.xml that does not parse, an id that is not its folder's name, a zip that is not a zip, a schema that is wrong) is in packages.Problems, not an exception: one broken mod does not stop the game. PackageSolver.Solve is the same decision on a plain list of candidates, which is what the tests drive.

docs.title: Running packages in Luau (PackageLoader)
docs.text:
PackageLoader (in Apogee.Scripting) runs the packages of a PackageSet in a VM. A game wires its hooks into the VM's options and then loads:

var loader = new PackageLoader(files, packages);
var vm = new LuauVm(new LuauVmOptions
{
    Files = new VfsScriptFiles(files),          // scripts are read through the file system
    FileSystem = files,                         // the fs library
    OwnerOfModule = loader.OwnerOfModule,       // a module runs as the owner of the package it is in
    CanLoadModule = loader.CanLoadModule,       // require confinement
    CanAccessFile = loader.CanAccessFile,       // fs confinement
});
vm.Defs = packages.LoadDefs();
IReadOnlyList<PackageRunResult> results = loader.Load(vm);
  • Order and owners. Scripts run packages in load order, each package's <Script>s in the order written. A base package's scripts run as the VM's base owner; a mod gets an owner of its own (PackageLoaderOptions: a soft memory limit, 256 MiB by default, and a time budget per call, 2 s), so one mod cannot use up the memory or the frame of the others, and it cannot use classes marked ModsBlocked. A module runs as the owner of the package it is in, whoever required it: a mod that requires a base-game module does not give it the mod's limits.
  • Aliases. @<id>/… is an alias for each package (require("@base_game/lib/util")), in every script. A .luaurc alias of the same name wins.
  • Confinement. A mod may require files of its own package, of the packages it depends on (however far), and res://; ../other_mod/x resolves to another mod's folder and is refused, and so is @other_mod/x. The base game may require anything.
  • Failure. A script that raises an error stops its package: the error is logged and in PackageRunResult.Error, the package's remaining scripts and the packages that need it are not run, and everything else goes on. A mod that never returns is stopped by its time budget. Content a package brought stays loaded.

docs.title: The fs library
docs.text:
Scripts read and write through the virtual file system with virtual paths only (res://…, user://…, mod://<id>/…):

local text, err = fs.read_text("mod://my_mod/config.xml")      -- text, or nil and a message
local ok, err = fs.write_text("user://moddata/my_mod/save.xml", xml.encode(node))
fs.exists(path)  fs.read_bytes(path)  fs.write_bytes(path, data)  fs.list(dir, "*.xml", true)  fs.list_dirs(dir)  fs.make_dir(path)  fs.remove(path)

Functions return nil and a message instead of raising an error for what can go wrong. A mod may read res://, its own package and its dependencies', and user://moddata/<its id>/, and may write only user://moddata/<its id>/ (folders are made as needed): the game's content is read-only to it, and so are the player's saves and other mods' data. The base game may write wherever the file system allows (user://). Messages name the virtual path (user://x: access denied, res://y: not found), never a path on the disk, and a path that is not valid (.., a backslash, a drive) is refused before anything is looked up. fs.exists says false for what a script may not see.

docs.title: Shaders in a mod
docs.text: A mod may bring Slang shaders. The shipped game has no shader compiler, so a mod's shaders must be compiled by the modder: run the engine's dev runtime on the mod's folder (Apogee.Runtime --import <mod folder>) and ship the result with the mod. The compiled files are in the mod's imported/ folder (imported/shaders/x.slang.ashader and an index.xml), which ShaderLibrary and ContentLoader find at mod://id/imported. A bundle records the engine's shader ABI; after an engine update that changes it, the game says to import the mod again. In development, where the compiler is present, a mod's .slang source loads without importing. See Asset import.

docs.title: Apogee.Runtime --game <folder>
docs.text:
Apogee.Runtime --game Samples/Mods [--user <folder>] [--headless --frames 60 | --headless --screenshot out.png | (a window)]

The folder is res:// (its packages/ hold the game's packages), user:// is --user or the platform's folder for the game's name (the player's mods are in user://mods). The runtime logs every package and why one does not load, loads the definitions and their problems, runs the scripts, and then runs the frame loop of --run. A mod that fails is logged and left out; a base package that fails is an error of the game (exit code 2).

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Tests/Apogee.Content.Tests: versions and ranges, the manifest (every field, every kind of problem), the solver (each reason to disable, cascade, cycles, order independent of discovery order, duplicate ids) and PackageSet over real folders and a zip (places, mounting, switched-off mods, problems, definitions built from the packages, disposal). Tests/Apogee.Scripting.Tests runs PackageLoader over real folders (order, owners and limits, aliases, require and fs confinement including that no real path leaks, failures that stay inside their package, a runaway mod stopped by its budget, definitions seen by scripts), and Tests/Apogee.Runtime.Tests runs --game end to end.

docs.title: Packs
docs.text: A pack is one file (or a few) that holds a game's content: compressed with zstd, optionally encrypted with AES-256-GCM, and mounted in the file system like a folder. A shipped game's res:// is its packs; during development it is a folder. Mods are not packs: they stay folders or zips so that players can make them without tools.

docs.title: Making one
docs.text:
./build.sh pack Samples/Mods/res Bin/data/game.pack                      # every file under the folder (Apogee.Runtime --pack, with .env loaded)
./build.sh pack Content Bin/data/game.pack --split-mb 1024 --level 15      # parts of about 1 GiB, a smaller (slower) compression
./build.sh pack Content Bin/data/patch.pack --base Bin/data/game.pack      # a patch pack

./build.sh pack runs Apogee.Runtime --pack (the engine's host program has the content library and the native libraries, and the editor and the export step use the same PackWriter); the wrapper loads .env, so APOGEE_PACK_KEY applies. Run Apogee.Runtime --pack <folder> <out.pack> yourself to pack without the wrapper. Paths in the pack are relative to the folder (packages/core/mod.xml); files and folders whose name starts with a dot are left out; every name must be valid in a virtual path (no .., no nul…), and the tool says which are not. From code: GamePacker (below), or PackWriter (Add, AddFile, Remove, Finish) to write the files yourself.

  • Compression. Each file is compressed with zstd when it has 64 bytes or more and that saves at least 10%; the rest (PNG, KTX2, OGG…) is stored as it is. --level is zstd's 1 to 22 (default 12). Large files are compressed on several threads.
  • Splitting. A pack grows to --split-mb (default 1536) and then continues in the next part: game.pack, game_001.pack, game_002.pack… A file is never split, so one that is bigger than the limit gets a part to itself. Opening the first part finds the others; a part that is missing is an error that says which.
  • Patch packs. With --base the packs you name (in order, with the same key) are what the game has already: the new pack holds only the files that are new or different, and a removal for each file that is gone. Mounted over the base, it replaces, adds and removes.

With --cooked the pack is what a shipped game needs: the imported artifacts instead of the sources they replace and their .import.xml files (Asset import), the authored documents (scenes), the definitions of the base packages (the .xml files in the Content folders of packages/<id>/mod.xml) and the UID list imported/assets.xml as cooked XML at the same paths, everything else as it is: mod.xml, schemas, .rml documents, scripts and mods stay text. It needs the folder to be imported first. The summary line says how many documents were cooked (game.pack: 14 files (5.5 MiB) in 1 part(s), 4.9 MiB, 2 cooked). Files under dev_mods/ are never cooked, and a scene or a definition file that is not well-formed XML is an error (exit code 1) that names its path. A script that read such a file as text with fs.read_text gets bytes from a cooked pack: it reads definitions with defs, scenes with world:load_scene_file and other XML with xml.load, which work on both forms (Tests/Fixtures/ShippedGame is packed --cooked and run from the pack by a test).

docs.title: From code: GamePacker
docs.text:
Apogee.Runtime --pack is a thin command over GamePacker in Apogee.Content.Packs, which an export or a tool calls directly:

PackReport report = GamePacker.Pack(new PackRequest
{
    Folder = "Content",                   // the game folder: it is res://
    Output = "build/data/game.pack",      // the first part; more are game_001.pack…
    Cooked = true,                        // artifacts instead of sources, cooked documents (needs an import first)
    AllowNothingImported = true,          // a game with nothing to import is packed as it is, not an error
    Key = PackKey.FromEnvironment(),      // the caller asks; the packer never reads the environment
    Exclude = ["dev_mods/", "data/"],     // folder-relative prefixes left out
    // Bases, SplitBytes (1536 MiB) and CompressionLevel (12) as for the options above
});
Console.WriteLine($"{report.Added} files, {report.CookedDocuments} cooked, {report.PackedBytes} bytes in {report.Parts.Count} part(s)");

IReadOnlyList<string> paths = GamePacker.PathsOf(request);   // what Pack would pack, without writing: for an export that lists or checks them

Pack throws a ContentException when the folder is not a folder, when a cooked pack has nothing imported (unless AllowNothingImported), when a path cannot be in a pack, or when an authored document does not parse; and an IOException when writing fails. PackReport says how many files were added, left unchanged and removed (the last two for a patch pack), how many of the added files were cooked documents, the bytes before and after compression, and the part files. Packing the same folder twice gives the same files, so a patch pack over a cooked base holds only what changed.

docs.title: Using one
docs.text:
PackKey? key = PackKey.FromEnvironment();                    // null when APOGEE_PACK_KEY is not set
using var pack = PackSource.Open("data/game.pack", key);     // the key is ignored for a pack that is not encrypted
files.Mount("res://", pack);                                  // later mounts override earlier ones: a patch pack goes after

Apogee.Runtime --game <folder> mounts the folder as res:// and then every *.pack in <folder>/data, by name (so patch.pack goes over game.pack), with the key from the environment, before it looks for packages. Reads are safe from several threads; a file is read, decrypted, decompressed and checked when it is asked for, a file that is neither compressed nor encrypted is streamed without being read whole (and without its hash checked).

docs.title: Encryption and the key
docs.text:
If APOGEE_PACK_KEY is set (64 hexadecimal digits: 32 bytes) the pack is encrypted; if it is not, it is not. No key is set up for your game: the repository has none, so packs are plain. (The continuous integration uses a public test key for its export test only, see Testing an export; never ship a game with it.) When you want one, put it in .env (which git ignores and the ./build.sh wrapper loads), make the same key available to everything that makes or opens packs (the editor, the tools, a CI secret), and never commit it or print it (a PackKey writes itself as PackKey(…)). A pack made with one key cannot be read with another, and changing the key means making the packs again.

Where each program gets the key:

  • Development runs (--game <folder>, the editor, --pack, --export) read APOGEE_PACK_KEY from the environment.
  • An exported game has it in its executable: --export encrypts the pack with the key it finds in the environment and writes the key, masked, into a reserved slot of the copy of the runtime (PackKeySlot; into every copy of it, when the compiler emitted the data more than once). The game reads the slot first and the environment after it, so it needs no variable (and a variable does not override the embedded key).

The embedded key is obfuscation, not protection

The slot keeps the key out of strings and out of a casual look at the file: the 32 bytes are XORed with a hash of a random salt and a constant, all of which are in the file next to them, and the format is documented here. Anyone who wants the key can read it from the executable or from the memory of the running game. Use a key for one game, and expect it to be found.

What it does, in detail (PackFormat has the layout):

  • Each part has a random 32-byte salt; the key that seals a part is HKDF-SHA256(key, salt), so the pack key never encrypts anything directly and two packs of the same files differ.
  • Every file and the index is its own AES-256-GCM blob (nonce | tag | ciphertext, a random nonce each time). A wrong key, or a single changed byte, fails the check instead of producing garbage. The file's path is authenticated with it, so a file cannot be moved to another path in the pack.
  • The first four bytes of the pack are APGK without a key, and with one a few bytes of a hash of the key: an encrypted pack has no signature to search for, and opening one with the wrong key, or with none, is an error that says so (without the key in it).
  • Compression comes first and encryption after it (encrypted data does not compress). Without a key, damage is found by the zstd checksum of a compressed file and by a hash (the first 16 bytes of the SHA-256 of the file) that is checked for every file read whole.

AES-GCM comes from the platform: Windows and macOS have it, and on Linux it needs OpenSSL (libssl), which desktops and Steam's runtime have.

What it is not. A game has to be able to open its own packs, so the key is in the game (the embedded slot above); a determined person can get it out. The encryption keeps the content from being taken apart casually and makes a changed pack fail to load. It is not copy protection.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Tests/Apogee.Content.Tests: the key, a round trip of every kind of file (empty, text, noise, nested), compression only where it pays, mounting, streaming, encryption (the content and the magic are not in the file, a salt per pack, no key and a wrong key), tampering (a flipped byte in a file or the index of a sealed pack, in a stored and in a compressed file of a plain one, a truncated file, a part missing), split parts (also a file bigger than a part, and sealed), patch packs, path rules, and many threads reading at once. Tests/Apogee.Runtime.Tests runs a game from a pack with a patch pack over it, and an encrypted game with the key from the environment. GamePackerTests covers the library: plain and cooked packs, sources dropped and artifacts kept, authored documents cooked at their paths and reading back equal to their source, UIDs surviving the dropped sidecars, excluded prefixes, nothing imported (an error, and not one when asked), a document that does not parse, patch packs over a cooked base, and an encrypted split pack.

docs.title: Prefabs
docs.text:
A prefab is a piece of a scene that can be made again and again: one entity with everything below it, saved as an XML document, a .aprefab file. A lamp with its model and its bulb, a crate with its lid. A script or a tool instantiates it where it is needed, and every instance starts out the same. Like a scene it is XML, so a person can read it, a diff of two versions makes sense, and it has a UID in its root that survives renaming and moving the file.

This page is the format of a prefab file, the numbers its entities keep, how to make instances and save a prefab from C# and Luau, and how a scene or another prefab holds an instance: as one element that names the prefab and says only what it changes. An instance is a set of ordinary entities that came from the file: changing them does not change the file, and a scene saves the changes as overrides of the prefab.

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<Prefab version="1" uid="uid://7h2k4m6p8q0rs" nextId="4">
  <Components>                                  <!-- only components a script defined, as in a scene -->
    <Component name="Flicker"><Field name="speed" kind="Float32"/><Field name="lamp" kind="Entity"/></Component>
  </Components>
  <Entity id="1" name="Lamp">                   <!-- exactly one root entity -->
    <Transform Position="0 0 0" Rotation="0 0 0 1" Scale="1 1 1"/>
    <ModelRenderer Model="res://models/lamp.glb|uid://3c5v7b9n1m2kx"/>
    <Entity id="2" name="Bulb">
      <Transform Position="0 1.8 0" Rotation="0 0 0 1" Scale="1 1 1"/>
      <Light Color="1 0.9 0.7" Intensity="80" Range="12" InnerCone="0" OuterCone="0" Kind="1"/>
      <Flicker speed="2" lamp="1"/>             <!-- an Entity field holds an id of this file: 1 is the root -->
    </Entity>
    <Entity id="3" name="Base"><Transform Position="0 0 0" Rotation="0 0 0 1" Scale="1 1 1"/></Entity>
  </Entity>
</Prefab>

docs.title: The format
docs.text:
A prefab file is a scene with one root and stable ids. Everything inside <Entity> (components as elements, a field per attribute, child entities, field text, tags) is exactly the scene format; what differs is the root and the numbers.

  • <Prefab version="1" uid="…" nextId="…"> is the root. version is the format's version: a file from a newer engine (a larger number) is refused. uid is the file's identity, given when it is first saved or imported and kept after.
  • One <Entity> is the root of the prefab, with everything else below it. A file with none or with two is a FormatException.
  • <Components> is as in a scene: the components that scripts defined, so that the file defines them again when it is instantiated.
  • id is the entity's number in the file: a whole number from 1 up, used once in the file. Entity-typed fields refer to it. Unlike a scene's, it does not change when the file is saved (see below). The id of the root need not be 1.
  • name is optional, as in a scene. The root's name is the name the instance's root gets (a free one, Lamp 2, when its parent already has a Lamp).
  • nextId is the id the next new entity takes. It is above every id in the file and is never lowered. A file written by hand without it, or with one that is not above every id, gets it worked out from the highest id (and the engine logs a warning), which is only wrong if the last entity was deleted.
  • A prefab keeps its instances' references inside it: an Entity field of the file means an entity of the same instance, so two lamps each point at their own root.
  • The component names PrefabInstance and PrefabMember are written by the engine, never to a file; a file that has them is skipped with a warning. Entity and Override cannot be component names (RegisterComponent and DefineComponent refuse them): <Entity> is a child entity, and <Override> is how an instance of a prefab will hold its changes.
  • An <Entity> with a prefab attribute is an instance of another prefab inside this one; see Nested prefabs. Its id is in this file's numbering like any entity's.

prefab.xsd (embedded in Apogee.Ecs, and at Source/Apogee.Ecs/Scene/prefab.xsd) describes the structure; the writer is tested against it.

docs.title: Ids stay the same
docs.text:
A scene numbers its entities 1..n in order every time it is saved, so an id means nothing from one save to the next. A prefab's ids are the opposite on purpose: scenes that instance the prefab will name its entities by id, and renumbering would silently point them somewhere else.

  • Loading a prefab tags every entity it makes with PrefabMember { Id, Prefab }: its id in the file and the file (a handle of the world's library). The root also gets PrefabInstance { Prefab } (and is a member of its own file, with the id of the file's root). A prefab nested in another has its own entities tagged with its file, and its root is a member of the outer file with the id of the instance element there.
  • Saving (SavePrefabFile) keeps the id of every entity that is a member of that file. A new entity (one made in code, or in an editor) takes nextId and raises it, and is tagged a member right away, so saving again keeps its id. An id that was deleted is never used again: nextId is read from the file being overwritten and kept. What is added to a nested instance is numbered in the file too.
  • A copy of a member has its original's id until it is saved: the first of two with the same id keeps it, and the other takes a new one.

The two components are plain data and need no remapping: Clone, Snapshot, Restore and undo copy them as they are, and a snapshot names the prefab by its file, as it does a model, so it is still the same prefab in the next session.

docs.title: From C
docs.text:
Entity lamp = world.Instantiate("res://prefabs/lamp.aprefab", parent);   // parent is optional
Entity same = world.Instantiate("uid://7h2k4m6p8q0rs");                   // the file that has that UID, wherever it moved to

world.PrefabOf(lamp);                  // "res://prefabs/lamp.aprefab|uid://7h2k4m6p8q0rs"; null for an entity that is not an instance root
world.IsPrefabInstance(lamp);          // true
world.InstanceOf(world.Children(lamp)[0]);   // lamp: the instance an entity is part of, or none
world.IsPrefabMember(world.Children(lamp)[0]);   // true: part of an instance without being its root, so it cannot be moved under another parent

world.SavePrefabFile("res://prefabs/crate.aprefab", crate);   // one entity and everything under it
  • Instantiate takes a path, a uid://… or path|uid://… (the text form of an AssetRef), or a handle (world.Instantiate(uint prefab)). It returns the root, and the entities under it are made in the order of the file, the prefabs inside it expanded. It reads without a game's per-mod confinement. Errors: a uid:// no file has is a ContentException, a missing file a FileNotFoundException, a file that is not a prefab (another root, none or two roots, a bad or repeated id, a newer version, a root that is itself an instance of another prefab) or that would make more than world.MaxLoadEntities entities a FormatException, and a world without Files an InvalidOperationException. Nothing is made when it fails.
  • SavePrefabFile(path, root) writes the entity and everything below it. The path must end in .aprefab. The file keeps its UID (a new one gets a new UID), the ids are kept as above, and an Entity field that points at something outside what is saved is left out. An instance of another prefab inside the tree is written as one element with its overrides, numbered in this file; the root is written as an ordinary entity even when it is an instance (a prefab saved from an instance of itself holds its entities). A tree that holds an instance of the file being written, directly or through another prefab, is an InvalidOperationException, and nothing is written. A path that is not in a writable source is an UnauthorizedAccessException.

docs.title: The library
docs.text: world.Prefabs is a PrefabLibrary: one number per prefab file, the same for a path, a uid://… or both. It is made when first asked for from the world's Files and Assets; a host that runs several worlds hands them one library, so their numbers agree. Load(pathOrRef) gives the handle; RefOf, PathOf and Document go back from it, and a prefab is read from its file once. A reference that names no file still gets a handle, which keeps its text (and is that file's handle once the file exists), so an instance of a prefab that is missing keeps what it was made from. The handle is only meaningful in the run that made it: scenes and snapshots hold the reference (the field's [Property(Asset = "prefab")] is saved through the world's prefab asset type).

docs.title: From Luau
docs.text:
local lamp = world:instantiate("res://prefabs/lamp.aprefab", parent)   -- or "uid://…"; parent is optional
print(world:prefab_of(lamp))     -- res://prefabs/lamp.aprefab|uid://7h2k4m6p8q0rs
print(world:prefab_of(some))     -- nil: not the root of an instance

instantiate returns the root. Like load_scene_file it reads without the per-mod confinement check of fs.read_text: a script can instantiate a prefab of any package or of the game by its path or UID, in a shipped game too (a pack holds it at the same path). The failures above are Luau errors. There is no Luau call that writes a prefab file.

docs.title: Nested prefabs
docs.text:
A prefab can hold instances of other prefabs: an <Entity> with a prefab attribute, the same text an AssetRef has (a path, a uid://…, or both). Its id is its number in the file, like any entity's, and its name is the name the root of the nested instance gets.

<Prefab version="1" uid="uid://9w1e3r5t7y9ua" nextId="5">
  <Entity id="1" name="Corner">
    <Transform Position="0 0 0" Rotation="0 0 0 1" Scale="1 1 1"/>
    <Entity id="2" name="Lamp" prefab="res://prefabs/lamp.aprefab|uid://7h2k4m6p8q0rs">   <!-- an instance: its id is in the corner's numbering -->
      <Transform Position="2 0 0"/>                                     <!-- a patch of the lamp's root: only the fields that change -->
      <Override entity="2"><Light Intensity="120"/></Override>          <!-- the lamp's Bulb (entity 2 of the lamp), in the lamp's numbering -->
    </Entity>
    <Entity id="3" name="Lamp 2" prefab="res://prefabs/lamp.aprefab|uid://7h2k4m6p8q0rs">
      <Transform Position="-2 0 0"/>
      <Override entity="3" remove="true"/>                              <!-- this one has no Base -->
    </Entity>
    <Entity id="4" name="Bench"><Transform Position="0 0 3" Rotation="0 0 0 1" Scale="1 1 1"/></Entity>
  </Entity>
</Prefab>

Loading a scene or a prefab, and Instantiate, expand every instance element by the rules below (PrefabExpander, in Apogee.Ecs) and then create all the entities. Prefabs are read from the world's library, so an instance names its prefab by a path, a UID or both and finds the same file whichever it uses.

Addresses. Ids repeat from one prefab to the next (every lamp has an entity 2), so an entity is named by a path of ids, its address: 4 is entity 4 of the document, 4/2 entity 2 of the prefab instanced as entity 4, 4/3/2 entity 2 of the prefab instanced as entity 3 of the prefab instanced as entity 4. Each id is a whole number from 1 up with no leading zero, and an address has at most 17 segments (the document's, and one for each of the 16 levels of nesting). The root of an instance is the instance's own address; address/rootId (the root's id in its own file) is accepted as another name for it. An address does not follow the hierarchy: if the author of the prefab moves entity 3 under another entity, …/3 is still entity 3.

Scopes. An Entity-typed field means an entity of the document that holds it. Inside a prefab file that is an id of the file (lamp="1" is the lamp's root), and it becomes an address under wherever the file is instanced (5/2 for the lamp that is entity 2 of a corner instanced as 5). Everything an instance element and its overrides hold is written in the scope of the document the instance is in, so a field in an override inside corner.aprefab is an id of the corner, and one in a scene is an address of the scene. A field that names nothing (an id nobody has, text that is not an address) stays as it is and, as in a scene, means no entity.

Inner before outer. The instances inside a prefab are expanded first, each with its own patches and overrides; the instance that holds the prefab then applies its overrides on top. An outer override may reach into a nested instance with a longer address (2/2 in an instance of the corner is the lamp's bulb).

Names. Siblings get unique names the way the scene loader gives them: the members of the prefab in file order, then the entities that were added, and a name that is already taken gets a number after it (Part, Part 2, Part 3…).

docs.title: Overrides
docs.text:
An instance element changes its prefab in three ways: component elements directly inside it, <Entity> children, and <Override> elements for any other entity of the instance.

<Entity id="2" name="Corner" prefab="res://prefabs/corner.aprefab|uid://9w1e3r5t7y9ua">
  <Transform Position="10 0 4"/>                         <!-- a modified field on the root: the other fields stay the prefab's -->
  <Health max="200" current="200" append="true"/>        <!-- a component the prefab does not have, written whole -->
  <Override entity="4" name="Old bench"><Transform remove="true"/></Override>   <!-- a renamed entity, and a removed component -->
  <Override entity="2"><Health max="50" current="50" append="true"/></Override> <!-- a component added to the nested lamp's root -->
  <Override entity="2/2"><Light Intensity="40"/><Flicker lamp="1"/></Override>  <!-- into the nested lamp's bulb; lamp="1" is entity 1 of THIS scene -->
  <Override entity="3" remove="true"/>                   <!-- a removed entity, and everything under it -->
  <Override entity="2/3">                                <!-- an entity added under a member, numbered in this document -->
    <Entity id="3" name="Sign"><Transform Position="0 0.5 0" Rotation="0 0 0 1" Scale="1 1 1"/></Entity>
  </Override>
  <Entity id="4" name="Trash can"/>                      <!-- an entity added directly under the root -->
</Entity>
  • <Override entity="address"> is required and is an address relative to the instance (the root of the instance is its id in the prefab, 1 for a prefab whose root is entity 1; the root's own patches are component elements directly inside the instance element). Its children are component patches and added <Entity> elements; name renames the entity and remove="true" removes it with everything under it (not the root of the instance: remove the instance instead).
  • A component element changes a component the entity has: its attributes replace the prefab's, and the fields it does not name keep the prefab's value. remove="true" removes the component. append="true" adds the component, written whole; if the prefab has (or later gets) the component, the instance's wins. These three words, with patch, are the same ones DefDatabase.Merge uses and are never kept in what an instance expands to.
  • Added entities are ordinary entities of the document that writes them (their ids are numbered there, so a scene's own ids, or the prefab file's), and may themselves be instances. They come after the prefab's own children.
  • There is no order to override: siblings are in creation order, the prefab's entities first and then the added ones.

Strict matching. An override applies only to what is there. The expander reads each element and, when it cannot apply it, keeps it aside instead of guessing:

  • an address that names nothing (the prefab lost that entity, or an earlier override removed it), a malformed or missing address, or an <Override> with an attribute this version does not know: the whole element;
  • a patch of a component the entity does not have (the prefab dropped it: a half component would be made), or a remove of one it does not have: that component element, under an <Override> with the same address (what could apply did);
  • an entity added under a member that another override of the same instance removes: its element, under an <Override> with the address of the removed member.

Each is logged with its file and line (once per line however many instances there are, and at most 200 lines per load, then one line saying so), and kept as written so that saving the scene does not lose it; if the prefab gets the entity or component back, the override applies again. A prefab that is not there is the same: the instance is a single entity with nothing in it, and every element of the instance element is kept. What is kept belongs to the document the expansion was asked for: the leftovers of an instance element inside a prefab file are that file's, are logged, and are worked out again at every expansion, so they do not appear on the scene's instance.

DefDatabase.Merge is used for the part it fits: the fields of one component (and the remove/append words). It is not used to find entities, which it would do by name and id among direct children only: an entity that the author moved would stop matching, ids repeat across nested prefabs, and a patch that matches nothing would add a half-made entity. Overrides address entities by path instead.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
A prefab file is read by anyone who installs a mod, so expansion is bounded and never trusts a file:

  • Nesting depth: 16 (World.MaxPrefabDepth). A chain of prefabs (one inside the next) may be 16 long; the 17th is missing (an instance of it is one empty entity, with a warning). Entities may be nested at most 128 deep in what results (the limit a document already has), or the whole expansion fails.
  • Cycles. A prefab that contains itself, directly or through others (a → b → c → a), is not followed: the instance that would repeat it is missing, and the warning shows the chain. The rest expands.
  • Entity budget: 262,144 (World.MaxLoadEntities, settable). The expansion counts each entity as it is about to make it and stops with a FormatException when a load (a scene with all its instances, its own entities are not counted: they are the size of the file and cannot multiply, and a scene with more than the limit entities loaded before there were prefabs) would go over, so a few small files that nest ten instances sixteen levels deep cost at most the budget, not memory without end. Nothing is made when a load fails. The budget is one number for a whole load, and a save gives each instance a budget of its own (the one an Instantiate of it had), so a world that was made of many instances can always be saved.
  • Work budget: 64 steps for each entity of the budget (16,777,216). A file's content is repeated for every instance of it, so entities alone do not bound a load: ten thousand overrides in a prefab that a thousand prefabs hold are ten million merges for a handful of entities. Every component or override handled, attribute copied, component merged (by its size) and name tried while making a name unique counts, and the expansion stops with a FormatException over the limit, with the same effect as the entity budget. An entity may have any number of components within it (the lookup is by name, not a scan). A load, each Instantiate, and each save (which expands the instances again to see what they changed) takes a new budget; one that failed is spent.
  • Missing prefabs. A reference that names no file, a file that cannot be read, is not a prefab (another root element, none or two root entities, a repeated id, a newer version), or whose root entity is itself an instance of another prefab (an entity would be the root of two instances: put it under an entity of its own) leaves the instance missing, as above.
  • Addresses. An instance at an address of 17 segments (the longest there is) is missing, since what is in it would need 18. A field that holds text that is not an address means no entity, so a loader resolves only text that is a valid address; an entity that nothing can refer to has an address that starts with ~, which no file can write.
  • Ids. Ids of entities an <Override> adds count in the prefab's numbering like any other: they may not repeat one, and nextId stays above them. An entity with no usable id, or one that repeats an address, is made but cannot be referred to.

docs.title: How overrides are stored
docs.text:
An instance is saved as the element of Overrides above, written for you: the world compares each instance with what its prefab expands to on its own, and writes what differs. Nothing is recorded while you edit, so a change made by the editor, by a script or by code is saved the same way, and a field set back to the prefab's value is no longer an override.

  • What is compared is the value the loader would make, not the text. 1.0 and 1 are one number, a field an element leaves out is zero, a true may be written 1; an asset reference with a UID and one without (or after the file moved) is the same asset, and two references with different UIDs are two assets; an entity field is the entity it names, wherever it is written from. A component is compared field by field and only the fields that differ are written, a field that was set to nothing as "".
  • Which entities pair up. The live instance and the expansion are paired from the root down by the id every member keeps (PrefabMember). A member the live instance no longer has is written as a removal (<Override entity="…" remove="true"/>, only the topmost of a removed branch). An entity of the instance that is not a member (made in the scene, or a copy of a member) is an added entity, written under the override of its parent (or directly in the element for the root's children), and it may itself be an instance. A member moved under another parent by code (the editor does not allow it) is written as both: the member removed from where it was, and a plain copy under its new parent. A member of the wrong prefab for its place, or a second entity with a member's id (a copy of its components), is an added entity.
  • The text is stable. The element is written in a fixed order: the root's changes (components in the prefab's order, those added last), an <Override> for each changed entity in the prefab's order (name, then components, then entities added below it), the entities added to the root, and the elements kept aside last. A scene that is loaded and saved again is byte for byte the same text.
  • Kept aside is kept. What an instance element held that could not be applied (see Overrides) is not in the live entities, so it is stored with the instance root (it travels with snapshots, which is why Play and Stop keep it, and with a clone of the root) and written back first, before what the live entities say: an instance element is applied in the order it is written, so an old element that has become applicable (a patch of a component the entity did not have, and has now) cannot win over what was done since. It is written as it was read, except that XML comments and layout are not kept, and that the numbers in it follow the scene: an entity it adds gets a number of this save, and an entity field in it that named an entity of the scene (or the instance root, and what follows, of an instance whose prefab is missing) is written with that entity's address now, empty if the entity is gone. Fields of components the world does not know (the prefab that defines them is missing) cannot be told from numbers and keep the number they had.
  • References to what was not made. A field of the scene that names an entity inside an instance whose prefab is missing (2/2), or one that a kept element would add, loads as no entity; the world remembers what it named and writes it back as the address that entity will have, so it names it again when the prefab is back. The same is kept for an asset field that did not load: it is 0, it is not an override of the prefab's model, and a plain entity writes the reference it had.
  • A reference that is not one. A prefab attribute that is not an asset reference (a damaged UID, text) makes an empty instance with the text kept as it was written, and everything the element holds kept.
  • A prefab that moved on. The comparison is with the prefab as it is now. New fields, components and entities of the prefab are not overrides when a scene is loaded with the new prefab, since the instance had nothing to say about them; a deleted entity that the scene had overrides for keeps them aside, and they apply again if the entity returns. But the live entities of a world that was running when the file changed (it is saved from this world, which then reads the file again) still have the old prefab's entities and values, and the next save of an instance of it writes every difference as an override: the new entity as a removal, the old value of a changed field pinned. Instances do not follow their prefab yet: until something refreshes them (loading the scene again does), that is what saving writes.
  • A prefab that cannot be read while the world holds its instance (the file was deleted, or replaced by one that contains itself) is compared as the single root it expands to: the live entities that came from it are written as additions and nothing is dropped. A scene loaded without the prefab keeps its element intact and saves it as it was. An instance whose prefab is missing is only its root: what is edited in it (a component added to the root, an entity added below it) is saved, and goes aside again when the scene is loaded again before the prefab is back, so a tool should treat it as read-only.

What is never an override: the order of siblings (they are in creation order, the prefab's entities first), WorldTransform and the other components scenes leave out (IgnoreInScenes), components the world cannot describe, a name that was cleared, PrefabInstance and PrefabMember (the engine makes them), and what the prefab's own nested instances could not apply (that belongs to the prefab's file).

A scene that holds an instance is version 2; one without is written as version 1, as before. The schemas (scene.xsd, prefab.xsd) describe prefab and <Override>, but leave what is inside an <Override> open: the rules above are what check it when a scene is read.

docs.title: Files
docs.text: .aprefab is an authored asset (AuthoredAssets.Extensions): --import gives a file without a uid one by adding the attribute to its root, the asset database finds a prefab by its UID, --pack stores it (--cooked as cooked XML, at the same path), and renaming or moving it keeps its UID (and what refers to it by path|uid still finds it).

docs.title: Scenes
docs.text:
A scene is the entities of a world, with their components, saved as an XML document: a .ascene file. The editor saves and opens them, a game's entry scene is one, and scripts and tools make and read them as text. Because a scene is XML like the rest of the game's data, a mod can patch it (see Patching a scene), and a diff of two scenes is something a person can read.

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<Scene version="1">
  <Components>                                   <!-- only components a script defined -->
    <Component name="Ticker">
      <Field name="count" kind="Int32"/>
      <Field name="target" kind="Entity"/>
      <Field name="look" kind="AssetRef" assetType="model"/>
    </Component>
  </Components>
  <Entity id="1" name="ground">
    <Transform Position="0 -0.5 0" Rotation="0 0 0 1" Scale="1 1 1"/>
    <ModelRenderer Model="res://models/ground.glb|uid://8c1q0w3e5r7ty"/>
    <Entity id="2" name="crate">                  <!-- children nest; there is no parent attribute -->
      <Transform Position="1.25 0 0" Rotation="0 0 0 1" Scale="1 1 1"/>
      <Ticker count="3" target="1"/>
    </Entity>
  </Entity>
  <Entity id="3" name="camera">
    <Transform Position="0 2 -6" Rotation="0 0 0 1" Scale="1 1 1"/>
    <MainCamera/>                                  <!-- a tag: an empty element -->
  </Entity>
</Scene>

docs.title: The format
docs.text:
• <Scene version="1"> is the root. version is the format's version; a scene from a newer engine (a larger number) is refused. It is 1, and 2 for a scene that holds a prefab instance (so that an engine that does not know instances refuses the file instead of loading them empty); the engine reads both. A scene file may also carry a uid attribute, its identity; text made by SaveScene has none, because a copy must not carry one.
  • <Entity id="…" name="…"> is an entity. name is optional. Its children are its components, as elements, and its child entities, as more <Entity> elements; a child entity is under its parent, so there is no parent attribute. Entity is therefore not a name a component can have (RegisterComponent and DefineComponent refuse it, and Override, which prefab instances use).
  • id is the entity's number in the file, not its id in a world. Entity-typed fields refer to it, and a patch matches on it. It is a whole number from 1 up: an entity with another id (or none) loads, but nothing can refer to it, and when two entities have the same one, references go to the first and the engine warns. This is stricter than version 1 scenes were read before prefabs: two entities with one id used to send references to the later one, and 0, a negative number, +5 or 05 were accepted as ids and are not now (a field that holds such a number warns). Scenes the engine writes are not affected.
  • A component is an element named after it, and each of its fields an attribute named after the field. A tag (or a component with no fields) is an empty element. A field the element does not name is zero when the scene is loaded.
  • What is written: every field of every component, so that a scene reads without the code at hand and diffs cleanly; components in the order of their names (an entity keeps them in the order of their ids in a world, which another world numbers differently, and a scene must be the same text whichever world saves it), entities in hierarchy order (parents first, children in creation order). Saving a loaded scene again gives the same text.
  • What is left out: WorldTransform (derived), components given to IgnoreInScenes (the host leaves out physics Body, which only means something in the run that made it), and an Entity or AssetRef field that points at nothing the file can name (an attribute left out; see below).

docs.title: Field text
docs.text:
The text is the same in every culture. Booleans are true and false, integers are decimal, floats are the shortest text that reads back as the same number (NaN, Infinity and -Infinity are the special values), and a Vector3, a Double3 position or a Quaternion is its numbers separated by spaces (1 2 3, 0 0 0 1). 64-bit integers keep all their digits. FieldText.Format and FieldText.Parse (in Apogee.Reflection) do this for every kind that needs no context.

Two kinds need a world:

  • Entity is the id of the entity it points to in the same file; for an entity inside a prefab instance its address, 2/3. A field that points outside the scene (a branch saved on its own, an entity not in the file) has its attribute left out, and loads as no entity. An id the file does not have, and text that is not an id or an address, is the same.
  • AssetRef is an asset reference: path|uid://…, a path alone, or uid://… alone. In memory the field is a number, a handle that only means something in this run (a model's number in the model library); the scene holds what it names. The host says how each asset type is saved with RegisterAssetType, and registers model for ModelRenderer.Model. When the path leads to no file, the UID finds the asset where it was moved; a reference that leads nowhere leaves the field 0 and logs a warning, and the scene loads on. An asset the type cannot name (a model made in code has no path) is left out.

docs.title: Components made by scripts
docs.text: A component that a script defined (world:component("Ticker", { … })) has no code behind it, so the scene carries its fields in <Components>: the name, and per field its name and its kind (Bool, Int8, UInt8, Int16, UInt16, Int32, UInt32, Int64, UInt64, Float32, Float64, Vector3, Double3, Quaternion, Entity or AssetRef). Loading a scene into a world that has not heard of the component defines it. A field of kind AssetRef also says what it names with assetType="model" (C#: the assetTypes argument of World.DefineComponent); without it the field cannot be saved, and the world warns once. A component of the engine or the game (a C# struct) is not listed: its layout is the code's. If the world already has a component of that name with other fields, the scene's is skipped with a warning and the existing one is used.

docs.title: Reading
docs.text: Loading is forgiving, so that a scene outlives the code around it. A component or an attribute the world does not have is logged (with the line) and skipped; an attribute whose text is not a value of its field is logged and the field stays zero; a name that is taken among the entities with the same parent (or among the top-level ones) gets a free one (crate 2, crate 3…, also for the entities of the world the scene is loaded into). What is an error (a FormatException) is a document that is not a scene: XML that is not well-formed, a root other than <Scene>, and a version newer than the engine's.

docs.title: Prefab instances
docs.text:
An <Entity> with a prefab attribute is an instance of a prefab: a whole piece of scene (an entity with everything below it) that lives in a .aprefab file and is made again at each instance. The element does not repeat what the prefab holds, only what this instance changes:

<Scene version="2">
  <Entity id="1" name="Player">…</Entity>
  <Entity id="2" name="Corner" prefab="res://prefabs/corner.aprefab|uid://9w1e3r5t7y9ua">
    <Transform Position="10 0 4"/>                         <!-- a field of the root changed: the other fields stay the prefab's -->
    <Override entity="4" name="Old bench"><Transform remove="true"/></Override>   <!-- another entity of the prefab, found by its address: renamed, and one component removed -->
    <Override entity="3" remove="true"/>                   <!-- an entity removed with everything below it -->
    <Entity id="4" name="Trash can">…</Entity>              <!-- an entity added below the root -->
  </Entity>
  <Entity id="5" name="Switch"><Door target="2/2"/></Entity>   <!-- a scene entity pointing into the instance: entity 2 of the prefab instanced as 2 -->
</Scene>
  • prefab is an asset reference to the file: a path, a uid://…, or both (the engine writes both, so the instance still finds a prefab that moved). The id and name are the instance root's, as for any entity; the name is the scene's, and always written.
  • Component elements directly inside change the root of the instance; <Override entity="address"> changes any other entity of it; <Entity> children are added below the root. Prefabs has the rules: how an entity is addressed (4, 2/2), what append="true" and remove="true" mean on a component, and what is kept aside when the prefab no longer has what an override names.
  • Addresses in Entity fields. An entity of the scene is its id; an entity that a prefab made is the address of its instance followed by its id in the prefab (2/3: entity 3 of the prefab that is instance 2), and 2/2/1 reaches into a prefab nested in it. What an override or an added entity holds is in the scene's numbering, so lamp="1" in the scene is the scene's entity 1; inside the prefab file the same text is the prefab's entity 1. Entities the instance made have no id of their own in the scene, which is why they are named by address.
  • Loading makes the prefab's entities, applies the element on top, and creates the added entities after them. The entities of an instance are ordinary entities: world:children, components, scripts and physics see no difference, and world:prefab_of(entity) tells the root of an instance. An instance whose prefab file cannot be found or read is one empty entity, with a warning, and what its element holds is kept: saved again, the scene has the same instance, so a prefab that is missing for a moment (a disabled mod) costs the scene nothing.
  • Saving writes the instance back as the same kind of element, working out what differs from the prefab. A scene numbers its own entities again at each save, so the id of an instance and of what is added to it may change from one save to the next; what refers to them follows, and a scene saved and loaded again saves to the same text. The entities an instance made keep the place the prefab gives them, and a member of an instance cannot be moved under another parent.
  • A branch of an instance saved or copied without its root (the clipboard of a selected member) is written as plain entities; a whole instance is one element.

docs.title: The schema
docs.text: scene.xsd (embedded in Apogee.Ecs, and in the repository at Source/Apogee.Ecs/Scene/scene.xsd) describes the structure for people and editors: the root, <Components>, the entity element with its id and name, and the form of a uid. It cannot describe the components, because those are the registry's; they are checked when the scene is loaded. The writer is tested against the schema.

docs.title: From C
docs.text:
string text = world.SaveScene();                  // every user entity
string branch = world.SaveScene(crate);           // one entity and everything under it: a prefab, the clipboard
List<Entity> made = world.LoadScene(text);        // in file order, parents first
world.LoadScene(text, parent: holder);            // the scene's entities become children of holder

XmlNode document = world.SaveSceneDocument(world.Roots());   // the same as a tree, to patch or inspect
world.LoadScene(document);

LoadScene returns the entities it made, so a caller can move or select them. SaveScene and LoadScene read and write text; the editor and the host decide where it is kept.

docs.title: Scene files and their UID
docs.text:
A scene kept as a file has an identity, a UID in the uid attribute of its root, that survives renaming and moving the file. The world reads and writes files through World.Files and World.Assets, which the host sets (a game's session and the editor do; a bare new World() has neither and cannot load a file).

world.SaveSceneFile("res://scenes/level.ascene");              // every user entity
world.SaveSceneFile("res://prefabs/crate.ascene", crate);      // one entity and everything under it
List<Entity> made = world.LoadSceneFile("res://scenes/level.ascene", parent);
world.LoadSceneFile("uid://4k2m9x7q1w3ze");                    // the file that has that UID, wherever it is now
  • SaveSceneFile keeps the UID of the file it overwrites: the old file's uid is read and written again, so a reference to the scene keeps meaning the same asset after every save. A new file gets a new UID. SaveScene() makes text with no uid, because a copy must not carry the identity of a file.
  • LoadSceneFile takes a path or uid://…. It reads the file with XmlFile.Read (cooked XML), so a scene cooked into a pack (--pack --cooked keeps its path) loads the same as the text one. A uid:// that no file has is a ContentException, a missing file a FileNotFoundException and a file that is not a scene a FormatException.
  • A scene that is renamed or moved keeps its UID, so LoadSceneFile and SaveSceneFile find it by uid://…; the asset database is read again with Refresh() after files move on disk (an import does it).

The game's entry scene is loaded with LoadSceneFile.

docs.title: From Luau
docs.text:
local text = world:save_scene()
for _, entity in world:load_scene(text, parent) do   -- parent is optional
    print(world:get_name(entity))
end

local made = world:load_scene_file("res://scenes/level.ascene", parent)   -- or "uid://…"; parent is optional

save_scene returns the text and load_scene the list of entities it made; text that is not a scene is an error. load_scene_file returns the same list from a file. It reads without the per-mod confinement check of fs.read_text, as models.load and ui:load_document do: a script can load a scene of any package or of the game by its path or UID. It loads a scene cooked into a shipped pack as well as the text file, at the same path. fs.read_text of a cooked scene gives binary, so a script that wants the scene's XML itself reads it with xml.load. There is no Luau call that writes a scene file; a script saves text with fs.write_text, which keeps the confinement of a mod's files (and a file written that way has no UID until the next import gives it one).

docs.title: Cooked scenes
docs.text: --pack --cooked stores each .ascene as cooked XML at the path of its source: the same tree (names, attributes, text, the lines of the source) in a binary encoding, which is not tied to the components the engine had when it was cooked, and keeps the uid of the root. LoadSceneFile and world:load_scene_file read both forms, and so does the asset database that finds a scene by uid://…, so a game needs no change to ship its scenes cooked. The fixture game of the tests (Tests/Fixtures/ShippedGame) loads mod://core/scenes/start.ascene this way from an encrypted cooked pack. A scene in a mod is never cooked (mods are Luau and data, shipped as folders and zips), and LoadScene(text), which takes text, is for text.

docs.title: Patching a scene
docs.text:
A scene is an ordinary XML document, so it merges like a definition (DefDatabase.Merge): children are matched by name and id, an attribute of the patch replaces the original's, and what the patch does not name stays. A patch that moves entity 2 and nothing else:
