<Scene version="1">
  <Entity id="2">
    <Transform Position="5 0 0"/>
  </Entity>
</Scene>

Merged into the scene above, crate keeps its rotation and scale and its Ticker; only Position changes. Because entities nest, a patch for a child names its parents too, each by id. patch, remove and append are the attributes the merge reserves, so a field cannot be called any of them if its component is meant to be patched.

The merged tree loads with world.LoadScene(node).

docs.title: Core
docs.text: Apogee.Core: the small things every other library uses.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
Log.Info("Category", "message") (also Trace, Debug, Warn, Error) writes a LogEntry to every registered ILogSink. Sinks can be called from any thread. Log.MinimumLevel filters, Log.IsEnabled(level) avoids building a message that would be dropped. The sinks that ship:

  • ConsoleSink: stderr for warnings and errors, stdout for the rest.
  • FileLogSink: one file per run in a folder that keeps the newest ten, flushed line by line.
  • RecentLogSink: the last N lines in memory, which a crash report quotes.

LogEntry.ToLine() is the one line format they share: HH:mm:ss.fff LVL [Category] message.

Log.AddSink(new ConsoleSink());
Log.Info("Runtime", "started");

The runtime and the editor write each run's log and, when an exception ends the program, a crash report: see Logs and crash reports.

docs.title: Arena
docs.text: Arena is a fixed-size bump allocator over unmanaged memory. Allocate<T>(count) returns a zeroed Span<T> that stays valid (the memory never moves) until Reset(mark); take Mark before, reset to it after, to free a scope. It is not thread safe: use one per thread or per job.

docs.title: NativeList
docs.text: NativeList<T> is a growable list in unmanaged memory for unmanaged elements: Add, RemoveAtSwapBack, a ref indexer and AsSpan(). Dispose it.

docs.title: Jobs
docs.text: JobSystem is a worker pool: Schedule(group, job) queues a job on a JobGroup, group.Wait() returns when all of its jobs ran and rethrows the first failure. ParallelFor(count, batchSize, body) splits a range across the workers and waits.

docs.title: Logs and crash reports
docs.text: Every run of a game writes its log to a file of its own, and a program that dies leaves a crash report. Both stay on the player's machine: nothing is sent anywhere. A player who has a problem sends the files, or you ask for them.

docs.title: The log file
docs.text:
A game started by Apogee.Runtime (--game <folder>, or a shipped game starting itself) and the editor open a FileLogSink when they start. It writes the same lines as the console (HH:mm:ss.fff LVL [Category] message), one Log entry per line, and flushes after every line, so that the end of the file survives a crash. The first lines say which engine version, which OS and which command line the run had. Log.MinimumLevel filters what reaches it, as it filters the console.

  • The file is <yyyyMMdd-HHmmss>-<pid>.log (UTC) in <user>/logs: one per run, so that two instances of a game do not mix their lines. The newest 10 are kept; older ones are deleted when a run starts.
  • A file that passes 64 MiB gets the line Log truncated and nothing more. A normal run is a few hundred kilobytes.
  • A clean end writes End of run. as the last line. A file without it is a run that died.
  • A file that cannot be written (a read-only disk, no space) switches the sink off with one line on stderr. The game goes on.
  • A single script run with --run is a development tool: it has the crash handler but no log file.

docs.title: Where the files are
docs.text:
<user> is the player's folder of the game (user://): --user <dir>, else <local application data>/<organization>/<userFolder> from game.xml (see The game manifest).

OS <local application data> Example Linux $XDG_DATA_HOME, else ~/.local/share ~/.local/share/Acme/Truck/logs/20261115-120000-4242.log Windows %LOCALAPPDATA% C:\Users\you\AppData\Local\Acme\Truck\crashes\ macOS ~/Library/Application Support ~/Library/Application Support/Acme/Truck/crashes/

The editor keeps its own logs and crashes in <local application data>/Apogee/Editor. Before a game's folder is known (while the program parses its arguments), and for commands that are not a game (--pack, --import, ...), reports go to <local application data>/Apogee/Runtime/crashes.

docs.title: Crash reports
docs.text:
A crash report is a plain text file crash-<yyyyMMdd-HHmmss-fff>-<number>-<kind>.txt (the number orders reports made in the same millisecond) in <user>/crashes. The newest 20 are kept. It holds:

  • the kind and the time (UTC);
  • the engine version, the .NET version and whether it is a NativeAOT build;
  • the OS and its architecture, the processor count and the memory;
  • the game, its version, and the GPU once the device is created (CrashHandler.SetContext adds more lines);
  • the thread, and the exception with its inner exceptions and stack trace;
  • the last lines of the log (200 by default).

The kinds:

Kind When The program unhandled an exception that nothing caught ends the program (AppDomain.UnhandledException) ends. The log gets the exception, the line A crash report was written to ..., and End of run.; the path is also on stderr task a task failed and nobody looked at its exception (TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException) goes on. Only the first one of a run gets a report; every one is in the log unclean-exit the previous run did not end cleanly is starting normally

A stack trace of a NativeAOT build has the method names but no source lines. The report's other lines tell which build it was.

A Luau error is an error of the script, which the engine reports and logs; it is not an unhandled exception. The reports are for engine bugs, bad native libraries and mistakes in a game's C# code.

docs.title: A run that did not end cleanly
docs.text:
A crash in native code (a Vulkan driver, SDL, Jolt, a bug in an engine shim), kill -9, the task manager, a power cut or an out-of-memory kill take the process down without running any managed code, so nothing can write a report at that moment. The next start finds out instead:

  1. While a run lives, <user>/logs/<run>.running holds its process id, the time the process started and the name of its log.
  2. A clean end deletes it, and so does the crash handler once it has written a report for an unhandled exception.
  3. At the next start, every marker whose process is gone (or whose process id belongs to a newer process, which a reboot makes common) gets a report of kind unclean-exit with the last 200 lines of that run's log, and the marker is removed. A marker of a process that still runs, another instance of the game, is left alone.

So the report comes one start late, and says only what the log said; for the native stack, see below. A player who closes a frozen game from the task manager gets one of these reports too, which is accurate: the run did not end by itself.

docs.title: Getting a native stack from the OS
docs.text:
The operating system captures native crashes better than a program can from inside itself. To find the cause of a crash in native code:

  • Linux. Allow core dumps (ulimit -c unlimited in the shell that runs the game), and see where they go with cat /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern. On systemd machines coredumpctl list and coredumpctl gdb open the last one. gdb with bt (and thread apply all bt) prints the stacks. ./build.sh aot keeps the symbols in Apogee.Runtime.dbg next to the program: keep that file for every build you ship, and load it in gdb with symbol-file.
  • Windows. Turn on Windows Error Reporting's local dumps: in the registry key HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\Windows Error Reporting\LocalDumps set DumpFolder (a folder that exists) and DumpType to 2 (a full dump), or add a key named after the executable to limit it to the game. Open the .dmp in Visual Studio or WinDbg with the .pdb files that the build kept. The Event Viewer (Windows Logs, Application) also lists the faulting module and offset.
  • macOS. The crash reporter writes an .ips file to ~/Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports (the Console app shows it under Crash Reports) with the stack of every thread. Keep the .dSYM of each build to read the frames.
  • CoreCLR (the editor, dotnet run). DOTNET_DbgEnableMiniDump=1 makes the runtime write a minidump of a crash, which dotnet-dump analyze reads (see Profiling for the other tools).

docs.title: What is deliberately not done
docs.text:
• No handler for fatal signals (SIGSEGV, SIGABRT, Windows structured exceptions). Both CoreCLR and NativeAOT own those signals (they turn a fault in managed code into a NullReferenceException), and a handler added later would see the runtime's own faults first and have to chain to it in a way that differs per runtime and OS. The OS already does the job above. If games turn out to need a report at the moment of the crash, a small C shim for it is possible future work.
  • No upload and no telemetry. Files never leave the machine on their own.
  • No symbolication, no minidump writing from the engine, no crash-time screenshot.

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text: A report and a log may contain the command line, folder names (which often include the user name), the GPU's name and anything the game logs. Tell players what the files hold before they send them.

docs.title: Using it from C
docs.text:
Apogee.Runtime and the editor do all of this themselves. A program of your own does the same in a few lines:

var recent = new RecentLogSink();                       // the lines a report quotes
Log.AddSink(recent);
CrashHandler.Install(Path.Combine(userDirectory, "crashes"), recent);   // as early as possible

using FileLogSink logFile = RunDiagnostics.Start(userDirectory, "My Game", "1.2.0");  // checks the previous run, then opens <user>/logs/<run>.log
CrashHandler.SetContext("GPU", device.Name);            // any more lines for the reports

RunDiagnostics.Start also moves the reports to <user>/crashes; ScriptSession.UserDirectoryFor gives the same <user> that StartGame mounts as user://. Dispose the returned sink when the run ends cleanly: until then the run counts as one that died.

docs.title: ECS
docs.text: Apogee.Ecs wraps a Flecs world (Apogee.Native.Flecs). World is an EngineObject, so scripts get a handle to it, and its [Method]s (create_entity, lookup, progress…) are in the registry. Use a world from one thread.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
A component is an unmanaged struct marked [Component] (see Reflection); its fields are the memory layout:

[Component] public struct Position { public Vector3 Value; }
[Component] public struct Health { public int Current; public int Max; }
[Component] public struct Frozen { }                       // no fields: a tag

using var world = new World();
Entity e = world.CreateEntity("hero");
world.Set(e, new Health { Current = 5, Max = 10 });
ref readonly Health health = ref world.Get<Health>(e);      // valid until the next structural change
world.Ensure<Health>(e).Current = 8;                       // a writable reference; the component is added when missing
world.Modified<Health>(e);                                 // tell observers about it
world.Add<Frozen>(e);                                      // tags: Add, Has, Remove

The first use of a component registers it in the world: an entity with the component's name, its size and alignment, and its fields as Flecs reflection data (world.ToJson(value) prints {"Current":5,"Max":10}; Flecs' own tools can read it too). Entity ids are Entity structs. Ids are never reused as such: deleting an entity and creating another gives a different id, and IsAlive is false for the old one.

docs.title: Components a script defines
docs.text: world.DefineComponent("Spin", [("speed", FieldKind.Float32), ("axis", FieldKind.Vector3)]) lays the fields out in name order (each aligned to its own size, a vector to four bytes), so a schema always gives the same layout. The same schema again returns the same component; another schema under a known name is an error. GetComponentInfo(id) gives the layout, and FieldAccess.Read/Write (in Apogee.Reflection) read and write a field of the component's memory as a Value, with range checks. The pointer API (GetPointer, EnsurePointer, SetPointer) works on any component id.

docs.title: Asset fields
docs.text:
A uint field marked [Property(Asset = "model")] has the kind FieldKind.AssetRef and FieldDef.AssetType = "model" (see reflection). In memory it is four bytes, a uint handle into the host's library of that asset type; Flecs describes it as a 32-bit number, FieldAccess reads and writes it as a number, and scripts see a number. The kind is what tells a scene file or an inspector that the number names an asset. DefineComponent takes the kind too (("model", FieldKind.AssetRef)) and, in its assetTypes argument, the asset type of each such field by name (new Dictionary<string, string> { ["model"] = "model" }); a scene carries it as assetType="model" in the component's schema, so a script-defined component saves its asset fields too. Luau's world:component cannot name an asset type yet.

A scene does not store the handle, which only means something in the run that made it. The host says what each asset type's handles name with RegisterAssetType(type, toRef, fromRef): toRef turns a handle into the AssetRef it names (null for a model made in code, which has no path), fromRef turns a reference into this run's handle, loading the asset when needed. The host registers model (ModelRenderer.Model) with the model library and the asset database, so a scene holds Model="res://models/car.glb|uid://4k2m9x7q1w3ze": the path is tried first, and when its file is gone the UID finds it where it moved. A scene written before UIDs holds the path alone, which loads as well. A reference that leads to no asset leaves the field 0 with a warning, and the scene loads on. A field of a type nobody registered (and a script-defined field with no assetType) is left out of the scene, with one warning per field.

Entity is not a component name: RegisterComponent and DefineComponent refuse it (InvalidOperationException), because a scene file writes a child entity as <Entity>.

docs.title: Editing: hierarchy, copies, snapshots and scenes
docs.text:
What an editor needs of a world, in World.Editing.cs and World.Scene.cs. "User entities" are the ones a game or an editor made (IsUserEntity): not Flecs' own entities (modules, systems, observers), not the entities of registered components and the reflection data under them, not what is marked EditorOnly (the editor's own camera) or under such an entity.

  • Hierarchy: Roots(), Children(entity) (in creation order) and Subtree(entity) (parents first). ComponentsOf(entity) lists the components and tags the registry describes (not relationship pairs or the name), with their ComponentInfo; Components is every component the world has registered. SetParent and GetParent were there before; Trs.InLocalOf gives the local transform that keeps an entity where it is under a new parent.
  • Names: a name is unique among the children of one parent, and among the top-level entities. SetName gives an entity a free name when a sibling has the one asked for (Lamp, Lamp 2, Lamp 3…; read it back with GetName), SetParent does the same when the new parent has a child of that name, and an empty name takes the name away (no name never clashes). UniqueName(name, parent?) says what a name would become. The loader, Clone, Restore and the editor's paste all use it. Names are compared as written (lamp and Lamp differ), and only the siblings count: a child and a top-level entity may share a name, and so may the entity and the engine's own entities of the same name (Flecs has one called Empty in its core module). The one exception is a top-level name that a component or system of the world already has (Health, Transform): Flecs keeps one entity of a name in a scope, so that entity would take its place in the index, and the user's entity gets Health 2. A load of many entities of one name takes as long as a load of distinct ones.
  • Copies: Clone(entity, parent?) copies the components and the whole branch under the same parent, naming the copies name (copy), name (copy 2) so they stay unique. A copy of an instance of a prefab is another instance; a copy of a branch of one, without its root, is plain entities (the entities' links to their prefab are kept only when the instance they belong to is copied too).
  • Snapshots: Snapshot() takes every user entity (ids with their generation, names, parents, component bytes), SnapshotTree(entity) one branch. Restore(snapshot) puts the world back: user entities that are not in it are destroyed, the ones that are come back under the same ids (made alive again with ecs_make_alive when they were destroyed) with their components, names and parents as they were; RestoreEntities(snapshot) only brings back and overwrites, destroying nothing (an undo of a deletion). The same ids are what keep a selection and an undo history valid across a play session. Asset fields travel by reference: for each field of an asset type (ModelRenderer.Model, anything [Property(Asset = "…")]) the snapshot also keeps the AssetRef (path and UID) its handle named, through the type registered with RegisterAssetType. Restored into the world it was taken from, the bytes come back as they are; restored into another world (the new session after a play run), each such field is set to that world's handle for the same asset, so a model is still the same model although the new session numbered its models afresh. An asset that world cannot find, or that has no path or UID, comes back as 0 with a warning. Any other handle of the run (a physics body's id) is still bytes and comes back with the old value, so such components are left to the code that made them. What a prefab instance's element held that could not be applied (see prefabs) travels with the instance's root, so Play and Stop, undo and redo do not lose it.
  • Scenes (.ascene): SaveScene() writes the user entities as XML text, SaveScene(entity) one branch, and LoadScene(text, parent?) creates the entities (under parent when given) and returns them in the order of the file. SaveSceneDocument(roots) and LoadScene(node, parent?) do the same with an XmlNode tree, for code that patches or inspects it. Each component is an element and each field an attribute (<Transform Position="0 -0.5 0" Rotation="0 0 0 1" Scale="1 1 1"/>), a child <Entity> is a child entity, and the format needs no reflection, so it works in NativeAOT. Flecs' own JSON was not used: it would carry the entities the engine registers for its types and systems. Components a script defined are written with their schema and defined again when the scene is loaded into a world that has not heard of them. On loading, a component or a field the world does not have is logged and skipped, a name that is taken gets a free one (name 2), and text that is not a scene is a FormatException. WorldTransform is derived and never saved; IgnoreInScenes(name) leaves others out (the host does it for physics Body), and RegisterAssetType (see asset fields) is how a field that holds a handle is saved as the asset it names: ModelRenderer.Model, a number in this run's model library, is saved as the model's path and UID. The format, the schema and how to patch a scene are in Scenes.
  • From scripts: world:save_scene() returns the text, world:load_scene(text, parent?) the list of entities it made, world:roots() and world:children(entity) the hierarchy. A script reads and writes the file itself with fs.read_text and fs.write_text, which keeps the confinement of a mod's files.

docs.title: Transforms
docs.text: Every world has Transform (local to the parent) and WorldTransform (in the world, computed top down once a frame by a system that every world installs), with a Double3 position: see Math and the double-precision world. A query term can read a component from the entity's parent with new QueryTerm(id, QueryOperator.Optional, QuerySource.ParentCascade): the field is a single element shared by the table (view.FieldPointer(index, size)), and parents are visited before their children. World.ComputeWorldTransform(entity) computes the world placement now, from the entity's Transform and its parents', for code that changes transforms and needs the result before the next Progress (physics placing a body it was just given).

docs.title: Queries
docs.text:
using Query<Position, Velocity> moving = world.Query<Position, Velocity>();
moving.Each((Entity e, ref Position p, ref Velocity v) => p.Value += v.Value);
int count = moving.Count();

A query matches the entities that have all of the components (up to four typed ones; CreateQuery takes any number of QueryTerms, with QueryOperator.Not to exclude a component). It is cached by Flecs. Iterating defers structural changes (adding or removing components, deleting entities): they are applied when the iteration is over, so a callback may do them without breaking it. ForEachTable gives a TableView for each table: Entities, Count, and Field<T>(index) for the component of the term with that index. Dispose a query when done with it; the world disposes the rest.

docs.title: Systems and observers
docs.text:
world.AddSystem<Position, Velocity>("Move", Phase.OnUpdate, (Entity e, ref Position p, ref Velocity v) =>
    p.Value += v.Value * world.DeltaTime);
world.Progress(1f / 60);

Progress runs one frame: the phases in order (OnLoad, PostLoad, PreUpdate, OnUpdate, OnValidate, PostUpdate, PreStore, OnStore), and within a phase the systems in the order they were added. AddSystem also takes terms and a TableAction for the raw form scripts use. Destroy the system's entity to remove it.

An observer runs at once when its event happens to an entity that matches: AddObserver<Health>("Watch", ObserverEvent.OnSet, …) (also OnAdd and OnRemove).

Exceptions never unwind through Flecs. A system or observer that throws is recorded, the others still run, and Progress throws when the frame is done: the exception itself when there was one, an AggregateException when there were several.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Flecs copies the names it is given (entities, struct members), and a system's callback is kept alive by a GCHandle that Flecs frees together with the system; a world that is destroyed frees them all. This is checked under NativeAOT by the runtime's smoke test, which CI runs.
  • Relationship pairs are World.Pair(first, second); the child-of relation and the other builtin ids are Ecs.ChildOf… in the Flecs binding.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Tests/Apogee.Ecs.Tests (needs the flecs native library): the transform hierarchy (TransformTests), registration and reflection JSON, set/get/ensure, tags, runtime components, names and parents, ids that stay dead, queries (with Not, with structural changes inside), systems in phases, failing systems, observers, and disposal; and EditingTests: which entities are the user's, hierarchy order, the components of an entity, clones, snapshots and restoring (ids that come back, names that swapped, a deleted branch); SnapshotAssetTests (asset fields restored into a world that numbers its assets differently); and scenes (a round trip with the hierarchy, references, doubles and script components, converters, unknown things, bad files). The scene round trip also runs in the NativeAOT smoke test (Apogee.Runtime --smoke) and from Luau (Tests/Luau/ecs.test.luau).

docs.title: Interop
docs.text: Apogee.Interop is what the generated bindings stand on.

docs.title: NativeLibraries
docs.text: Generated DllImports name a logical library (SDL3, flecs). Each binding assembly registers the file names to try per operating system (NativeLibraries.Register, called from the generated *.Library.g.cs). Resolution tries, per candidate: next to the executable, then runtimes/<rid>/native, then the system search. TryLoad lets a test or a tool ask whether a library is installed without failing.

docs.title: CBool
docs.text: CBool is a one-byte C bool/uint8_t flag with implicit conversions to and from bool, so signatures stay blittable (a managed bool is not).

docs.title: Utf8
docs.text:
Utf8.ToZeroTerminated(string) gives the bytes of a C string (pin them with fixed to pass them to native code) and Utf8.FromPointer(byte*) reads one back (null stays null).

fixed (byte* name = Utf8.ToZeroTerminated("Apogee"))
{
    SDL.SetWindowTitle(window, name);
}
string? error = Utf8.FromPointer(SDL.GetError());

docs.title: Math and the double-precision world
docs.text: Everything the GPU and the shaders see is float; the world is not. A float has 24 bits of precision, so 5.8 km from the origin (the corner of an 8192 m map) it moves in 0.5 mm steps, which shows as jitter in physics and in the picture. So positions are double, and every other quantity (directions, rotations, scales, velocities, everything on the GPU) stays float.

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
The engine does not have a math library of its own. It uses System.Numerics (Vector2/3/4, Quaternion, Matrix4x4, Plane): the JIT and NativeAOT treat those as SIMD intrinsic types (a Vector3 lives in one register and +, Dot, Normalize compile to a few vector instructions), which a struct of our own would only match by wrapping them. Apogee.Core.Numerics adds what System.Numerics has no type for:

Type What it is Double3 A world position: three doubles, 24 bytes, scalar code (positions are added and subtracted, not crunched in bulk). Converts implicitly from Vector3 and explicitly to it. Trs A placement: Double3 position, Quaternion rotation, Vector3 scale. InWorldOf(parent), TransformPoint, InverseTransformPoint, TransformVector, ToMatrix(origin).

Conventions (the same as the renderer's): right-handed, +Y up, an object or camera looks down -Z, angles are radians, matrices are row-major and used with row vectors (Vector3.Transform(v, m); a * b applies a first), and quaternions compose as in mathematics: (q1 * q2) * v == q1 * (q2 * v), so q2 applies first.

docs.title: Relative to an origin
docs.text:
Double3.RelativeTo(origin) subtracts in double and then narrows to float, so the result is exact however far both points are from the world's origin:

Vector3 onScreen = enemy.Position.RelativeTo(camera.Position);     // a few meters, precise to a micrometre, 10 000 km from the origin
Matrix4x4 world = placement.ToMatrix(camera.Position);             // the translation is relative to the camera

That is how positions reach the GPU: the renderer works camera-relative (see Rendering: Camera.Position and a scene's Origin are Double3). Jolt is built with JPH_DOUBLE_PRECISION (see Native libraries), so that body positions are double too.

docs.title: Transforms in the ECS
docs.text:
Transform (Position: Double3, Rotation: Quaternion, Scale: Vector3) is a component of every world. It is local: relative to the entity's parent (the ChildOf relationship), and in the world for an entity with no parent. Set the scale to one (Transform.Identity, Transform.At(position)): a zeroed transform, which is what Add gives, has no size.

WorldTransform is the same placement in world space, and the transform system computes it once a frame (in the PostUpdate phase) top down: a Flecs query with the parent's WorldTransform as a cascade term, so parents are always done before their children, whatever order they were created in. Adding a Transform adds its WorldTransform (Flecs' With trait). Read WorldTransform; do not write it.

Entity truck = world.CreateEntity("truck");
Entity wheel = world.CreateEntity("wheel", parent: truck);
world.Set(truck, Transform.At(new Double3(5_000_000, 0, 0)));
world.Set(wheel, new Transform(new Double3(1, 0.4, 2), Quaternion.Identity, Vector3.One));
world.Progress(0.016f);
Double3 where = world.Get<WorldTransform>(wheel).Position;       // (5 000 001, 0.4, 2)

Limits. Scale may differ per axis, but there is no shear: a child's world scale is the product of its own and its parent's, which is exact when the parent's scale is uniform or its rotation lines up with the child's axes (the rule most engines use). The child's position inside its parent is narrowed to float while it is rotated, so keep children within about ten kilometres of their parent; the parent itself can be anywhere.

docs.title: In scripts
docs.text:
Luau's vector is three floats (LUA_VECTOR_SIZE 3), so scripts see positions as vectors: a Double3 is narrowed when it goes into Luau and widened when it comes back. A float is good to about a millimetre at 8 km from the origin, which is enough for gameplay logic, and nothing is lost where it matters, in the physics and the renderer, which keep the doubles. A script that needs an exact far position works with offsets from a known place instead.

Quat is an immutable userdata:

local turn = Quat.axisAngle(Vector3(0, 1, 0), math.rad(90))      -- Quat.new(x, y, z, w), Quat.euler(vector(pitch, yaw, roll)), Quat.lookAt(forward, up?)
turn * Vector3(0, 0, 1)                                          -- rotates a vector: (1, 0, 0)
turn * other                                                     -- composes: `other` applies first
turn:inverse(), turn:normalized(), turn:slerp(other, t), turn:dot(other), turn:toEuler()
turn.x, turn.y, turn.z, turn.w; Quat.identity; turn == other

The built-in components are reachable by name: world:component("Transform") and world:component("WorldTransform"), with fields Position, Rotation and Scale. A component a script defines can have fields of type "dvec3" (a Double3, seen as a vector) and "quat".

docs.title: In the registry and in files
docs.text:
• [Component] structs may have Double3 and Quaternion fields (FieldKind.Double3, FieldKind.Quaternion), and [Property]/[Method] members may use both types. A Double3 member crosses to scripts as ValueKind.Vector3, a Quaternion as ValueKind.Quaternion. Flecs knows both as struct types, so its JSON keeps all 17 digits of a position.
  • Value carries a quaternion in the spare float next to a vector's z (a Value is 32 bytes); it has no room for a Double3, which is why positions cross as vectors.
  • In XML definitions a vector3 attribute (type="xs:vector3"; any prefix) is three numbers, at="1 2.5 -3" (spaces or commas), decoded as a DefVector and a vector in Luau.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Tests/Apogee.Core.Tests (Double3, Trs: composing, inverting, precision at 10 000 km, the camera-relative matrix), Tests/Apogee.Ecs.Tests (propagation through three levels created in any order, reparenting, the With trait, the layout and the JSON of the components), Tests/Apogee.Reflection.Tests (the new field kinds, members and values), Tests/Luau/quat.test.luau (Quat and the transform from a script), the vector3 case of Tests/Apogee.Content.Tests and, in Tests/Apogee.Rendering.Tests, the golden scene rendered 100 km and 10 000 km from the origin.

docs.title: Profiling, SIMD and the shipped instruction set
docs.text: The rule for speed is measure, then write SIMD where a measurement says so. System.Numerics is already intrinsic (see Math), so most code needs nothing. This chapter says how to look, what the shipped programs are compiled for, and where hand-written vector code exists.

docs.title: Where to look
docs.text:
• The dev overlay (Dev tools): the CPU frame time history, the GPU time of each pass (FrameLoop.Timings, from timestamp queries, per frame in flight), the render graph and the draw, culled and light counts. Start here: it says whether a frame is CPU- or GPU-bound.
  • RenderDoc shows the same pass names (frame.Scope(name) and recorder.Label(name) are debug labels).
  • CoreCLR (the editor and dotnet run): dotnet-trace collect -- <program> and dotnet-counters monitor (install them with dotnet tool install -g dotnet-trace dotnet-counters).
  • NativeAOT (a shipped build): a native program, so the platform's profiler reads it: perf record -g on Linux, Instruments on macOS, Windows Performance Analyzer or Visual Studio on Windows. ./build.sh aot keeps the symbols (Apogee.Runtime.dbg next to the program on Linux, .pdb files on Windows).
  • Micro-benchmarks: ./build.sh bench [filter] runs BenchmarkDotNet over Samples/Benchmarks (a sample: benchmarks are run by hand) in Release (the raw results go to Bin/benchmarks, which is not committed) (for example ./build.sh bench '*Culling*' --job short). BenchmarkDotNet is used there only (MIT, a test dependency, never shipped), and CI builds the project but does not run it: benchmarks are noisy on shared machines. Remember that BenchmarkDotNet's NativeAOT mode compiles for the CPU it runs on, which is not what a game ships with; to measure the shipped baseline publish a small program with -p:PublishAot=true instead.

docs.title: The instruction set of a shipped game
docs.text:
The JIT asks the CPU which instructions exist when the program starts. NativeAOT cannot: it compiles for a fixed set, and a CPU without it does not start the program. Measured with a small program on an AVX2 machine:

IlcInstructionSet Vector128.IsHardwareAccelerated Vector256.IsHardwareAccelerated, Avx2.IsSupported, Fma.IsSupported (not set) true false x86-64-v2 true false x86-64-v3 true true

So the default of x64 is x86-64-v2 (SSE4.2 and POPCNT, practically every PC since 2009), and AVX2 code is simply compiled out of a default NativeAOT build; it is not a run-time check. Our choice, in Directory.Build.props for PublishAot builds:

  • x64: x86-64-v2, written down so that it is a decision. -p:ApogeeAotInstructionSet=x86-64-v3 builds for AVX2, BMI and FMA (Intel since Haswell in 2013, AMD since Excavator in 2015 and Zen) at the price of the older CPUs, which then do not start the game; the next section says what that buys.
  • osx-arm64: apple-m1 (atomics, CRC, rounding multiply, dot products): every Apple-silicon Mac has at least that.
  • Other arm64 and anything else keep the compiler's default (ARMv8.0 with NEON).

The CoreCLR editor and development runs use the JIT and so do get AVX2 on a CPU that has it. That is why the code that can use 256-bit vectors checks Vector256.IsHardwareAccelerated and falls back.

docs.title: Where there is SIMD
docs.text:
Only where it was measured to pay, and with a scalar twin that the tests compare it with.

Frustum culling (Apogee.Core.Numerics.FrustumCulling, used by SceneRenderer): the bounds of every draw are kept as six arrays (centers and half extents, structure of arrays, padded to a multiple of eight), and each frame the five planes of the camera's view volume are tested against all of them, four or eight boxes per instruction, producing a bit per draw. The three kernels (CullScalar, CullVector128, CullVector256) do the same arithmetic in the same order, so they set the same bits, which FrustumCullingTests checks on random boxes and frusta; Cull picks the widest that is hardware accelerated. Because the scene's boxes are relative to its origin, the frustum is moved to them with Frustum.Offset (the plane constants absorb the offset) and the arrays never change.

Measured for 100 000 boxes (Core i7-14700K, .NET 10):

scalar Vector128 (NativeAOT x86-64-v2, the shipped default) Vector256 (NativeAOT x86-64-v3; CoreCLR) time 1.66 ms 0.18 ms (9x) 0.064 ms (26x)

So a shipped game culls 100 000 draws in under a fifth of a millisecond without AVX2, and AVX2 would save about 0.1 ms more per 100 000: not worth turning players away. For 1 000 boxes the whole cull is about 1.5 µs (128-bit). ./build.sh bench '*Culling*' reproduces the table; *RelativePosition* measures Double3.RelativeTo (100 000 positions: about 0.11 ms, scalar double code, which is fast enough that it has no SIMD twin).

Not done, on purpose (nothing measured yet, so nothing written): density-map sweeps and the instancer (terrain), skinning, particles. They get a benchmark first.

docs.title: Reflection
docs.text: Apogee.Reflection is the registry of everything scripts, serialization and inspectors see: classes with properties, methods and signals, enums, ECS components and script libraries. It is written by a Roslyn source generator (Apogee.Reflection.Generator), so there is no runtime reflection and it works under NativeAOT.

docs.title: Describing a class
docs.text:
A class derives from EngineObject, is partial, and is marked [ApogeeClass]. Members are opted in:

public enum Mode { Idle, FastMove }

/// <summary>Something that moves.</summary>
[ApogeeClass(Creatable = true)]
public partial class Actor : EngineObject
{
    /// <summary>How fast it goes, in meters per second.</summary>
    [Property] public float Speed { get; set; } = 2;
    [Property] public Mode Mode { get; set; }
    [Property] public int Count { get; private set; }              // no public setter: read-only

    [Method] public bool TryMove(Vector3 to, float speed = 1f) { … }
    [Method] public (int, string) Pair() => (7, "seven");            // a tuple is several results in a script
    [Method] public static int Twice(int x) => x * 2;

    [Signal] public Signal<int, string> Damaged { get; } = new();
}
  • Names in scripts are snake_case (TryMove → try_move, FastMove → "fast_move"); Name = "…" on an attribute overrides it. Classes keep their C# name ([ApogeeClass(Name = "…")]).
  • Options: Scriptable = false keeps the class out of scripts, ModsBlocked = true refuses its objects to mods, and Creatable = true gives scripts a new() (it needs a parameterless constructor).
  • Documentation: the <summary> above a member is copied into the registry, for the generated .d.luau and the inspectors.
  • Types a member may have: bool, the integer types, float, double, string, Vector3, Double3 (seen as a vector in scripts), Quaternion, enums (a [Flags] enum is a list of names in scripts), Entity, AssetRef (a string in scripts, see asset fields), Value (any), ScriptFunction, EngineObject classes, and T[], List<T> and IReadOnlyList<T> of those. T? is nullable. Anything else is error APG002 that names the member, as are non-partial classes (APG001), two members with one script name (APG003), a component that is not an unmanaged struct or has an unsupported field (APG004) and a member that cannot be described, such as a ref parameter or a signal of the wrong type (APG005), and Asset where it does not belong (APG006). A type with an error writes nothing, so the first error is the only one.

docs.title: Components and libraries
docs.text:
[Component]
public struct Position { public Vector3 Value; }               // fields: bool, integers, float, double, Vector3, Double3, Quaternion, Entity

[Component] public struct Frozen { }                           // no fields: a tag

[ScriptLibrary("imgui")]
public static partial class ImGuiLibrary
{
    [Method] public static bool Button(string label) { … }
}

A component's ComponentInfo has its size, alignment and every field's offset, taken from the compiled struct. A library is a global table of its static [Method]s in scripts.

docs.title: What an inspector shows
docs.text:
[Property] carries hints for inspectors, on a class's properties and on a component's fields (FieldDef.Meta, PropertyDef.Meta: an InspectorMeta). All are optional:

[Component]
public struct Engine
{
    [Property(Min = 0, Max = 100, Step = 0.5, Category = "Power")] public float Throttle;   // a slider from 0 to 100 under the heading "Power"
    [Property(Min = 0)] public int Gear;                                                    // a drag field that does not go below 0
    [Property(Hidden = true)] public uint Handle;                                           // an inspector does not show it
    [Property(ReadOnly = true)] public double Hours;                                        // shown, not editable
}

Min, Max and Step are hints for widgets: they do not stop a script or a file from setting another value. InspectorMeta.HasRange says both ends are given (a slider can be drawn), RangeText is 0 to 100 for the generated Luau definitions, which add (Range: 0 to 1.) to the doc of a property. A field without [Property] has no hints. A component a script defines gives them in a table: world:component("Vehicle", { speed = { type = "f32", min = 0, max = 90, step = 0.5, category = "Motion" }, gear = "i32", token = { type = "u32", hidden = true } }); the plain name = "type" form still works.

docs.title: Asset fields
docs.text:
A component is made of unmanaged memory, so a field that names an asset (a model, a texture) is a uint handle in the loaded library of that asset type. [Property(Asset = "model")] on a uint field says so: the field's FieldDef.Kind is FieldKind.AssetRef (four bytes, like a uint) and FieldDef.AssetType is "model". Scripts still read and write a number; scenes and the editor use the kind and the type to turn the handle into a reference by path and UID.

[Component]
public struct Furnished
{
    [Property(Category = "Model", Asset = "model")] public uint Model;   // FieldKind.AssetRef, AssetType "model"
}

Asset is only for uint fields of a [Component] struct, and needs a non-empty type name; anywhere else it is error APG006. Without it a uint stays a number.

On a class, a property that names an asset has the type Apogee.Core.Assets.AssetRef (path and UID). Scripts see its text form as a string (res://models/car.glb|uid://4k2m9x7q1w3ze, a path alone or a uid://… alone), and the generated .d.luau says string (string? for AssetRef?). Text that is not an asset reference is an error in the script (Value.ToAssetRef throws a ValueException) and the property keeps its value.

docs.title: Using the registry
docs.text:
TypeRegistry.GetClass("Actor") gives a ClassInfo; FindProperty("speed"), FindMethod("try_move") and FindSignal("damaged") look a member up by its script name, inherited ones included. Everything crosses as a Value, a 24-byte struct with no boxing:

var results = new Value[1];
actor.Class.FindMethod("try_move")!.Invoke(actor, [Value.Vector(target), Value.Float(2)], results);
bool moved = results[0].ToBool();

MethodDef.Invoke checks the argument count; the To… methods check kind and range and throw a ValueException whose message a script can show (expected number, got string, 300 is out of range for byte). Registration happens in a module initializer of each assembly that has described types, so the registry is complete before the first lookup.

docs.title: Objects and handles
docs.text: Every EngineObject takes a slot in one table: its Handle is an index and a generation (SlotTable<T> in Apogee.Core). Scripts hold the handle, never the object. Destroy() frees the slot and bumps the generation, so a handle to a destroyed object, or to one whose slot was reused, is recognised (attempt to use a destroyed object). An object a script creates is destroyed when the script lets go of it unless the engine calls Adopt() on it (see Scripting).

docs.title: Signals
docs.text: Signal, Signal<T1> … Signal<T1, T2, T3, T4>: Connect(handler) returns a Connection (Disconnect(), IsConnected) and Emit(…) calls a snapshot of the handlers, so a handler may disconnect itself while it runs. A handler that throws is logged and the others still run; the emitter never sees it. SignalDef.Connect connects a handler that receives the arguments as Values.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Tests/Apogee.Reflection.Tests compiles C# snippets with the generator (CSharpGeneratorDriver), checks the generated text and the diagnostics, loads the result and drives it through the registry; it also tests Value, handles, signals and the registry itself.

docs.title: Graphics
docs.text: Apogee.Graphics is the GPU layer. The renderer, the dev tools and the content pipeline talk to a small portable API: GraphicsDevice and the objects it makes (buffers, images, samplers, pipelines, a command recorder, a swapchain and a frame loop). Each graphics API implements it in its own namespace: Apogee.Graphics.Vulkan and Apogee.Graphics.Metal. The renderer on top of it is in Rendering.

docs.title: Backends: the seam
docs.text:
Everything above the backends is abstract classes with the portable surface, and each backend has one sealed class for each:

Portable (Apogee.Graphics) Vulkan (Apogee.Graphics.Vulkan) What it hides GraphicsDevice VulkanDevice instance, physical device choice, queue, memory allocator, the window's surface GpuBuffer, GpuImage, ImageView, GpuSampler VulkanBuffer, VulkanImage, VulkanImageView, VulkanSampler VkBuffer, VkImage and views (VMA allocations) Pipeline VulkanPipeline pipeline objects and the shared pipeline layout CommandRecorder VulkanCommandRecorder command buffers, barriers (VulkanStates maps an ImageState to layouts, stages and accesses), dynamic rendering BindlessHeap VulkanBindlessHeap the descriptor set of texture, sampler and storage-image arrays ImmediateContext VulkanImmediateContext a command buffer and a fence for loading and tools Swapchain, FrameLoop VulkanSwapchain, VulkanFrameLoop acquiring and presenting, the timeline semaphore of the frames in flight, timestamp queries

The portable names of things are the engine's own: PixelFormat (in Apogee.Core.Graphics; its numbers are Vulkan's VkFormat numbers, which are also the vkFormat of a KTX 2 file, so a texture's format is read by a cast, and another backend maps the ones it supports with a table), BufferUsage, ImageUsage, SampleCount, CullMode, FrontFace, CompareOp, PrimitiveTopology, Filter, MipmapMode, AddressMode and IndexFormat (all with Vulkan's numbers too), and ShaderCode (the compiled code of one entry point and which ShaderBackend it is for). Apogee.Graphics.Vulkan.VulkanConvert turns them into Vulkan's enums; the barrier states (ImageState, BufferState) were already abstract. A device refuses ShaderCode of another backend.

A test keeps the seam closed. BackendSeamTests reads the public surface of Apogee.Graphics, Apogee.Rendering, Apogee.DevTools, Apogee.Content and Apogee.Platform by reflection and fails on any signature that names a type of Apogee.Native.Vulkan, outside Apogee.Graphics.Vulkan. Code that does need Vulkan (the backend's own tests, tools) casts: (VulkanDevice)device.

Creating a device.

using var window = new Window("My game", 1280, 720, WindowOptions.Resizable | GraphicsDevice.RequiredWindowOptions());   // a window is made for one API
using var device = GraphicsDevice.Create(new GraphicsDeviceOptions { Window = window });                              // no window: headless
using var swapchain = device.CreateSwapchain(vsync: true);
using var loop = device.CreateFrameLoop(swapchain);

GraphicsDeviceOptions.Backend chooses the API; when it is null the platform's is used (GraphicsDevice.DefaultBackend: Metal on macOS, Vulkan elsewhere; APOGEE_GRAPHICS=vulkan|metal overrides it for development). TryCreate returns the reason instead of throwing, for a machine without a usable GPU or driver (GraphicsException is what the creation functions throw). GraphicsDevice.EnumerateDevices lists every GPU with the reasons it cannot be used. device.Name, Kind, Backend, ShaderBackend and the capabilities (SupportsBc, SupportsAstc, SupportsAnisotropy, MaxSamplerAnisotropy) are portable; device.ValidationErrorCount / TakeValidationErrors() count what the API's validation layer reported, which is how the tests fail on any validation error.

docs.title: Other backends
docs.text: Direct3D 12 is not planned: Vulkan already covers Windows (AMD, NVIDIA and Intel ship Vulkan 1.3 drivers), Linux and the Steam Deck. The seam does not rule one out (push constants of 128 bytes fit root constants, the bindless heap maps to a descriptor heap, the render graph's states are abstract, and the shader bundle reserves a slot for DXIL), but the engine's shaders read buffers through pointers (device addresses), which HLSL does not have.

docs.title: The Metal backend
docs.text:
Status: written, never run on a GPU (help wanted). It compiles, the shim builds on macOS CI, Apple's compiler accepts every shader, and the native bindings are tested; GitHub's macOS runners have no Metal 3 GPU, so the device, rendering and swapchain code has not run.

Apogee.Graphics.Metal is the default on macOS. It needs macOS 15, Metal 3 and tier 2 argument buffers, which is Apple silicon and the Intel Macs of 2017 and later; EnumerateDevices says why a GPU does not qualify. Metal is Objective-C, so it is reached through a small C API, Native/metal_c (see ThirdParty/README.md), bound by Apogee.Native.Metal. Nothing Objective-C crosses it: objects are opaque handles, and completion is a shared event's value rather than a block.

Portable Metal GpuBuffer MTLBuffer: shared (mapped for life) for upload and readback; device-local is private, filled through a staging buffer. Its Address is gpuAddress, which is what the push constants carry GpuImage, ImageView, GpuSampler MTLTexture and MTLSamplerState; PixelFormat is mapped by a table in the shim BindlessHeap one argument buffer of 8-byte gpuResourceIDs in runs: 16 384 2D textures, 256 samplers (slot 0 is a white texel and a linear-repeat sampler), then 16 384 each of cube, 2D-array, 3D and unsigned-integer textures, and 256 storage images CommandRecorder an MTLCommandBuffer; the render, compute or blit encoder a command needs is opened on demand and ended by the next kind of command or by a barrier Pipeline MTLRenderPipelineState / MTLComputePipelineState from the bundle's MSL (compiled with newLibraryWithSource when loaded); a compute pipeline's thread-group size comes from Slang's reflection Swapchain, FrameLoop a CAMetalLayer (SDL creates it for a WindowOptions.Metal window) and an MTLSharedEvent as the timeline, with the same frames in flight as Vulkan

Two things differ from Vulkan and shape the code:

  • Residency. Buffers are reached by address and textures by the argument buffer, so Metal does not know the GPU uses them. Every buffer and texture is added to one MTLResidencySet when it is made (this is why macOS 15 is the minimum), and the set is committed before a submission when something was added.
  • Hazards. Metal does not order what shaders reach through an address. Encoders are chained with an MTLFence (each waits for the one before), which is what the render graph's barriers mean on Metal. Image layouts do not exist, so Barrier only ends the current encoder.

Not done yet: GPU timings (FrameLoop.Timings is empty on Metal), Metal's binary archive cache for compiled shader libraries. The Metal tests (MetalBackendTests, and every shared GPU test when the device is Metal) skip without a qualifying GPU, unless APOGEE_REQUIRE_METAL=1. How to check a build on a Mac: Metal on a Mac; the open tasks: Help wanted.

docs.title: The Vulkan backend: instance and device
docs.text:
GraphicsDevice.Create makes a VulkanInstance and, for a window, its VkSurfaceKHR (through SDL), and the VulkanDevice owns both; a caller that keeps its own instance uses VulkanDevice.Create(instance, options).

VulkanInstance asks for Vulkan 1.3, turns on the Khronos validation layer when it is installed (APOGEE_VULKAN_VALIDATION=0 turns it off, =1 makes a missing layer an error), and installs a debug messenger: warnings and errors from the layers and the driver go to the log, and ErrorCount / TakeErrors() count them. On macOS the loader's portability enumeration is enabled so MoltenVK is listed.

The device picks the best GPU that meets the engine's baseline: Vulkan 1.3 with dynamic rendering, synchronization2, maintenance4, buffer device addresses, timeline semaphores and descriptor indexing (runtime arrays, partially bound, sampled images update after bind, non-uniform indexing), plus a graphics and compute queue that can present to the window when one is given. Discrete GPUs win over integrated ones, then virtual, then software. PreferredDeviceName or APOGEE_GPU=llvmpipe picks by name (a substring), and a GPU that fails the baseline is skipped with its reason.

The device owns the VMA allocator (created with bufferDeviceAddress; VMA loads Vulkan through the device's own entry points), and VulkanDevice.SetDebugName names objects for the validation layer and RenderDoc.

docs.title: Buffers, images, samplers
docs.text:
All GPU memory comes from VMA through three small classes. GpuBuffer always gets a device address (buffer.Address), which is how shaders reach buffers: a pointer in push constants, no descriptors. MemoryKind says where it lives: DeviceLocal (fastest, filled by copying), Upload (the CPU writes it, the GPU reads it; mapped for its whole life) and Readback.

using GpuBuffer vertices = device.CreateBuffer(vertexBytes, BufferUsage.Storage, "mesh vertices");   // uploads through staging
using GpuBuffer perFrame = device.CreateBuffer(256, BufferUsage.Uniform, MemoryKind.Upload);
perFrame.Write(frameConstants);

using GpuImage albedo = device.CreateImage(new ImageDescription(PixelFormat.R8G8B8A8Srgb, 1024, 1024, ImageUsage.Sampled, MipLevels: 11));
device.UploadImage(albedo, texels, regions, ImageState.ShaderRead);

GpuImage knows its description, has a view of everything (the depth aspect only, for depth-stencil formats) and makes extra views for one mip or layer. Memory from VMA is not zeroed. UploadBuffer, UploadImage, ReadBuffer and ReadImage go through staging and wait for the GPU: they are for loading, tools and tests, not for every frame (per-frame data goes in Upload buffers). ImmediateContext (device.Immediate.Submit(recorder => …)) is the same machinery for your own one-off GPU work, and is safe from several threads.

docs.title: Resource states and barriers
docs.text: An image or buffer is always in one ImageState / BufferState (ShaderRead, ColorAttachment, StorageReadWrite, …), and ResourceStates.Describe maps each to the Vulkan layout, pipeline stages and access mask. CommandRecorder.Barriers records any number of transitions as one synchronization2 vkCmdPipelineBarrier2; the render graph computes them from what each pass declares. recorder.Label("Shadow pass") opens a named group that shows up in RenderDoc and in validation messages.

docs.title: The bindless heap
docs.text:
Every pipeline has the same layout: descriptor set 0 is device.Bindless, three big arrays (sampled images, samplers, storage images, partially bound and update-after-bind) that shaders index with integers, plus 128 bytes of push constants. AddSampledImage(image) returns the index to read it with, RemoveSampledImage frees it for reuse; AddStorageImage(view) does the same for a view a shader writes (any mip or layer: make the view with GpuImage.CreateView). Slot 0 of the images and samplers is a white texel and a linear repeat sampler, so an unset index still reads something sane; slot 0 of the storage images is never handed out, so 0 means "none".

common.slang declares the arrays a shader can use. The sampled images are one binding whatever their dimension, so the shader declares one array per type, all on that binding, and a texture is read through the array of its own type at the index the heap gave it:

Slang Reads gTextures[i] (Texture2D<float4>) a 2D view (also a depth image's) gCubes[i] (TextureCube<float4>) a view of six layers of a cube image gArrays[i] (Texture2DArray<float4>) a 2D-array view gVolumes[i] (Texture3D<float4>) a 3D image gUintTextures[i] (Texture2D<uint>) a view of an unsigned-integer format (Load only) gStorage[i] (RWTexture2D<float4>) a 2D view added with AddStorageImage (a mip or a face of a cube is a 2D view) gSamplers[i] a sampler from AddSampler

A view's type follows the image: the whole of a cube image is a cube, one layer of it a 2D view, a whole 2D-array image a 2D array, one layer a 2D view. Reading a texture through an array of another type is undefined, as reading an index nobody added; the validation layer does not complain about the unused aliases because the arrays are partially bound.

docs.title: Shaders
docs.text:
Shaders are Slang. In development they are compiled at run time by ShaderCompiler; a shipped game never loads the compiler: its shaders were compiled ahead of time by the importer (below) and are loaded from their artifacts. ShaderCompiler targets Vulkan 1.3 (SPIR-V 1.6) or Metal (below) with row-major matrices, and entry points keep their names.

var compiler = new ShaderCompiler(new ShaderCompilerOptions { SearchPaths = [shaderFolder], CacheDirectory = cacheFolder });
CompiledShader shader = compiler.CompileFile(Path.Combine(shaderFolder, "tonemap.slang"));   // throws ShaderCompileException with file:line
using Pipeline pipeline = device.CreateComputePipeline(shader.Code("main"), "tonemap");     // the code of the compiler's backend, as the device runs it

A CompiledShader has the code of each entry point for one backend (Spirv(entry), Msl(entry) or Code(entry) for a pipeline), Slang's reflection of the program as JSON, warnings, and the list of files it read. CompileSource(name, text) compiles text. The cache (CacheDirectory) keeps SPIR-V between runs (the Vulkan build only): an entry is named by a hash of the source, the options and the Slang version, and remembers the hash of every file the compile read, so editing an imported module invalidates it. A corrupt or unwritable cache only costs a recompile. Compiles are serialized process-wide: Slang's global session is not safe to use from two threads at once.

docs.title: Compiled ahead of time: ShaderBundle
docs.text:
Apogee.Runtime --import <folder> compiles every .slang module that has a [shader(…)] entry point into imported/<path>.ashader (the importer is ShaderImporter in Apogee.Rendering, see Asset import). A bundle holds one or more variants of the module, each the module compiled with one set of preprocessor defines (the variant without defines is always there; more are listed in the shader's .import.xml), and for each variant its reflection and the code of every entry point per backend. The importer writes SPIR-V and Metal shading language into the same file; a reader takes the code of the backend of its device (ShaderBundle.Read(…, backend), ShaderLibrary.Load(path, backend: device.ShaderBackend)) and skips the others, and the format reserves DXIL (Direct3D 12). A shader that does not compile for every backend fails the import, so it is found on the author's machine and not on a Mac. Specialization constants need no variant: they stay in the SPIR-V and are in the reflection (pipelines do not set them yet).

A bundle records ShaderAbi.Version (2: it added the Metal code and the bindless parameter block), which is bumped when the shared pipeline layout below changes, on any backend, and an engine refuses a bundle of another version with "import it again" instead of crashing in the driver. That matters for mods, which may ship their own compiled shaders (a mod's folder imported with --import; mod://id/imported).

ShaderCache stores its entries as bundles, so there is one format on disk.

docs.title: Metal: the same shaders
docs.text:
ShaderCompilerOptions.Backend = ShaderBackend.Msl makes the compiler produce Metal shading language source instead of SPIR-V (text, so any machine can make it; the Metal driver compiles it when the shader is loaded). It is the same Slang source for both backends, which is why the engine's shaders follow a few rules, checked by MetalShaderTests:

  • Buffers are pointers (Foo* in the push constants), which Slang writes as device Foo* in MSL: nothing to change.
  • The push constants are Metal buffer 0 (setBytes), and the bindless textures, samplers and storage images are one argument buffer, buffer 1. In Slang the Metal build declares them as ParameterBlock<BindlessResources> gBindless with gTextures, gSamplers, gCubes, ... as macros for its members; the Vulkan build declares the same names as globals with explicit bindings (0 for every sampled array, 1 for the samplers, 2 for the storage images: Slang has no other way to alias several types on one binding, and a parameter block would give each its own). Metal cannot alias: each member of the block is its own run of resource ids, in declaration order, so MetalBindlessHeap writes a sampled texture's id into the same index of every sampled run (the shader reads the run of its type) and keeps its table of runs (MetalBindlessHeap.Members) in step with the block; BindlessTests compares that table with the Metal shading language Slang writes, so reordering the block without the heap fails a test. Metal has no descriptor sets and Slang numbers buffers in declaration order, so the compiler defines APOGEE_METAL for the Metal build only, and the shaders pin the indices with : register(b0) / : register(b1) (PUSH_SLOT, BINDLESS_SLOT in common.slang). The Vulkan build never sees those annotations: the same register annotations changed the SPIR-V's bindings and crashed lavapipe.
  • No other buffer, texture or sampler is bound directly: everything else is reached through an address or an index.

AppleCompilesEveryEngineShaderToMetal hands every entry point to Apple's compiler (xcrun metal -c) when it runs on a Mac with Xcode; the macOS CI job requires it. Slang's reflection is that of the SPIR-V build; the bundle keeps the first backend's.

All pipelines share one layout (the bindless set and 128 bytes of push constants), so a pipeline is just shaders plus state. CreateGraphicsPipeline takes a GraphicsPipelineDescription: geometry is pulled from buffers by the vertex shader (no vertex input state), depth is reverse-Z (near plane = 1, so the compare is greater-or-equal, and the clear value is 0), blending is one of Opaque, Alpha, Premultiplied, Additive, and rendering is dynamic rendering into attachments of the given formats.

Buffers are reached through pointers: put a buffer's Address in the push constants and read it in Slang as a pointer.

struct Push { float* output; uint count; float scale; };
[[vk::push_constant]] ConstantBuffer<Push> push;

[shader("compute")] [numthreads(64, 1, 1)]
void main(uint3 id : SV_DispatchThreadID) { if (id.x < push.count) push.output[id.x] = id.x * push.scale; }

recorder.BindPipeline(pipeline);                  // also binds the bindless set
recorder.PushConstants(new Push { Output = buffer.Address, Count = n, Scale = 0.5f });
recorder.Dispatch((n + 63) / 64);

For drawing, BeginRendering(width, height, colorTargets, depthTarget) starts a pass and sets viewport and scissor, Draw/DrawIndexed draw, EndRendering ends it; images are moved to ColorAttachment/DepthAttachment with Barriers first.

docs.title: Fill, clear and indirect calls
docs.text:
The calls GPU-driven passes are made of, all on CommandRecorder:

Call What it does State the resource is in FillBuffer(buffer, value, offset, size) sets a range (a multiple of four bytes; WholeSize is the rest) to a 32-bit pattern: zero a counter or a histogram buffer: TransferDestination ClearImage(image, color, baseMip, mipCount, baseLayer, layerCount) sets mips and layers of a colour image to one colour; a count of uint.MaxValue means all that remain image: TransferDestination, outside a rendering pass ClearDepthImage(image, depth, ...) the same for a depth image (the stencil to zero) image: TransferDestination DispatchIndirect(buffer, offset) a compute dispatch whose group counts are a DispatchIndirectCommand in a buffer buffer: IndirectRead DrawIndexedIndirect(buffer, offset, drawCount, stride) drawCount draws from DrawIndexedIndirectCommands (20 bytes each); an instance count of 0 draws nothing, which is how culling removes a draw buffer: IndirectRead DrawIndexedIndirectCount(buffer, offset, countBuffer, countOffset, maxDrawCount, stride) the same, with the number of draws in a buffer too (capped at maxDrawCount): the output of a culling pass both buffers: IndirectRead

A buffer a compute shader writes the commands into needs the BufferUsage.Indirect usage and a barrier from ShaderWrite to IndirectRead before the call (the render graph does this for a pass that calls pass.ReadIndirect(buffer)). The commands may use a first instance: the Vulkan device turns on drawIndirectFirstInstance and, when multiDrawIndirect is missing, issues the commands of a multi-draw one by one.

Two optional features are switched on when the GPU has them, and are GraphicsDevice flags like SupportsBc:

  • SupportsDrawIndirectCount (Vulkan's drawIndirectCount): DrawIndexedIndirectCount works. Without it the call throws NotSupportedException; draw with DrawIndexedIndirect and the maximum count instead, and let the pass that fills the commands zero the instance count of the unused ones.
  • SupportsSamplerFilterMinMax (samplerFilterMinmax): SamplerDescription.Reduction (SamplerReduction.Min or Max, or SamplerDescription.MinMax(...)) makes a sampler that returns the smallest or largest texel of its filter footprint instead of the average, so a Hi-Z depth pyramid takes one linear sample per texel. Asking for one without the feature throws.

On Metal (never run, see above) the recorder differs in four ways. There is no clear command, so ClearImage and ClearDepthImage clear with a render pass of their own per mip and layer and need the image to have ImageUsage.ColorAttachment (or DepthStencilAttachment); 3D textures are not cleared. FillBuffer is a blit fill of one byte, so the four bytes of the pattern must be equal (zero and 0xFFFFFFFF are). An indirect draw makes one draw per call, so DrawIndexedIndirect loops over the commands, which have the layout Metal reads. And a draw cannot take its count from a buffer: SupportsDrawIndirectCount is false, as is SupportsSamplerFilterMinMax (Metal has no reduction samplers; a shader takes the minimum of four texels itself).

docs.title: Swapchain and the frame loop
docs.text:
using var swapchain = device.CreateSwapchain(vsync: true);
using var loop = device.CreateFrameLoop(swapchain);

while (!window.CloseRequested)
{
    PlatformHost.PumpEvents();
    Frame? frame = loop.BeginFrame();           // null: minimized, or the swapchain was just recreated
    if (frame is null) continue;

    Backbuffer back = frame.Backbuffer!.Value;   // starts in ImageState.Undefined
    using (frame.Scope("Clear"))
    {
        frame.Recorder.Barrier(new ImageBarrier(back.Image, ImageState.Undefined, ImageState.ColorAttachment));
        frame.Recorder.BeginRendering(back.Width, back.Height, [new ColorTarget(back.View, Clear: true)]);
        frame.Recorder.EndRendering();
        frame.Recorder.Barrier(new ImageBarrier(back.Image, ImageState.ColorAttachment, ImageState.Present));
    }
    loop.EndFrame(frame);                        // submits, then presents
}
loop.WaitIdle();

Swapchain picks a UNORM format (B8G8R8A8 or R8G8B8A8; shaders write sRGB-encoded values themselves, which lets the dev overlay draw onto it directly), FIFO presentation (mailbox or immediate without vsync), and the window's size. A resized window, an out-of-date or suboptimal result all recreate it; a minimized window skips frames. Present semaphores are per image, so one is never signalled while an earlier present still waits on it.

FrameLoop keeps two frames in flight. Each has its own command pool and buffer, upload arena, timer queries and acquire semaphore, and one timeline semaphore counts finished submissions, so BeginFrame waits only for the frame that used its slot two frames ago. Without a swapchain it runs headless: the same frames with no window image, for screenshots, tests and servers.

  • frame.Allocate(size) gives per-frame host-visible memory with a GPU address (a 4 MB arena per frame, reset when the slot is reused): per-draw constants, instance data. It is valid until the GPU finishes the frame.
  • frame.Defer(resource) disposes something once the GPU has finished the frame, which is how a transient resource a frame's commands use is freed.
  • frame.Scope("Shadow pass") is a RenderDoc debug label plus a GPU timer; loop.Timings lists the sections of the most recent finished frame in order, with their GPU milliseconds.

The window tests open a real window, so they only run with APOGEE_WINDOW_TESTS=1 ./build.sh test.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: The GPU tests share one device and fail on any validation error. They skip without a GPU, unless APOGEE_REQUIRE_VULKAN=1 (CI, on lavapipe) or, with the Metal backend, APOGEE_REQUIRE_METAL=1. Run them on a specific GPU with APOGEE_GPU=nvidia ./build.sh test or APOGEE_GPU=llvmpipe ./build.sh test.

docs.title: Metal
docs.text:
The Metal backend (Graphics) was written without a Mac in front of the developer, and has never run on a GPU. The macOS jobs of the CI build it on every push and run the tests that can run there; a Mac that meets the baseline can check the rest. This page is for whoever has one, and the open tasks are in Help wanted.

Needs: macOS 15 or later, and a Mac with Metal 3 and tier 2 argument buffers: an Apple silicon Mac, or an Intel Mac from 2017 on with a recent GPU. The same checks apply to both.

docs.title: What CI does
docs.text:
• Builds metal_c (the Objective-C shim), the bindings and the backend, and runs the native binding tests (Tests/Apogee.Native.Tests) against the real library.
  • Compiles every engine shader's Metal shading language with Apple's own compiler (xcrun metal -c; AppleCompilesEveryEngineShaderToMetal).
  • Runs Apogee.Runtime --gpu-info. If the runner's GPU meets the baseline (the line metal: … ok), the GPU tests are required to run on it (APOGEE_REQUIRE_METAL=1); if not, they skip and the log says why.
  • Does all of this on an Apple-silicon runner and an Intel one, and uploads each NativeAOT build as the artifact apogee-osx-arm64 / apogee-osx-x64. When the probe finds a qualifying GPU it also renders the fixture game on Metal (uploaded as metal-screenshots-*).

docs.title: Checking on a Mac
docs.text:
Clone the repository, download the artifact for your Mac (apogee-osx-arm64 or apogee-osx-x64) from the CI run and unzip it into Bin/publish (so that Bin/publish/runtime exists). A downloaded binary needs chmod +x Bin/publish/runtime/Apogee.Runtime and xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine Bin/publish first. Then, from the repository's root:

Bin/publish/runtime/Apogee.Runtime --gpu-info                       # which GPUs, and whether they qualify; send this line first
Bin/publish/runtime/Apogee.Runtime --game Tests/Fixtures/ShippedGame --user /tmp/game-user --headless --size 640x360 --frames 10 --screenshot game.png
Bin/publish/runtime/Apogee.Runtime --run Samples/Scripting/main.luau --headless --size 640x360 --frames 30 --screenshot scripting.png   # a sample, run by hand
Bin/publish/runtime/Apogee.Runtime --luau-test Tests/Luau

Then a window, which tests the swapchain: run the lighting sample (./build.sh aot-viewer, then Bin/publish/viewer/Apogee.Samples.Viewer) and look at it for a few seconds (fly with the mouse and WASD; resize the window).

Report (an issue, or a pull request with the fix) the output of --gpu-info, the PNGs, and anything printed in the terminal. There are no reference images: a few pixels of difference at edges between GPUs is the rasterizer, a black or garbled image is a bug.

To run the engine's tests from a checkout instead: APOGEE_REQUIRE_METAL=1 ./build.sh test (a missing or unqualified GPU is then a failure, not a skip).

docs.title: What is not covered
docs.text:
GPU timings (Timings is empty on Metal: Metal samples counters only at encoder boundaries, and not on every GPU) and a binary archive cache for shader libraries.

The recorder's fill, clear and indirect calls (FillBuffer, ClearImage, DispatchIndirect, DrawIndexedIndirect; see Graphics) and the extra bindless arrays (cube, array, 3D and storage textures) are written and tested by the shared GPU tests (RecorderTests, BindlessTests), but only the Metal-specific restrictions they have are known from reading Metal's documentation: a render-pass clear needs the attachment usage, a buffer fill is bytewise, and there is no draw count in a buffer. Confirm them with APOGEE_REQUIRE_METAL=1 ./build.sh test on a Mac.

The images are compared with the references that Mesa's software rasterizer made, so the Metal tests allow a mean difference of 2 (worst channel 64) instead of Vulkan's 0.5 (24); APOGEE_IMAGE_TOLERANCE=<mean> sets it. These numbers are a guess until a real Mac has measured the difference: report the "mean difference" lines, and the bound can be tightened (or the Metal reference images split off).

docs.title: Rendering
docs.text: The renderer is built on Graphics: a render graph, the Forward+ lighting pipeline and the dev overlay.

docs.title: The render graph
docs.text:
A frame's rendering is a graph of passes over images and buffers. A pass says how it uses each resource; the graph works out what runs, where the memory comes from, and every barrier. You build a new graph every frame (it is cheap); the memory persists in a pool.

using var pool = new TransientPool(device);                       // lives as long as the renderer

void RenderFrame(Frame frame, Backbuffer back)
{
    var graph = new RenderGraph(device, pool);
    ImageHandle backbuffer = graph.ImportBackbuffer(back);        // starts undefined, ends ready to present
    ImageHandle hdr = graph.CreateImage("HDR color", new ImageDescription(PixelFormat.R16G16B16A16Sfloat, back.Width, back.Height,
        ImageUsage.ColorAttachment | ImageUsage.Sampled));

    graph.AddPass("Scene", PassType.Graphics, pass =>
    {
        pass.WriteColor(hdr, clear: new Vector4(0, 0, 0, 1));     // the graph begins and ends the rendering
        pass.Execute(ctx => DrawScene(ctx.Recorder));
    });
    graph.AddPass("Tonemap", PassType.Graphics, pass =>
    {
        pass.ReadSampled(hdr);
        pass.WriteColor(backbuffer, clear: Vector4.Zero);
        pass.Execute(ctx => Tonemap(ctx.Recorder, ctx.Image(hdr).SampledIndex));    // the bindless index to read it by
    });
    graph.Execute(frame);
}

Declaring. AddPass(name, type, setup) runs setup immediately; it declares uses on the PassBuilder and sets the callback that records the commands (pass.Execute). Images: ReadSampled, WriteColor, WriteDepth, ReadDepth, WriteStorage, ReadWriteStorage, CopyFrom, CopyTo. Buffers: Read, Write, ReadWrite, ReadIndirect (the arguments of an indirect dispatch or draw), CopyFrom, CopyTo. The difference between write and read-write matters: a write replaces everything (so whatever wrote it earlier is no longer needed, and a fresh transient can be written first), a read-write needs the previous contents. Attachments are begun and ended by the graph for graphics passes, with clear (give a value) or load (give none); depth is reverse-Z, so its default clear is 0. A pass the graph cannot see the effect of calls NoCull().

Mips and layers. Every image method takes an optional SubresourceRange (SubresourceRange.Mip(2), Layer(3), Of(mip, layer), Mips(1), Layers(0, 2); a count of uint.MaxValue means all that remain). Without one a pass uses the whole image; with one, only that part, and the graph keeps a state for each mip level and layer. So one pass can read level n while it writes level n+1 of the same image, a mip chain or a cube map is built a level or a face at a time, and the barrier in front of a pass moves only the parts it uses (a whole image in one state is still one barrier). A transient may have several mips and layers (ImageDescription.MipLevels, ArrayLayers, Cube; not multisampling); an attachment is one mip level, so a range is required for an image with several.

ImageHandle chain = graph.CreateImage("Bloom", new ImageDescription(PixelFormat.R16G16B16A16Sfloat, w, h, ImageUsage.Storage | ImageUsage.Sampled, MipLevels: 6));
for (uint mip = 1; mip < 6; mip++)
{
    uint level = mip;
    graph.AddPass($"Down {level}", PassType.Compute, pass =>
    {
        pass.ReadSampled(chain, SubresourceRange.Mip(level - 1));
        pass.WriteStorage(chain, SubresourceRange.Mip(level));
        pass.Execute(ctx =>
        {
            ResolvedImage source = ctx.Image(chain, SubresourceRange.Mip(level - 1));      // a view of that level alone
            ResolvedImage target = ctx.Image(chain, SubresourceRange.Mip(level));
            Downsample(ctx.Recorder, source.SampledIndex, target.StorageIndex, target.Width, target.Height);
        });
    });
}

Compiling (graph.Compile(), done by Execute if you did not) is pure and needs no GPU:

  1. Culling. Walking back from the outputs (the backbuffer, and imports marked output: true), a pass runs only if it writes something that is needed; what it reads becomes needed. A pass that overwrites a resource completely (all its mips and layers) makes earlier writers of it unneeded; one that writes a part of it does not.
  2. Validation. A read of something no earlier pass wrote is a RenderGraphException (for an image, every mip and layer the read covers must have been written), as are one part of a resource used two ways in a pass, a range outside the image, attachments of different sizes (an attachment is the size of its mip level), and attachments in a compute pass.
  3. Memory. Transients whose lifetimes do not overlap and whose descriptions are equal share one image (buffers: equal size and usage).
  4. Barriers. In front of each pass, one batched barrier brings each resource from its last state to the one the pass declared. Reading a resource again in the same state needs none; anything after a write does, even in the same state. Imported resources leave in the state you gave (Present for the backbuffer). graph.Plan describes the result (ToString() prints it for the dev overlay); PassPlan.ImageBarriers lists the image rectangles (mips and layers, before and after) of each pass.

Executing. Each live pass runs inside frame.Scope(name), so it is a RenderDoc label and a GPU timer. PassContext resolves handles: ctx.Image(h) gives the VkImage, view, size and, for transients created with Sampled / Storage usage, the bindless index to read or write it by; ctx.Image(h, range) gives the same for a part of the image: a view of just those mips and layers, the bindless indices for that view, and the size of its first mip (the indices exist when the image has the Sampled / Storage usage, and a storage view is a 2D view, which RWTexture2D in common.slang reads: see the bindless heap). ctx.Buffer(h) gives the GpuBuffer (use .Address in push constants).

Transients come from TransientPool, one set per frame in flight, so a steady-state frame allocates nothing; resources unused for eight frames are freed. A transient image with Sampled or Storage usage keeps its bindless slot for as long as it lives, and so do the views of its parts that passes asked for (made the first time and kept with the image). The views of a part of an imported image are made per frame and destroyed when the same frame slot next starts a graph, after the GPU has finished with them. Limits: transients have no multisampling, a storage view of a cube or array is read as RWTexture2D (one face or layer at a time), and everything runs on the one queue.

new RenderGraph() without a device can only be compiled, which is how the planner is unit tested.

docs.title: Where shaders come from: ShaderLibrary
docs.text: Renderers get their shaders from a ShaderLibrary (SceneRenderer(device, shaders); the default is ShaderLibrary.Standard(cacheDirectory), the Shaders folder next to the program mounted as shaders://). Load("shaders://forward.slang") takes the compiled artifact when the folder was imported (imported/forward.slang.ashader, made by Apogee.Runtime --import, which ./build.sh aot runs on the published programs) and never touches the Slang compiler. A module without an artifact is compiled (development), if the compiler library is there; if it is not, the error says to import the folder. A mod's shaders are loaded the same way from mod://id/… and its own imported/.

docs.title: Rebuilding pipelines when a shader changes
docs.text:
