ShaderLibrary.NotifyChanged(paths) takes the virtual paths of changed files (HotReloader.ShadersChanged reports them, or a VfsWatcher over the shaders' folders) and raises ModulesChanged with the modules it had loaded that are one of those files or were made from one (the files a compile read are in CompiledShader.Dependencies, the artifact's in the index), so an edit to common.slang reaches every shader that imports it. SceneRenderer and ImGuiRenderer keep their pipelines in ReloadablePipelines<T> groups, one per shader module (the two cluster shaders are one group), and only the groups that use a changed module are rebuilt:

  1. Off the render thread. The change starts a build on another thread: the module is compiled through the library and the pipelines are made (pipeline creation needs no external synchronization). The frame is not held up; the renderer keeps drawing with the pipelines it has. Changes that arrive during a build start one more right after it.
  2. Swapped at a frame boundary. Render (or AddPasses) calls Apply(frame) first: if a build has finished, its pipelines become the current ones there, so a frame never mixes old and new.
  3. Destroyed when the GPU is done. The old pipelines go through frame.Defer, which frees them when that frame's slot comes round again, after the frames that used them have completed. The tests record several frames without waiting, rebuild in the middle, and the validation layer must stay silent (it does not when the old pipelines are destroyed at once).
  4. A shader that does not compile changes nothing. The old pipelines stay, the error (file, line, message) is logged and held in ShaderLibrary.Errors for the dev overlay, and the next edit that compiles clears it. Pipelines that are made lazily per target format are made again for the formats already seen, in the same build.

The runtime's --watch mounts the shaders' source folders when it runs from the repository, and the viewer's --watch does the same, so saving a .slang file changes the picture of the running program.

docs.title: Forward+
docs.text:
SceneRenderer draws a RenderScene (a ModelData on the GPU) with a Camera, using a render graph it builds every frame.

using var renderer = new SceneRenderer(device, cacheDirectory: shaderCache);     // loads the shaders in <program>/Shaders (compiled ahead of time, else compiled now)
using RenderScene scene = renderer.CreateScene(GltfLoader.Load("Sponza.gltf", options));
var camera = new Camera { Position = new Vector3(0, 2, 8) };
camera.LookAt(Vector3.Zero);

Frame frame = loop.BeginFrame()!;
renderer.Render(frame, scene, camera, RenderTarget.Window(frame.Backbuffer!.Value), new RenderSettings { Tonemapper = Tonemapper.Gt7, ExposureMode = ExposureMode.Auto });
loop.EndFrame(frame);

The frame. Depth prepass (opaque and alpha-masked geometry into a reverse-Z D32 image) → Build clusters (only when the projection changed) → Cull lights → Forward (PBR into an RGBA16F image, opaque and masked, then blended surfaces far to near, depth-tested against the prepass; the camera's exposure is applied here) → Luminance histogram and Resolve exposure (auto-exposure only) → Tonemap (the GT7 or the Khronos PBR Neutral tone mapper, and the sRGB transfer function, into the target). The units of the lights, the exposure and the tone mappers are in Exposure and tone mapping. renderer.LastPlan is the graph and LastStats the draw, light and cluster counts.

Clusters. The view is cut into 16 x 9 cells over the screen and 24 slices in depth, spaced exponentially between the camera's Near and ClusterFar (a slice is thin close to the camera and long far away, so every cell holds a similar amount of space as seen from the eye). A compute shader builds each cluster's view-space box; another tests every light's sphere against every box and keeps at most 64 lights per cluster in a fixed-size list, so there are no atomics and nothing to clear. The forward shader finds the pixel's cluster from its screen position and depth and loops over only those lights. ClusterGrid has the same arithmetic on the CPU. A cluster's bounds are per frame-in-flight and are rebuilt only when the projection changes. Spot lights are culled by their bounding sphere (the cone is applied when shading).

Lighting. glTF metallic-roughness materials with Cook-Torrance GGX: Smith visibility, Schlick Fresnel, Lambert diffuse, base color, metallic-roughness, normal, occlusion and emissive textures with KHR_texture_transform, alpha mask and blend, double-sided, and unlit. Lights are point and spot (RenderScene.Lights, editable every frame; light is photometric, see Exposure and tone mapping; intensity is candela, falling off as the inverse square and reaching zero exactly at the light's radius, which is its glTF range or where it fades below a faint threshold) plus one directional sun (SunDirection, SunColor, in lux) and a two-colour ambient. No shadows and no image-based lighting yet, so a smooth metal reflects only the lights. RenderSettings.Debug = DebugView.ClusterLights tints each pixel by its cluster's light count (dark: none; blue to red: one to eight or more).

Conventions. Right-handed, +Y up, a camera looking down -Z at yaw 0. Reverse-Z with an infinite far plane: depth 1 at the near plane, 0 at infinity, compare greater-or-equal. The projection flips y (Vulkan's normalized y points down), which keeps the image and so the winding: front faces are counter-clockwise, as in glTF. Matrices are row-major and used with row vectors, as in System.Numerics.

Culling. Before the passes are recorded, every draw's bounds (the mesh's box carried to the camera's axes, written each frame into six float arrays together with the instance) are tested against the camera's view volume (Frustum: left, right, bottom, top and the near plane; the far plane is at infinity) with SIMD, and only the draws inside go into the depth and forward passes. It is exact for the planes, so it never drops a draw that touches the view and may keep one near a corner that is not visible. LastStats.Culled counts what was left out, RenderSettings.CullDraws = false turns it off to compare (CullingTests requires the same picture either way, and that a camera turned away culls everything). The measurements and the instruction set shipped games are built for are in Profiling and SIMD. The per-pass lists of draws are reused from frame to frame instead of allocated.

A double-precision world, rendered camera-relative. Camera.Position and RenderScene.Origin are Double3 (see Math): renderer.CreateScene(model, at: new Double3(5_000_000, 0, 2_000_000)) puts a model 5 000 km out, and the model's own coordinates (instances, lights, bounds) stay relative to that origin. Nothing on the GPU is in world coordinates. Each frame:

  • Camera.View has the camera at the origin (rotation only; camera.WorldToView(point) takes a world point there, subtracting in double first);
  • the renderer writes the frame slot's instance records with their translation (placement position - camera.Position) + offset, subtracted in double and then narrowed, so a scene 10 000 km away is as precise as one at the origin (the instance buffer is per frame in flight, like the cluster buffers, and grows when a frame needs more; the matrices' linear part is stored once at load);
  • lights and the blend sort are moved the same way, and GpuFrameData.CameraPosition is zero, which the shaders (that subtract it from a surface position) need no change for.

ForwardPlusTests.TheSceneLooksTheSameFarFromTheWorldsOrigin renders the golden scene at the origin, at 100 km and at 10 000 km and requires the same picture.

Data for the shaders. One GpuFrameData per frame (in the frame's upload arena) holds the matrices, the screen, the sun, and the addresses of the instance (rewritten every frame), light and cluster buffers; a draw pushes the frame's address, the instance number and the addresses of the vertices and materials of its model (a model has buffers of its own). Shaders/common.slang is the Slang side of GpuStructs.cs; the structs use only 16-byte aligned members (and the vertex is twelve explicit floats) so that every layout rule agrees, and tests pin the sizes and offsets.

Tests. The planner and the math run without a GPU. On a GPU: a GPU-vs-CPU comparison of the light lists of all 3456 clusters (every light that is inside by a margin must be listed, every listed light inside by a margin), the sky tone-mapped exactly like the CPU twin, lights brighten what they should and nothing beyond their radius, spot cones, the sun, alpha mask and blend, double-sided surfaces, the heatmap, the 64-light cap, 600 lights, and a golden image rendered by the software rasterizer (Golden/forward_plus.png; APOGEE_UPDATE_GOLDEN=1 rewrites it). The discrete GPU matches it to a mean of 0.02 out of 255.

docs.title: Drawing a world of entities
docs.text:
A RenderScene is one model with its own lights. A game draws entities: any number of models, each placed by an entity, lit by light entities, seen through a camera entity. The pieces:

  • GpuModel is a ModelData on the GPU: its vertex, index and material buffers, its textures in the bindless heap, and a record per mesh instance (ModelNode: its matrices without the translation, its box, its first index). It is placed any number of times at no cost but one instance record per mesh. renderer.CreateModel(data) makes one; a RenderScene is a GpuModel plus an origin, a sun and lights.
  • ModelLibrary gives models ids: Load(path) returns the same id for the same path, however many entities show it, and reads the model through the virtual file system (imported .amodel when there is one). Ids exist before there is a GPU, because a game's scripts run before the renderer is made: the model is read and uploaded the first time a frame needs it (Attach(renderer, caps) says where), a file that does not load is logged once and draws nothing, and Reload(path) swaps a changed file in under the same id (the runtime does it for the --watch run, after the importer). Detach() frees the GPU side before the device goes. Scripts see the library as the global models: models:load("res://packages/car/car.glb") (or models:load("uid://…"), see asset identity). It reads any mounted path, as audio does: the engine's classes do not know which mod called them.
  • Components (Components.cs, all visible to scripts and, later, the editor): ModelRenderer { Model } draws the model at the entity's WorldTransform (position, rotation and scale place every mesh); Light { Color, Intensity, Range, InnerCone, OuterCone, Kind } is a point, spot or (kind 0) directional light shining along the entity's -Z, and the first directional one is the sun; CameraComponent { FovDegrees, Near, ClusterFar } is a lens, and the entity that also has the MainCamera tag is the eye. The lights a model came with move with its entity.
  • RenderWorld(world, models) reads those entities when a frame is rendered (queries over WorldTransform, so what the systems moved this frame is what is drawn; nothing is copied or kept in sync) and SceneRenderer.Render(frame, renderWorld, camera, target) draws it. renderWorld.TryGetMainCamera(camera) fills a Camera from the main camera entity (roll is ignored: yaw, then pitch). DefaultSunDirection, DefaultSunColor and the ambient colours are what a world without a directional light uses.

Both kinds of scene go through one renderer core. It gathers placements (a model, a double-precision position, a rotation, a scale) and lights, writes one GpuInstance per mesh instance with the placement's rotation and scale composed in (normals take S^-1 * R, so non-uniform scale lights correctly) and its translation relative to the camera, builds the boxes from the same numbers, culls, and draws by pass. A draw binds its model's index buffer when the model changes and pushes the model's vertex and material addresses, so many models share one frame without sharing buffers.

In the runtime. --game and --run draw the world through its main camera when it has one, with the ImGui frame over it; the scene renderer is not even made (and its shaders not compiled) until then, so a script that only has panels keeps drawing them over the plain background, exactly as before. Without a GPU (--headless without --screenshot) ids and entities exist and nothing is drawn.

local Transform, ModelRenderer = world:component("Transform"), world:component("ModelRenderer")
local CameraComponent, MainCamera = world:component("CameraComponent"), world:component("MainCamera")

local car = models:load("res://packages/garage/car.glb")
local e = world:create_entity("car")
world:set(e, Transform, { Position = Vector3(0, 0, 0), Rotation = Quat.identity, Scale = Vector3(1, 1, 1) })
world:set(e, ModelRenderer, { Model = car })

local eye = world:create_entity("eye")
world:set(eye, Transform, { Position = Vector3(0, 1.5, 6), Rotation = Quat.identity, Scale = Vector3(1, 1, 1) })
world:set(eye, CameraComponent, { FovDegrees = 60, Near = 0.05, ClusterFar = 100 })
world:add(eye, MainCamera)

RenderWorldTests check, on a GPU, that an entity draws what a scene of the same model draws, that five entities share one model (draw counts), that scale and rotation place the model, that lights and the sun light the world, that an unknown or removed id draws nothing, that a model 3 000 km out looks the same as at the origin, that the main camera entity drives the camera, and that models load once per path and reload in place; WorldRenderingTests run a game folder with a model, a light and a camera through --headless --screenshot.

docs.title: Debug drawing
docs.text:
DebugDraw (in Apogee.Core, so anything can add to it without knowing about rendering) is immediate mode: lines and triangles in double-precision world positions that live for one frame. Line, Triangle, Box (turned, or from two corners), Circle, Sphere, Arrow and Axes add them; colors are bytes r, g, b, a as a uint (DebugColor.Rgba, DebugColor.Red, ...). It keeps at most Capacity (a million) lines and as many triangles and counts the rest in Dropped, so a loop that draws too much costs detail, not memory. Physics adds to it with PhysicsWorld.DrawDebug (physics); scripts use the debug_draw library (debug_draw.line(from, to, color), box, sphere, arrow, axes; a color is a vector of red, green and blue from 0 to 1, white without one), called every frame for as long as the picture should stay.

RenderSettings.DebugDraw is the instance to draw; the renderer reads it and does not clear it (whoever fills it clears it: the runtime does after every frame). When it is not empty a pass, Debug draw, is added between the forward pass and tone mapping: it loads the HDR image, depth-tests against the scene's depth without writing it, and so draws over the lit picture before the tone mapper, as display-referred colors (the exposure does not change them; debug_draw.slang takes the colors as sRGB). The tone mapper then treats them like any other color: with Tonemapper.PbrNeutral they come out as they went in, with GT7 the brightest and most saturated ones are pulled a little towards white.

  • Lines are quads of two triangles, widened to RenderSettings.DebugLineWidth pixels (1.5 by default) in the vertex shader: hardware line width is not portable (Metal has none). A quad cannot be left to the clipper, so the shader cuts a line at the near plane itself, and a line wholly behind the camera is not drawn. The part of a line that is behind something is drawn again without the depth test, at DebugHiddenAlpha (0.25; 0 hides it).
  • Triangles are drawn solid with flat shading from a light at the eye, so a face looking at the camera is bright and one seen edge-on is dim.
  • Camera-relative, like the scene: DebugDrawRenderer writes the positions as offsets from the camera, subtracting in double first, so a line 3 000 km out lands on the same pixels as one at the origin (DebugDrawRenderingTests render both). The buffers are per frame in flight and grow when a frame needs more.

DebugDrawRenderingTests read pixels back: a line is a stripe of its color and a wider one covers more, hidden parts follow DebugHiddenAlpha, a line behind the camera changes nothing and one crossing the near plane is cut there, triangles are shaded, and an empty DebugDraw adds no pass.

docs.title: Exposure and tone mapping
docs.text:
The renderer lights the scene in physical units, exposes it like a camera, and then tone maps the exposed image to the screen. This page describes the three steps, the settings that control them, and the units the lights are in. The code is in Source/Apogee.Rendering (ExposureMath.cs, Gt7ToneMapping.cs and the shaders forward.slang, exposure.slang and tonemap.slang).

lights (lux, candela)  →  forward pass: luminance in cd/m²  →  × exposure  →  HDR image (exposed values)
                                                                                    │
                                          luminance histogram → auto-exposure ──────┤  (next frame's exposure)
                                                                                    ▼
                                                          tone mapper (GT7 or PBR Neutral) → sRGB → screen

docs.title: Units: light is photometric
docs.text:
The forward pass computes luminance in cd/m² (nits) from lights in the units the glTF format uses (KHR_lights_punctual):

What Unit In the code The sun (Light.Sun, RenderScene.SunColor) lux (illuminance on a surface facing the sun) SunColor is color × lux; a surface facing the sun is lit with that many lux Point and spot lights (Light.Point, Intensity) candela (luminous intensity) color × candela, divided by the squared distance: lux on a surface facing the light Ambient (AmbientSky, AmbientGround) cd/m²: the radiance of the environment multiplied by the surface's albedo (not by π: a radiance is not an illuminance) Emissive (MaterialData.EmissiveFactor, KHR_materials_emissive_strength) cd/m² (nits) added as it is Unlit materials, the sky color, debug lines display-referred colors not light: the exposure does not change them

A surface of albedo a lit by E lux straight on, seen from the front, has the luminance E · (a / π) (plus a little specular): 100 000 lux of sun on a white wall of 0.8 is about 25 000 cd/m². The tests check this: a sun of 2 lux and a point light of 200 cd 10 m above the same ground give the same picture, and its luminance is the one the BRDF gives.

A point light's fall-off is the inverse square with a smooth window that reaches exactly zero at its radius (Range, or where it falls below 0.05 lux when it has none, at most 500 m). That radius is a culling bound and does not depend on the exposure, so a very dark scene, exposed for starlight, can show the edge of a light whose range is left to the default; give such lights an explicit Range.

Content authored before this page (suns of 3, lamps of 80 candela) is far too dim to be real, which is why the default exposure is automatic: whatever the scale of the lights, the image is exposed for it. When you author in real units (a sunny day is about 100 000 lux, a lit room 100 to 500 lux, moonlight 0.1 lux) the exposure also tells you what a camera would see.

docs.title: Exposure
docs.text:
A camera's exposure is one number, the EV100 (exposure value at ISO 100). For an aperture f/N, a shutter time t in seconds and a sensitivity S:

EV100 = log2(N² / t) − log2(S / 100)

One stop of aperture, shutter or ISO is one EV. A sunny day with f/16 at 1/100 s and ISO 100 is EV100 14.6; a lit room is about 5.

The forward pass multiplies the luminance by 1 / (1.2 · 2^EV100) (the saturation-based exposure of a camera at that EV100) before it writes the HDR image. The HDR image therefore holds exposed values: 1.0 is the luminance that just saturates the sensor, a bright sun does not overflow the half-float image the way raw cd/m² would, and everything after the forward pass (tone mapping, the debug draw) works on numbers around 0 to 1. A half float tops out at 65 504, and a very bright highlight at a low EV100 can still reach it (at EV100 −6 the exposure is 53), so the forward pass clamps its result to 65 504 instead of letting it become an infinity, which would turn into NaN in later passes; the tone mapper also takes an infinity as 65 504.

RenderSettings.ExposureMode chooses the EV100:

Mode EV100 Settings Fixed the value you set Ev100 Camera from the physical camera Aperture, ShutterSeconds, Iso Auto (default) measured from the scene every frame, adapted over time Ev100 (first frame), MinEv100, MaxEv100, AdaptationSpeedBright, AdaptationSpeedDark, AutoLowPercentile, AutoHighPercentile

RenderSettings.Exposure is an exposure compensation as a factor (2 is one stop brighter) on top of any mode.

var settings = new RenderSettings
{
    ExposureMode = ExposureMode.Camera,
    Aperture = 8f, ShutterSeconds = 1f / 125f, Iso = 100f,   // EV100 ≈ 13
    Exposure = 1.5f,                                          // and a little brighter
};

docs.title: Auto-exposure
docs.text:
Two compute passes run after the forward pass, and nothing is read back to the CPU:

  1. Luminance histogram (buildHistogram). Every pixel where something lit was drawn adds one to a bin of a 256-bin histogram of its luminance's log2. Bin 0 counts what is not measured (black, below the range, NaN or infinite), bins 1 to 254 divide the range 2⁻¹⁰ to 2¹⁸ cd/m² (0.001 to 262 000, 28 stops, about a ninth of a stop per bin) evenly, and bin 255 holds what is at or above the top. A pixel's luminance is its value divided by the exposure the frame was drawn with. What is not light is left out: pixels where nothing was drawn (the sky color), found by their depth, and opaque unlit pixels, which the forward pass writes with alpha 0 (an unlit color divided by the exposure would read as a luminance that moves with the exposure, and push it further every frame). A blended unlit surface mixes with what is behind it and is measured with it. The group counts in shared memory and adds its counts to the global histogram.
  2. Resolve exposure (resolveExposure). One thread averages the histogram without its darkest 10 % and brightest 10 % of pixels (a few lamps should not darken the image, a dark corner should not brighten it), gets the EV100 log2(L · 100 / 12.5) that exposes that luminance as a mid-gray (12.5 is the reflected-light meter's calibration constant), clamps it to MinEv100 and MaxEv100, and moves the exposure towards it: ev += (target − ev) · (1 − e^(−speed · dt)), with AdaptationSpeedBright (default 3 per second) when the scene got brighter and AdaptationSpeedDark (1) when it got darker, as an eye does. It writes the exposure into a small persistent buffer and clears the histogram for the next frame.

The forward pass of the next frame reads the exposure from that buffer, on the GPU, so no frame waits for the previous one. The consequences:

  • The first frame of auto-exposure, and the first after another mode, is drawn with Ev100; the histogram then sets the exposure to the target at once (no crawl from a stale value), and the second frame is right.
  • The frame time for the adaptation is measured between calls to Render (clamped to a quarter of a second); RenderSettings.DeltaTime sets it, which the tests use to be repeatable.
  • There is no way yet to snap the adaptation on a camera cut or a scene load while staying in Auto (it restarts only after another mode); after a cut the exposure takes a second or two to settle. Not done.
  • The state belongs to the SceneRenderer: two views drawn by one renderer share an exposure. Give each its own renderer when they should adapt separately.

ExposureMath is the CPU twin of all of this (EV100, the scale, a bin, the percentile average, the adaptation), and the tests run the shader passes against it.

docs.title: Tone mapping
docs.text: RenderSettings.Tonemapper chooses what turns the exposed image into the display's range. The result is encoded with the sRGB transfer function in the shader (the swapchain is UNORM).

docs.title: Tonemapper.Gt7 (default)
docs.text:
Gran Turismo 7's operator, from Polyphony Digital's sample implementation (gt7_tone_mapping.cpp, MIT licence; the notice is in Legal/THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md), ported to tonemap.slang and, as its twin, to Gt7ToneMapping.cs. It works like this:

  1. The color goes to linear Rec.2020 (the renderer's working space is Rec.709, the sRGB primaries) and is scaled to the operator's frame-buffer units, where 1.0 is 100 cd/m².
  2. Each channel goes through a curve: a power-law toe, a linear section (the identity from 0.538 up to 0.444 of the peak) and an exponential shoulder that levels off just above the display's peak.
  3. The result is also taken to ICtCp (a perceptual color space with the lightness I apart from the chroma Ct and Cp). The curved color's lightness is combined with the input's chroma, which is faded out as the lightness nears the peak. Per-channel curves alone shift hues (saturated bright colors skew towards yellow or cyan); keeping the chroma fixes the hue, and fading it makes the brightest colors go to white.
  4. The two results are blended (60 % of the chroma-preserving one), cut to the peak, and scaled so that the peak is the display's white.

SDR mode is the one the renderer uses: the display's white is the operator's paper white of 250 cd/m² (2.5 in frame-buffer units), which is where the curve's parameters were tuned. The renderer maps the exposed value 1.0 (the luminance that saturates the sensor) to that paper white, so a mid-gray at 18 % is shown as a mid-tone and the sensor's saturation just under white. The output is converted back to Rec.709 (colors outside the sRGB gamut are clipped) before the sRGB encoding.

Two small differences from the original, both for the GPU: negative and NaN channels are taken as 0 and an infinity as 65 504 before the operator (it assumes valid input, and an infinity makes NaN in the ICtCp conversion), and the constants it sets up once for the SDR peak (the shoulder's kA, kB, kC and the lightness of the peak) are literals in the shader, which a test compares with the C# twin's. The C# twin clamps an HDR peak to the original's 250 to 10 000 cd/m². HDR output (the operator's HDR mode on an HDR10 swapchain) is not implemented. The twin is also tested against the original's own test inputs (SDR and HDR peaks of 1000, 4000 and 10 000), with the outputs computed from the original's source.

docs.title: Tonemapper.PbrNeutral
docs.text: The Khronos PBR Neutral tone mapper, as before. It leaves colors below a compression point alone, so a base color texture shows as it was authored, which suits product views and flat-lit stylized scenes. Its input is the exposed value as it is.

docs.title: Reading the settings together
docs.text:
I want Use A scene lit in real units that adapts like an eye ExposureMode.Auto (the default), with MinEv100/MaxEv100 to keep it in a plausible range A scene that stays the same brightness whatever the camera sees ExposureMode.Fixed and an Ev100 (about 15 for sun, 12 overcast, 6 to 8 indoors) Photographic control ExposureMode.Camera with aperture, shutter and ISO The brightness of the previous renderer for unit-scale content Tonemapper.PbrNeutral, ExposureMode.Fixed, and Ev100 = -log2(1.2) (an exposure of exactly 1)

The dev overlay's exposure slider is the compensation (RenderSettings.Exposure).

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
• Gt7ToneMappingTests: the curve (toe, linear section, continuity, monotonic, the shoulder's asymptote), PQ against its known values, ICtCp round trips, the gamut matrices against the Rec.709 and Rec.2020 primaries they are derived from, infinities, the shader's literal constants, and the original's outputs for its test inputs.
  • ToneMappingGpuTests: an image of gradients (gray and colors, 0.002 to 30, the last column infinite) goes through tonemap.slang and every pixel is compared with the CPU twin, for GT7 and for Neutral.
  • ExposureMathTests: EV100, the scale, the bins, the percentile average and the adaptation.
  • ExposureTests: the histogram pass against the CPU's bins on an image whose size is not a multiple of the group; the exposure pass against ExposureMath (first frame, brighter, darker, clamped, cleared); an unlit quad covering most of the view not moving the exposure; an emitter of known luminance at several EV100s; the physical camera against the same EV100 set by hand; a lux and a candela giving the same picture with the luminance the BRDF predicts; and auto-exposure following a scene four stops darker with the adaptation's rate and restarting after another mode.

docs.title: Native bindings
docs.text:
Raw bindings for each C library are generated by our own tool, Tools/Apogee.Build/Bindings (ClangSharp.Interop over libclang). Output goes to Source/Apogee.Native.<Lib>/Generated/ and is committed; nothing in Generated/ is edited by hand.

./build.sh bindings           # all libraries
./build.sh bindings sdl flecs # some

Each library has a JSON config in Tools/Apogee.Build/Bindings/Configs/: headers and include directories, ownDirs (declarations found elsewhere are foreign and not bound), prefixes and suffixes to strip, renames, macro groups that become [Flags] enums, and regexes for functions and constants to leave out. What was skipped, and why, is written to Bin/bindings/<lib>.skipped.txt.

A config can name a type that another binding defines (foreignTypes, a regex on C names mapped to a namespace): it is then referenced and not bound again, by the name that binding gives it (the same stripPrefixes and renames, as rmlui.json and cimgui.json have). Enum members lose the common prefix they share with their enum (JPH_MotionType_Static is MotionType.Static), and members whose C name starts with an underscore (_JPH_MotionType_Count, _JPH_MotionType_Force32: reserved names, not values) are left out.

Vulkan is generated from the Khronos registry ("kind": "vulkan") rather than headers, and loads commands through vkGetInstanceProcAddr into VkGlobalCommands, VkInstanceCommands and VkDeviceCommands.

Steamworks ("kind": "steam") is generated from Valve's steam_api.json and the S_API declarations of its flat API, because the headers are C++: the config names the interfaces to bind (interfaces) and the core functions (includeFunctions). libclang parses the headers only to measure the structs, once with Linux's 4-byte callback packing and once as Windows (8), and the structs whose size differs are emitted with Pack = SteamPack.Callback (Native libraries).

docs.title: What is generated
docs.text: Blittable structs, unmanaged function pointers for callbacks, opaque handles as readonly structs, DllImports with ExactSpelling (runtime marshalling is disabled in every binding assembly), a module initializer that registers the library with NativeLibraries, and a Sizes table of every struct's C size.

docs.title: Build defines
docs.text: The headers are read with the defines the native library is built with ("defines" in the config, and the same ones in Native/<lib>/CMakeLists.txt). Struct layouts can depend on them: Flecs has more fields in ecs_ref_t and ecs_map_t in a debug build, so its binding is generated with FLECS_NDEBUG and the library is always compiled with it. The struct size test cannot catch this, because it compares with what clang saw, not with the compiled library; FlecsRefsHaveTheLayoutOfTheCompiledLibrary calls a function that returns such a struct by value.

docs.title: Exported variables
docs.text:
extern variables (extern const ecs_entity_t EcsOnUpdate;) become ref properties that look the symbol up by name the first time they are used, so the value is always the library's, filled in by its init function:

ulong phase = Ecs.OnUpdate;        // ref readonly ulong: the variable is const in C
Ecs.ComponentId                    // ecs_id(EcsComponent), the symbol FLECS_IDEcsComponentID_

globalRenames (regex → replacement, first match wins, applied before the usual stripping) maps odd symbol names; excludeGlobals leaves out variables the library does not export (debug-only ones, or ones declared without a definition). Arrays are not bound. A variable whose name is a function's keeps the full C name (EcsDelete next to Delete).

docs.title: Array parameters
docs.text: A C parameter written as an array (float color[4]) is a pointer to its first element: the binding takes float*, not an inline array by value (libclang reports the written type, and passing the bytes where an address is expected crashes). Fields of structs are different: they are fixed buffers or inline arrays.

docs.title: Types from another binding
docs.text:
A library whose headers use another library's types (VMA uses Vulkan's) lists them in foreignTypes: a regex on the C type name and the C# namespace of the binding assembly that has it under the same name.

"foreignTypes": { "^Vk": "Apogee.Native.Vulkan" },
"typeMap": { "VkBufferUsageFlags": "VkBufferUsageFlagBits", "VkBool32": "uint", "VkDeviceSize": "ulong" }

Those types are referenced (the generated files get a using for the namespace, and the project references the other binding), never generated again. The Vulkan binding names flags typedefs differently from C (VkBufferUsageFlags is the VkBufferUsageFlagBits enum, VkBool32 is uint), so those go in typeMap, which is looked at first. A name that the other assembly lacks is a compile error in the generated code, not a silent void*.

docs.title: Vulkan structure types
docs.text:
Every Vulkan struct that starts with sType has a parameterless constructor that sets it from the registry, so new VkRenderingInfo { … } is correct by default:

var rendering = new VkRenderingInfo { LayerCount = 1, RenderArea = area };   // SType is VkStructureType.RenderingInfo

default(T), stackalloc and arrays of the struct do not run it: set SType yourself there (or loop over the array).

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Tests/Apogee.Build.Tests runs the generator on fixture headers and on the Vulkan registry, and checks that the committed Vulkan bindings are what the generator writes now (it needs clang; the tests skip without it).

Tests/Apogee.Native.Tests checks, for every binding assembly, that every entry point resolves in the native library, that every exported variable is found, that every struct size equals the one clang computed, and calls into each library. Library assemblies are skipped, with a message, when the native library is not installed.

docs.title: Native libraries
docs.text: What is bound and how to use it. Where each library comes from and how it was built is in ThirdParty/README.md.

docs.title: Luau (Apogee.Native.Luau)
docs.text:
The VM, the compiler and the native code generator in one library, plus our layer over them, Native/luau/apogee_luau.h. Luau is built with LUA_USE_LONGJMP: an error is a longjmp to the nearest protected call, and a longjmp must never cross a managed frame. So the binding leaves out what raises an error on input a script controls: lua_error, lua_call, the luaL_check*/luaL_opt* family, lua_gettable/lua_getfield and the other calls that run metamethods, lua_yield, and lua_pushcclosurek. What is bound can raise only on a programming error (writing to a read-only table, pushing without Checkstack) or when memory runs out, and the layer deals with that one.

State* state = Lua.NewVm(memoryLimit: 64 * 1024 * 1024);          // allocator, interrupt and accounting installed
Lua.LuaLOpenlibs(state);
Lua.PushManagedFunction(state, &Add, name, 0);                       // [UnmanagedCallersOnly] static int Add(State*)
Lua.Rawsetfield(state, Lua.Globalsindex, name);
if (Lua.LoadSource(state, chunk, source, size, 0) == CallResult.Ok)  // compiles, loads, native code for --!native chunks
    result = Lua.ProtectedCall(state, 0, 1, budgetMilliseconds);     // traceback on errors, time budget, memory errors
Lua.CloseVm(state);
  • A managed function returns its number of results, or Lua.Raise with the error value on top of the stack; the wrapper turns that into lua_error once managed code has returned. Its own upvalues start at index 2 (Globalsindex - 2).
  • Memory: NewVm takes a hard limit (SetMemoryLimit changes it: set it after the libraries are open). An allocation over it fails, and Luau raises the memory error, only while Luau code is the topmost thing running. One made by a managed function, or by the host outside a call, is never refused (nothing could catch the error, or it would unwind managed code); the error is raised when the managed function returns. SetCategoryLimit is a soft limit for a memory category (Setmemcat), raised at the next call or loop iteration, which is how each script owner gets its own cap in one VM.
  • Time: the budget of ProtectedCall/ProtectedResume (or SetTimeBudget) is armed by the outermost call. Once it has passed every call and loop iteration raises, so pcall in a script cannot swallow it. A long native function (string.rep) is not interrupted.
  • Bytecode from LuauCompile is freed with Lua.Free: it comes from the library's C runtime, which is not necessarily the caller's. LoadSource keeps it inside the library.
  • Native code (--!native, Luau::CodeGen) is on where the machine supports it (x64 and arm64); NativeEnabled says. It needs executable memory: a macOS app that is signed with the hardened runtime needs the allow-jit entitlement.
  • One state belongs to one thread at a time.

docs.title: Vulkan Memory Allocator (Apogee.Native.Vma)
docs.text:
VMA suballocates GPU memory. Its binding is Vma (functions) plus Allocator, Allocation, Pool… (the opaque structs behind VMA's handles; you only hold pointers to them).

var functions = new VulkanFunctions { VkGetInstanceProcAddr = …, VkGetDeviceProcAddr = … };
var info = new AllocatorCreateInfo
{
    PhysicalDevice = physicalDevice, Device = device, Instance = instance,
    VulkanApiVersion = Vk.ApiVersion13, PVulkanFunctions = &functions,
};
Allocator* allocator;
Vma.CreateAllocator(&info, &allocator);

The library is built without static Vulkan functions: it loads the rest through the two pointers you pass, so it works with whatever Vulkan loader the process uses. Flag typedefs are the *FlagBits enums (AllocationCreateFlagBits), already [Flags].

VirtualBlock needs no GPU: it hands out offsets from a range (used for sub-allocating our own buffers, and in tests).

docs.title: meshoptimizer (Apogee.Native.Meshopt)
docs.text:
Mesh processing: vertex deduplication, vertex cache / overdraw / vertex fetch optimization, simplification, meshlets and quantization. The binding is Meshopt and keeps the C spelling of the parameters. The content loader runs every mesh through it at import: GenerateVertexRemap → RemapIndexBuffer/RemapVertexBuffer → OptimizeVertexCache → OptimizeVertexFetch.

nuint unique = Meshopt.GenerateVertexRemap(remap, indices, indexCount, vertices, vertexCount, vertexSize);
Meshopt.RemapIndexBuffer(indices, indices, indexCount, remap);
Meshopt.OptimizeVertexCache(indices, indices, indexCount, unique);

docs.title: zstd (Apogee.Native.Zstd)
docs.text:
Compression, for packs and for libktx's KTX 2 supercompression. The binding is Zstd and covers the stable API of zstd.h and zstd_errors.h: one-shot Compress/Decompress (with CompressBound and GetFrameContentSize to size the buffers), streaming through CompressStream2/DecompressStream with InBuffer/OutBuffer, contexts (CreateCCtx, CCtxSetParameter), and dictionaries (CreateCDict/CreateDDict). Functions that fail return a size that IsError recognizes; GetErrorName and GetErrorCode say what happened. The library is built with worker threads, so CParameter.NbWorkers compresses on several threads.

byte[] frame = new byte[(int)Zstd.CompressBound((nuint)data.Length)];
nuint size = Zstd.Compress(target, (nuint)frame.Length, source, (nuint)data.Length, 3);
if (Zstd.IsError(size) != 0) throw new InvalidDataException(Marshal.PtrToStringUTF8((IntPtr)Zstd.GetErrorName(size)));

Zstd.ContentSizeUnknown and ContentSizeError are what GetFrameContentSize returns for a frame that does not say its size and for non-frames. libktx links this library (they have to sit next to each other, which the build arranges), so a zstd-compressed KTX 2 file is inflated by the same code.

docs.title: FreeType (Apogee.Native.FreeType)
docs.text:
Font rasterization, for the dev tools' text now (Dear ImGui's FreeType loader) and for RmlUi's. The binding is class FT over the public headers of the modules we build: loading a face (NewMemoryFace, NewFace), sizes, glyph loading and rendering (LoadChar, RenderGlyph, with the Load… flags and the RenderMode enum: anti-aliased, light, monochrome, LCD and signed distance fields), outlines, strokes, glyph and bitmap helpers, variable fonts (ftmm) and colour tables. The names drop the FT_ prefix (FT_Init_FreeType is FT.InitFreeType); FT_Library is LibraryRec* and FT_Face is FtFaceRec*; a C long is CLong.

LibraryRec* library;
FT.InitFreeType(&library);
FtFaceRec* face;
fixed (byte* font = fontBytes)   // the face reads this memory for as long as it lives: keep it pinned (or in native memory)
{
    FT.NewMemoryFace(library, font, new CLong(fontBytes.Length), new CLong(0), &face);
    FT.SetPixelSizes(face, 0, 16);
    FT.LoadChar(face, new CULong('A'), FT.LoadRender);
    Bitmap bitmap = face->Glyph->Bitmap;               // Rows, Width, Pitch, Buffer: 8-bit coverage
}

Every function returns an FT_Error: zero is success. The modules are TrueType and OpenType (tt, cff, sfnt), Type 1, CID and Type 42, the PostScript helpers, the auto-hinter, and the smooth, monochrome and SDF renderers; zlib is FreeType's own copy (WOFF 1 fonts and .gz files). Left out: the bitmap and Windows fonts, PFR, the SVG and colour-PNG glyphs, WOFF 2 (brotli) and HarfBuzz; ThirdParty/README.md lists them and how the library is configured (Native/freetype/apogee_ftoption.h, apogee_ftmodule.h). FreeType is used under the FreeType License (BSD-style, with a credit clause: a game that ships the library says so in its credits, see Legal/THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md). Dear ImGui's font atlas is rasterized by it: cimgui links this library (they sit next to each other) and ImGui makes it the default font loader. FreeTypeSmokeTests renders a glyph of a font loaded from memory through every renderer, and the common binding tests check the entry points and struct sizes.

docs.title: cgltf (Apogee.Native.Cgltf)
docs.text:
A glTF 2.0 parser (.gltf and .glb). Cgltf.Parse reads a file from memory and Cgltf.ParseFile from a path; both give a Data* that owns the parsed document and that you release with Cgltf.Free. Cgltf.LoadBuffers reads the binary buffers (external files and data URIs), Cgltf.Validate checks the document, and Cgltf.AccessorUnpackFloats / AccessorReadIndex read accessor data whatever its component type.

var options = new Options();
Data* data;
if (Cgltf.Parse(&options, bytes, size, &data) == Result.Success && Cgltf.LoadBuffers(&options, data, path) == Result.Success)
{
    Accessor* positions = data->Meshes[0].Primitives[0].Attributes[0].Data;
    Cgltf.AccessorUnpackFloats(positions, destination, floatCount);
}
Cgltf.Free(data);

The names are the C names without cgltf_; its booleans are plain ints.

Keep the parsed memory alive

For a .glb cgltf's buffers, and for any file its strings, point into the memory you passed to Parse, so that memory has to stay valid until Free. Pinning a managed array only for the call works under CoreCLR by luck (the array does not move) and breaks under NativeAOT. GltfLoader copies the file into native memory and frees it after Free.

docs.title: stb_image (Apogee.Native.Stb)
docs.text:
Decodes the common image formats (PNG, JPEG, BMP, TGA, GIF, PSD, HDR, PIC, PNM) from memory. The class is Stbi.

int width, height, channelsInFile;
byte* pixels = Stbi.LoadFromMemory(data, length, &width, &height, &channelsInFile, Stbi.RgbAlpha);
if (pixels == null) throw new InvalidDataException(Marshal.PtrToStringUTF8((IntPtr)Stbi.FailureReason()));
// …upload width * height * 4 bytes…
Stbi.ImageFree(pixels);

Asking for Stbi.RgbAlpha always gives four 8-bit channels, whatever the file has. Stbi.InfoFromMemory reads the size without decoding. There is no file API: read the bytes through the engine's file system first.

docs.title: libktx (Apogee.Native.Ktx)
docs.text:
Reads KTX 1 and KTX 2 textures, and writes KTX 2 with the Basis Universal encoder. Basis Universal data (ETC1S/BasisLZ and UASTC) is transcoded to whatever the GPU supports. The asset importer encodes UASTC with ktxTexture2_CompressBasisEx and supercompresses it with ktxTexture2_DeflateZstd (BasisEncoder, Asset import); the game only loads, but the encoder is in the same library (libktx is 2.1 MB on Linux with it; a shipped game never calls the encoder). Not built: the ASTC encoder (UASTC is transcoded to ASTC instead), and the OpenGL/Vulkan upload (the renderer uploads the bytes itself).

Texture2* texture;
Ktx.Texture2CreateFromMemory(bytes, size, TextureCreateFlagBits.LoadImageData, &texture);
if (Ktx.Texture2NeedsTranscoding(texture))
{
    // BC7 on desktop GPUs, ASTC 4x4 on mobile and Apple, RGBA8 as the fallback that always works.
    Ktx.Texture2TranscodeBasis(texture, TranscodeFmt.TtfBc7Rgba, 0);
}
nuint offset;
Ktx.Texture2GetImageOffset(texture, level, layer, face, &offset);   // texture->PData + offset: that level's bytes, texture->VkFormat: their format
Ktx.Texture2Destroy(texture);

Names are the C names without ktx, with the _ after Texture2 dropped (Texture2CreateFromMemory); enums lose _e.

docs.title: Slang (Apogee.Native.Slang)
docs.text:
The shader compiler. Slang's own API is C++ and COM, so the binding is over a small C API of ours (Native/slang_c) that compiles Slang source to SPIR-V for Vulkan 1.3 (SPIR-V 1.6, row-major matrices, entry points keep their names). The compiler library ships with the game: shaders compile at run time, and a mod can bring its own .slang files.

Session* session;
var desc = new SessionDesc { SearchPaths = paths, SearchPathCount = pathCount, Optimization = 1 };
Slang.SessionCreate(&desc, &session);

Result* result;
Slang.Compile(session, moduleName, path, source, null, 0, &result);   // entry points: all the module defines
if (Slang.ResultStatus(result) < 0) Log.Error("Shaders", Marshal.PtrToStringUTF8((IntPtr)Slang.ResultDiagnostics(result)));
byte* spirv = (byte*)Slang.ResultSpirv(result, 0, &size);              // entry point 0
Slang.ResultDestroy(result);

Passing source = null loads <moduleName>.slang from the search paths. Besides the code, a result carries the diagnostics (warnings too), the program's reflection as Slang's JSON, and the files the compile read, which is what a shader cache keys on.

docs.title: Jolt Physics (Apogee.Native.Jolt)
docs.text:
Jolt Physics, behind our own C API, Native/jolt/apogee_jolt.h (about 80 functions, written for what the engine needs; no third-party wrapper), in one shared library, jolt. The binding is a class Jolt (Jolt.WorldCreate, Jolt.BodyCreate) with structs that keep their Aj prefix (AjBodyDesc, AjVec3, AjWorld*) because BodyDesc, VehicleDesc and World are the engine's own names for other things. Physics is the engine's use of it; this is the raw binding.

The API is handles and plain structs: a world owns its job system, temp allocator, collision layer filters and event queue; shapes are reference counted (ShapeBox, ShapeMesh, ShapeStaticCompound, MutableCompound… each returns one reference that ShapeRelease gives back); bodies are made from an AjBodyDesc (layers, mask, motion, mass, damping, sensor, events, bullet) and are 32-bit ids; there are queries (Raycast, CastSphere, OverlapSphere, OverlapBox, with a layer mask and an ignored body, filtered natively), a character (CharacterCreate, CharacterStep), vehicles (VehicleCreate from a flat AjVehicleDesc, then VehicleSetGearbox, VehicleDriveWheeled, VehicleGetWheelState…) and a drawbar joint. Nothing throws; functions that can fail return false or null.

How it is built decides what the binding means, so these are fixed in Native/jolt/CMakeLists.txt:

  • Double precision (JPH_DOUBLE_PRECISION): AjRVec3 is three doubles, and so are the positions in every call (BodyGetPose, Raycast, AjEvent.Position). Rotations, scales, velocities and everything else are floats. It is the physics side of the double world (see Math).
  • Cross-platform determinism (JPH_CROSS_PLATFORM_DETERMINISTIC): the same inputs give the same results on Windows, Linux and macOS, on any CPU and with any number of threads (no fused multiply-add, strict float contraction). It costs about 8% of the simulation. Tests/Apogee.Native.Tests/JoltSmokeTests simulates a pile of bodies and compares the bits of their final positions with a recorded hash; it was the same on SSE 4.2 and AVX2 builds, with 1, 2 and 7 threads, and before and after the move from JoltC to our own API.
  • 32-bit object layers (JPH_OBJECT_LAYER_BITS=32): the low 16 bits are a body's group (its 14 layers, plus a marker for static and one for sensor bodies, which only choose the broad phase tree), the high 16 its mask. Two bodies collide when each is in a layer the other's mask holds; static bodies never collide with each other.
  • Instruction set: SSE 4.2 (the engine's x86-64-v2 baseline). cmake -DAPOGEE_JOLT_AVX2=ON builds for AVX2, BMI, LZCNT and F16C, any CPU since Haswell, and Jolt's code is then faster; the library picks its instruction set when it is built, there is no run-time dispatch. FMA is never used.
  • No C++ exceptions and no RTTI, as Jolt does not use them, and none may cross managed frames. No GPU compute, no profiler, no assertions in Release. The debug renderer is compiled in: aj_world_draw_debug collects what it draws (see Physics).
Jolt.Init();                                                     // registers Jolt's types; Jolt.Shutdown() at the end
var desc = new AjWorldDesc { MaxBodies = 10240, MaxBodyPairs = 65536, MaxContactConstraints = 20480, TempBufferBytes = 32 << 20, Threads = 4, EventCapacity = 4096,
                             VelocitySteps = 10, PositionSteps = 2, Gravity = new AjVec3 { Y = -9.81f } };
AjWorld* world = Jolt.WorldCreate(&desc);
AjShape* ball = Jolt.ShapeSphere(0.5f);
uint body = Jolt.BodyCreate(world, &bodyDesc);                   // bodyDesc.Shape = ball
Jolt.WorldUpdate(world, 1f / 60);                                // one collision step

Events. Jolt calls its contact and activation listeners on its worker threads, inside WorldUpdate, where managed code must not run. The world's listeners only append to a queue in native memory (a mutex, and a fixed capacity: what does not fit is counted, EventsDropped), and EventsTake copies them out after the update:

  • ContactAdded: two bodies started touching; the point (a double position), normal and depth are the first contact point's. ContactRemoved: they stopped (also when one of them goes to sleep: Jolt ends the contacts of a sleeping body).
  • BodyActivated and BodyDeactivated.
  • Only bodies that ask are reported (AjBodyDesc.Events); a sensor always reports its contacts, with Jolt.EventSensor in the flags. The UserData of a body is yours, whole, and comes back in the event.
  • IgnorePair(a, b) makes two bodies pass through each other (a truck and its trailer) until AllowPair; the world's contact validation looks the pair up only while some pair is ignored.

A step that needs more working memory than TempBufferBytes allocates from the heap instead of failing.

docs.title: RmlUi (Apogee.Native.RmlUi)
docs.text:
RmlUi 6.3 (HTML and CSS style game UI), behind our own C API, Native/rmlui/apogee_rmlui.h (85 functions), in one shared library, rmlui. RmlUi's own API is C++ with inheritance, templates and ownership by unique_ptr, which a C# program cannot call, so everything goes through handles and plain structs. RmlUi is compiled into the library as a static one would be (RMLUI_STATIC_LIB, hidden symbols): the library exports what the header declares and nothing else. Its font engine is FreeType, our own freetype library (it has to sit next to this one). The binding is a class Rml (Rml.ContextCreate, Rml.ElementAppendChild) with Ar-prefixed structs (ArHost, ArVertex, ArRect). UI is the engine's use of it; this is the raw binding.

  • The host. RmlUi needs a few things from its host, and ArHost is how it gets them: a table of function pointers (a C# program fills it with [UnmanagedCallersOnly] methods). Drawing: RmlUi compiles geometry (ArVertex lists, 20 bytes each, with the alpha already multiplied into the color) and asks for it to be drawn with a translation and a texture, under a scissor rectangle and a transform; textures come from load_texture (an image path) or generate_texture (RGBA pixels, for font atlases). System: time, a log, the mouse cursor, the clipboard. Files: read_file hands over a whole file to the library (ar_sink_write), which serves RmlUi's reads and seeks from memory, so every document, stylesheet and font is read through whatever file system the host has. Any function may be NULL; its work is then skipped (no drawing, no files).
  • Elements are handles, 64 bits with a generation, not pointers. A slot watches its element with RmlUi's observer pointer, so a handle to an element that has been destroyed (it was in a document that was unloaded, or in a branch someone destroyed) answers "not alive" and every call refuses it; a released slot that is used again does not answer to the old handle. An element made with DocumentCreateElement or DocumentCreateText is owned by its handle until ElementAppendChild or ElementInsertBefore puts it in a tree (RmlUi's ElementPtr rule), ElementRemoveChild gives it back, ElementDestroy ends it. Handles that calls return are the caller's to ElementRelease; so are the ones an event gives (EventTarget, EventCurrent).
  • Events. ElementAddListener(element, "click", capture) returns a token, and every event reaches the host's one on_event(user, token, event) synchronously, with the type, target, current element, phase and the event's parameters (EventGetString, EventGetNumber: mouse_x, key_identifier, value...), and EventStopPropagation. A listener dies with its element or at ElementRemoveListener; the only place one is freed is RmlUi's OnDetach.
  • Text results (ElementGetId, TextGet...) are written into a caller's buffer with the length the whole text needs, like snprintf; -1 is "no such thing".
  • Input is ContextMouseMove, ContextMouseButton, ContextMouseWheel, ContextKey (ArKey is RmlUi's key list, its values checked at compile time) and ContextText; each returns false when a document consumed the input.
  • Scripts in documents. Every document is an ArDocument, so that <script> and <script src> reach the host (load_inline_script, load_external_script, with a document id that is the same for every call about the document until document_closed) and on* attributes become listeners whose code the host compiles (compile_inline_handler, when the first event comes: the attribute is read before the element is in its document). RmlUi runs the scripts of a document when its <head> is read, before the body.
  • Data models. DataModelCreate, DataModelBind (a top-level variable, by ref and ArDataKind), DataModelBindEvent (for data-event-*), DataModelDirty, DataModelIsDirty and DataModelRemove. The values stay the host's: RmlUi asks data_get, data_set, data_size and data_child with the refs the host gave out, so one VariableDefinition per kind serves every variable. ArVariant carries the value (nil, bool, integer, double, string).
  • A base stylesheet. RmlUi has no user-agent stylesheet: a div is display: inline and ignores its width and height until a stylesheet says div { display: block }. SetBaseStyle gives it one, put under the rules of every document loaded afterwards (in its head, so the text the body makes already has a font); the tests of this binding that do not set one write the rule themselves.
  • Fonts are copied (LoadFont keeps its own copy until after shutdown, which RmlUi requires of the memory).
  • Effects. The host gets what RmlUi 6 asks of a render interface beyond geometry: enable_clip_mask and render_to_clip_mask (an ArClipOperation, geometry and translation), layers (push_layer, composite_layers with the filter handles and a blend mode, pop_layer), save_layer_as_texture and save_layer_as_mask_image, filters (compile_filter gets an ArFilterDesc: a blur, a drop shadow, or a 4x5 color matrix that opacity, brightness, contrast, invert, grayscale, sepia, saturate and hue-rotate are turned into) and shaders (compile_shader gets an ArShaderDesc: a linear, radial or conic gradient with its stops), with render_shader and the matching releases. Every callback is optional: one left null is a feature RmlUi then draws without. backdrop-filter is not forwarded.
var host = new ArHost { Size = (uint)sizeof(ArHost), User = state, CompileGeometry = &CompileGeometry, RenderGeometry = &RenderGeometry, /* ... */ ReadFile = &ReadFile, OnEvent = &OnEvent };
Rml.Initialize(&host);                                           // once; Rml.Shutdown() at the end
ArContext* context = Rml.ContextCreate(name, 1280, 720);
ulong document = Rml.ContextLoadDocumentText(context, rml, url);
Rml.DocumentShow(document);
Rml.ContextUpdate(context);                                      // layout and animations
Rml.ContextRender(context);                                      // calls host.RenderGeometry for what is visible

Tests/Apogee.Native.Tests/RmlUiSmokeTests runs all of it against a recording host: layout in pixels, the geometry and its colors, text with a real font, building and editing a tree (and what a stale handle does), listeners (bubbling, capture, stopping, removal, parameters), clicking by pointer position, files and stylesheets through the host, images, added stylesheets, typing into a text field, the debugger, resizing.

docs.title: ImGuizmo, ImPlot and imnodes
docs.text:
Dear ImGui add-ons for the dev tools and the editor: ImGuizmo (3D manipulation gizmos and a view cube), ImPlot (plots) and imnodes (node editors). All three use ImGui's C++ API and its context, and the symbols of ImGui are hidden in cimgui, so they are compiled into the cimgui library (Native/imgui/CMakeLists.txt), each with a C API of ours over it (apogee_imguizmo.h, apogee_implot.h, apogee_imnodes.h: plain functions over floats, ints and opaque handles, no C++ types, no cimguizmo / cimplot / cimnodes). Three binding projects are generated from those headers, all on the library name cimgui: Apogee.Native.ImGuizmo (class Gizmo, functions Gizmo.Manipulate, Gizmo.ViewManipulate...), Apogee.Native.ImPlot (class Plot: Plot.BeginPlot, Plot.PlotLineF...) and Apogee.Native.ImNodes (class Nodes: Nodes.BeginNode, Nodes.Link...). Their enums are checked against the library's own at compile time (static_asserts in the shims).

  • They act on ImGui's current context, which is in the same library: make ImGui's context current, create an ImPlot and an imnodes context (Plot.CreateContext, Nodes.CreateContext), and make those current too. ImGuiHost does all of that.
  • ImPlot's templates are exported as _f (float) and _d (double) functions: Plot.PlotLineF(label, values, count, xScale, xStart, spec) and Plot.PlotLineXyD(label, xs, ys, count, spec), and the same for shaded areas (PlotShadedBetweenF is an area between two lines), bars and scatter. AplotSpec is the look of an item; Plot.DefaultSpec fills it with automatic colors.
  • ImGuizmo's matrices are 16 floats, column-major; Gizmo.Manipulate changes the object's matrix in place and can give the change since the drag began (deltaMatrix).
  • imnodes' ids are the caller's integers: nodes, attributes (pins) and links each have their own.
  • The library exports exactly the three headers and ImGui's cimgui.h: nm -D libcimgui.so | grep -c _Z is 0, no C++ symbol of ImGui, ImPlot or imnodes leaks.
  • Tests: the three bindings are in NativeBindingTests (every entry point resolves; they have no struct of a known size but ImPlot's AplotSpec), and Tests/Apogee.DevTools.Tests/ImGuiExtensionTests runs a headless frame through each.

docs.title: OpenAL Soft (Apogee.Native.OpenAL)
docs.text:
OpenAL 1.1 with OpenAL Soft's extensions, through its C API with no shim: class OpenAL. OpenAL Soft is LGPL, so it is its own shared library beside the program (see Legal/THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md); Audio is built on it.

  • Names keep the C names with the first letter in capitals: alGenBuffers is OpenAL.AlGenBuffers, alcOpenDevice is OpenAL.AlcOpenDevice, AL_SOURCE_RELATIVE is OpenAL.AlSourceRelative. The extensions OpenAL Soft exports as plain functions are bound too (AL_ALEXT_PROTOTYPES): EFX effects, filters and auxiliary slots (AlGenEffects, AlFilterf), and ALC_SOFT_loopback (AlcLoopbackOpenDeviceSOFT, AlcRenderSamplesSOFT), which renders to memory with no sound card.
  • Left out: the direct-context variants (...Direct), EAX, the debug extension, the functions the header declares that the library does not export, and the effect parameters' default, minimum and maximum (float macros).
  • Every call can leave an error that is read with AlGetError / AlcGetError; the audio system checks them where a failure matters.
ALCdevice* device = OpenAL.AlcLoopbackOpenDeviceSOFT(null);          // or AlcOpenDevice(null) for the speakers
int[] attributes = [OpenAL.AlcFormatChannelsSoft, OpenAL.AlcStereoSoft, OpenAL.AlcFormatTypeSoft, OpenAL.AlcFloatSoft, OpenAL.AlcFrequency, 48000, 0];
fixed (int* a = attributes) { context = OpenAL.AlcCreateContext(device, a); }
OpenAL.AlcMakeContextCurrent(context);
// ... buffers, sources, then, once per update on a loopback device:
OpenAL.AlcRenderSamplesSOFT(device, mix, 1024);

docs.title: Audio decoders (Apogee.Native.AudioDecode)
docs.text:
WAV, FLAC, Ogg Vorbis and MP3 behind four functions of ours (Native/audio_decode/apogee_audio.h, built from dr_libs and stb_vorbis): Open takes a whole file in memory and tells the format from its first bytes, Read gives interleaved 32-bit float samples at the file's channel count and sample rate, Rewind starts over, Close ends it. The memory must stay valid until Close. The files come from the engine's file system, so the decoders never touch the disk.

AaInfo info;
AaDecoder* decoder = AudioDecode.Open(bytes, (nuint)length, &info);   // null if it is not audio we can read
ulong frames = AudioDecode.Read(decoder, samples, 4096);              // 0 at the end
AudioDecode.Close(decoder);

docs.title: GameNetworkingSockets (Apogee.Native.Net)
docs.text:
Valve's GameNetworkingSockets behind our own small C API (Native/net/apogee_net.h, shim apogee_net), class Net: GNS's flat C API takes C++ references and structs packed differently by platform, which the shim's compiler lays out instead. A host owns a listen socket and connections (GNS's handles, as uint); Poll returns what happened as AnEvents (Incoming, Connected, Message, Disconnected), whose message bytes and strings stay valid until the next Poll, so managed code never runs inside a GNS callback or on one of its threads. Network is built on it; Tests/Apogee.Network.Tests is its test. Without libGameNetworkingSockets next to it the shim does not load (NativeLibraries.TryLoad fails) and networking is off.

Net.Init(error, size);                       // counted: every Init needs a Shutdown
AnHost* host = Net.HostCreate();
ushort port; Net.Listen(host, 27020, &port);
uint connection = Net.Connect(host, "127.0.0.1:27020"u8);
AnEvent* events = ...; int n = Net.Poll(host, events, 256);   // once a frame
Net.Send(host, connection, bytes, length, reliable: true, lane: 0);

docs.title: Steamworks (Apogee.Native.Steam)
docs.text:
Valve's flat C API (steam_api.dll / libsteam_api.so / libsteam_api.dylib), class Steam. The three libraries are Valve's redistributable_bin, committed unchanged (Git LFS, ThirdParty/steamworks/lib); the SDK headers are not (Valve's agreement lets us distribute only the redistributables), so the bindings are generated code and committed, and the headers are needed only to regenerate them (./build.sh sdk steam <zip>, then ./build.sh bindings steam). Without the library NativeLibraries.TryLoad fails and Steam is off.

The headers are C++, and the bindings are generated from what Valve publishes for other languages instead: steam_api.json (interfaces, structs, enums, constants) plus the S_API function declarations in steam_api_flat.h, steam_api.h and steam_api_common.h, with libclang measuring the structs ("kind": "steam", SteamApiParser).

  • Interfaces are opaque pointers. Steam.SteamUserV023() returns an ISteamUser* that Steam owns; its methods take it first (Steam.UserGetSteamID(user), the flat API's SteamAPI_ISteamUser_GetSteamID). Only the interfaces in steam.json are bound (user, friends, utils, apps, user stats, remote storage, UGC, screenshots, timeline); networking, matchmaking, Steam Input and the game server API are left out.
  • Callbacks use manual dispatch (ManualDispatchInit, ManualDispatchRunFrame, ManualDispatchGetNextCallback into a CallbackMsg, ManualDispatchGetAPICallResult), so nothing runs on Steam's threads. Every callback struct has its id as a constant (Steam.GameOverlayActivatedId).
  • Packing. Valve packs its callback structs to 4 bytes on Linux and macOS and to 8 on Windows, and a few structs are #pragma pack(4) or (2) on every system. The structs that depend on the system say Pack = SteamPack.Callback, a constant chosen when the project is built (APOGEE_STEAM_PACK8 for a Windows build), and the layout test checks the size clang computes for both packings (SteamLayout.CallbackPackSizes). Build the binding for the operating system it runs on.
  • Names lose Valve's Hungarian prefixes (m_unAppID is AppID, m_eResult is Result); _t and the E/I prefixes of enums and interfaces stay as Valve writes them.
  • Constants that are plain numbers (or a * b, a + b) are bound; strings and macros are skipped (Bin/bindings/steam.skipped.txt).
byte* message = stackalloc byte[1024];
if (Steam.InitFlat(message) == ESteamAPIInitResult.OK)       // Steam client running, steam_appid.txt next to the program in development
{
    Steam.ManualDispatchInit();
    ISteamUser* user = Steam.SteamUserV023();
    ulong id = Steam.UserGetSteamID(user);
}

docs.title: Network
docs.text:
Apogee.Network connects the game to other programs over UDP: GameNetworkingSockets (GNS, Valve's open-source transport, BSD-3-Clause) behind one NetSystem, in scripts the global net. Connections are encrypted, messages are reliable (arrive once, in order) or not (may be lost, never twice), large messages are split and put back together, and lanes keep a slow message on one from holding up the others. There is no replication: what is sent, and what it means, is the game's.

The base game's only: NetSystem is ModsBlocked, as are connections. The library is a prebuilt, self-contained shared library beside the program (ThirdParty/gns/lib, see ThirdParty/README.md); without it net.is_active is false and every call does nothing and returns nothing, so a game that can also play alone works the same.

-- the server
local port = net:listen(27020)            -- 0: a free port; returns the port, or 0 if it is in use
net.connection_requested:connect(function(connection, address)
    if banned[address] then connection:refuse() end    -- accepted when the handlers return, unless one refused
end)
net.connected:connect(function(connection)
    connection:send('{"hello":"player"}')
end)
net.message:connect(function(connection, text, lane)
    local command = json.decode(text)
    ...
end)
net.disconnected:connect(function(connection, reason, code) ... end)

-- a client
local connection = net:connect("192.168.1.20:27020")    -- "[::1]:27020" for IPv6; a name is looked up first
net.connected:connect(function(c) c:send("hello") end)
connection:send(positionText, false)                  -- unreliable: for what is out of date a moment later

docs.title: The system
docs.text:
ScriptSession makes the NetSystem (the global net) and calls Update() once a frame, after Steam's and before the input and the world, so what arrived is a signal before the systems and scripts run. Nothing of the game runs on GNS's threads: the library's callbacks are queued and become signals inside Update, all on the calling thread, in this order: connections requested and made, then messages, then connections ended (a message sent just before a close is delivered before the close is announced). Opening a socket costs nothing until listen or connect is called. The system is disposed with the session.

  • listen(port) listens on a UDP port for IPv4 and IPv6 and returns the port (0 if it is in use). With 0 a free port from 49152 up is chosen. One port at a time; stop_listening(); listening_port.
  • connect(address) returns a NetConnection that is connecting, or nil when the address cannot be used. The outcome is a connected or a disconnected signal. A name in the address is looked up with the system's resolver, which can block for a moment; an IP address does not.
  • NetSystem.create() makes a system of its own (the tests talk to themselves over the loopback interface), NetSystem.create_inactive() one that does nothing, NetSystem.is_installed() says whether the library loads.

docs.title: Connections
docs.text:
NetConnection: address, is_incoming, state (connecting, connected, closed), ping (ms, -1 until known), quality (0 to 1), bytes_out and bytes_in (a second), send(text, reliable = true, lane = 0) (false when it could not be queued), configure_lanes(count), close(reason, linger = true) and refuse().

  • Messages are text in scripts: UTF-8, such as JSON. C# also has SendBytes(span, reliable, lane) and the event BytesReceived, which carry any bytes.
  • Lanes. configure_lanes(3) before the first message gives the connection three lanes of equal priority; each is in order on its own. Both sides configure the same number. The lane a message arrived on is the last argument of message.
  • Closing. close ends the connection and, with linger, sends what is still waiting first. The other side gets disconnected with the text and the code (1000 and up are the application's: a refused request is 1001). Here no signal comes (you asked for it). A connection that ended is closed and destroyed a frame later.
  • A connection that is not answered gives up after GNS's connect timeout (10 seconds) with a disconnected.

docs.title: With Steamworks
docs.text: GNS's interface is Steam's: ISteamNetworkingSockets in libsteam_api is the same class with the same functions, and the Steam Datagram Relay (connections by Steam id, through Valve's network, with no open port) is the same API with another way to address the peer. A Steam transport would therefore replace Native/net/apogee_net.cpp's calls (CreateListenSocketP2P, ConnectP2P, the identity instead of the IP address) and leave Apogee.Network, the scripts and these signals as they are. It is not built: the Steam wrappers of steam.md leave networking out on purpose (steam.json).

docs.title: How it is built
docs.text: GNS is C++ with a flat C API that takes C++ references and structs packed differently on each platform, so it is not bound as it is. Native/net/apogee_net.h is our own small C API over it (a host, connections as integers, an_poll returning events), compiled against GNS's headers (ThirdParty/gns/include) and linked to its shared library. Apogee.Native.Net is the generated binding of that header. Every GNS call is in apogee_net.cpp. ./build.sh native builds the shim when libGameNetworkingSockets is in Bin/native/<rid> or ThirdParty/gns/lib/<rid>, and skips it with a message otherwise.

docs.title: Not done
docs.text: Peer-to-peer connections and signaling, Steam's relay (above), the datagram-only ISteamNetworkingMessages, NAT punch-through, a server browser or lobby, and replication (entities, snapshots, prediction): the game builds those on messages. Messages in scripts are text only.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Tests/Apogee.Network.Tests runs two network systems in one process over the loopback interface: a client connects and messages go both ways (reliable and unreliable, with non-ASCII text), 300 reliable messages arrive in order, bytes are not changed, a 200 kB message is split and put back together, a close is announced after the messages that came before it, a handler can refuse a connection (the other side sees code 1001), a connection to a port nobody listens on stays pending without blocking, lanes carry their number, addresses are parsed and names resolved, and an inactive system does nothing. Tests/Luau/net.test.luau runs the same through the script surface. They skip where the library is not installed; Tests/Apogee.Native.Tests checks the shim's entry points and struct sizes.

docs.title: Steam
docs.text:
Apogee.Steam connects a game to Steam: the player's name and language, the overlay, achievements, stats and leaderboards, rich presence, the timeline, cloud saves, and Workshop mods. In a game, scripts see it as the global steam (the SteamSystem class). It is the base game's: a mod cannot use it (ModsBlocked), and a base-game function a mod calls still acts as the base game.

Steam's library (steam_api) is Valve's redistributable and is in the repository; the Steam client is the player's. When Steam is not running, or the game was not started with an app id, steam.is_active is false and every call does nothing and answers with something inert (the log says why, once, and steam.status has the words), so a game works the same on a machine without Steam, under --headless, and in a test. A real, windowed run connects; --headless and tests do not.

if steam.is_active then
    print(steam.user_name, steam.language)          -- "Ada", "english"
end

steam:unlock_achievement("ACH_WIN_ONE_GAME")        -- shows the pop-up, and sends it to Steam
steam:set_stat_int("NumGames", steam:stat_int("NumGames") + 1)
steam:store_stats()                                  -- stats are in memory until stored

steam:set_rich_presence("status", "Delivering hay")  -- the line friends see
steam:add_timeline_event("Crash", "Hit a tree", "steam_death")

steam.overlay_activated:connect(function(open: boolean) paused = open end)

docs.title: The frame and the signals
docs.text:
ScriptSession.Progress calls steam:update() first in every frame. It uses Steam's manual dispatch: Steam's callbacks and the results of asynchronous calls are collected there, on the calling thread, and turn into signals. Nothing runs on a thread of Steam's. A script never waits: a call that needs Steam to answer returns at once, and a signal carries the answer.

Signal When overlay_activated(open) the overlay opened or closed: pause the game while it is open shutdown_requested() Steam is shutting down and wants the game to exit stats_received(ok), stats_stored(ok) the player's stats arrived; a store_stats finished achievement_stored(name, current, max) an achievement unlocked or progressed leaderboard_found(name, found), score_uploaded(name, ok, rank), scores_downloaded(name, users, ranks, scores) the answers of the leaderboard calls (ok false and no entries when it failed or Steam is off) text_input_dismissed(submitted, text) Steam's on-screen keyboard closed workshop_item_installed(id), workshop_item_downloaded(id, ok), workshop_subscribed(id, ok), workshop_unsubscribed(id, ok) Workshop

Steam's 64-bit ids (the player, a Workshop item) are decimal strings in scripts, because a script number cannot hold them.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• The user and the app: user_id, user_name, app_id, build_id, language (the language the player chose for the game, as Steam names it: english, french, schinese; a game can take it as the default language), ui_language, country, is_subscribed, is_steam_deck, is_big_picture, owns_dlc(app_id), is_dlc_installed(app_id).
  • Overlay: activate_overlay("friends" | "community" | "players" | "settings" | "stats" | "achievements" | ""), open_web_page(url), open_store(app_id), is_overlay_enabled, and show_text_input(description) for the Deck's on-screen keyboard.
  • Achievements and stats: achievement(name), unlock_achievement, clear_achievement, achievement_progress(name, current, max), achievement_names(), stat_int/stat_float, set_stat_int/set_stat_float, store_stats, reset_all_stats(achievements_too). Steam loads the stats when the game starts: stats_received says when. Achievements and stats are defined in Steamworks (the partner site), by name; this only sets them.
  • Leaderboards: find_leaderboard(name), upload_score(name, score, keep_best), download_scores(name, from, to, "global" | "around_user" | "friends"). A leaderboard that was not looked up yet is looked up by the call that needs it.
  • Rich presence: set_rich_presence(key, value) (status is the line shown in the friends list), clear_rich_presence().
  • Screenshots and the timeline: trigger_screenshot(), add_screenshot(path, width, height); add_timeline_event(title, description, icon, priority, offset_seconds, featured), set_timeline_state(text) and set_timeline_mode("playing" | "staging" | "menus" | "loading") give the player's Steam timeline (the game recording) its markers.

docs.title: Cloud saves
docs.text:
ScriptSession.StartGame mounts cloud:// in the game's file system. With Steam running and the cloud on (steam.is_cloud_enabled: the player has it on for the account and for the game) it is the player's Steam Cloud files for the game; otherwise it is a plain folder (<user folder>/cloud). A game saves to cloud:// in both cases, with the same code:

fs.write_text("cloud://slot1/save.json", json)       -- follows the player to their other machines
local text = fs.read_text("cloud://slot1/save.json")

Steam keeps cloud files flat, with / in their names, so a folder exists only as far as a file's name says; a write that Steam refuses (too big, or the space is used up) fails like a write to a full disk. steam:cloud_quota() gives the total space and what is left. The game must also turn the cloud on for its files in Steamworks (the app's Steam Cloud settings: a byte and a file count quota). What is saved in the plain folder while Steam was off is not copied into the cloud later.

docs.title: Workshop mods
docs.text:
A Workshop item is a mod: a folder with a mod.xml at its root, uploaded by its author, that Steam downloads and keeps up to date for subscribers. When Steam runs, the game mounts the installed items at workshop:// (Steam's own folders, read-only), each listed under its mod.xml id, and the package finder searches it (PackageOptions.ExtraUserModsPaths) next to user://mods: a Workshop mod is one of the player's mods in every way (the same solver, the same "switch it off" list in user://mods.xml, the same limits for mods). If an own mod and a Workshop item share an id, the one found first (the player's own) wins.

Mods are read when the game starts. workshop_item_installed(id) says a subscription finished installing: tell the player to restart. subscribe(id), unsubscribe(id), subscribed_items(), workshop_item_folder(id) and download_workshop_item(id) are there for a mod browser in the game's menu.

docs.title: Uploading a mod
docs.text:
cd path/with/steam_appid.txt          # the game's app id; the Steam client must be running and signed in as a partner of the game
Apogee.Runtime --workshop-upload Mods/my_mod --title "My mod" --description "What it does" --preview preview.png --tags Vehicles,Tools --visibility private
Apogee.Runtime --workshop-upload Mods/my_mod --title "My mod" ... --confirm      # this one really uploads
Apogee.Runtime --workshop-upload Mods/my_mod --item 1234567890 --note "Fixed the hitch" --confirm   # an update of an item
