Function What it does tween.value(from, to, seconds, set, options?) Calls set(value) every step with a number, a vector or a Quat between from and to. Both ends must be the same kind. tween.property(object, name, to, seconds, options?) Animates a property of an engine object (a number, vector or Quat property with a setter) from its value to to. tween.field(world, entity, component, field, to, seconds, options?) Animates a field of a component in place: a number (f32, f64 or an integer, which is rounded), a vec3, a dvec3 (a world position, interpolated in double precision) or a quat. tween.ease(ease, t) The easing curve at time t, from 0 to 1.

Each of the first three returns a Tween.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
The last argument is an optional table:

Option Default Meaning ease "linear" The curve, from the table below. delay 0 Seconds to wait before it starts. property and field read their start value when the delay ends, not when the tween is made. repeats 0 The number of extra passes; -1 repeats for ever. reverses false Every other pass plays backwards, so a repeating tween goes there and back. unscaled false Use the real clock instead of the game clock (below).

An unknown option, a bad ease name, or the wrong type is a script error at the call. Nothing is written when the tween is made: the first write is in the next step, and the last write is exactly to. A tween with seconds <= 0 finishes on its first step. With reverses, a tween whose last pass runs backwards (an odd number of extra passes) ends on from.

docs.title: The Tween handle
docs.text:
Member playing True while the tween runs: not paused, not over. paused True while it is paused. progress How far the current pass has got, 0 to 1 in time (the curve is not applied). 1 once it has completed. duration The seconds of one pass. ease The curve. cancel() Stops it where it is, keeps the value it has, and emits cancelled. complete() Jumps to the end value, writes it, and emits completed. On a tween that repeats for ever it stops it at to. pause(), resume() Hold and release it (the delay too). A paused tween is still alive. completed, cancelled Signals, emitted at most once each, and only one of them. wait() Yields the running task until the tween ends. Returns true if it completed and false if it was cancelled.

cancel() and complete() do nothing once the tween is over. completed is emitted after the last value is written, and never by a tween that repeats for ever (apart from complete()).

wait() is task.wait for a tween: it works only in a task (task.spawn, task.defer, task.delay, task.every) and is the same error anywhere else ("must run in a task"), see Tasks and game time. On a tween that is over it returns at once, in a task or not. A task that is cancelled while it waits is not woken.

docs.title: Easing
docs.text:
Linear, and ten families with an _in, an _out and an _in_out form each: quad, cubic, quart, quint, sine, expo, circ, back, elastic and bounce. The names are the snake_case ones: quad_in_out, bounce_out. in starts slowly, out ends slowly, in_out does both. The curves are Robert Penner's, written from the formulas. Every curve is exactly 0 at time 0 and exactly 1 at time 1.

Family in Shape quad, cubic, quart, quint t^2 … t^5 A smoother and smoother start (or end). sine 1 - cos(t * pi / 2) The gentlest. expo 2^(10t - 10) Almost still, then fast. circ 1 - sqrt(1 - t^2) A quarter of a circle. back 2.70158 t^3 - 1.70158 t^2 Pulls back before it goes, or overshoots the end. Goes outside 0 to 1. elastic a decaying sine Swings like a spring. Goes outside 0 to 1. bounce a ball dropped Bounces on the end (out) or off the start (in).

tween.ease("quad_in", 0.5) is 0.25. The same curves are Easing.Apply(Ease, t) in C#.

docs.title: Clocks
docs.text:
A tween follows the game clock of the task library (Tasks and game time): at game.set_time_scale(0.5) it plays at half speed, and at 0 it stands still (it does not rewrite its value either). With unscaled = true it follows the real clock, which the time scale does not change: a fade of a pause menu. The editor's pause stops both.

Tweens are stepped by LuauVm.AdvanceTime, after the due tasks and before the deferred ones, in the order they were made. A tween made by a task in a step first moves in the next step; one made anywhere else (a system, a module, an event) moves in the next step too, so the first write is never in the call that made the tween. A task that waits for a tween that ends in a step resumes in that same step.

A field tween writes the component's memory and calls World.Modified, so observers see each write. The world transform system runs in World.Progress, which comes before the tweens in a frame: a tween on Transform is seen by the transform system, and so by rendering, one frame later.

docs.title: Lifetime, owners and reloading
docs.text:
While a tween plays the engine keeps it, so a script may drop the handle (tween.value(...) as a statement is the usual way to use it). When it ends the engine lets go of it, and it is collected when no script holds it; a script that kept the handle can still read it (playing is false).

A tween is cancelled, without emitting cancelled, when:

  • the module that made it (or a task of that module) is reloaded or fails to load (Hot reload) — a failed reload cancels the new run's tweens and keeps the old ones;
  • its owner is unloaded: a mod that fails to load has its tweens cancelled, as its tasks are;
  • the VM ends, with the session.

The handlers of those tweens belong to what is being taken away, so they are not called; a task that waits for one is woken with false.

A tween is cancelled, with cancelled, when a script calls cancel(), when the setter of a tween.value or the setter of a property raises an error (the error is logged for the owner that made the tween, as Script:<owner>, with "tween failed"), when a value is out of range for the field (an integer field that would overflow), or when its target is gone: the object was destroyed, the entity died, or the component was removed. A target that goes away is not an error and is not logged.

docs.title: Cost
docs.text: tween.property and tween.field make no Luau call per frame: the engine reads the start once, then interpolates and writes the property or the memory of the component itself. Only tween.value calls a Luau function (its setter) every step, under the time budget and memory category of the owner that made it. Use the first two for anything that has a property or a field.

docs.title: From C
docs.text:
ScriptScheduler tasks = vm.Scheduler;     // TweenCount, TweenCountOf(owner), CancelOwner(owner), CancelAll()
vm.AdvanceTime(1.0 / 60, 1.0 / 60);       // one frame: tasks, then tweens, then the deferred tasks
double eased = Easing.Apply(Ease.QuadInOut, 0.25);

Tween is an engine class (Tween.Playing, Tween.Cancel(), Tween.Completed…), so it is in the generated definitions and reference. The tests of the library are in Tests/Apogee.Scripting.Tests/TweenTests.cs and Tests/Luau/tween.test.luau, whose cases count frames at the runner's 60 Hz clock.

docs.title: Dev tools
docs.text: Apogee.DevTools is Dear ImGui (the docking branch, through cimgui) wired into the engine: an SDL3 input backend and a Vulkan renderer backend written in C#, a thin C# layer over ImGui's C API, and the engine's debug window. The editor and the game's own dev windows use the same pieces.

docs.title: Using it
docs.text:
using var imgui = new ImGuiHost();
imgui.Attach(window);                                              // input from this window
using var imguiRenderer = new ImGuiRenderer(device);               // draws ImGui's output
var overlay = new DevOverlay();

// each frame
imgui.BeginFrame(deltaSeconds);                                    // display size and scale come from the window
overlay.Draw(new DevOverlayData { GpuName = gpuName, CpuFrameMilliseconds = cpuMs, GpuTimings = loop.Timings,
                                  Plan = renderer.LastPlan, Stats = renderer.LastStats, Settings = settings, Camera = camera });
Ui.Begin("My window"); Ui.Text("anything"); Ui.End();             // any ImGui widgets
imgui.EndFrame();

renderer.Render(frame, scene, camera, target, settings, overlay: imguiRenderer);   // the overlay is the last pass of the frame's graph

imgui.WantsMouse / WantsKeyboard say when ImGui has the pointer over a widget or a text field active: the game should not also react then.

docs.title: Docking
docs.text:
The vendored Dear ImGui is the docking branch (the tag v1.93.0-docking, see ThirdParty/README.md; before 2026-11-05 it was by mistake a master commit without the docking API). Docking is off until a host asks for it, because the dev overlay's windows are meant to float:

imgui.EnableDocking();
// each frame, before the windows that should dock:
uint dockspace = ImGui.DockSpaceOverViewport(0, ImGui.GetMainViewport(), ImGuiDockNodeFlags.PassthruCentralNode, null);

Windows dock inside the one SDL window. ImGui's multi-viewport (windows that leave the main window as OS windows) is not enabled, so there is one swapchain. The editor builds its layout on this.

docs.title: The SDL input backend
docs.text: ImGuiHost.Attach(window) listens to PlatformHost.RawEvent, so ImGui gets its input as the platform pumps events: the pointer and buttons (SDL's left, middle, right are reordered to ImGui's), the wheel, every key (an SDL scancode to an ImGuiKey table: letters, digits, function keys, arrows, the keypad, modifiers), typed text (UTF-8), window focus, and the pointer leaving the window. Each frame it also sets the OS mouse cursor to the one ImGui asks for (arrow, text beam, resize arrows) and starts or stops SDL text input as text fields appear. The clipboard goes through SDL. Events of other windows are ignored; AttachToAllWindows() is for headless use.

docs.title: Text
docs.text: Dear ImGui rasterizes its fonts with FreeType (imgui_freetype.cpp is part of the cimgui library, see Native libraries): text is hinted and anti-aliased by FreeType instead of ImGui's built-in stb_truetype (which is still compiled in, because cimgui calls it, but is not the default). The loader's name (FreeType (2.15.0; 2.15.0), compiled against and linked) is atlas->FontLoader->Name, which TheGlyphsAreRasterizedByFreeType checks. Colour glyphs are off (ImGuiFreeTypeLoaderFlags.LoadColor), so the atlas stays a single-channel coverage image that ImGuiRenderer expands to RGBA8; the flags can be set per font through ImFontConfig.FontLoaderFlags.

docs.title: The Vulkan renderer backend
docs.text: ImGuiRenderer is an IRenderOverlay: it adds one pass to the frame's render graph that draws on the output after tone mapping. It follows Dear ImGui 1.92's texture protocol: ImGui says which textures to create, update and destroy, and the backend answers with an id per texture. The font atlas becomes an RGBA8 image with a bindless slot; an update creates a new image and defers freeing the old one until the GPU has finished the frame that may still sample it. Vertices and indices of every draw list are copied into per-frame-in-flight buffers that grow when needed, and the shader pulls the vertices (imgui.slang, ImGui's 20-byte vertex) with push constants for the projection and the texture. Clip rectangles become scissors, alpha blending is straight alpha, and the output image is the (UNORM) swapchain so the colours ImGui chose reach the screen unchanged.

docs.title: The overlay window
docs.text:
DevOverlay.Draw shows one window with four sections, and above them, in red, the shader errors (DevOverlayData.ShaderErrors, fill it with ShaderLibrary.Errors) while a shader that was edited does not compile: the renderers keep using the shader as it was, and the message, with the file and line, stays until an edit that compiles:

  • Frame: frames per second, average, minimum and maximum frame time, and an ImPlot plot of the last 240 frames, newest on the right (the history keeps filling while the window is hidden, Visible = false).
  • GPU passes: a stacked ImPlot plot of the GPU milliseconds of each top-level render graph pass over the last 240 frames (DevOverlay.GpuHistory; a pass that did not run in a frame has 0 there, and a section inside a pass, Forward/lights, is part of it), and under it the table of every section of the last finished frame, with bars.
  • Render graph: the passes that ran and the ones culled, their type, barriers and what they write, and how many images the graph shares.
  • Lighting: draws, lights, whether the clusters were rebuilt; exposure, the view (final image or the cluster-light heatmap), the camera's field of view and the cluster range, all edited live.

Ui has the ImGui calls the dev tools need with C# strings and ref values (windows, text, sliders, checkboxes, combos, plots, tables, headers); for anything else call ImGui from Apogee.Native.CImGui directly.

docs.title: ImPlot, ImGuizmo and imnodes
docs.text:
Three more libraries sit in the same shared library as Dear ImGui (they use its C++ API and its context, and ImGui's symbols are hidden), each with a small C API of ours over it (see ThirdParty/README.md, and the native libraries):

  • ImPlot (Apogee.Native.ImPlot, class Plot) draws plots. Plots in Apogee.DevTools is the surface the overlay uses, with strings and spans: if (Plots.Begin("id", size)) { Plots.Axes(...); Plots.Limits(...); Plots.Line("label", values, spec); Plots.Shaded(...); Plots.Band(...); Plots.Bars(...); Plots.End(); }.
  • ImGuizmo (Apogee.Native.ImGuizmo, class Gizmo) draws move, rotate and scale gizmos and a view cube over a viewport: Gizmo.BeginFrame(), Gizmo.SetRect(...), then Gizmo.Manipulate(view, projection, operation, mode, matrix, ...) changes the matrix in place while the player drags (the matrices are 16 floats, column-major).
  • imnodes (Apogee.Native.ImNodes, class Nodes) draws node editors: nodes with title bars and pins, links, a minimap, selection and positions.

ImGuiHost makes an ImPlot context and an imnodes context with the ImGui one and makes them current at the start of every frame; they are destroyed with it.

docs.title: Dear ImGui for Luau scripts
docs.text:
ImGuiLibrary ([ScriptLibrary("imgui")]) is the global table imgui, written with the same source generator as everything else, so its declarations in the .d.luau definitions cannot drift from the code. Functions are snake_case; a widget returns changed, value; a window, tree, table, menu, tab or popup that can be open returns whether it is, and every begin_… has its end_… (a script that forgets one, or fails between them, is put right at the end of the frame by ImGui's error recovery). Colors are tables of 3 or 4 numbers from 0 to 1, a combo's index counts from 1, flags and conditions are the names of ImGui's enums ({ "no_title_bar", "no_resize" }, "always"), and ids are the labels, with ImGui's ## and ###.

devtools.on_gui(function()                                 -- called every frame, inside the ImGui frame
    if imgui.begin_window("Spawner", nil, { "always_auto_resize" }) then
        imgui.text("entities: " .. world:count({ Position }))
        local changed, rate = imgui.slider_float("Rate", rate, 0, 10)
        if imgui.button("Spawn") then spawn() end
        devtools.watch("rate", rate)                        -- shown in the engine's debug window
    end
    imgui.end_window()
end)

With no frame open (a headless run, a shipped game that has no overlay) every imgui call does nothing and returns what it was given, so tool code can stay in the game. devtools.frame_open() says which it is. devtools.on_gui(fn) registers a drawing function and returns an id for devtools.remove_gui(id); the host calls ScriptGui.RunGui() once a frame between ImGuiHost.BeginFrame and EndFrame, and a function that raises is logged and removed. devtools.watch(name, value) adds a row to the debug window. The runtime's --run does this every frame, headless. The surface is: windows, text, widgets, layout, ids, trees, tables, menus, tabs, popups, tooltips, style, show_demo_window); ImPlot, ImGuizmo and imnodes are not in the Luau library yet: they are for the dev overlay and the editor, in C#.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
The Luau library runs against real ImGui frames with no window and no GPU: widgets return what they were given, draw data is produced, a mouse click on a button reaches the script, a script that forgets an end or fails in the middle does not break later frames, gui functions run and are removed when they fail, and the idle behavior.

ImGuiExtensionTests calls each of the three libraries in a headless frame (a quiet gizmo changes nothing and draws, a plot draws its four kinds of item in float and double, a node editor keeps the positions it was given and draws two nodes and a link) and reads how many vertices the frame produced. The overlay's GPU history (a line per top-level pass, zero where it did not run, the last 240 frames) is tested without a window.

The input translation runs on SDL's dummy video driver with synthetic events: the key table, buttons, the wheel, text, window filtering, display size and who wants the mouse. The renderer tests draw to an offscreen target and check where pixels land (a window and nothing outside it, glyphs from the atlas, clipping at the corners), that the atlas's bindless slot is released with the renderer, that the buffers grow, and that the overlay is the last pass of a real SceneRenderer frame. ImGui keeps a process-wide current context, so these tests run one at a time.

docs.title: The editor
docs.text:
Very bare-bones for now

The editor is very bare-bones for now: files are brought in by dragging them from the system (there is no import dialog or import settings editor), and it has no materials, no animations and no Export dialog (a game is exported from the command line). See What is not here.

Source/Apogee.Editor is an ImGui editor for a game folder. It is a CoreCLR program (a tool, never published with NativeAOT) built on Dear ImGui with docking, ImGuizmo, ImPlot and imnodes, Apogee.Host and the scene format.

dotnet run --project Source/Apogee.Editor -- [game folder] [--user <folder>]

With no game folder the editor shows its start screen.

The layout (a dock space: hierarchy on the left, inspector on the right, the viewport in the middle, tabs of assets, console, profiler and render graph below) is saved to imgui.ini in ~/.local/share/Apogee/Editor (the platform's local application data folder); the first run, with no file, builds the default one. Quitting with unsaved changes asks first.

docs.title: The panels
docs.text:
• Viewport. The world drawn into an image that ImGui shows as a texture (RenderTarget.Texture; one image per frame in flight, so the GPU never samples what the frame is writing). The editor's camera is not an entity: right mouse button looks around and, with W A S D Q E (Shift is faster), flies; middle button pans; the wheel zooms; F frames the active entity. A click that does not drag picks the entity under the pointer: a ray against the models' bounds (measured from the file, so no GPU is needed), and a small sphere for entities that have no model (lights, cameras, empty entities). Ctrl-click toggles the entity in the selection, Shift-click adds it, and a click on nothing clears the selection (unless Ctrl or Shift is held). Dragging from empty space (not on an entity, not on the gizmo) draws a selection box; letting go selects every entity whose bounds touch it (its model's bounds, projected; an entity without a model counts by its origin) and that is in front of the camera: with Ctrl the box toggles them, with Shift it adds them, otherwise it replaces the selection. Escape clears the selection (while a box is being dragged it cancels the box instead). ImGuizmo moves, rotates and scales the whole selection (W, E and R choose; local or world axes; optional snapping; the Pivot box chooses where a group turns, see Group transforms); a drag is one undo step. The view cube in the corner turns the camera. The helpers drawn as debug lines (a ground grid, the bounds of every selected entity, the active one brighter, a mark for each light and camera) can be turned off. Dropping a .glb or .gltf from the assets panel makes an entity at the point of the ground under the pointer; dropping model files from the system copies them into the game, imports them and does the same (see Bringing files in).
  • Hierarchy. The scene as a tree: click to select, Ctrl-click to toggle, Shift-click to select a range (in the order the tree shows, so entities inside a collapsed branch are skipped), drag on the empty space to select with a box, Ctrl+A for all and Escape for none. Double click or F2 renames the active entity, Ctrl+X, Ctrl+C, Ctrl+V and Ctrl+D cut, copy, paste and duplicate the selection (see Copy and paste), Delete removes every selected entity as one undo step ("Delete 3 entities"), right click opens the menu, and dragging a node drags the whole selection (or only that node when it is not selected) onto another to make them children (onto the empty space below to make them roots), as one step. An entity keeps its place in the world when it changes parent, and a name a sibling already has is made unique, also between the entities that move together.
  • Inspector. The components of the active entity (the last one picked; editing several at once comes later), drawn from the registry's descriptions: a checkbox, drag field, slider (when [Property] gives a Min and a Max), three drag fields for a vector or a double position, three angles for a rotation, a drop target for an entity reference, and for ModelRenderer.Model the model's path (type one, or drop a model file on it). Fields are grouped under their Category, Hidden ones are left out and ReadOnly ones greyed; right click a component to remove it; Add component lists every registered component. See what an inspector shows.
  • Assets. The virtual file system: res:// and, when listed, the packages' mod://id/ folders; each importable file shows whether it is imported, out of date, or not imported yet (AssetImporter.StatusOf), and Re-import imports one file again (Reimport). Double click a .ascene to open it; drag a model into the viewport or the inspector; drop files from the system on the panel to add them to the folder it shows (see Bringing files in).
  • Console. The log, filtered by level; while files are being imported its header shows the progress and a Cancel import button.
  • Profiler. The dev overlay's ImPlot plots: frame times, and the GPU time of every pass stacked over the last 240 frames, with the table.
  • Render graph. The last viewport frame's render graph as a read-only imnodes view: a node for each pass that ran, its inputs and outputs, and a link from the pass that last wrote a resource to the passes that read it.

docs.title: Selection
docs.text:
The selection is a list of entities in the order they were picked, and one of them is the active entity: the last one picked, the one the inspector shows and the gizmo sits on (when the active one is deleted, the last of the others takes over). Several entities can be selected in the hierarchy and in the viewport (see the panels above). What a delete, a drag in the hierarchy, a group transform (and, later, a copy) acts on (and a copy, a cut and a duplicate) is the selection's top level: the selected entities that have no selected ancestor, because a branch is carried by its top and its selected descendants would be handled twice.

The selection is not an undo step. It is kept as entity ids: an entity that was destroyed drops out of it, and comes back into it when an undo brings the entity back under the same id; creating an entity selects it, deleting entities takes them out of the selection (undoing the delete does not select them again), and the selection survives Play and Stop like the history does. While the game plays, selecting works and every edit stays disabled. The code is Source/Apogee.Editor/Editing/Selection.cs (plain classes over a world, with no ImGui, so it is tested without a window); the hierarchy panel only translates the requests of ImGui's multi-select (a click, a range, the box, Escape) into SelectionRequests, which SelectionRequests.Apply applies against the list of visible nodes.

docs.title: Group transforms
docs.text:
The gizmo acts on the selection's top level (the selected entities that have a Transform and no selected ancestor: a selected child rides on its selected parent and is never moved twice). A drag is one undo step ("Move 3 entities", "Rotate Cube"), however many frames it takes. Pivot in the viewport's toolbar chooses what a rotation or a scale turns around:

  • Center: the centre of the selection. It is the middle of the box that contains every member's model bounds when all of them have a model; when one does not (a light, a camera, an empty entity) it is the mean of the origins. Only a member's own model counts, not those of its descendants, so a group of empty parents is centred on the mean of their origins. One selected entity always uses its own origin.
  • Active: the origin of the active entity (the last one picked); when the active entity is a child of a selected entity, the origin of that selected parent, which is the one that moves.
  • Individual: the gizmo sits at the centre, but every entity turns and scales about its own origin, so a group of crates each spin in place (about the gizmo's axes: with World off those are the active entity's, not each crate's own). A move carries every entity by the same amount in all three modes.

The gizmo's axes are the world's, or, with World off (and always when scaling), those of the active entity. Snapping applies to the gizmo, that is to the pivot, so the group moves by whole steps and the members keep their offsets from each other.

What happens to a member, in world space: its offset from the pivot is stretched by the scale ratio (along the gizmo's axes) and then swung by the rotation of the drag, the pivot's translation is added, and its own rotation is turned by the same rotation. The result is taken into its parent's space, so a member under a rotated or scaled parent still moves the way the gizmo does. Positions are double and only differences (a delta, an offset) are ever floats. A move adds the gizmo's float difference to the double position, so it is exact in double for entities at the root of the scene, however far out (ten million metres from the origin still moves to the millimetre), and a move never turns or scales anything; a rotation or a scale reads only the rotation or the scale back from the gizmo. Offsets between members are floats, so a rotation or scale about a pivot a kilometre away is good to about a tenth of a millimetre. An entity under a parent has a local position that the engine stores relative to the parent and handles as a float: far from its parent's origin (everything under a root at the origin while the group is ten million metres out) it is only as exact as that float, which is how every transform in the engine works. A scale ratio below 0.001 is raised to 0.001 (the gizmo never goes lower), so a group is flattened but never mirrored or collapsed to zero. A drag that is cut short (Play, a failed Play, Escape or a click that changes the selection) ends where it is as its own undo step, and a new drag cannot begin until the mouse button has been let go.

Scaling a group is exact only in some cases. A transform here has a per-axis scale and no shear. Stretching a member along axes that are not its own would shear it, which cannot be stored. Each of a member's axes takes the length ratio that the stretch gives its direction, so a member whose axes line up with the gizmo's (or are turned a quarter turn) gets exactly the ratio you dragged, but a member turned 45 degrees under a non-uniform stretch is only approximated (its axes stay perpendicular and only their lengths follow the stretch). A uniform scale is always exact. Scaling about Individual or Active has the same rule. The maths is in Source/Apogee.Editor/Editing/GroupTransform.cs, TransformGesture.cs and GizmoDrag.cs (plain functions over placements, with no ImGui, tested without a window); the undo step is SetTransformsCommand in Apogee.Host.

docs.title: Copy and paste
docs.text:
Ctrl+C copies the selection (its top level, each entity with everything below it) to the system clipboard as scene text: the same XML a scene file holds (scenes), written by World.SaveSceneDocument, with no uid, because a copy is not a file. Several selected entities are one document. Ctrl+V reads the text back with World.LoadScene, so it works between scenes, between projects and between editor instances, and the text can be edited or written by hand. Ctrl+X is a copy followed by a delete (one step). Ctrl+D duplicates without touching the clipboard. The same commands are in the Edit menu and the hierarchy's context menu, which also has Paste as child (Ctrl+Shift+V).

  • Where it goes. A paste lands next to the active entity (under the same parent; at the root when nothing is selected); Paste as child puts it under the active entity. The new entities are selected, and the paste is one undo step ("Paste Cube", "Paste 3 entities"); undoing removes them, redoing brings them back under the same ids. A pasted entity keeps its local transform, so under another parent it moves with that parent.
  • Names. The pasted top-level entities get names no sibling has ("Cube", then "Cube 2"), also among themselves when they come from different parents; the loader decides, among the real siblings, so a pasted "Empty" stays "Empty" when no sibling has that name. Names below them are kept.
  • References. An Entity field that points to an entity inside the copied set is written as that entity's number in the document, and a paste points it at the new copy, so a copied branch stays wired to itself (and several selected entities to each other). A field that points outside the copied set is left empty: the scene format cannot name an entity that is not in the document. Asset fields travel as path|uid (the model's path, and its UID once it is imported) and are found again by the pasting project; one that cannot be found is left empty and logged. Components that a script defined travel in the document's <Components> header. A prefab instance is copied as one element that names its prefab and what it changes, and pasted as an instance (a selected member of one, without its root, as plain entities).
  • Duplicate is not a paste: it clones each top-level entity with World.Clone under the same parent ("Cube (copy)") as one step, and a clone keeps the references of its components as they are, so one that pointed at another entity still points at the original (including inside the duplicated branch).
  • Playing. Copy works while the game plays (it copies the running state); Cut, Paste and Duplicate are off, like every edit.
  • Bad text. Whatever is on the clipboard is untrusted. Text that is not a scene (not XML, another root element, a DTD, nesting that is too deep, more than 16 MB), a scene of a newer version, or one with no entities changes nothing: the console says why. Paste is greyed in the menus when the text cannot be a scene.

The code is Source/Apogee.Editor/Editing/ClipboardScene.cs (the IClipboard interface, SdlClipboard over SDL's clipboard, MemoryClipboard for tests, and the checks of the text), the project's Copy, Cut, Paste and Duplicate, and CreateEntitiesCommand in Apogee.Host (the undo step that makes several branches).

docs.title: Shortcuts
docs.text:
Every shortcut is a row of one table, the keymap (Source/Apogee.Editor/Input/Keymap.cs): an action id (edit.undo), the chord or chords that fire it, and the context it applies in. The menus show the shortcut text from the same table, so a label never disagrees with the key. On macOS the primary modifier is Cmd, shown as Cmd+Z; everywhere else it is Ctrl.

Action Shortcut Where Undo Ctrl+Z Anywhere Redo Ctrl+Y or Ctrl+Shift+Z Anywhere Save Ctrl+S Anywhere Save as Ctrl+Shift+S Anywhere Play or stop F5 Anywhere Cut Ctrl+X Anywhere Copy Ctrl+C Anywhere Paste Ctrl+V Anywhere Paste as child Ctrl+Shift+V Anywhere Duplicate Ctrl+D Anywhere Delete Delete Hierarchy focused Rename F2 Hierarchy focused Clear the selection Escape Viewport focused Frame the selection F Viewport focused Move tool W Viewport focused Rotate tool E Viewport focused Scale tool R Viewport focused Fly forward W Viewport, right mouse button held Fly back S Viewport, right mouse button held Fly left A Viewport, right mouse button held Fly right D Viewport, right mouse button held Fly up E Viewport, right mouse button held Fly down Q Viewport, right mouse button held
  • Contexts. Anywhere shortcuts work whichever panel has the keyboard; the others only while that panel is focused. While the right mouse button is held in the viewport the camera flies: the fly keys are held rather than pressed (extra modifiers, such as Shift to go faster, do not stop them), and the viewport's own keys (W, E, R, F, Escape) are off so that W flies instead of choosing the Move tool.
  • Exact modifiers. A chord fires only with exactly its modifiers: Ctrl+Shift+V pastes as a child and does not also paste, Shift+Z is not Z.
  • Typing. While a text field (or any widget that uses the keyboard) is active, no shortcut fires, so typing a name never deletes entities or switches the tool.
  • Conflicts. Keymap.Conflicts() reports two actions that share a chord where both could be active: in the same context, or when one of them is Anywhere. The defaults have none (a test checks it); a rebinding that collides is reported, not refused. Preferences rebinds, saves and resets the table.
  • ImGui's own keys. Ctrl+A (select all), Shift-click ranges, Ctrl-click and Escape in the hierarchy are ImGui's multi-select, not keymap rows.

The matching is Keymap.Pressed and Keymap.IsHeld over IKeyState (ImGui's keyboard in the editor, a fake in the tests), so it is tested without a window. The manual's table above is checked against the real one by a test.

docs.title: Preferences
docs.text:
The editor remembers its preferences, the recent projects and the key bindings in preferences.xml in the editor's own folder (the platform's local application data folder: ~/.local/share/Apogee/Editor on Linux and macOS, %LOCALAPPDATA%\Apogee\Editor on Windows; next to imgui.ini and the logs). It is never written into a game folder, and it is not the game's user://settings.xml: that file belongs to one game and its mods, is replaced when Play starts, and every mod can read it. The file is the engine's settings store over a file system of the editor's folder alone, so it has the same shape (<settings version="1"> with <value key="..."> lines), only what differs from the default is written, writes are atomic (a temporary file moved over the old one), and a key this editor does not know is kept. The dock layout stays in imgui.ini.

<settings version="1">
  <value key="editor.camera.speed">12</value>
  <value key="keys.edit.undo">Ctrl+Alt+U</value>
  <value key="recent.0">/home/me/games/farm</value>
  <value key="project.5b0c7e1d2a9f4c38.scene">res://scenes/barn.ascene</value>
</settings>
Keys Holds editor.camera.speed the fly speed of the camera in metres per second (6; Shift is three times as fast) editor.gizmo.mode, .world, .pivot, .snap the tool (move, rotate, scale), world or local space, the pivot of a group (center, active, individual) and whether it snaps editor.gizmo.snap_move, .snap_rotate, .snap_scale the snap steps (0.5 m, 15 degrees, 0.1) editor.helpers, editor.game_camera the viewport's helpers, and the game camera while playing editor.ui.scale the interface scale (1; 0.5 to 3) recent.0 to recent.9 the recent projects as full paths, the latest first project.<16 hex digits>.scene the scene that was open last in a project (the first 16 hex digits of the SHA-256 of the project's full path), reopened the next time the project opens if it is still there keys.<action id> a key binding that differs from the default

The gizmo's state is kept as you work (the toolbar and the window edit the same values), the scene is noted when it changes, and the file is written within a second of a change and when the editor quits (a slider that is dragged writes once a second, not once a frame).

Edit > Preferences... (also on the start screen) opens a window with two tabs. General edits the values above (Reset to defaults puts them back; it does not touch the recent projects or the keys). Keys lists every action with its shortcut and where it applies. Rebind waits for the next key you press and binds the action to it with the modifiers held (Ctrl+Shift+K); Escape alone gives up (to bind Escape itself, hold a modifier, or use Reset on an action whose default it is); a modifier alone is not a chord. Clear unbinds the action, Reset puts its defaults back (it is greyed when it is on them), Reset all does it for every action. While a key is awaited no shortcut fires, so the key you choose does not also do what it is bound to. A chord that another action already has (where both could be active) is accepted and shown in red with the name of the other action: both fire, and the window says so. The menus and the toolbar show the new chords at once.

Key bindings are a difference from the defaults. An action on its default chords has no key in the file, so a later editor with another default reaches everyone who never changed it. keys.edit.redo holds the chords joined with | (Ctrl+Y | Ctrl+Shift+Z), none for an unbound action. The primary modifier is always written Ctrl and shown as Cmd on macOS, so a file reads the same on every platform. Bindings for actions this editor does not have stay in the file untouched. When the file is read, a chord that does not parse is reported and the action keeps its default, and collisions the saved bindings cause are reported (nothing is refused).

Recent projects. File > Open recent and the start screen list the last ten game folders, the latest first, without duplicates (the same folder spelled differently counts once). A folder that is gone from the disk is dropped when the file is read, and when you choose one that turned out to be gone (or is no game folder any more) the editor says so and removes it; Clear recent empties the list. Opening a project adds it, the same way as the dialog.

A file that does not read never crashes the editor and is never lost. A file that is not XML (or has another root element) is kept as preferences.bad.xml next to it; one written by a newer editor (a version above 1) is kept as preferences.v<N>.xml; in both cases the defaults are used, a message at the start says so, and the next change writes a new preferences.xml. A file that cannot be read at all (locked, no permission) is left exactly as it is and nothing is saved in that run. A value of the wrong type or outside its range falls back to its default (numbers are clamped). The window shows where the file is and whether it is being saved.

The code is Source/Apogee.Editor/EditorPreferences.cs (the typed keys, the recent list, the keymap diff), Source/Apogee.Editor/Input/KeyBindingEditor.cs (the rows and the capture of a chord over IKeyState, with no ImGui) and Source/Apogee.Editor/Panels/PreferencesWindow.cs (only draws them). The folder is a parameter of EditorPreferences.Open, so tests use a temporary one.

docs.title: Scenes and undo
docs.text:
File creates, opens and saves scenes (.ascene XML, see scenes); Open scene... and Save as... use the system's file dialogs. Every edit is a command on an EditHistory (Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Y or Ctrl+Shift+Z): component values (a drag is one step), adding and removing components, creating, duplicating and deleting entities (a deleted branch comes back under the same ids; deleting or moving several at once is one step), renaming and reparenting. Opening or creating a scene clears the history.

The history remembers the state the scene was saved in (its save point): the scene is modified (the * after its name, and the question when quitting) only when it differs from the file. Undo back to the saved state and the mark goes away; undo past it, or make a new edit after undoing from it, and it comes back. A drag that is still going (its steps merge) is not the saved state either. With more than 500 steps (the history's Limit) the oldest are forgotten, and if the saved state was among them the scene stays modified until it is saved again.

docs.title: File dialogs
docs.text:
Open scene..., Save as... (Ctrl+Shift+S, and Save on a scene that has no file yet) and Open project... show the operating system's own dialog: the open dialog starts in the game's scenes folder (or the game folder) and filters on .ascene; the save dialog adds .ascene when the name has none. The dialogs come from SDL (FileDialog); they are asynchronous, so the editor goes on running while one is open, and the New scene, Open scene, Save as and Open project entries are greyed until it closes (a second dialog is never opened; a shortcut pressed meanwhile opens the editor's own entry instead). A dialog that is cancelled changes nothing. A dialog that never answers (a desktop portal that crashed) is given up on after ten minutes: the editor is free again, and an answer that arrives later is ignored.

A scene belongs to the game, so only a file inside the game folder can be opened or saved: the dialog gives an operating system path, and the editor turns it into the game's virtual path (<game folder>/scenes/level.ascene becomes res://scenes/level.ascene). A path outside the folder (a game folder that is a symbolic link, or sits at the root of a drive, is understood), a file that is not an .ascene, a name the game cannot use, a place in a read-only part of the game, or a file that a pack of the game already answers for is refused with a message that says why, and nothing is written. If the project was switched while a dialog was open, its late result is dropped; a result that arrives while the game is running is applied like the menu entry would: Open scene and Save as end the run first (the scene saved is the edited one, not the run's).

A scene that cannot be opened (it does not parse, it is from a newer engine) or saved (a read-only file, a full disk) is reported in a message and changes nothing: the open scene stays as it was, with its path, its undo history, its selection and its modified mark, so the next Save cannot write an empty scene over it. Save and quit and Save and open do not go on when the save failed. Known limits: Windows 8.3 short names and macOS file names written in another Unicode form than the folder's are reported as outside the game folder.

On Linux SDL asks the desktop's file chooser through xdg-desktop-portal, or runs zenity. A machine with neither has no system dialog: the editor then falls back to its own entries (a list of the game's scenes for Open scene, a path field for Save as and for Open project), so everything stays reachable.

docs.title: The start screen and opening a project
docs.text: Started without a game folder, the editor opens its window on a start screen with an Open project... button (and File > Open project...) and the list of recent projects: choose a game folder in the system's folder dialog, or click a recent one. Only a folder that has a game.xml or a packages folder is taken for a game (a mistaken pick, such as the home folder, is refused with a message and nothing closes); choosing the folder that is already open does nothing. The same entry in the File menu of an open project switches projects inside the same process: if the scene has unsaved changes the editor asks first (Save and open, Open without saving, Cancel); then the old project is closed (the GPU is waited for, the viewport and the session are disposed, since one session exists at a time) and the new folder is opened at the start of the next frame, with a fresh camera, panels and undo history. The window title and the crash reports' Edited game line follow the project. --user <folder> belongs to the game folder given on the command line: a project opened later from the dialog gets its own user folder (what its game.xml says), so two games never share user://. If the folder cannot be opened (a game.xml that is wrong, say) the editor says why and opens the previous project again. A folder that does not exist is refused without closing anything.

docs.title: Bringing files in
docs.text:
Drag files or folders from the system's file manager onto the editor's window. The editor accepts the drop only when it can do something sensible with it, and says why when it cannot (a message, and the console lists every file it left out): no project is open, the game is playing, a dialog is open, an import is already running, a question about names is waiting, or the files landed on a panel that takes none (the hierarchy, the inspector).

Where they go. The panel under the pointer decides, using what it showed when you let go:

  • On the Assets panel: into the folder it shows (a dropped folder is recreated under it). The files are copied and imported; nothing is added to the scene.
  • On the Viewport: model files (.glb, .gltf) go to the asset browser's folder when it is inside res:// below the top, otherwise to res://models; once they are imported, one entity per model is made, as one undo step, at the point of the ground under the pointer where you let go (five metres along the view when the pointer was above the horizon; several models are put side by side, two metres apart). The files are not undone by the undo, only the entities. Other files in the drop are added too. A model that fails to import makes no entity.
  • No position: some systems (Wayland compositors without the protocol) do not say where the drop happened. The editor never guesses a point: such a drop goes to the Assets panel's folder.

Only folders of the game itself take files: res://, which must be writable. A folder of a package (mod://) or of a pack is read-only, and the drop is refused.

What is taken. Files the game can use: what an importer takes (.glb and .gltf, .png, .jpg and .jpeg, .slang shaders), scenes and prefabs (.ascene, .aprefab), and scripts, definitions, sounds, fonts and UI documents (.luau, .xml, .wav, .ogg, .flac, .mp3, .ttf, .otf, .rml, .rcss). Anything else is refused by name with the list of what is taken. Also refused, each with its reason: a name the game cannot use on every system (a colon, a trailing dot or space, a Windows device name such as con), a hidden file or folder (a name that starts with a dot; hidden entries inside a dropped folder are skipped without a word), the game folder itself or a folder that holds it (it would copy the game into itself), anything into res://imported (the importer's own folder: its index and UID list; a dropped folder of that name too), an empty file, a file over 512 MB or a drop over 2 GB in all, and links: a symbolic link or a junction (dropped or inside a dropped folder) is never followed, because its target can be anywhere. A dropped folder is read to at most 10,000 files, 10,000 folders and 64 levels (this walk, and the reading of a .gltf, run on the main thread when the files are dropped: they are capped for that reason). The paths the files get are built only from names that passed these checks, so a name cannot climb out of the folder.

Models with files of their own. A .gltf brings the buffers and images its uris name (beside it or below it, %20 and other escapes read as the glTF standard has them, so a.bin and a%2Ebin are one file; a file or a folder on the way that is a link is refused; data URIs need nothing). A model that names a file that is missing, an absolute path, a drive, or a path that climbs (..) is refused whole, with the reason. The companions are copied with it and imported as part of the model, not as assets of their own. A file's .import.xml beside it comes along; a dropped .import.xml without its asset is refused. A sidecar that arrives with a UID that another asset of the project has (you copied an asset together with its settings) gets a new UID, so two assets never share one; the console says which.

Names the project has. A dropped file is never written over a file the project has unless you choose it. When some names clash, a question lists them: Keep both (the default: the new file gets a free name, car 2.glb; a model with files of its own goes into a new folder, since the names inside it cannot change), Skip them, Replace (overwrites; this cannot be undone; the asset keeps its own .import.xml, so its UID and settings stay; a link in the project is never written through, that file is kept and the new one gets a free name instead) or Cancel. A name that appears between the plan and the copy (another program wrote it) is left alone and reported. Two dropped files with the same name both arrive (the second is numbered).

The copy and the import run on a worker thread, so a large model or a texture compression does not stop the editor. The menu bar and the console header show the progress (Importing 2/5: res://models/car.glb), and the console lists each step. Cancel import stops at the next file; what was copied stays (nothing is rolled back), and the files not yet imported can be imported with Re-import in the Assets panel. A file that fails to import (a damaged model) stays copied, and the console says why. Files are written through the game's file system, whole or not at all (a crash leaves the old file). A file is read whole before it is written, which is why a single file is limited to 512 MB, and a file that is being read cannot be cancelled until it has been read. Files are read again just before they are copied and must be exactly what the plan saw (the same size, not a link, not swapped for a pipe), so a file that changed meanwhile fails on its own and cannot hold the worker. Play is disabled while a job runs (and until its report has been taken), and a drop or a Re-import is refused. Closing the project, or the editor, during a job stops it at the next file (or the next megabyte of a big one) and waits up to 20 seconds for the worker; a texture compression cannot be interrupted, so a longer one ends by itself in the background, while the gate of that game folder stays held (there is one gate per game folder for the whole process, not one per open project), so opening the same folder again does not start a second importer.

The hot reloader and the importer. The editor's session normally imports changed files itself, on the main thread, every frame (HotReloader). Two importers must never write imported/index.xml at the same time, so the editor holds one import gate: a job takes it for its whole run, the reloader's poll and the Re-import menu entry take it for theirs, and whoever finds it taken does nothing that frame (the main thread never waits). While a job runs the reloader is therefore not polled; what it missed is kept, and when the job ends it notices the new files, finds their artifacts current (the job imported them), and reloads the models that changed without importing anything a second time. A project that was never imported has no imported/index.xml, and its models and textures are loaded from their sources. Importing one dropped file would make an index, and from the next frame the reloader would import the whole project on the main thread (every model, every texture compression). So a drop on such a project only copies: the console says "the project has not been imported", models dropped on the viewport still become entities (they load from their source), and nothing is imported until the project is: with Apogee.Runtime --import, or Re-import on a file in the Assets panel (which starts the index; the reloader then imports the rest of the project's out-of-date assets as well, on the main thread).

Dropped files arrive as one event for the whole drag-and-drop (see Platform). On X11 and Windows the position is reliable; on macOS it is in points like the rest of the window; on Wayland it depends on the compositor and SDL's version. Dropping from a file manager into a sandboxed editor (Flatpak or Snap) may give the editor a path that is not the real one: add files by copying them into the game folder instead.

docs.title: Play
docs.text:
Play (F5) runs the game inside the editor. The editor keeps a snapshot of the world, replaces its session with the game's (the same ScriptSession the runtime makes: packages, mods and scripts, physics, audio, the UI) over a copy of the scene, loaded before the scripts run, and shows the game in the viewport through the world's main camera (or the editor's camera when it has none, or when Game camera is off). The game gets the pointer and the input actions while the viewport is hovered or focused; keys and typed text also go to the game's own UI (its text fields) while the viewport has the keyboard; the pointer reaches it through the panel, in the panel's coordinates. Pause and Step freeze and advance the world. Stop makes an editing session again and puts the world back as it was under the same entity ids, so the selection and the undo history still point at the same entities. A game whose scripts fail does not start: the editor says why and stays in editing. Only one session exists at a time (the UI library and others hold process-wide state), which is why Play and Stop replace it. Debug toggles the physics shapes and RmlUi's debugger while playing.

Editing is off while playing: the panels show the game's world, read-only.

docs.title: What is not here
docs.text: An import settings editor and an import dialog (files are dropped in; their settings are the .import.xml next to them, see Asset import), materials, animations, an Export dialog (a game is exported with ./build.sh export), editing several selected entities at once in the inspector (it shows the active one), material and logic graph editors (imnodes is ready for them), multi-viewport windows, and a physics ray cast for picking (an editing session has no physics bodies). Sound plays in play mode through OpenAL Soft (Audio), which ships beside the editor like any other library.

docs.title: Tests

with what is behind the camera left out), the selection model (toggle, ranges in the visible order, top level, dead entities, the active entity, the multi-select requests), copy, cut, paste and duplicate through a memory clipboard (the same tree under new ids as one step, next to the active entity or under it, unique names, references inside the copy followed and outside ones dropped, models by path, undo of a cut, text that is not a scene, duplicating several, playing), the group transforms (the pivots, moving at ten million metres, rotating and scaling about the centre or in place, local axes, a member under a turned, non-uniformly scaled or mirrored parent, a selected child not moved twice, exactness of a move with a turned pivot, ten million metres out, the scale caveat and its 45 degree value, and the life of a drag: dropped when cut short, sealed, blocked until the button is let go), the keymap (chords parsed and printed for each platform, the defaults and their menu
