docs.title: Exporting a game
docs.text:
An export turns a game folder into a folder that runs on its own: the runtime built for a platform, renamed to the game's executable name, its native libraries and compiled shaders, the game's files in data/game.pack, and the game's game.xml. It is made from the command line (Apogee.Runtime --export, wrapped by ./build.sh export) or from code (GameExporter in Source/Apogee.Export). The editor has no Export dialog yet.

./build.sh aot                                                          # publish the runtime for this machine: Bin/publish/runtime
./build.sh export Tests/Fixtures/ShippedGame Bin/export/linux --target linux-x64 --cooked
Bin/export/linux/FixtureGame                                           # runs from anywhere, with no environment variable

Apogee.Runtime --export <game folder> <out folder> --target <rid> [--cooked] [--runtime <dir>] [--console]
<game folder> the game: a folder with a game.xml. It is never written to. <out folder> where the export goes: it does not exist, is empty, or is an earlier export (it holds a file .apogee-export), which is then replaced. Anything else is an error, so that nothing of yours is deleted. It cannot be inside the game folder, nor contain it. --target <rid> the platform: linux-x64, win-x64, osx-arm64 or osx-x64 (the platforms the engine has complete native libraries for). Anything else is an error that lists these. --cooked pack the imported artifacts and the cooked documents instead of the sources they replace (the game is imported first, in a copy). --runtime <dir> the folder the runtime for the target was published to. Default: the folder of the running program when it is the NativeAOT runtime, else the Bin/publish/runtime above the program or the current folder. --console Windows only: keep the console subsystem, so that the game opens a console window (to read its log). Without it the program is a windowed one, see Windows.

Exit codes: 0 fine, 1 bad arguments (an unknown target, a bad APOGEE_PACK_KEY), 2 the export failed (the message says why). Warnings are printed to stderr, for example that no key is set.

docs.title: Where the runtime for a platform comes from
docs.text:
The runtime is a NativeAOT program, so it can only be built on its own operating system (./build.sh aot), and the folder that command publishes already holds every native library of that platform. An export copies from such a folder. It reads the header of the program in it (PE, ELF or Mach-O, with its processor) and refuses a folder of another platform with what to do:

/path/runtime holds a linux-x64 runtime; --target win-x64 needs one published for win-x64 (./build.sh aot on that operating system, or the CI artifact apogee-win-x64), passed with --runtime <dir>.

So exporting for the machine you are on needs nothing but ./build.sh aot; exporting for another platform needs a runtime published there (or downloaded from CI) and --runtime. A macOS runtime has to be a thin binary for one processor, not a universal one. Left out of the copy: debug files (*.pdb, *.dbg, *.dSYM), import libraries (*.lib, *.exp), the Slang compiler's libraries and the shader sources and their import settings (Shaders/*.slang and Shaders/*.slang.import.xml; the compiled Shaders/imported stays: a shipped game never loads the compiler), steam_appid.txt, and the runtime folder's own game.xml and data/.

The continuous integration publishes the runtime of each platform it builds (apogee-linux-x64, apogee-win-x64, apogee-osx-arm64, apogee-osx-x64) as a workflow artifact for 14 days: download one, unzip it (an archive does not keep the executable bit; the export sets it on the program it writes), and pass the folder with --runtime. This is how to export for Windows or macOS without a computer of that kind.

docs.title: The layout
docs.text:
Linux and Windows macOS executable and native libraries, Shaders/ <out>/ <out>/<Name>.app/Contents/MacOS/ game.xml, data/game.pack <out>/ <out>/<Name>.app/Contents/Resources/ executable name <executable> (.exe on Windows), from game.xml the same; the bundle is <name>.app

The folder that holds game.xml and data/ is the game's root: the runtime finds it next to its executable, or in ../Resources from a bundle's MacOS folder (see how the runtime finds it), and mounts only data/*.pack as res://. A game that is exported does not read the files of the folder it came from, only its pack.

data/game.pack holds the game folder as GamePacker packs it (a very big game continues in game_001.pack…), less what a shipped game does not have: data/ (the packs of the development folder), dev_mods/ (a shipped game has no development mods), game.xml (it is written beside the pack), the icon file, steam_appid.txt (the Steam app id comes from game.xml), and names that start with a dot. A cooked export imports a copy of the game folder (the existing imported/ is reused, so only what changed is imported again), so the game folder gets no imported/ and no changed file.

The exported game.xml is the game's, with the icon changed: the icon is in the executable or the bundle on Windows and macOS, and a file icon.png beside game.xml on Linux, which the platform steps below write.

docs.title: The pack key
docs.text:
If APOGEE_PACK_KEY is set (64 hexadecimal digits, in the environment or in the .env file that the ./build.sh wrapper loads), the export encrypts the pack with it, and writes the key into the executable, so that the game opens its own pack without the variable. Without a key the packs are plain, and the export warns about it. See Encryption and the key.

The key goes into a reserved slot of the runtime (PackKeySlot): the executable holds 68 bytes in its read-only data, which start with a 16-byte magic that appears nowhere else, and the export patches the copy: it finds every copy of the whole slot (at least one, else it is not this engine's runtime and the export fails; a magic that is not followed by the rest of a slot is other data and is left alone, and a file that ends inside a slot is refused), and writes the same key, masked with one random salt, into each. A compiler may emit the slot's data more than once (the NativeAOT executable for macOS on Apple silicon has two copies), and the game reads whichever copy its code refers to, so all of them are patched; the export log says how many places it wrote when there is more than one. The running game reads the key back before it looks at the environment. No recompiling is needed, which is why an export can be made for any platform.

Obfuscation, not protection

The key is in the file, one XOR away from anyone who reads this page and the source, and in the memory of the running game. The slot keeps it out of strings, out of a quick look in a hex editor, and away from the pack. It does not stop a determined person from reading your game's files. Do not put a key in an export that you cannot afford to have extracted, and use a key only for this game.

docs.title: Arguments a shipped game ignores
docs.text: A game started with no command takes the runtime's options (--user, --headless, --frames, --size...) and logs and ignores any other argument, because Steam appends +connect_lobby <id> when a player accepts an invitation. Every runtime command stays in the shipped program (there are no feature toggles).

docs.title: Platform steps
docs.text: The last step of an export depends on the operating system (IPlatformPackaging): the executable's icon and version information on Windows, the .app bundle on macOS, the icon file and desktop entry on Linux. The Windows, Linux and macOS steps are described below. Code signing with a certificate (Authenticode, Developer ID) and notarization are outside the export: sign the result.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
The export copies the runtime built for win-x64, renames it <executable>.exe, and then changes the file in place with the export's own PE writer (Source/Apogee.Export/Windows). It reads and writes the executable's headers and resource section itself, with no Windows API, rc.exe or rcedit, so a Windows export can be made on Linux or macOS from a runtime published on Windows (--runtime). Three things change:

  • The icon. The game's Icon (a square PNG, 256x256 or more advised) is written as an icon group with seven images: 16, 24, 32, 48, 64 and 128 pixels as 32-bit images with an alpha channel (what every Windows version reads), and 256 pixels as a PNG (Windows Vista and later), each scaled from your image with a box filter. Explorer picks the size it needs; the window and the task bar take the first group, which is number 1. A smaller image is scaled up for the sizes above it and the export warns. A game without an icon keeps the runtime's.
  • The version information (the Details tab of the file's properties, the name task managers show) is made from game.xml: CompanyName is the organization, FileDescription the description (the name when there is none), FileVersion and ProductVersion the version as major.minor.patch.0, InternalName the executable's name, OriginalFilename the executable's file name, LegalCopyright the copyright, ProductName the name; language English (United States), code page Unicode. Each part of the version must be at most 65535. Any version or icon resource the runtime had is replaced; its other resources (the application manifest above all) are kept as they are.
  • The subsystem. The runtime is a console program; a game started by a double-click would open a console window beside its own. The export makes it a windowed program (IMAGE_SUBSYSTEM_WINDOWS_GUI). A windowed program has no standard output: run the game from a terminal and nothing is printed. --console keeps the console subsystem for when you want to read the log.

How the file is changed: the resource section is rewritten where it is when it is the last section of the file and nothing else points into it; otherwise (linkers put the relocations last) a new .rsrc section is added after the last one, and the old one is renamed .rsrc0 and left in the file as unused data. No existing section moves, so the code, the pack key and everything that points into the program stay where they are, and the key is written before this step so that the checksum in the header, which is written last, covers the final file. Adding a section header needs 40 free bytes between the section table and the first section's data; a linker leaves hundreds, but an executable made some other way may not, and the export then stops with an error saying so. It also stops if the declared image size is larger than where the last section ends. The export refuses an executable that has other data after its sections (an installer, an attached archive), and one that is damaged: the message says what is wrong.

  • Signing. Signing the game (Authenticode, signtool sign) is outside the export: sign <executable>.exe, and the DLLs if you like, after the export. An unsigned program from the internet is held by Windows SmartScreen until enough people have run it, or until it is signed with a certificate that has a reputation; a game on Steam is not affected by that.
  • Version suffixes. The version in game.xml is major.minor.patch and nothing else: a suffix such as -beta or +build is an error when the manifest is read. The file version, the product version and the strings FileVersion and ProductVersion all say 1.2.3.0. Put a label such as "beta" in the description if players should see it.
  • Signed runtimes. A signed runtime loses its signature (the changes invalidate it) and the export warns. A runtime with IMAGE_DLLCHARACTERISTICS_FORCE_INTEGRITY, which Windows loads only when signed, is refused instead, because the unsigned result could not start.

What the tests prove, and what they do not. The unit tests write executables with the PE writer and read them back with System.Reflection.PortableExecutable, with their own parser of the resource tree and version block, and with an independent sum for the checksum: the sections are contiguous and aligned, SizeOfImage is where the last one ends, every resource directory is ordered (names first, then numbers) with the entry counts it declares, the checksum is right. They do this on small executables made by the tests, on the engine's vendored MSVC-linked SDL3.dll and on the signed steam_api64.dll (a signature to strip, a resource type with a name), where the original sections, the import, exception, relocation, debug and load-configuration tables and the other resources must come out byte for byte. They also damage the headers (truncations, every field set to the edge values, random bytes) and expect an ExportException every time. They cannot show that the Windows loader accepts the file: nothing in the project's tests runs an exported program on Windows, and PEReader is more lenient than the loader. On Windows one test asks FileVersionInfo for the version information.

To look at an export with a second, independent implementation of the format, on Linux or macOS with LLVM installed (one test does this when llvm-readobj is on the PATH):

llvm-readobj --file-headers --sections --coff-resources Bin/export/win/FixtureGame.exe

Expected: Subsystem: IMAGE_SUBSYSTEM_WINDOWS_GUI (0x2) (without --console), a non-zero CheckSum, a section .rsrc that is the last one and, usually, .rsrc0 before it (the old resources, now unused), and under .rsrc the types ICON (ID 3) with 7 entries, GROUP_ICON (ID 14), VERSIONINFO (ID 16) and MANIFEST (ID 24). That Explorer shows the icon and the Details tab, and that a double-click opens no console, is checked by hand on a Windows computer.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
An export for linux-x64 is a folder that runs from anywhere:

FixtureGame                      the program (mode 755), the game's executable name
lib*.so, libSDL3.so.0 ...        the native libraries, beside it
Shaders/imported/                compiled shaders
game.xml, data/game.pack         the game
icon.png                         the icon, 256x256
org.apogee.fixturegame.desktop   the desktop entry
  • The executable bit. The step sets the executable's mode to rwxr-xr-x (File.SetUnixFileMode). On a Windows computer there are no Unix modes, so the export warns that the bit is not set: set it (chmod +x) when the folder is unpacked on Linux, or export Linux from Linux or WSL, where the bit is kept (an archive made on Windows loses it again).
  • The icon. The game's Icon is written as icon.png, scaled to 256x256 (a smaller icon is made bigger and the export warns, as it does for an icon below 256 pixels), and the exported game.xml names it (<Icon path="icon.png"/>), which is the file the runtime draws the window's icon from. A game without an icon gets no icon.png and no Icon line.
  • The desktop entry, <identifier>.desktop, follows the Desktop Entry Specification: Type, Name and Comment (from game.xml's name and description), Exec=<executable>, Icon=<identifier>, Categories=Game; and StartupWMClass=<identifier>, which is the application id the runtime gives its window, so that a desktop matches the window to the entry. Values are escaped as the specification says (a backslash, a line break and a leading space). It is a template for whoever packages the game (a distribution package, a Flatpak, an AppImage, an installer): Exec is the program's name as found on the PATH and Icon is the name of an icon in a theme, which is where an installer puts icon.png. Nothing in the export reads it, and a game run through Steam does not use it.

It does not depend on the working directory. The runtime finds the game (game.xml, data/), the compiled shaders and the native libraries from the folder of the executable, not from where it was started (AppContext.BaseDirectory), and the libraries that load other libraries (for example libcimgui.so, librmlui.so, libktx.so) have the run path $ORIGIN, so they find them beside themselves. No LD_LIBRARY_PATH is needed: cd /tmp && /path/to/export/FixtureGame works. The player's files are written under ~/.local/share/<organization>/<user folder> (or --user <dir>), never in the game's folder.

What the player's system provides. The native libraries are shipped; these are not:

  • The C and C++ libraries: glibc, and libstdc++ (libstdc++.so.6) for the libraries that use it. How new a glibc and libstdc++ the export needs is decided by where its parts were built. SDL, OpenAL Soft and GameNetworkingSockets are the prebuilt libraries in ThirdParty, built in Valve's Steam Runtime "sniper" and needing glibc 2.31 at most (ThirdParty/README.md). The NativeAOT program and the libraries built by ./build.sh native (Flecs, Luau, Jolt, ...) need the glibc and libstdc++ of the computer that built them: a runtime published on a current rolling distribution needs a current glibc (one published on Arch Linux in November 2026 needed 2.44) and will not start on an older one. Publish the runtime (./build.sh aot) on the oldest distribution you want to support, or in a container of it, and export from that. Steam's "sniper" runtime is the baseline to aim for for a game on Steam.
  • Vulkan: the Vulkan loader (libvulkan.so.1) and a driver for the graphics card. The engine does not ship them (ThirdParty/README.md, "Not vendored").
  • OpenSSL (libssl): the packs are encrypted with AES-GCM, which .NET takes from the system's OpenSSL on Linux. A game with encrypted packs needs it; a plain one does not.
  • Audio and windowing: SDL and OpenAL Soft load the desktop's backends at run time (X11 or Wayland; PipeWire, PulseAudio or ALSA), so whatever the player's desktop has is used.

The unit tests export from a synthesized runtime folder, so they check the step's files, not that a real export starts on a given distribution.

docs.title: macOS
docs.text:
An export for osx-arm64 or osx-x64 is an application bundle. The runtime for the target must be a thin (single processor) one, see above.

Fixture Game.app/                      the bundle, named after the game's name
  Contents/
    Info.plist                         generated from game.xml
    PkgInfo                            APPL????
    MacOS/
      FixtureGame                      the program (mode 755), the game's executable name
      lib*.dylib                       the native libraries, beside it
      Shaders/imported/                compiled shaders
    Resources/
      game.xml, data/game.pack         the game: its root, see "The layout"
      game.icns                        the icon
  • Info.plist is written as an XML property list (the text of game.xml is escaped, so a name with & or < is fine). It holds CFBundleName and CFBundleDisplayName (the game's name), CFBundleIdentifier (its identifier), CFBundleExecutable, CFBundleVersion and CFBundleShortVersionString (its version, major.minor.patch: game.xml accepts no suffix such as -beta, which CFBundleVersion could not hold, since it takes only integers separated by dots), CFBundlePackageType APPL, CFBundleIconFile game.icns (when the game has an icon), CFBundleInfoDictionaryVersion 6.0, LSMinimumSystemVersion, NSHighResolutionCapable, LSApplicationCategoryType public.app-category.games and NSHumanReadableCopyright (its copyright, when it has one). LSMinimumSystemVersion is the newest minimum system version (LC_BUILD_VERSION) among the program and the .dylib files beside it, for the target's processor, and never below 11.0, the first macOS for Apple silicon (also what it is when none of them says).
  • The icon is made into game.icns, with PNG images at 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512 and 1024 pixels and the @2x images of 16 to 256 (the sizes Finder and the Dock use). A size above the game's icon is left out, not enlarged: macOS then scales the biggest image there is. 1024x1024 is advised; below that the export warns that the 512 and 1024 pixel images are missing. The window's icon is the application's icon, so the exported game.xml names no Icon.
  • The executable bit is set as on Linux (rwxr-xr-x); a Windows computer has no Unix modes, so the export warns that it must be set where the bundle is unpacked, and an archive made on Windows loses it again. Archive a bundle on a Mac with ditto -c -k --keepParent "Fixture Game.app" Game.zip.

docs.title: The code signature
docs.text:
An Apple-silicon Mac only runs a program that is signed, and the NativeAOT runtime comes with an ad-hoc signature: the linker signs it with no certificate, only hashes (codesign -s - makes the same kind, with an empty signature slot, and is accepted too). The signature is a table at the end of the file (the CodeDirectory) with the hash of every 16 KiB page of the program; the kernel checks a page's hash when it is loaded and kills the program if it does not match (Killed: 9). The export changes a page of the program, for it writes the pack key into it (into each copy of the slot), so it has to make the hashes right again. MachOSignature.Rehash does that once, after the key is written everywhere and as the last change to the program:

  1. It reads the Mach-O header and finds the LC_CODE_SIGNATURE load command, which says where the signature is.
  2. It reads the signature's SuperBlob and finds every CodeDirectory in it (a program can have an alternate one with another hash function).
  3. For each, it hashes every page of the program, from the start of the file up to where the signature begins, with that CodeDirectory's own hash function (SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-256 cut to 20 bytes, or SHA-384) and page size, and writes the hashes over the old ones in place.

Nothing else is touched: not the length of the file, the header, the position of the signature, the identifier, or the other blobs. All of it is checked first: a file that is not a thin 64-bit Mach-O, or whose lengths and offsets do not fit it (or whose CodeDirectory is shorter than its version needs, or uses a scatter vector, or does not have every copy of the pack key slot inside the hashed code), fails the export and is not written (the program is untrusted input to this code, so every length is checked against the file with 64-bit arithmetic, and nothing is allocated or looped over by what the file claims).

What it does not do:

  • It does not sign. A program without a signature (an x86-64 build the linker did not sign) is left as it is, which macOS runs; for an arm64 one the export warns that it will not run until it is signed (codesign --force --sign - <executable>, on a Mac).
  • It does not repair a signature made with a certificate. Such a signature (a CodeDirectory without the ad-hoc flag, or a signature slot with a CMS message in it; an empty slot is what codesign -s - writes) also signs the CodeDirectory, so changing the CodeDirectory breaks it, and only the private key can make it again. The export stops with that message: publish the runtime unsigned, and sign the bundle after the export.
  • There is no Developer ID signing and no notarization. The bundle is not sealed either: no signature covers Info.plist or the files in Resources; only the program (and each library, by the signature it came with) is signed.

docs.title: Gatekeeper, signing and notarization
docs.text:
• Downloaded builds (a browser, a message, a mail attachment) get the quarantine attribute, and Gatekeeper refuses to open an application that is not notarized: the player has to open it with Control-click and Open, or allow it in System Settings, Privacy & Security, or remove the attribute (xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine "Fixture Game.app"). Files that Steam installs are not quarantined, so a game distributed through Steam opens without any of this.
  • Developer ID signing and notarization are outside the export, and an exported bundle is not ready for them: the compiled shaders are data files in Contents/MacOS, which is for code only, and codesign --strict and notarization reject data there. The engine looks for them next to the program (AppContext.BaseDirectory), so moving them to Contents/Resources is a change to the engine's shader loading that has not been made. When it has, signing is done after the export, with Apple's tools and your own certificate, from the inside out as Apple advises (--deep is discouraged): sign each .dylib, then the executable with --options runtime, then the bundle, and then submit it (xcrun notarytool submit) and staple the ticket (xcrun stapler staple). Signing again replaces the ad-hoc signature this step repairs, so it comes after the export, never before.
  • Checking an export on a Mac. codesign judges an executable inside a bundle as part of the bundle, which is not sealed and may fail --strict for reasons that have nothing to do with the program. To check only the program's own signature, copy it out of the bundle: cp "Fixture Game.app/Contents/MacOS/FixtureGame" /tmp/exe && codesign --verify --strict --verbose=4 /tmp/exe (exit status 0), and codesign -dvvv /tmp/exe shows its flags (adhoc) and CDHash. codesign --verify --strict --verbose=4 "Fixture Game.app" is informational. plutil -lint "Fixture Game.app/Contents/Info.plist" checks the plist, and starting the game with its encrypted pack and no key in the environment is a check of the page that holds the key slot, since the game reads it. The unit tests cannot run these tools; the macOS job of the continuous integration is to.
  • Metal. Whether an exported game draws on a Mac depends on the engine's Metal backend, which is written but not tested yet (see help wanted), not on the export.

Not run on a Mac

The bundle step was written and tested without a Mac. The tests build Mach-O programs and signatures by hand and check the hashes against an independent computation (the SHA-1 and SHA-256 of each page), and they rehash the real signatures of the libraries in ThirdParty to see that the result is byte for byte what the linker and codesign -s - made; codesign --verify and plutil -lint have not been run on an export. The macOS job of the continuous integration is where they will be.

docs.title: Testing an export
docs.text:
The three aot jobs of the continuous integration (.github/workflows/*_builds.yml) export Tests/Fixtures/ShippedGame for their own platform with the runtime they just published, --cooked, and then check and run the result:

  1. The export step sets APOGEE_PACK_KEY to a fixed test key, 000102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f101112131415161718191a1b1c1d1e1f, on that step only. The key is public and worthless: it is made up, nothing is protected by it, and an exported game carries its key anyway. Never ship a game with it.
  2. The result is checked: the pack does not start with the plain magic (it is encrypted), no debug file, Slang library, shader source or steam_appid.txt was copied, and the game folder in the repository has no changed or new file. On Windows the version information says Fixture Game; on macOS the program's signature is verified (codesign --verify --strict --verbose=4 on a copy outside the bundle, then codesign -dvvv) and Info.plist and game.icns are read by plutil -lint and iconutil.
  3. The exported game is run headless from another folder, with APOGEE_PACK_KEY not in the environment (so the key can only come out of the executable's slot), a player's mod copied to the user folder, and +connect_lobby 1 on the command line, which a shipped game ignores. The files that the fixture leaves in the user folder (ran.txt, scene.txt, def.txt, document.txt and the mod's moddata/patcher/ran.txt) must exist. On Linux it is run once more, rendered, on the software rasterizer.
  4. The export is uploaded as the artifact export-<rid>.

This is the test that runs an export on each operating system: the unit tests build the files for all platforms from any computer, but only these jobs start the result.

docs.title: From code
docs.text:
ExportResult result = GameExporter.Export(
    new ExportOptions
    {
        GameFolder = "Game",
        OutputFolder = "Bin/export",
        Target = new ExportTarget("linux", "x64"),
        RuntimeDirectory = null,                 // look for a published runtime
        Cooked = true,
        Key = PackKey.FromEnvironment(),
        Importers = ScriptSession.Importers,     // the importers of the game (models, images, shaders); null: models and images
    },
    Console.WriteLine);
foreach (string warning in result.Warnings) { /* ... */ }

ExportResult has the executable, the game's root and the files written. ExportException is the one error an export throws. IconImages.Load(png) makes the sizes the platform steps need from the game's icon (Rgba(size), Png(size): a box filter down, with a warning for an icon below 256 pixels or a size above the image).

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Tests/Apogee.Export.Tests: the targets, reading the platform from an executable header, what is left out of a runtime folder, the key slot (written into every copy of the slot and read back, a magic without the rest of the template left alone, no slot, a slot cut by the end of the file and too many copies an error, the key is not in the file in the clear), the icon sizes, the PE writer (the resource tree, the section that is rewritten or added, header room, signatures and overlays, the subsystem, the checksum, files that are damaged or hostile, the engine's vendored Windows libraries, damaged and hostile files), the Windows step (the version information and the icon images read back, every copy of the key kept), the Linux step (the executable bit, icon.png and the manifest's icon, the escaping of the desktop entry), the macOS step (the plist and its escaping, the icns structure and sizes, the bundle layout, the minimum system version, and the Mach-O signature: page hashes of every hash type and page size checked against an independent computation, real signatures from ThirdParty reproduced, and hostile lengths and offsets, truncation and random damage all ending in an ExportException), and exports for all four targets from any host with a synthesized runtime folder (layout, renamed executable, what is packed, the game folder untouched, encrypted packs, the output folder rules). Tests/Apogee.Runtime.Tests runs an exported game from its folder, headless, on its encrypted pack.

docs.title: User interface
docs.text:
Apogee.UI is the game's UI: RmlUi (HTML and CSS as the game UI world knows them, in RML and RCSS) on the engine's renderer, file system and input, behind the script global ui. A UI is a document (RML text, from a file or built in code) of elements that scripts make, move, style and listen to. Luau-only mods author UI the same way the base game does, with documents that carry their own scripts and data models. The ImGui of the dev tools is a different thing: it is for tools and the editor, this is for players.

local doc = ui:load_document("res://ui/menu.rml")          -- or ui:load_document_text(rml), or ui:create_document() for an empty one
doc:show()
doc:by_id("start"):listen("click", function(event)
    print("clicked", event.target.id, event:get_number("mouse_x"))
end)

local note = doc:create_element("div")                     -- made in code, in no tree yet
note.class_name = "toast"
note:append(note:create_text("Saved"))
doc:append(note)                                           -- the document owns it now

docs.title: The pieces
docs.text:
• UiSystem (Source/Apogee.UI/UiSystem.cs) starts RmlUi with one context, the screen, and owns what RmlUi asks of its host: files (read through the virtual file system, so res://, mod://<id>/ and user:// paths work in documents' <link>s and srcs, and relative ones resolve against the document), images (decoded by the content loader, premultiplied on loading), the clipboard, the cursor, the clock and the log. There is one at a time, because RmlUi has one state per process. Update(dt) lays out and runs animations; SetSize(width, height, density) follows the window.
  • UiElement is an element as a script holds it: a handle. It names the element without keeping it alive, so one whose element was destroyed (its document was closed, an ancestor destroyed) answers is_alive = false and every call on it does nothing. An element made with create_element or create_text belongs to the object that holds it until append or insert_before puts it in a tree, which owns it from then on; remove(child) gives it back; letting go of an element that no tree ever held destroys it, and destroy_element() destroys one now.
  • UiEvent is what a listener receives: type, target, current, phase, stop_propagation(), and the event's parameters (get_number("mouse_x"), get_string("value"), has(key)). It is good only inside the handler.
  • UiRenderer draws the picture, as a pass of the render graph over the finished image (IRenderOverlay); OverlayChain puts it under the dev tools. UiInput feeds one window's events to the UI.

docs.title: Documents
docs.text:
RmlUi has no built-in stylesheet: a div is display: inline and takes no width or height, text has no font, body is only as big as its content. ui_base.rcss (Source/Apogee.UI, embedded in the assembly) is added under every document's own rules, so a document, or a mod, overrides anything in it: block elements, box-sizing: border-box for everything, headings, lists, links, a look for form controls and scrollbars, tables, and a body as big as the screen with the default font. The default font is Inter (regular, bold and italic, SIL OFL 1.1; Source/Apogee.UI/Fonts), registered as the family Inter; ui:load_font(path, family, bold, italic, fallback) adds more from any mounted file. Documents loaded from text have [document from memory] as their source unless load_document_text is given a URL.

doc:close() unloads a document with everything in it. A module that is reloaded (--watch) closes the documents it loaded and the listeners it added, and loads them again.

docs.title: Events and input
docs.text:
element:listen(type, handler, capture?) returns a number for ui:unlisten. Events are the DOM's: click, mousedown, mouseup, mouseover, mouseout, mousemove, keydown, keyup, textinput, focus, blur, change, submit, scroll, resize, transitionend, animationend... They go down to the target (capture) and back up (bubble); event:stop_propagation() ends the trip. A handler that throws is logged and the event goes on: nothing may unwind through RmlUi's native frames. Listeners go when their element does (the system forgets their handlers within a couple of seconds).

The host gives the UI the player's input: UiInput turns SDL's events into the UI's (buttons: SDL's left, middle, right are RmlUi's 0, 2, 1; the wheel's y is flipped; keys by USB scancode; typed text; modifiers) and starts SDL's text input when a text field has the focus. Every call says whether the UI used the input, and ui.wants_mouse (the pointer is over an element) and ui.wants_keyboard (a text field is focused) tell the game to leave it alone: the runtime's input actions are not fed while they are true. A host that shows the UI inside something else (the editor shows the game in a panel) sets UiInput.PointerEnabled = false when it feeds the pointer itself, and UiInput.KeyboardEnabled to a function that says whether keys and text may go to the UI now.

docs.title: Scripts in documents
docs.text:
A document can carry its own Luau, the way RmlUi's Lua plugin lets a document carry Lua. The engine implements the same model on Luau (there is no Lua in the engine): <script> tags, on* attributes and data models.

<rml>
<head>
  <link type="text/rcss" href="menu.rcss"/>
  <script src="menu.luau"/>                       <!-- a file next to the document -->
  <script>
    clicks = 0
    function bump(element, event)                  -- a function in the document's globals
      clicks += 1
      element.inner_rml = "Clicked " .. clicks
    end
  </script>
</head>
<body>
  <button id="b" onclick="bump(element, event)">Click</button>
</body>
</rml>
  • Scripts run in the head, when it has been read and before the body is: define functions and open data models there, and do the rest when the document says it has loaded (document:listen("load", function() ... end)).
  • Each document has globals of its own over the ones every script sees. What a <script> defines is there for that document's on* attributes and for nothing else; use require for state that documents share. document is the document's UiElement.
  • An on* attribute is the body of a function with event (the UiEvent) and element (the element the attribute is on, event.current) in scope. It is compiled when its first event comes, because the element is not in its document yet when its attributes are read. A syntax error is logged then.
  • An attribute runs as whoever wrote it. One in the document's own RML runs as the script that loaded the document, with the document's globals. One that another script puts in with inner_rml or set_attribute (a mod adding to the game's HUD) runs as that script, in globals of its own: it has the mod's limits and file rules, and cannot call the game's functions through the document.
  • <script src> is read through the virtual file system with the rules of the script that loaded the document: a mod can read its own files and the ones it depends on, not another mod's (CanAccessFile). require("./helper") in it is relative to the script's file. The path may be relative to the document or a res:// or mod:// one.
  • Scripts run as the script that called ui:load_document: its memory category and its time budget apply, and a mod's UI scripts cannot do what the mod cannot.
  • A script that fails is logged with the document's name and line, and the rest of the document loads.
  • Without a scripting layer (a bare UiSystem in a C# test) scripts and attributes are ignored with a warning; set UiSystem.ScriptEnvironments to give it one.

docs.title: Data models
docs.text:
A data model ties a table of the script to a document: RmlUi's {{value}}, data-if, data-for, data-class-*, data-style-*, data-value and data-event-*. Open the model before the document that uses it loads (a <script> in the document's head can).

-- menu.luau, a <script src> of menu.rml
local game = { volume = 0.8, name = "Ada", items = { { name = "Sword", qty = 1 } }, player = { hp = 100 } }
function game.buy(event, amount) -- data-event-click="buy(3)"
    table.insert(game.items, { name = "Arrow", qty = amount })
    model:dirty("items")
end
model = ui:open_data_model("game", game)

<body data-model="game">
  <p>{{name}} has {{player.hp}} hp</p>
  <div data-for="item : items">{{item.name}} x{{item.qty}}</div>
  <div data-if="player.hp < 20">Low health!</div>
  <input type="range" min="0" max="1" step="0.1" data-value="volume"/>
  <button data-event-click="buy(3)">Buy</button>
</body>
  • The table is read when RmlUi needs a value, so it is the one source of truth. When you change it, say so: model:dirty("items") for one top-level field (a change inside a struct or a list dirties the field that holds it), model:dirty() for everything, or model:set("volume", 0.5) to write a top-level field and dirty it. The elements update at the next ui:update.
  • The top-level fields are bound when the model opens. Each has to exist then (use false, 0, "" or {} for a value that comes later) and keeps its kind: a number stays a number, a list a list, a table with named fields a struct. A table with elements, or an empty one, is a list (counted from 1 in Luau, from 0 in data-for addresses).
  • Functions in the table are events for data-event-*. They get the UiEvent and the arguments of the expression (buy(3, 'sword') calls game.buy(event, 3, "sword")).
  • data-value writes back: typing in a field, or moving a slider, sets the field in the table (text is converted to the field's number or boolean).
  • A model belongs to the script that opened it and is closed when its module reloads; model:close() closes it now (close its documents first). ui:open_data_model returns nil, with a message in the log, when the name is taken.
  • Integers show without a decimal point (5, not 5.0).

docs.title: The Lua manual, in the engine's names
docs.text:
RmlUi's Lua manual describes the plugin; the engine keeps the model and uses its own snake_case names, like every other script API.

RmlUi Lua plugin Here <script>, <script src>, onclick="..." the same; event, element and document are in scope rmlui.contexts["main"] the ui global (one context, the screen) context:LoadDocument(path) ui:load_document(path), ui:load_document_text(rml), ui:create_document() document:Show(), :Hide(), :Close() doc:show(), doc:hide(), doc:close() document:GetElementById(id) doc:by_id(id) element:AppendChild(e), :RemoveChild(e) el:append(e), el:remove(e) element.inner_rml, .class_name, .id the same properties element:SetAttribute(n, v), :GetAttribute(n) el:set_attribute(n, v), el:get_attribute(n) element.style["width"] = "10px" el:set_property("width", "10px") element:AddEventListener(type, fn) el:listen(type, fn) (a number for ui:unlisten) event.parameters.mouse_x, event:StopPropagation() event:get_number("mouse_x"), event:stop_propagation() context:OpenDataModel(name, table) ui:open_data_model(name, table) assigning to a model field model:set(name, value) or change the table and model:dirty(name) Lua 5.x Luau only; its require is Luau's, relative to the file

docs.title: In the runtime
docs.text: --game and --run give every script ui. Each frame the runtime sizes it to the window (in pixels, with the window's pixel density as the dp unit), feeds it input, steps it after the world and the scripts have run, and draws it over the picture (the 3D world if there is a camera, the plain background otherwise) with the dev overlay on top. The UI renderer is made the first frame after a document was loaded, so a script that only has ImGui panels never compiles its shader. ui.debugger = true shows RmlUi's element inspector over the UI.

docs.title: Drawing
docs.text: RmlUi compiles geometry (vertices with positions in pixels, premultiplied-alpha colors and texture coordinates) and asks to render it with a translation, a texture, a scissor rectangle and an optional transform. UiRenderer keeps the compiled vertices and indices in memory and, when a frame's graph is built, packs the geometry that frame draws, once each however often it is drawn, into per-frame upload buffers (as the ImGui backend does), so nothing on the GPU depends on when RmlUi releases a piece of geometry. ui.slang pulls the 20-byte vertices from a buffer, applies the element's CSS transform and the translation, and maps pixels to clip space at the context's size; the pipeline blends premultiplied (source + destination * (1 - source alpha)), the textures are premultiplied when they are made, and colors go to the (UNORM) target as authored, like ImGui's. Textures are bindless images whose index is the handle RmlUi holds (0 is the white texel that untextured geometry samples); a released texture is freed when the frame that last used it is done.

docs.title: Effects
docs.text:
RmlUi 6 asks the host for more than geometry, and UiRenderer records everything it asks for, in order, then turns the list into passes of the render graph.

RCSS What RmlUi asks What we do overflow: hidden with a border-radius, or a transform a clip mask (EnableClipMask, RenderToClipMask: set, set inverse, intersect) a texture the size of the context whose red channel is the coverage. Every operation draws its shape into a new one (an intersection samples the one before), and ui.slang multiplies what it draws by the mask. This is a coverage texture, not a stencil buffer: it needs nothing from the graphics device's pipelines, and it is the same on every backend. A plain rectangle stays a scissor. filter: opacity() blur() drop-shadow() brightness() contrast() grayscale() hue-rotate() invert() saturate() sepia() layers (PushLayer, PopLayer, CompositeLayers) and filters (CompileFilter) what is inside a filtered element is drawn into a transient RGBA8 layer (an image of the render graph, as large as the context), and the filter chain runs on it as full-screen passes: a 5x4 color matrix for the color filters, a separable Gaussian for blur, shifted and tinted blur under the source for drop-shadow. The result is composited onto the layer below, inside the scissor and the clip mask. box-shadow, mask-image SaveLayerAsTexture, SaveLayerAsMaskImage the box shadow is drawn once into a layer, blurred, and kept as a texture RmlUi gives back to draw; a mask image is drawn into a layer whose alpha multiplies the element when it is composited. decorator: linear-gradient(), radial-gradient(), conic-gradient() (and repeating- forms) shaders (CompileShader, RenderShader) a branch of uiFs: the gradient's stops are in a per-frame storage buffer and the fragment computes its color from its position in the element.

The opacity property is not a layer: RmlUi folds it into the colors of each element, so overlapping children of a half-transparent element show through each other. filter: opacity() is the one that makes a group. Not supported: backdrop-filter (it would sample the frame under the UI, which is not an image the pass can read) and a filter on the root of the context. UiRenderer.LastEffects says how many masks, layers and composites the last frame had; the tests in UiRenderingTests read pixels back for each of the rows above.

docs.title: Animations
docs.text: Animations and transitions run on the sum of the Update steps, so a paused game pauses its UI and a test is deterministic. RmlUi limits one step to a tenth of a second per animation (a long frame does not skip one). Tween names are RmlUi's (linear-in, quadratic-out, cubic-in-out); a transition starts counting at the first update after the change; transition: width 1s linear-in in a rule and a class change is the usual shape.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Tests/Apogee.UI.Tests runs RmlUi through the whole engine: the base stylesheet under a document's own rules, the default font and its bold face, making and moving and destroying elements from the script surface (and what a handle to a destroyed one does), attributes, inline styles and pseudo-classes, listeners (bubbling, capture, stopping, a handler that throws, pruning), typing into a text field, documents and their stylesheets read through the file system, resizing and density, transitions and the step limit, the debugger, the SDL key and button tables; and on a GPU, pixels read back from the render graph: a box at its place in its color, premultiplied blending over black and white, overflow: hidden clipping, CSS transforms (a translation and a rotation), text from the default font, an image with straight alpha from the file system, the geometry cache across frames, edits showing on the next frame, resizing. RuntimeTests runs a game folder with a document through --headless --screenshot and clicks an element from a Luau system, whose handler writes a file.
